units.label: Earth Materials and the Rock Cycle

lessons.label: What a Mineral Is: Crystals, Composition, and the Silicate Family

sections.heading: Five criteria, one word
sections.body: A mineral must satisfy five conditions: naturally occurring, inorganic, solid, possessing an ordered internal crystal structure, and having a definite (though not perfectly fixed) chemical composition. Each clause excludes something that looks like a mineral but is not. Coal fails "inorganic." Obsidian fails "ordered crystal structure" — it is volcanic glass, chemically similar to rhyolite but cooled too fast for atoms to organize into a lattice, so mineralogists call it a mineraloid. Lab-grown diamond fails "naturally occurring." Water fails "solid" but ice passes. The composition clause allows solid solutions: olivine ranges continuously from forsterite (Mg2SiO4) to fayalite (Fe2SiO4) and is still called one mineral. Why silicates dominate is a matter of raw supply: eight elements make up roughly 98% of continental crust by mass — oxygen 46.6%, silicon 27.7%, aluminum 8.1%, iron 5.0%, calcium 3.6%, sodium 2.8%, potassium 2.6%, and magnesium 2.1%. Oxygen and silicon alone are nearly three-quarters of that mass, so it is almost inevitable that most crustal minerals are built from oxygen-silicon frameworks.

sections.heading: The SiO4 tetrahedron
sections.body: The silicate building block is the [SiO4]4- tetrahedron: one silicon ion at the center, four oxygen ions at the corners. The shape follows from ionic size. Using Pauling crystal radii, Si4+ is near 0.41 angstroms against O2- near 1.40 angstroms; that radius ratio (about 0.29) falls in the range that favors four-fold (tetrahedral) coordination rather than the six- or eight-fold packing bigger cations like Mg2+ or Ca2+ prefer. The bare tetrahedron carries a net negative charge, so isolated tetrahedra must be charge-balanced by surrounding cations, or the tetrahedra must share corner oxygens with each other.

sections.heading: A ladder of polymerization
sections.body: How much oxygen-sharing occurs sorts silicates into a structural ladder that also tracks bulk SiO2 content. Isolated tetrahedra, no shared oxygens, held together by cations: olivine. Single chains, each tetrahedron sharing two of four oxygens with neighbors: pyroxene (e.g., augite). Double chains, alternating tetrahedra sharing two or three oxygens: amphibole (e.g., hornblende). Sheets, each tetrahedron sharing three oxygens, producing a plane of weakly bonded layers: the micas (biotite, muscovite) and clay minerals (kaolinite). Full three-dimensional frameworks, all four oxygens shared: quartz (pure SiO2) and the feldspars (orthoclase, plagioclase), where some silicon is substituted by aluminum. Rounding out the roughly ten rock-forming minerals a student actually meets: calcite, the non-silicate carbonate that shows up constantly alongside this list.

lessons.workedExample: A specimen has formula Mg2SiO4. The silicon-to-oxygen ratio is 1:4, meaning each SiO4 tetrahedron shares none of its oxygens with another tetrahedron — the charge is balanced entirely by Mg2+ ions sitting between isolated tetrahedra. That is olivine, a nesosilicate. Compare enstatite, MgSiO3: the ratio is 1:3, meaning each tetrahedron shares two of its four oxygens with a neighbor, forming an endless single chain — that is pyroxene. The same two elements, silicon and oxygen, in a different sharing pattern produce a different structural family, different cleavage, and a different rock-forming role.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks "why classify minerals by structure instead of just chemical formula" is testing whether a student understands polymorphism — the same composition, radically different behavior, because the atoms are wired together differently (graphite versus diamond is the classic case; calcite versus aragonite, both CaCO3, is the geology-specific one). A student who can explain that the SiO4 tetrahedron's sharing pattern, not just its ingredients, sets a silicate's cleavage and hardness has grasped the actual physics behind a rock's mineralogy, not just memorized a name list.

questions.prompt: Which of these four is NOT a true mineral, and why?

options.text: Halite
Quartz
Obsidian
Ice

explanations.a: Halite (NaCl) is naturally occurring, inorganic, solid, has an ordered cubic lattice, and a fixed composition — it passes all five criteria.
explanations.b: Quartz is a crystalline framework silicate (SiO2) that meets every criterion.
explanations.c: Correct — obsidian is volcanic glass. It cooled too quickly for atoms to organize into a lattice, so it fails the ordered-crystal-structure requirement; it is classified as a mineraloid, not a mineral.
explanations.d: Ice is a solid, naturally occurring, inorganic substance with an ordered hexagonal crystal structure and fixed composition (H2O) — it is a genuine mineral.

questions.prompt: Why is silicon surrounded by exactly four oxygen ions in the fundamental silicate building block, rather than six or eight?

options.text: Because silicon and oxygen always form double bonds
Because the small radius of Si4+ relative to O2- favors four-fold coordination
Because oxygen is the most abundant element in the crust
Because four is the only coordination number found in nature

explanations.a: Coordination number is a geometric packing question, not a bonding-order question.
explanations.b: Correct — Si4+ (about 0.41 angstroms, Pauling crystal radius) is small relative to O2- (about 1.40 angstroms); that radius ratio (about 0.29) geometrically favors four oxygens packing around one silicon, rather than the six- or eight-fold coordination larger cations like Mg2+ or Ca2+ adopt.
explanations.c: Oxygen's abundance explains why oxygen is in the structure at all, not why the coordination number is specifically four.
explanations.d: Six-fold and eight-fold coordination are both common for other cations in silicate minerals; four is specific to silicon's size.

questions.prompt: Match each silicate structural family to its example mineral.

left.text: Double chain (two or three oxygens shared)

right.text: Olivine
Pyroxene (augite)
Amphibole (hornblende)
Mica (biotite)
Quartz

questions.explanation: The polymerization ladder runs from isolated tetrahedra (olivine) through single chains (pyroxene) and double chains (amphibole) to sheets (mica) and full frameworks (quartz), with each step sharing more oxygens between tetrahedra.

questions.prompt: Order these silicate structures from fewest to most oxygens shared between adjacent tetrahedra.

items.text: Isolated tetrahedra (olivine)
Single chain (pyroxene)
Double chain (amphibole)
Sheet (mica)
Framework (quartz)

questions.explanation: Sharing increases from zero oxygens shared (isolated tetrahedra, olivine) to two (single chains, pyroxene) to two-or-three alternating (double chains, amphibole) to three (sheets, mica) to all four (frameworks, quartz), tracking rising bulk SiO2 content along the way.

lessons.label: Identifying a Hand Sample: Hardness, Cleavage, Streak, and Luster

sections.heading: Hardness: a scratch test, not an absolute unit
sections.body: Friedrich Mohs built his ten-point hardness scale in 1812 by ranking common minerals (talc 1 through diamond 10) purely on which scratches which — it is an ordinal ranking, not a linear physical measure (the jump from 9 to 10, corundum to diamond, represents a far bigger real-world hardness gap than 1 to 2). Field geologists substitute everyday objects for the reference minerals: a fingernail scratches anything softer than about 2.5, a pre-1982 US copper penny scratches anything softer than about 3.5, and a steel knife blade or window glass scratches anything softer than about 5.5. The penny caveat matters: in 1982 the US Mint switched penny composition from 95% copper to a zinc core with only a thin copper plating, so a modern penny's edge behaves differently and is a less reliable field proxy than an older coin.

sections.heading: Cleavage versus fracture: reading the bonds
sections.body: Cleavage is a mineral breaking along flat, repeatable planes that trace its weakest atomic bonds; fracture is breaking with no such preferred plane (irregular, or curved conchoidal fracture as in quartz). Mica shows one perfect cleavage direction — its sheet-silicate structure has strong bonds within each layer and weak bonds between layers, so it peels into thin flat sheets. Halite shows three cleavage directions meeting at 90 degrees, producing cubic fragments, because its ionic lattice is a literal cube of alternating Na+ and Cl-. Calcite also shows three cleavage directions but NOT at 90 degrees — closer to 75 and 105 degrees — yielding rhombohedron-shaped fragments, a direct fingerprint of its underlying crystal geometry.

sections.heading: Streak, luster, and the carbonate-specific tests
sections.body: Streak is the color of a mineral's powder, obtained by rubbing it on unglazed porcelain — it is often diagnostic where the surface color is not, because surface color can vary with impurities while the fine powder is more consistent (hematite always streaks reddish-brown regardless of whether the specimen looks black and metallic or reddish and earthy). Luster describes how a surface reflects light: metallic, glassy (vitreous), pearly, silky, or dull/earthy. Two tests are specific to carbonates: dilute hydrochloric acid causes calcite to fizz vigorously (effervesce) as it releases CO2, while dolomite only fizzes when scratched or powdered first; and clear calcite (Iceland spar) famously shows double refraction, splitting a single light ray into two, visible as a doubled image through a clear cleavage rhomb.

lessons.workedExample: A student has an unlabeled clear crystal. A fingernail does not scratch it, but a penny does, so hardness is between 2.5 and 3.5 — consistent with calcite (hardness 3). It breaks into rhomb-shaped fragments along three cleavage planes that are clearly not square (not 90 degrees), ruling out halite. A drop of dilute HCl on a corner produces vigorous bubbling. Looking through the crystal at printed text underneath, the letters appear doubled. Every observation — moderate hardness, rhombohedral cleavage, effervescence, double refraction — is individually consistent with calcite, and together they rule out the lookalikes (quartz would not scratch with a penny; halite would cleave into cubes and would not fizz).
lessons.judgeFraming: A fair judge asks a student to identify a mystery mineral on the spot because the sequence of tests reveals whether the student ran a real diagnostic process or is guessing from memorized appearance. The tell is language: a student who says "I observed rhombohedral cleavage and effervescence in HCl, which together indicate calcite" is separating observation from inference correctly, while a student who says "it looks like calcite" has skipped the test entirely. Judges specifically probe cleavage angle and the acid test because both are cheap, repeatable, and instantly falsifiable if the identification is wrong.

questions.prompt: A field geologist uses a modern (post-1982) US penny to test hardness. Why is this less reliable than using an older penny?

options.text: Modern pennies are made almost entirely of nickel, which is far harder than copper
Modern pennies are copper-plated zinc rather than solid copper, so the edge behaves differently
Modern pennies are larger and harder to hold against a specimen
The Mohs scale was redefined in 1982 to exclude copper as a reference point

explanations.a: Modern pennies are zinc-cored with a thin copper plating, not nickel; nickel is not the substitution metal used.
explanations.b: Correct — in 1982 the US Mint switched from 95% copper composition to a zinc core with only a thin copper coating, changing how the edge scratches a test surface compared to the older solid-copper coin.
explanations.c: Penny size did not change in 1982; the composition changed.
explanations.d: The Mohs scale (1812, Friedrich Mohs) has not been redefined; only the penny's composition changed, which affects it only as an informal field proxy, not the scale itself.

questions.prompt: Halite cleaves into cubes (three planes at 90 degrees) while calcite cleaves into rhombohedra (three planes, not at 90 degrees). What does this difference reveal?

options.text: Cleavage angle is random and carries no structural meaning
Cleavage planes trace the weakest bonds in each mineral's underlying crystal lattice, which differs between the cubic halite lattice and calcite's rhombohedral lattice
Halite is always harder than calcite, which causes the angle difference
The angle only depends on how the specimen was collected in the field

explanations.a: Cleavage angle is highly repeatable for a given mineral precisely because it is not random — it reflects a fixed atomic geometry.
explanations.b: Correct — cleavage breaks along a mineral's weakest atomic bond planes, and those planes sit at whatever angle the crystal's actual lattice geometry dictates: 90 degrees for halite's cubic ionic lattice, and roughly 75/105 degrees for calcite's rhombohedral lattice.
explanations.c: Hardness (a resistance-to-scratching property) and cleavage angle (a bond-geometry property) are independent; one does not cause the other.
explanations.d: Cleavage angle is intrinsic to the mineral's crystal structure and reproduces identically regardless of how or where a specimen was collected.

questions.prompt: Match each diagnostic test to what it is actually measuring or revealing.

right.text: The color of the mineral's powder, more consistent than surface color
Presence of carbonate (CO2 release), distinguishing calcite from dolomite
A crystal splitting one light ray into two, as in clear calcite
An ordinal ranking of which mineral scratches which, not a linear physical unit

questions.explanation: Streak reveals powder color (often more diagnostic than surface color, as with hematite); dilute HCl effervescence flags carbonate minerals and distinguishes calcite from dolomite; double refraction splits light through calcite's structure; and the Mohs scale, built by Friedrich Mohs in 1812, ranks scratch resistance ordinally rather than on a linear scale.

questions.prompt: A student is working a dichotomous key on an unknown mineral. Order these steps in the correct diagnostic sequence, from first observation to final conclusion.

items.text: Record the raw observation: hardness, cleavage angle, streak color, luster
Test hardness with fingernail, penny, and glass/steel to bracket a Mohs range
Compare the full set of observations against a dichotomous key
State the inferred mineral identity as a conclusion distinct from the raw observations

questions.explanation: Testing happens first (scratch tests establish a hardness bracket), the raw results are recorded as observations, those observations are then compared against a dichotomous key, and only at the end is an identity inferred — keeping inference clearly separated from what was actually observed.

lessons.label: Igneous Rocks: Magma, Cooling Rate, and Texture

sections.heading: Two independent axes: composition and texture
sections.body: Every igneous rock name encodes two independent pieces of information: what it is made of (composition) and how fast it cooled (texture). Composition is ranked by silica (SiO2) content: ultramafic under 45%, mafic 45-52%, intermediate 52-65%, and felsic above 65%. Texture is ranked by crystal size, which is a direct proxy for cooling rate: phaneritic (crystals visible to the naked eye, from slow cooling deep underground, giving atoms time to organize into large grains), aphanitic (crystals too small to see without a microscope, from fast cooling at or near the surface), porphyritic (large crystals suspended in a fine-grained matrix, from a two-stage cooling history — slow, then fast), glassy (no crystals at all, from cooling too fast for any lattice to form, as in obsidian), vesicular (gas bubbles frozen into the rock as it solidified, as in pumice and scoria), and pyroclastic (fragmented rock blasted out explosively, as in volcanic ash and tuff).

sections.heading: The compositional pairs
sections.body: Crossing the two axes gives every intrusive (plutonic, cooled slowly underground) rock a fine-grained extrusive (volcanic, cooled fast at the surface) twin of identical composition: granite pairs with rhyolite (felsic), diorite pairs with andesite (intermediate), gabbro pairs with basalt (mafic), and peridotite pairs with komatiite (ultramafic). Peridotite is the dominant rock of Earth's mantle; komatiite, its rare volcanic equivalent, is found almost exclusively in Archean-age terrains because it required mantle temperatures higher than those common today.

sections.heading: Bowen's reaction series
sections.body: In 1922, petrologist Norman Bowen published the reaction principle explaining why particular minerals crystallize from a cooling melt in a predictable order, along two branches. The discontinuous branch crystallizes a sequence of chemically distinct minerals as temperature drops: olivine first, then pyroxene, then amphibole, then biotite — each mineral reacting with the remaining melt to form the next, unless cooling is fast enough to skip a reaction. The continuous branch crystallizes a single mineral family, plagioclase feldspar, whose composition shifts smoothly from calcium-rich to sodium-rich as temperature falls, without changing structure. Because early-crystallizing minerals (olivine, Ca-rich plagioclase) pull mostly magnesium, iron, and calcium out of the melt, the leftover liquid is progressively enriched in silicon, sodium, and potassium — this is fractional crystallization, and it is one major reason magmas evolve toward more felsic compositions over time. Partial melting works in the opposite direction at the source: melting a mantle rock only part way preferentially produces a melt enriched in the lowest-melting-point (most felsic-leaning) components first.

lessons.workedExample: A rock sample is dark gray-green, has visible crystals of several millimeters, and a lab test shows 48% SiO2. Composition of 48% SiO2 falls in the mafic range (45-52%), and visible large crystals mean phaneritic texture, indicating slow cooling underground. Mafic plus phaneritic gives gabbro. If the identical 48% SiO2 melt had instead erupted at the surface and cooled in hours, the same chemistry would produce basalt — fine-grained, often with a few larger phenocrysts (porphyritic) if crystallization began slowly at depth before a fast eruption. The composition tells you the magma's chemistry; the texture tells you its cooling history — and both are needed for a correct rock name.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing igneous rocks wants to see the composition-texture split held apart cleanly, because collapsing them is the most common student error — calling any dark fine-grained rock "basalt" without checking silica content, or assuming granite must be felsic just because it is light-colored without connecting that to a slow-cooling plutonic origin. A strong answer explains that the same 48% SiO2 magma yields gabbro underground and basalt at the surface, showing the student understands texture as a record of cooling history layered on top of, not instead of, chemical composition.

questions.prompt: A magma with 68% SiO2 cools slowly at depth, producing large visible crystals. What is the rock?

options.text: Basalt
Granite
Peridotite
Rhyolite

explanations.a: Basalt is mafic (45-52% SiO2) and fine-grained (aphanitic) from fast surface cooling — wrong on both composition and texture here.
explanations.b: Correct — 68% SiO2 is felsic (above 65%), and large visible crystals from slow cooling mean phaneritic texture. Felsic plus phaneritic is granite.
explanations.c: Peridotite is ultramafic (under 45% SiO2), far below this magma's silica content.
explanations.d: Rhyolite is the correct composition (felsic) but the wrong texture — rhyolite is aphanitic (fine-grained, fast-cooled at the surface), not phaneritic.

questions.prompt: According to Bowen's reaction series (1922), which mineral crystallizes from a cooling basaltic melt at the HIGHEST temperature along the discontinuous branch?

options.text: Biotite
Amphibole
Olivine
Quartz

explanations.a: Biotite crystallizes near the cool end of the discontinuous branch, after olivine, pyroxene, and amphibole have already formed.
explanations.b: Amphibole crystallizes after olivine and pyroxene, at a lower temperature than either.
explanations.c: Correct — olivine crystallizes first, at the highest temperature, at the top of Bowen's discontinuous branch, before reacting toward pyroxene as the melt cools further.
explanations.d: Quartz is not on the discontinuous branch at all; it crystallizes last, from the residual silica-enriched melt, at the coolest end of Bowen's whole series.

questions.prompt: Match each plutonic (intrusive) rock to its fine-grained volcanic (extrusive) twin of identical composition.

right.text: Rhyolite
Andesite
Basalt
Komatiite

questions.explanation: Each pair shares composition but differs in cooling rate: felsic granite/rhyolite, intermediate diorite/andesite, mafic gabbro/basalt, and ultramafic peridotite/komatiite, with komatiite restricted almost entirely to Archean-age terrains that experienced higher mantle temperatures.

questions.prompt: Order these textures by decreasing cooling time (slowest-cooled first, fastest-cooled last).

items.text: Phaneritic (large visible crystals)
Porphyritic (large crystals in a fine matrix)
Aphanitic (crystals too small to see)
Glassy (no crystals at all)

questions.explanation: Phaneritic texture needs the longest, slowest cooling to grow large visible crystals; porphyritic reflects a two-stage history (slow, then fast); aphanitic reflects fast surface cooling that still allows microscopic crystal growth; glassy reflects cooling so fast that no crystal lattice forms at all.

lessons.label: Sedimentary Rocks: Weathering Products, Texture, and Cement

sections.heading: Three origins, one grain-size ruler
sections.body: Sedimentary rocks form three ways: clastic (broken mineral and rock fragments, physically transported and deposited), chemical (minerals precipitated directly from solution, as evaporating seawater precipitates halite and gypsum), and biochemical (organisms build or extract the material, as marine creatures secrete calcite shells that accumulate into limestone). Clastic rocks are classified by grain size using the Udden-Wentworth scale, built by Johan Udden in 1914 and refined by Chester Wentworth in 1922: clay is finer than 1/256 mm, silt runs from 1/256 to 1/16 mm, sand from 1/16 to 2 mm, and gravel-sized clasts (granule, pebble, cobble, boulder) extend upward past 256 mm. Because these boundaries are inconvenient fractions, geologists convert to the phi scale, phi = -log2(diameter in mm), turning the ruler into small, easy-to-plot whole numbers — sand runs roughly from phi 4 down to phi -1.

sections.heading: Reading transport history in the grains
sections.body: Three grain properties record how far and how energetically sediment traveled before burial. Rounding measures how sharp or worn a grain's corners are — angular grains have barely traveled, well-rounded grains have been abraded over long transport distances, as in a river or along a beach. Sphericity measures how equant (ball-like) versus elongate/flattened a grain is, largely inherited from the original mineral's cleavage and fracture habit rather than transport. Sorting measures how uniform the grain sizes are within a deposit — well-sorted sediment (nearly one grain size) indicates a sustained, selective transport agent like wind or a beach; poorly sorted sediment (a chaotic mix of sizes) indicates a short or unselective agent like a glacier or debris flow. Textural maturity combines rounding and sorting into a single measure of how long a sediment has been reworked; compositional maturity measures how thoroughly unstable minerals (feldspar, mica) have been weathered out, leaving only the most chemically durable grains, typically quartz.

sections.heading: Diagenesis: turning sediment into rock
sections.body: Loose sediment becomes rock through diagenesis: compaction squeezes grains together as burial pressure expels water and air from the pore spaces, and cementation precipitates minerals — most commonly silica, calcite, or iron oxide — into the remaining pores, gluing grains rigidly together. The cementing mineral often gives the rock its color: iron oxide cement produces the reddish-brown tint common in many sandstones. Common hand-sample rocks: sandstone (cemented sand grains), shale (compacted clay/mud, fissile — splits into thin sheets), conglomerate (cemented rounded gravel), breccia (cemented angular gravel, indicating little transport), limestone (calcite, often fossiliferous, fizzes in dilute HCl), chert (microcrystalline silica, very hard, conchoidal fracture), and evaporites like rock salt and gypsum (soft, soluble, precipitated as water evaporated).

lessons.workedExample: A student collects a rock made of gravel-sized clasts, each clast sharply angular with jagged edges, cemented in a fine matrix. Because grain size is in the gravel range but rounding is angular rather than worn smooth, this is breccia, not conglomerate — the angularity indicates the clasts traveled only a short distance before burial (a rockfall or fault zone, for instance), since abrasion during longer transport would have rounded the corners. If the same size clasts were well-rounded instead, the correct name would be conglomerate, implying a much longer transport history, such as a river system, that had time to wear the edges down.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about rounding and sorting because those two properties are the closest thing sedimentary petrology has to a transport-history readout, and testing whether a student can extract that history from a hand sample (rather than just naming the rock) reveals real understanding. The strong answer distinguishes breccia from conglomerate by rounding alone and explains why: angular clasts mean short transport, and a student who can reason from grain shape to transport distance has understood diagnosis, not memorized a rock chart.

questions.prompt: A sedimentary rock is made of well-rounded gravel-sized clasts cemented together. What is it, and what does the rounding imply?

options.text: Breccia; the rounding implies almost no transport
Conglomerate; the rounding implies substantial transport and abrasion
Sandstone; the rounding implies wind transport
Shale; the rounding is irrelevant to shale

explanations.a: Breccia is defined by angular clasts, the opposite of what is described here, and angular clasts (not rounded ones) imply minimal transport.
explanations.b: Correct — gravel-sized, well-rounded, cemented clasts define conglomerate, and rounding of that degree requires substantial abrasion during transport, typically in a river or along a wave-worked shoreline.
explanations.c: Sandstone requires sand-sized grains (1/16-2 mm), far smaller than gravel-sized clasts.
explanations.d: Shale is fine-grained compacted mud, not gravel; grain size alone rules this out.

questions.prompt: A deposit contains grains ranging chaotically from clay to boulder size, all mixed together with no separation by size. What does this poor sorting most likely indicate about the transport agent?

options.text: A slow, steady wind that sorted grains carefully over a long time
A beach environment reworked by waves over thousands of years
A short, unselective transport event such as a glacier or debris flow
Precipitation directly from evaporating seawater

explanations.a: Wind is a highly selective transport agent and typically produces well-sorted, narrow-grain-size deposits like dune sand, not chaotic mixtures.
explanations.b: Wave reworking over a long time tends to sort and separate grains by size, producing well-sorted beach sand, not a poorly sorted mix.
explanations.c: Correct — poor sorting (a chaotic mix of sizes) indicates an unselective, often short-duration transport agent like a glacier or a debris flow, which moves everything from clay to boulders together without separating by size.
explanations.d: Direct precipitation from evaporating water produces chemical sediment (like halite or gypsum), not a clastic mix of pre-existing grain sizes.

questions.prompt: Match each sedimentary rock to its defining origin or composition.

right.text: Calcite, often biochemical, fizzes in dilute HCl
Microcrystalline silica, very hard, conchoidal fracture
Compacted clay/mud, fissile, splits into thin sheets
Precipitated directly as water evaporated

questions.explanation: Limestone is calcite-based and often biochemical, fizzing in dilute HCl; chert is hard microcrystalline silica with conchoidal fracture; shale is compacted, fissile clay/mud; and evaporites like rock salt form by direct chemical precipitation as water evaporates.

questions.prompt: Order these Udden-Wentworth grain-size categories from finest to coarsest.

items.text: Clay
Silt
Sand
Boulder

questions.explanation: The Udden-Wentworth scale (Udden 1914, refined by Wentworth 1922) runs from clay (finer than 1/256 mm) through silt (1/256-1/16 mm) and sand (1/16-2 mm) up through gravel categories, with boulder (coarser than 256 mm) at the top.

lessons.label: Metamorphic Rocks: Pressure, Temperature, and Fabric

sections.heading: Solid-state change, three settings
sections.body: Metamorphism recrystallizes an existing rock's minerals and texture in the solid state, roughly between 200 and 800 degrees Celsius — hot enough to break and reform atomic bonds, but below the rock's melting point, so no melt is ever involved (cross that threshold and you have made igneous rock instead). Three settings produce it. Contact metamorphism bakes rock adjacent to a hot intrusion, driven by heat alone with little added pressure, producing fine-grained, non-foliated hornfels in a halo (aureole) around the intrusion. Regional metamorphism affects enormous volumes of crust during mountain-building, driven by both elevated temperature and elevated confining pressure over millions of years, and is the source of most foliated rock. Dynamic metamorphism occurs narrowly along active fault zones, driven primarily by shear stress (differential stress) as rock grinds past rock, producing crushed, sheared fabrics.

sections.heading: Differential stress builds foliation
sections.body: When stress is unequal in different directions (differential stress, as opposed to uniform confining pressure that squeezes equally from all sides), platy and elongate minerals like mica and chlorite rotate and grow with their flat faces perpendicular to the greatest compressive stress, producing foliation — planar fabric visible as parallel mineral alignment. Foliated rocks form a progressive series with increasing grade: slate (very fine, splits into flat sheets, from low-grade metamorphism of shale), phyllite (slightly coarser, has a silky sheen from barely-visible mica), schist (coarse enough that individual mica and other platy grains are visible to the eye, strongly foliated), and gneiss (high-grade, coarse, with light and dark minerals segregated into visible bands rather than uniform sheets). Non-foliated rocks form where the parent rock lacks platy minerals or where stress was uniform rather than differential: marble (recrystallized limestone/calcite), quartzite (recrystallized sandstone/quartz), and hornfels (from contact metamorphism, where heat dominates over directed stress).

sections.heading: Reading the thermometer: Barrow and Eskola
sections.body: In 1893, George Barrow mapped the Scottish Highlands and found that specific new minerals appeared in a fixed sequence as metamorphic grade increased across the same original shale-like rock: chlorite first (lowest grade), then biotite, then garnet, then staurolite, then kyanite, then sillimanite (highest grade). These Barrovian index minerals let a geologist read approximate temperature directly off a hand sample. In 1920, Pentti Eskola generalized this into the metamorphic facies concept: any rock reaching a given pressure-temperature range will converge on a characteristic mineral assemblage regardless of its original composition, letting facies (named after a mapped example, like greenschist or amphibolite) function as a P-T map. One well-defined checkpoint on that map is the aluminosilicate triple point: the three Al2SiO5 polymorphs — andalusite (low pressure), kyanite (high pressure), and sillimanite (high temperature) — are all stable simultaneously only at approximately 500 degrees Celsius and 0.4 GPa (about 4 kilobars), a single P-T coordinate that experimentally pins the boundaries between all three fields.

lessons.workedExample: A schist sample contains garnet crystals but no kyanite. According to the Barrovian sequence (chlorite, biotite, garnet, staurolite, kyanite, sillimanite), the presence of garnet without kyanite places this rock's peak metamorphic conditions between the garnet zone and the staurolite/kyanite zones, roughly mid-grade — hotter than chlorite- or biotite-grade slate/phyllite, but not as hot as a kyanite-bearing schist from deeper in the same mountain belt. If a second sample from the same field area contains sillimanite instead, that sample recorded a higher peak temperature than the garnet-bearing sample, even though both may have started as the same shale protolith — the index mineral is a direct temperature readout.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks a student to explain foliation is testing whether the student understands stress as a directional quantity, not just a magnitude — the giveaway answer names differential stress specifically and explains why platy minerals rotate perpendicular to the compression direction, rather than vaguely saying "pressure caused layering." A judge who follows up by asking what index minerals reveal is testing whether the student can connect Barrow's 1893 field observation to a quantitative P-T history, treating a mineral assemblage as data about the rock's buried past rather than a static label.

questions.prompt: Why does foliation form under differential stress but not under uniform confining pressure?

options.text: Uniform pressure destroys all minerals, leaving nothing to align

Differential stress is directional, so platy minerals rotate and grow perpendicular to the greatest compressive direction, producing a planar fabric; uniform pressure has no preferred direction to align against
Foliation only depends on temperature, not on any kind of stress
Uniform pressure always produces higher metamorphic grade than differential stress

explanations.a: Metamorphism recrystallizes minerals; uniform pressure does not selectively destroy them, and platy minerals like mica still exist under uniform stress — they simply have no preferred direction to align.
explanations.b: Correct — differential stress is unequal in different directions, giving platy and elongate minerals a directional cue to rotate and grow perpendicular to the greatest compression, producing foliation; uniform confining pressure squeezes equally from all sides and offers no such directional signal.
explanations.c: Temperature drives which minerals form (as in the Barrovian sequence), but the planar, aligned FABRIC specifically depends on differential stress, not temperature alone.
explanations.d: Grade (temperature and pressure magnitude) and stress directionality are independent variables; one does not automatically produce a higher grade than the other.

questions.prompt: At the aluminosilicate triple point (about 500 degrees Celsius, 0.4 GPa), what is true of andalusite, kyanite, and sillimanite?

options.text: Only sillimanite is stable; the other two have melted
All three polymorphs are simultaneously stable at that single pressure-temperature point
The three minerals combine into one new mineral at that point
The triple point marks where all metamorphism stops and igneous melting begins

explanations.a: Melting is not involved; all three are solid-state polymorphs of Al2SiO5 (aluminosilicate) under metamorphic conditions, well below melting temperatures.
explanations.b: Correct — the triple point is defined as the specific pressure-temperature coordinate, roughly 500 degrees Celsius and 0.4 GPa, where all three Al2SiO5 polymorphs (andalusite, kyanite, sillimanite) are simultaneously stable, and it is exactly this coordinate that experimentally fixes the boundaries between their three stability fields.
explanations.c: The three are polymorphs (same formula, different structure) of one compound, not separate minerals that combine into a fourth.
explanations.d: The triple point is a purely metamorphic (solid-state) reference point, unrelated to the melting threshold that would produce igneous rock.

questions.prompt: Match each foliated metamorphic rock to its diagnostic field appearance.

right.text: Very fine grained, splits into flat sheets
Slightly coarser, silky sheen from barely-visible mica
Coarse, individual platy mica grains visible to the eye
High-grade, coarse, light and dark minerals segregated into visible bands

questions.explanation: The foliated series runs from lowest to highest grade: slate (fine, flat sheets), phyllite (silky sheen), schist (visible platy grains), and gneiss (coarse, banded), tracking increasing metamorphic grade.

questions.prompt: Order these Barrovian index minerals from lowest to highest metamorphic grade, following Barrow's 1893 Scottish Highlands sequence.

items.text: Chlorite
Garnet
Staurolite
Sillimanite

questions.explanation: Barrow's 1893 field mapping in the Scottish Highlands established the sequence chlorite, biotite, garnet, staurolite, kyanite, sillimanite as grade increases, giving geologists a mineral-based thermometer for a rock's peak metamorphic conditions.

lessons.label: The Rock Cycle as a Mass Budget and a History

sections.heading: Two engines driving one cycle
sections.body: The rock cycle is not a single loop but a set of pathways powered by two independent energy sources. Earth's internal heat, left over from planetary accretion and ongoing radioactive decay, drives melting (making igneous rock from magma) and drives most metamorphism (recrystallizing existing rock under heat and pressure without melting it). Solar energy plus gravity drive the surface half of the cycle: solar-powered wind, rain, and rivers weather rock into fragments and dissolved ions, gravity moves those products downhill and downstream, and burial under accumulating layers compacts and cements sediment into sedimentary rock. Any rock type — igneous, sedimentary, or metamorphic — can become the raw material (protolith) for any other type, and a rock can also melt directly back into magma or be metamorphosed further without ever surfacing, so the "cycle" is really a branching set of possible paths, not one fixed loop.

sections.heading: A lopsided mass budget
sections.body: The three rock types are not evenly distributed. Sedimentary rocks make up only about 5-8% of crustal volume, yet because they form at the surface by definition, they blanket roughly 75% of the exposed continental land surface as a thin veneer over igneous and metamorphic basement rock. This mismatch matters for a science-fair-level argument: a shallow surface survey (walking transects, mapping outcrops) will oversample sedimentary rock relative to its true share of the crust, because most igneous and metamorphic rock is buried beneath that sedimentary veneer or exposed only where uplift and erosion have stripped it away, as in mountain cores or continental shields.

sections.heading: Reading a rock backwards
sections.body: A single hand specimen is not just a rock type but a compressed record of the last two or three events it experienced, and texture plus mineralogy are the tools for reading that record in reverse. A gneiss with visible banding and Barrovian-grade minerals like sillimanite records: an original protolith (possibly a shale or a granite), then burial and differential stress deep in a mountain belt reaching high metamorphic grade. A well-rounded, well-sorted quartz sandstone records: a felsic source rock that weathered chemically enough to leave only durable quartz grains (compositional maturity), then long transport by water or wind (rounding and sorting), then burial, compaction, and cementation. Framing a specimen this way turns "identify this rock" into a testable hypothesis about its history — one that competing observations (a differently shaped cleavage crystal, a fresh unweathered feldspar grain) can support or falsify, which is exactly the kind of reasoning a science-fair judge wants to see applied to a geologic sample.

lessons.workedExample: A student finds a rock that is fine-grained, foliated, and splits into flat sheets — consistent with slate. Reading it backwards: the fine grain size and low-grade foliation indicate the protolith was originally a fine clastic sedimentary rock (shale, itself made of compacted clay), which was then subjected to relatively low-temperature regional metamorphism with differential stress, just enough to align clay-derived minerals into planar fabric without producing coarser Barrovian minerals like garnet. The specimen therefore encodes at least three events in order: original deposition as mud, burial and compaction into shale, then low-grade metamorphism into slate — each step readable from a different textural clue in the same rock.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks a student to "read" a rock's history rather than just name it because that is the actual scientific skill the rock cycle is meant to teach: treating texture and mineralogy as evidence for a sequence of past events, not static labels. A student who can say "this gneiss's banding and sillimanite tell me it was buried to high-grade conditions, and before that its coarse-then-fine mineral zoning suggests an igneous protolith" is doing real historical inference; a student who only names the current rock type has skipped the inferential step the judge is actually testing for.

questions.prompt: Sedimentary rocks make up only about 5-8% of crustal volume, yet cover roughly 75% of the exposed continental land surface. Why does this create a sampling bias for a surface-only rock survey?

options.text: It doesn't — surface exposure accurately reflects the crust's true volumetric composition
A surface survey will oversample sedimentary rock relative to its true share of crustal volume, because it forms a thin veneer over buried igneous and metamorphic basement rock
Sedimentary rocks are actually the majority of crustal volume, so this is not a bias at all
Igneous and metamorphic rocks are too rare to ever appear at the surface

explanations.a: The volume and surface-coverage figures are mismatched (5-8% versus 75%) precisely because surface exposure does not reflect volumetric composition.
explanations.b: Correct — because sedimentary rock forms only at or near the surface, it caps most of the land surface as a thin veneer even though it is a small minority of total crustal volume, so a survey limited to surface outcrops will overrepresent sedimentary rock relative to the crust as a whole.
explanations.c: Sedimentary rock's crustal volume share (5-8%) is small, not a majority; the 75% figure describes surface coverage, not volume.
explanations.d: Igneous and metamorphic rock do reach the surface, notably in mountain cores, continental shields, and uplifted terrain where erosion has stripped away the sedimentary veneer.

questions.prompt: Which energy source primarily drives weathering, transport, and burial of sediment in the rock cycle?

options.text: Earth's internal radioactive decay heat
Solar energy and gravity
Residual heat from planetary accretion only
Differential stress from plate collisions

explanations.a: Internal radioactive decay heat drives melting and most metamorphism, not the surface processes of weathering and transport.
explanations.b: Correct — solar energy powers wind, rain, and rivers that weather and transport sediment, while gravity moves those products downhill and downstream toward burial.
explanations.c: Accretion heat is part of Earth's internal heat budget, which drives the melting/metamorphic side of the cycle, not surface weathering.
explanations.d: Differential stress produces foliation during metamorphism; it is not the driver of surface weathering and sediment transport.

questions.prompt: A student finds a slate specimen. Order the events it records, from earliest to most recent.

items.text: Original deposition of clay-sized sediment
Burial and compaction into shale
Low-grade regional metamorphism under differential stress into slate

questions.explanation: The specimen's history runs from original clay deposition, through burial and compaction into sedimentary shale, to low-grade metamorphism that aligns clay-derived minerals into the foliated fabric of slate — each step is read off a different textural clue in the same rock.

questions.prompt: Match each rock-cycle process to its primary energy source.

right.text: Earth's internal heat
Earth's internal heat and pressure
Solar energy
Gravity

questions.explanation: Melting and most metamorphism are driven by Earth's internal heat (and, for metamorphism, added pressure), while weathering is driven by solar-powered wind and water, and burial of sediment proceeds under gravity as material accumulates and sinks.

units.label: Earth Structure and Plate Tectonics

lessons.label: Layering by Composition and by Strength

sections.heading: Seismic waves found the layers before anyone could drill to them
sections.body: Nearly everything known about Earth's interior comes from timing seismic waves, because the deepest borehole ever drilled, the Kola Superdeep, reached only about 12 km. In 1909 the Croatian seismologist Andrija Mohorovicic noticed something odd in travel-time data from a Kupa Valley earthquake: at a certain distance, a second, faster wave arrived ahead of the direct one, meaning waves were refracting off a boundary where seismic velocity jumps sharply. That boundary, now called the Mohorovicic discontinuity or Moho, marks the base of the crust. In 1913 Beno Gutenberg located a much deeper boundary, now placed at 2891 km, where P waves slow down and S waves vanish entirely, defining the core-mantle boundary and revealing the outer core is liquid, since liquids cannot carry shear waves. In 1936 Inge Lehmann, studying earthquakes that should have left a P-wave shadow zone if the whole core were uniform, found faint arrivals inside it, evidence of a solid inner core that reflects and refracts waves differently than the liquid outer core surrounding it. Modern reference models, especially the Preliminary Reference Earth Model (PREM) built by Adam Dziewonski and Don Anderson in 1981, stitch thousands of these travel-time and normal-mode observations into a single depth profile of density, velocity, and pressure that is still the working standard today.

sections.heading: Two different maps of the same planet
sections.body: Composition and mechanical strength divide Earth along different lines, and conflating them is a common student error. Compositionally, Earth has crust, mantle, and core, distinguished by chemistry: oceanic crust is basaltic and thin, roughly 7 km thick, continental crust is granitic and averages 35-40 km, thickening to nearly 70 km beneath young mountain belts like the Himalaya. Rheologically, Earth has lithosphere, asthenosphere, and mesosphere, distinguished by how the material deforms: the lithosphere (crust plus uppermost mantle, roughly 100 km thick) is cold and rigid enough to fracture and ride as tectonic plates, the asthenosphere below it is hot enough to flow plastically over geologic time, and the mesosphere (lower mantle) is stiffer again under enormous pressure despite being hotter still. The two schemes do not line up: the lithosphere-asthenosphere boundary sits entirely within the mantle, far below the Moho, so 'crust' and 'lithosphere' are not synonyms.

lessons.workedExample: A seismogram from a distant earthquake shows P waves arriving on schedule out to about 103 degrees of arc from the epicenter, then nothing until about 143 degrees, where weak, delayed arrivals reappear. This gap is the P-wave shadow zone, produced because the outer core slows and bends P waves sharply at the core-mantle boundary Gutenberg located near 2891 km depth. If the whole core stayed uniform, the shadow zone should be seismically silent, but Lehmann found faint P' arrivals inside it in 1936, arrivals only explainable if a solid inner core sits within the liquid outer core, reflecting and refracting waves along an additional interior boundary near 5150 km depth.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks how you know what is hundreds or thousands of kilometers underground because the honest answer is never direct observation, and pressing on it separates students who memorized a labeled cross-section from those who understand travel-time seismology as indirect evidence. The strong answer names a specific discontinuity and the observation that revealed it, for instance the Moho as Mohorovicic's 1909 velocity jump or the inner core as Lehmann's 1936 shadow-zone arrivals, and the same rigor applies to the compositional-versus-rheological distinction: a judge testing whether 'lithosphere' means the same thing as 'crust' is checking whether the student can name the mechanism, rigidity versus chemistry, that separates the two maps.

questions.prompt: What observation led Andrija Mohorovicic to propose a boundary at the base of the crust in 1909?

options.text: A borehole sample changed from granite to basalt at a known depth
A faster refracted wave arrived ahead of the direct wave from a Kupa Valley earthquake
Gravity measurements showed a density anomaly under continents
The P-wave shadow zone disappeared at shallow depth

explanations.a: No borehole reaches crustal-base depths; the Moho was inferred from seismic travel times, not drilling.
explanations.b: Correct — Mohorovicic noticed a second, faster wave overtaking the direct wave at a critical distance, evidence of a sharp velocity increase at the crust-mantle boundary.
explanations.c: Gravity data support isostasy calculations but were not the observation that defined the Moho.
explanations.d: The P-wave shadow zone is a much deeper, core-related feature identified later by Gutenberg and Lehmann, unrelated to the shallow Moho.

questions.prompt: Why did Gutenberg's 1913 core-mantle boundary observation imply the outer core is liquid?

options.text: P-wave velocity increased continuously through the boundary
S waves failed to pass through the outer core
The boundary depth matched the Moho exactly
Surface waves stopped being recorded worldwide

explanations.a: P-wave velocity actually drops sharply at the core-mantle boundary, and this alone does not indicate a liquid state.
explanations.b: Correct — S waves cannot travel through a fluid, so their disappearance below 2891 km showed the outer core has no shear strength.
explanations.c: The core-mantle boundary near 2891 km is far deeper than the Moho (tens of km); the two are unrelated features.
explanations.d: Surface waves travel along Earth's exterior and are not diagnostic of deep interior state.

questions.prompt: Match each layering scheme's boundary or unit to its correct basis.

right.text: Compositional change from crust to mantle rock
Mechanical change from rigid to plastic flow
Averages 35-40 km, up to ~70 km under orogens
Solid despite extreme heat, due to immense pressure

questions.explanation: The Moho marks a compositional change (crust to mantle rock); the lithosphere-asthenosphere boundary marks a mechanical change in rigidity within uniform mantle composition; continental crust averages 35-40 km and thickens under mountain belts; the inner core is solid because pressure raises its melting point above ambient temperature.

questions.prompt: Order these discoveries about Earth's interior from earliest to most recent.

items.text: Mohorovicic identifies the crust-mantle discontinuity
Gutenberg locates the core-mantle boundary
Lehmann identifies the solid inner core
Dziewonski and Anderson publish the PREM reference model

questions.explanation: Mohorovicic's discontinuity (1909) came first, followed by Gutenberg's core-mantle boundary (1913), then Lehmann's inner core (1936), with PREM (1981) synthesizing decades of such observations into one modern reference profile.

lessons.label: Isostasy: Why Continents Float and Land Rebounds

sections.heading: A plumb line that pointed the wrong way
sections.body: The idea that crust floats on the mantle came from a measurement error. During the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India, surveyors used a plumb line to fix station positions, expecting the nearby Himalaya's mass to pull the plumb bob slightly off vertical. When they compared the observed deflection to the deflection predicted from the visible mountain mass, the actual deflection was several times smaller than calculated. In 1855, two explanations appeared almost simultaneously. John Henry Pratt proposed that crustal columns have varying density, with less-dense rock beneath high mountains compensating for the extra height, so every column exerts equal pressure at some depth of compensation regardless of elevation. George Airy proposed instead that crust has uniform density but variable thickness, with mountains floating on the denser mantle the way icebergs float on water, so a tall peak must be underlain by a deep root of low-density crustal material displacing mantle. Both models predict the same deflection deficit; they differ on whether density or thickness does the compensating.

sections.heading: Calculating the root, and watching isostasy happen today
sections.body: Airy's version yields a simple calculation once you assign crust and mantle densities of roughly 2.7 and 3.3 g/cm3. Because the root and the topography above sea level are both crustal material of the same density displacing denser mantle, buoyancy requires the root to be about 2.7 divided by (3.3 minus 2.7), or 4.5 times thicker than the visible relief: roughly 4.5 km of root for every 1 km of mountain above the surrounding plain. Isostasy is not just a fossil explanation for old survey errors, it is measurably active today through glacial isostatic adjustment. Fennoscandia and Hudson Bay were depressed by kilometers-thick ice sheets during the last glaciation; with that load removed over the last 11,000 years, the crust is still rising back toward equilibrium, with GPS stations in the Gulf of Bothnia and around Hudson Bay recording uplift rates approaching 10 mm/yr. Because that rebound is still happening thousands of years after the ice vanished, the rate directly constrains how viscous the underlying mantle is: it flows too slowly to keep pace with unloading in real time, so the crust visibly lags the load and keeps adjusting for millennia.

lessons.workedExample: A mountain range stands 3 km above the surrounding lowland. Using Airy compensation with crustal density 2.7 g/cm3 and mantle density 3.3 g/cm3, the required root thickness is 3 km multiplied by 4.5, or 13.5 km of extra low-density crust extending down into the mantle beneath the range, beyond whatever root the lowland crust already has. This is why seismic surveys under real mountain belts like the Himalaya and the Andes find crust thickened to 60-70 km, roughly double the 35 km continental average, rather than a thin crustal veneer simply piled higher.
lessons.judgeFraming: Isostasy is a favorite probe because it tests whether a student can move from a qualitative claim, 'mountains have roots,' to a quantitative one. A judge will ask for the density contrast and the resulting root-to-relief ratio, and a student who can derive roughly 4.5 km of root per km of topography from 2.7 and 3.3 g/cm3 shows real command of buoyancy reasoning rather than memorized vocabulary. Bringing in glacial isostatic adjustment and its measured GPS uplift rates further demonstrates that isostasy is not a static 19th-century curiosity but an ongoing, measurable process that also lets scientists estimate mantle viscosity, connecting a survey anomaly to a live geophysical measurement.

questions.prompt: What observation originally motivated the Airy and Pratt models of isostasy in 1855?

options.text: Seismic waves showed a sharp velocity jump beneath mountain ranges
A plumb line near the Himalaya deflected far less than predicted from the visible mountain mass
GPS stations recorded crustal uplift in Fennoscandia
Borehole samples under the Himalaya showed unexpectedly low density rock

explanations.a: Seismic methods for imaging crustal thickness came decades after 1855; the original evidence was a plumb-line deflection during the Great Trigonometrical Survey.
explanations.b: Correct — the observed plumb-line deflection near the Himalaya was several times smaller than calculated from the mountains' visible mass, implying hidden compensation below.
explanations.c: GPS-measured glacial rebound is a modern confirmation of isostasy, not the 1855 motivating observation.
explanations.d: No borehole reached such depths in 1855; the evidence was geodetic (plumb-line), not a rock sample.

questions.prompt: How do the Airy and Pratt models differ in explaining isostatic compensation?

options.text: Airy varies crustal thickness at uniform density; Pratt varies crustal density at uniform thickness
Airy varies crustal density at uniform thickness; Pratt varies crustal thickness at uniform density
Both models assume compensation occurs in the core, not the crust
Airy applies only to oceanic crust; Pratt applies only to continental crust

explanations.a: Correct — Airy's model gives mountains a deep root of uniform-density crust displacing mantle, while Pratt's model keeps a constant base depth but lets column density vary with elevation.
explanations.b: This reverses the two models; Airy is the thickness-varying (root) model, Pratt is the density-varying model.
explanations.c: Both models place compensation within the crust-mantle system, not the core, which was not yet even characterized in 1855.
explanations.d: Neither model is restricted to one crust type; both were proposed to explain continental topography specifically.

questions.prompt: Match each isostasy-related quantity to its approximate value from the lesson.

left.text: Crust and mantle densities used in Airy's calculation
Root thickness per km of topography
What the rebound rate helps scientists estimate

right.text: 2.7 and 3.3 g/cm3
About 4.5 km
Approaching 10 mm/yr
Mantle viscosity

questions.explanation: Airy's calculation uses crust at 2.7 g/cm3 and mantle at 3.3 g/cm3, giving a root-to-relief ratio near 4.5; modern GPS records Fennoscandian and Hudson Bay uplift approaching 10 mm/yr, a rate slow enough to reveal how viscous the mantle is.

lessons.label: The Three Plate Boundaries and What Each Produces

sections.heading: Divergent boundaries: pulling the lithosphere apart
sections.body: At a divergent boundary two plates move away from each other, and the lithosphere thins until hot asthenosphere rises and melts by decompression, feeding new oceanic crust at a mid-ocean ridge. The ridge crest typically has an axial valley where fresh basalt erupts, and spreading rate varies enormously between ridges: the Mid-Atlantic Ridge spreads at a full rate of roughly 2.5 cm/yr, a slow ridge with a pronounced rift valley, while the East Pacific Rise spreads at up to about 15 cm/yr, fast enough to build a broad, gentle swell with little to no median valley. Because divergent boundaries are shallow, thermally young, and under tension, they produce frequent but small, shallow earthquakes with normal-fault focal mechanisms.

sections.heading: Convergent boundaries: subduction, collision, and deep seismicity
sections.body: Where an oceanic plate meets another plate and is denser, it subducts, bending down into the mantle and dragging sediment into an accretionary prism at the trench while flux melting above the descending slab feeds a volcanic arc. Earthquakes along the subducting slab define a Wadati-Benioff zone that can extend to about 700 km depth, the deepest earthquakes on Earth, tracing the slab's geometry as it sinks. The same downward flexure that generates that deep seismicity also carves the deepest points on the seafloor: the Mariana Trench, above the fastest-subducting slab on the planet, bottoms out near 11 km below sea level, far deeper than any mid-ocean ridge relief. Where two continental plates converge, neither is dense enough to subduct far, and the result is continental collision, thickening crust into a mountain belt like the Himalaya rather than producing a trench and arc.

sections.heading: Transform boundaries and triple junctions
sections.body: At a transform boundary, plates slide past each other horizontally with no significant creation or destruction of lithosphere, producing shallow strike-slip earthquakes. The San Andreas Fault carries about 35 mm/yr of the roughly 50 mm/yr total relative motion between the Pacific and North American plates, with the remainder distributed across nearby faults in a broader deformation zone. Because boundary type sets the stress regime, focal mechanisms alone can classify a boundary: normal mechanisms flag divergence, thrust mechanisms flag convergence, and strike-slip mechanisms flag transform motion. Where three plates and three boundaries meet at a point, geologists call it a triple junction, and its stability depends on the geometry and relative velocities of the three boundaries involved.

lessons.workedExample: A seismologist locates an earthquake at 600 km depth beneath a volcanic arc, with a focal mechanism showing down-dip compression consistent with a subducting slab. This depth alone rules out a divergent or transform origin, since both are confined to shallow crust, and identifies the setting as a convergent, subducting margin, part of a Wadati-Benioff zone tracing the slab toward its maximum depth near 700 km. Compare this to a shallow, 10 km deep earthquake with a strike-slip mechanism recorded along a fault like the San Andreas, consistent with roughly 35 mm/yr of transform motion, and the same three clues, depth, mechanism, and rate, are enough to identify boundary type without ever seeing a map.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks a student to classify an unfamiliar earthquake or map feature by boundary type because it tests whether they understand tectonics as a predictive framework rather than a labeled poster. The strong answer reasons from depth and focal mechanism, deep and compressional means convergent, shallow and strike-slip means transform, shallow and extensional means divergent, and can cite a real spreading or slip rate as calibration, such as the East Pacific Rise's roughly 15 cm/yr versus the Mid-Atlantic Ridge's roughly 2.5 cm/yr. That numeric fluency, not just naming the three boundary types, is what shows the student has internalized how plate motion generates the specific hazards and landforms found at each one.

questions.prompt: An earthquake occurs at 650 km depth beneath a volcanic arc. What boundary type is this most consistent with?

options.text: Divergent
Convergent (subduction)
Transform
Continental collision

explanations.a: Divergent boundaries produce only shallow earthquakes near the ridge axis, not events at hundreds of km depth.
explanations.b: Correct — the Wadati-Benioff zone at a subducting convergent boundary can reach about 700 km depth, and a deep event under a volcanic arc fits this setting precisely.
explanations.c: Transform boundaries produce shallow, strike-slip earthquakes with no deep seismic zone.
explanations.d: Continental collision thickens crust but does not subduct a slab deep enough to produce 650 km earthquakes; that depth requires an actively subducting oceanic slab.

questions.prompt: Roughly how much faster does the East Pacific Rise spread compared to the Mid-Atlantic Ridge?

options.text: About the same rate
Roughly 2 times faster
Roughly 6 times faster
Roughly 50 times faster

explanations.a: The two ridges differ substantially, about 2.5 cm/yr versus about 15 cm/yr, so they are not comparable rates.
explanations.b: A doubling understates the gap between roughly 2.5 cm/yr and roughly 15 cm/yr.
explanations.c: Correct — about 15 cm/yr divided by about 2.5 cm/yr is roughly 6, making the East Pacific Rise a fast-spreading ridge compared to the slow Mid-Atlantic Ridge.
explanations.d: A 50-fold difference vastly overstates the actual spreading-rate contrast between these two ridges.

questions.prompt: Match each plate boundary type to the feature or process it produces.

right.text: Mid-ocean ridge with axial valley, normal faulting
Accretionary prism, arc volcanism, deep Wadati-Benioff seismicity
Crustal thickening into a mountain belt, no trench or arc
Shallow strike-slip faulting, e.g. San Andreas

questions.explanation: Divergent boundaries build mid-ocean ridges with normal faulting; subducting convergent boundaries build accretionary prisms, arc volcanoes, and deep seismicity; continental collision thickens crust without a trench or arc; transform boundaries produce shallow strike-slip faulting like the San Andreas.

questions.prompt: Order these plate-boundary rates from slowest to fastest.

items.text: Mid-Atlantic Ridge full spreading rate (~2.5 cm/yr)
San Andreas Fault slip rate (~35 mm/yr)
East Pacific Rise full spreading rate (~15 cm/yr)

questions.explanation: Converting to the same units, the Mid-Atlantic Ridge is about 2.5 cm/yr, the San Andreas is about 3.5 cm/yr, and the East Pacific Rise is about 15 cm/yr, making the slow Atlantic ridge the slowest, the transform fault intermediate, and the fast Pacific ridge by far the quickest.

lessons.label: The Driving Engine: Slab Pull, Ridge Push, and Mantle Convection

sections.heading: Weighing the candidate forces
sections.body: Plates do not simply drift; something must supply the force, and geophysicists have long debated which candidate dominates. Ridge push comes from the elevated, thermally young lithosphere at a mid-ocean ridge sliding gravitationally away from the ridge crest as it cools, thickens, and subsides toward the surrounding seafloor; it contributes on the order of 3x10^12 N per meter of ridge length, a real but comparatively modest push. Slab pull comes from a subducting plate's cold, dense lithosphere sinking under its own negative buoyancy relative to the warmer mantle around it, dragging the attached plate behind it, and is generally regarded as the dominant force, an order of magnitude or more larger than ridge push where a long subducting slab is attached. Basal drag, the shear traction where the base of the lithosphere contacts the asthenosphere below, is the most ambiguous term: depending on whether mantle flow moves faster or slower than the plate above it, drag can either help or resist plate motion, so its sign is not fixed.

sections.heading: Testing the forces against real plate speeds
sections.body: Donald Forsyth and Seiya Uyeda tested these candidates directly in 1975 by comparing plate velocities to plate boundary characteristics, and found that the strongest predictor of a plate's speed is the fraction of its boundary occupied by subduction zones, not the fraction occupied by ridges. Plates with a long attached subducting slab, like the Pacific and Nazca plates, move fast, while plates with little or no subducting boundary, like Eurasia and Africa, move slowly, a pattern that only makes sense if slab pull, not ridge push, supplies most of the driving force. This result reframed convection: rather than the mantle passively dragging plates along on top like a conveyor belt, the plates themselves, through sinking slabs, appear to be an active part of the convective system, a thermal boundary layer that cools at the surface and sinks under its own weight.

sections.heading: Whole-mantle convection and measuring plates directly
sections.body: Whether convection is layered, with separate circulation cells above and below about 660 km, or spans the whole mantle in a single system remains debated, though seismic tomography imaging slabs descending well past 660 km into the lower mantle favors whole-mantle convection for at least some subduction zones. Independent of the convection debate, plate motions are now measured directly rather than only inferred from magnetic stripes: NUVEL-1A (1994) used spreading rates, transform azimuths, and earthquake slip vectors averaged over roughly the last few million years, while MORVEL (2010) refined this with better data, and continuous GNSS/GPS networks now track plate motion in real time, generally confirming the geologically averaged rates.

lessons.workedExample: Compare the Pacific plate, whose boundary is dominated by long subducting margins along the western and northern Pacific, to the African plate, which is nearly surrounded by slow-spreading ridges and has little attached subducting slab. Forsyth and Uyeda's 1975 analysis found the Pacific among the fastest-moving plates and Africa among the slowest, exactly the pattern predicted if slab pull, not ridge push, is the dominant driver: more subducting boundary means more sinking slab weight pulling the plate along, while a ridge-dominated boundary supplies only the comparatively weak push of cooling, subsiding lithosphere near the crest.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge presses on 'what actually moves the plates' because it is easy to say 'mantle convection' as an unexamined black box, and much harder to say which force dominates and why. The strong answer cites Forsyth and Uyeda's 1975 correlation between plate speed and subducting-boundary fraction, names slab pull as the dominant term with ridge push an order of magnitude weaker, and can explain that basal drag's effect is genuinely ambiguous in sign, all showing the student understands convection as several competing, unequal forces rather than one vague label, and can connect that mechanism to a directly measurable quantity, like modern GNSS plate velocities.

questions.prompt: What did Forsyth and Uyeda's 1975 analysis find correlates most strongly with a plate's speed?

options.text: The fraction of its boundary occupied by mid-ocean ridges
The fraction of its boundary occupied by subduction zones
The plate's total surface area
The average depth of its transform faults

explanations.a: Ridge fraction was tested but did not predict plate speed as strongly as subduction-zone fraction did.
explanations.b: Correct — plates with more subducting boundary, like the Pacific and Nazca, move fastest, implicating slab pull as the dominant driving force.
explanations.c: Plate area alone was not the predictive variable in their analysis; boundary composition was.
explanations.d: Transform fault depth is not a driving-force variable considered in this analysis; transform boundaries are shallow and passive with respect to driving force.

questions.prompt: Why is basal drag considered ambiguous compared to slab pull and ridge push?

options.text: It only occurs at transform boundaries
Its magnitude is always zero
It can either resist or assist plate motion depending on relative mantle flow speed
It was disproven by the Forsyth and Uyeda study

explanations.a: Basal drag acts along the entire base of a plate, not just at transform boundaries.
explanations.b: Basal drag is not zero; it is a real shear traction, just one whose sign is not fixed.
explanations.c: Correct — depending on whether the asthenosphere below moves faster or slower than the plate above, basal drag can push the plate along or resist its motion.
explanations.d: The Forsyth and Uyeda study addressed slab pull versus ridge push via boundary-type correlation; it did not specifically disprove basal drag.

questions.prompt: Match each item to its role in plate-driving forces or plate-motion measurement.

right.text: ~3x10^12 N per meter of ridge, from subsiding young lithosphere
Dominant force, from cold dense slab sinking under negative buoyancy
Geologically averaged plate-motion models from spreading rates and slip vectors
Direct, continuous, real-time measurement of plate motion

questions.explanation: Ridge push contributes roughly 3x10^12 N per meter of ridge from subsiding young lithosphere; slab pull is the dominant force from sinking cold slabs; NUVEL-1A and MORVEL are geologically averaged plate-motion models; GNSS/GPS networks measure plate motion directly and continuously.

questions.prompt: Order these plate-motion models and measurement methods from earliest to most recent.

items.text: NUVEL-1A published
MORVEL published
Continuous GNSS/GPS tracking of plate motion

questions.explanation: NUVEL-1A (1994) came first as a geologically averaged model, MORVEL (2010) refined it with better data, and continuous GNSS/GPS tracking represents the most recent, direct real-time measurement approach.

lessons.label: Faults and Folds: The Structural Vocabulary

sections.heading: Anderson's theory: which stress axis is vertical decides the fault
sections.body: Anderson's 1905 theory of faulting explains fault type from the orientation of the three principal stresses, and the key insight is simple: because Earth's surface is a free surface that can support no shear, one principal stress must always be vertical, and which one it is determines the fault geometry. If the maximum principal stress is vertical (overburden weight dominates), the crust extends horizontally and produces a normal fault, where the hanging wall, the block above an inclined fault surface, slides down relative to the footwall below it. If the minimum principal stress is vertical, horizontal compression dominates and produces a reverse fault, where the hanging wall moves up relative to the footwall; a shallow-angle reverse fault, common where slip is large, is specifically called a thrust fault. If the intermediate principal stress is vertical, the crust shears horizontally and produces a strike-slip fault, where blocks slide past each other with negligible vertical offset. Faults that combine vertical and horizontal slip are oblique-slip faults, and where a block drops down between two normal faults it forms a graben, with the uplifted flanking blocks called horsts.

sections.heading: Folds: naming the bends, then orienting them in space
sections.body: Where rock deforms without breaking, it folds, and the vocabulary names both the shape and its parts. An anticline is a fold arching upward, oldest rock in its core; a syncline is a fold bending downward, youngest rock in its core; a monocline is a single, step-like bend between otherwise flat-lying layers. Each fold has two limbs meeting at a hinge, the line of maximum curvature, and an axial plane bisecting the fold, connecting hinges up and down through the structure; if the hinge line itself is not horizontal, the fold is described as plunging, at a specific plunge angle. To locate a planar surface, like a bed or a fault, in three dimensions, geologists record strike, the compass direction of the horizontal line within that plane, and dip, the angle the plane descends below horizontal, measured perpendicular to strike; by the right-hand rule convention, pointing the right hand's fingers along the strike direction so the thumb points in the dip direction resolves the otherwise ambiguous choice of which of two possible strike directions to report.

lessons.workedExample: A cross-section shows a shallow-angle fault where older limestone has been pushed up and over younger shale, with clear horizontal shortening. Applying Anderson's theory, horizontal compression means the minimum principal stress is vertical, identifying this as a reverse fault, and because the dip is shallow with large displacement, specifically a thrust fault, with the limestone forming the hanging wall riding up and over the shale footwall. A nearby outcrop shows the same shale layers arched upward with the oldest bed exposed at the crest, a plunging anticline, whose axial plane trace on a geologic map curves and narrows in the direction of plunge, letting a field geologist read the fold's three-dimensional geometry from a two-dimensional map pattern.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge shows a photo, a map, or a cross-section and asks a student to name the structure because vocabulary fluency signals whether the student can actually read geologic evidence rather than recite definitions. The strongest answers reason from mechanism, not just shape, connecting a normal fault to horizontal extension via Anderson's 1905 framework, or correctly distinguishing an anticline from a syncline by which age of rock sits in the core rather than by which way the beds appear to bend at the surface, a common error since erosion can make an anticline's surface expression misleading. Fluency with strike, dip, and the right-hand rule further shows the student can translate a field or map observation into the standard notation a real geologist would report.

questions.prompt: Per Anderson's 1905 theory of faulting, what stress condition produces a normal fault?

options.text: Maximum principal stress is vertical
Minimum principal stress is vertical
Intermediate principal stress is vertical
All three principal stresses are equal

explanations.a: Correct — when the maximum principal stress is vertical (overburden dominates), the crust extends horizontally, producing a normal fault with the hanging wall dropping relative to the footwall.
explanations.b: A vertical minimum principal stress implies horizontal compression, which produces a reverse or thrust fault, not a normal fault.
explanations.c: A vertical intermediate principal stress produces horizontal shear and a strike-slip fault, not a normal fault.
explanations.d: Equal principal stresses would produce no differential stress to drive faulting at all.

questions.prompt: In an anticline, where is the oldest rock found?

options.text: In the core of the fold
Along the limbs only
In the core of an adjacent syncline
At the plunging end only

explanations.a: Correct — an anticline arches upward with the oldest rock exposed in its core, since it was originally the deepest, earliest-deposited layer before folding lifted it.
explanations.b: The limbs contain progressively younger rock moving outward from the core, not the oldest rock itself.
explanations.c: A syncline's core holds the youngest rock, the opposite pattern from an anticline.
explanations.d: Age distribution follows the fold's core-to-limb structure everywhere along its length, not just at a plunging end.

questions.prompt: Match each structural term to its definition.

right.text: The block above an inclined fault surface
A block dropped down between two flanking normal faults
The compass direction of the horizontal line within a plane
The angle a plane descends below horizontal, perpendicular to strike

questions.explanation: The hanging wall sits above an inclined fault surface; a graben is a down-dropped block between two normal faults; strike is the compass bearing of a plane's horizontal line; dip is the angle that plane descends, measured perpendicular to strike.

questions.prompt: Order these terms from a single planar feature (a fault or bed) to a full three-dimensional fold structure, from simplest to most composite.

items.text: Strike (one direction on one plane)
Limb (one side of a fold)
