Griffith's model also explains a striking asymmetry every geologist relies on - tensile strength runs only about a tenth to a twentieth of compressive strength for the same rock. Under tension, a crack's tip concentrates stress and the crack propagates straight through; under compression, cracks tend to close and interact instead, so far more load is needed to link them into a through-going fracture. This is why rock almost always fails first in tension, and why engineered structures in rock are designed to keep tensile stress to a minimum wherever possible.

sections.heading: The Brittle-Ductile Transition
sections.body: Whether a given rock shatters or flows depends on three competing factors: confining pressure, temperature, and strain rate. Rising confining pressure suppresses crack opening (cracks need room to dilate to propagate) and pushes failure toward more ductile, distributed deformation; rising temperature makes crystal-plastic mechanisms - dislocation glide and climb - progressively easier, since these are thermally activated; and falling strain rate gives slow, thermally activated creep processes time to operate rather than snapping into brittle fracture. In average continental crust, these factors trade off around 10-15 km depth, where confining pressure and temperature (roughly 300-450 degrees C for quartz-rich crust) become high enough for crystal plasticity to dominate over brittle fracture. This brittle-ductile transition matches, closely, the observed base of the seismogenic layer - the depth below which earthquakes essentially stop, because rock there deforms by slow creep instead of by sudden slip.

sections.heading: Byerlee's Law: A Frictional Ceiling
sections.body: Above the brittle-ductile transition, rock strength is not set by the rock's own cohesion but by friction on pre-existing fractures - and remarkably, that frictional strength is nearly independent of rock type. Byerlee (1978) compiled sliding-friction data across many rock types and found a strikingly uniform relationship: for normal stress below about 200 MPa, tau = 0.85 * sigma_n; above 200 MPa, tau = 50 MPa + 0.6 * sigma_n. This 'Byerlee's law' sets a hard frictional ceiling on how much shear stress a fault can sustain before slipping, regardless of whether the fault cuts granite, sandstone, or limestone, and it is the standard baseline against which anomalously weak faults (explained by high pore pressure or weak clay gouge) are measured.

lessons.workedExample: A fault at 5 km depth has normal stress sigma_n = 130 MPa, below the 200 MPa Byerlee break, so its frictional strength ceiling is tau = 0.85 * 130 = 110.5 MPa - the fault slips once shear stress reaches that value. At 12 km depth in the same crust, sigma_n = 320 MPa exceeds 200 MPa, so the ceiling instead follows tau = 50 + 0.6 * 320 = 242 MPa. But at 12 km, temperature has also climbed enough (roughly 350 degrees C) that crystal-plastic creep may accommodate strain before frictional sliding ever reaches that ceiling - illustrating why the brittle-ductile transition, not Byerlee's law alone, ultimately caps the depth of large earthquakes.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe brittle-ductile behavior to see whether a student can explain, mechanistically, why deep earthquakes are rare without just citing a depth number. The strong answer names the three competing controls - confining pressure, temperature, strain rate - and explains why each pushes toward ductile flow at depth, rather than treating 10-15 km as an arbitrary cutoff. Citing Byerlee's law by name, with its two-part linear form and 200 MPa break, and connecting it to the seismogenic layer's base shows a student understands crustal strength as the product of two competing physical limits (frictional sliding above, plastic creep below) rather than a single rule of thumb.

questions.prompt: Why is a rock's tensile strength so much lower than its compressive strength?

options.text: Tension increases confining pressure, which weakens rock
Under tension, cracks propagate directly from stress concentrated at their tips, while compression tends to close cracks and requires them to interact before failure
Compressive strength is a purely theoretical value never observed in real rock
Tensile strength and compressive strength are actually equal for most crustal rocks

explanations.a: Tension does not increase confining pressure; if anything it works against it, which is part of why tension promotes crack growth.
explanations.b: Correct - Griffith's theory explains that stress concentration at crack tips lets tension propagate cracks straight through at low stress, while compression closes cracks and needs far more load to link them into a fracture.
explanations.c: Compressive strength is a real, measured property; it is simply much higher than tensile strength, not a theoretical abstraction.
explanations.d: The asymmetry is large - tensile strength is roughly a tenth to a twentieth of compressive strength - not approximately equal.

questions.prompt: A fault has normal stress sigma_n = 150 MPa. Using Byerlee's law, what shear stress is needed to cause frictional sliding?

options.text: tau = 150 MPa exactly
tau cannot be determined without knowing rock type

explanations.a: Correct - since sigma_n = 150 MPa is below the 200 MPa break, the low-pressure Byerlee relation tau = 0.85 * sigma_n applies, giving 127.5 MPa.
explanations.b: The tau = 50 + 0.6*sigma_n form only applies above 200 MPa normal stress; using it below that threshold gives the wrong branch of the law.
explanations.c: Byerlee's law is not a 1:1 relationship between shear and normal stress; the coefficient is 0.85, not 1.0, below 200 MPa.
explanations.d: Byerlee's law is notable precisely because it is nearly independent of rock type - only sigma_n matters.

questions.prompt: Match each factor to how it shifts rock behavior toward brittle or ductile.

right.text: Suppresses crack dilation, pushing toward ductile behavior
Thermally activates dislocation glide and climb, pushing toward ductile behavior
Gives slow creep processes time to operate instead of brittle fracture, pushing toward ductile behavior

questions.explanation: All three factors push rock toward ductile behavior when they increase (pressure, temperature) or decrease (strain rate) as depth increases, which is why the crust transitions from brittle to ductile with depth rather than staying brittle throughout.

questions.prompt: Order these depths in continental crust from shallowest to deepest based on where they fall relative to the brittle-ductile transition (roughly 10-15 km).

items.text: 3 km - clearly brittle, above the transition
12 km - within the brittle-ductile transition zone
25 km - clearly ductile, well below the transition

questions.explanation: Rock behavior shifts from brittle near the surface, through a transitional zone around 10-15 km where confining pressure and temperature are high enough for crystal plasticity to compete with fracture, to fully ductile flow well below that depth.

lessons.label: Soil as an Engineering Material: Texture, Classification, and Plasticity

sections.heading: Texture and the Unified Soil Classification System
sections.body: The USDA texture triangle sorts soil purely by grain size: sand spans 2 mm down to 0.05 mm, silt 0.05 mm down to 0.002 mm, and clay is anything finer than 0.002 mm (2 microns). Engineers instead use the Unified Soil Classification System (USCS), which sorts coarse-grained soils by gradation as well as size: well-graded gravel (GW) and poorly-graded gravel (GP), well-graded sand (SW) and poorly-graded sand (SP), and fine-grained soils by plasticity - low-plasticity silt (ML), low-plasticity clay (CL), high-plasticity silt (MH), high-plasticity clay (CH). Gradation itself is quantified with two coefficients read off a grain-size distribution curve: the uniformity coefficient Cu = D60/D10 (the ratio of the grain size at 60% passing to the size at 10% passing - a high Cu means a wide spread of grain sizes, filling voids and increasing strength) and the coefficient of curvature Cc, which checks the curve's shape between those extremes. A soil needs both Cu above about 4-6 and Cc between 1 and 3 to earn a 'well-graded' (W) designation rather than 'poorly-graded' (P).

sections.heading: Atterberg Limits and the Plasticity Chart
sections.body: For fine-grained soil, grain size alone says little about engineering behavior - two clays with identical texture can behave very differently depending on how much water they hold while remaining a coherent solid. The Atterberg limits, developed by Albert Atterberg and standardized by Casagrande, define this with two water-content thresholds found by standardized lab tests: the liquid limit (LL), the water content at which soil transitions from plastic to a viscous liquid, and the plastic limit (PL), the water content below which it becomes brittle and crumbles rather than deforms. Their difference is the plasticity index, PI = LL - PL, the size of the water-content window in which the soil behaves plastically. Casagrande's plasticity chart plots PI against LL and uses the empirical 'A-line' to separate clays (above the line) from silts (below it), and a vertical line at LL = 50 to separate low-plasticity from high-plasticity soils - giving the CL, CH, ML, MH labels their exact boundaries.

sections.heading: Why Clay Mineralogy Controls Everything
sections.body: The huge behavioral range within 'clay' traces back to which clay mineral dominates. Kaolinite has a tightly bonded, non-expanding structure and low plasticity and low shrink-swell. Illite bonds its layers with potassium ions, giving intermediate plasticity. Smectite (including montmorillonite) has a weakly bonded structure that lets water molecules force their way between mineral layers, so it swells dramatically when wetted and shrinks and cracks severely when dried - the mineral behind most expansive-soil damage to foundations and roads.

lessons.workedExample: A clay sample has liquid limit LL = 65% and plastic limit PL = 28%, so PI = 65 - 28 = 37. On the Casagrande chart, LL = 65 puts it past the LL = 50 line into the high-plasticity field, and PI = 37 sits above the A-line, so it classifies as CH (high-plasticity clay). A geotechnical report would flag this combination - high LL, high PI - as a red flag for smectite content and expansive-soil risk, meaning a foundation on it needs either deep piers past the active zone or moisture-control measures, unlike a low-PI kaolinitic clay (CL) that would need neither.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge testing soil mechanics wants to see whether a student treats 'clay' as one uniform material or understands that its engineering behavior swings wildly with mineralogy. The strong answer runs a sample's liquid limit and plastic limit through the plasticity index and places it on the Casagrande chart to justify a CL vs CH classification, then explains the classification in terms of clay mineral structure (kaolinite's tight, non-expanding layers versus smectite's water-absorbing interlayer) rather than treating classification as an arbitrary label. That link from lab-measured numbers to mineral structure to real-world consequence (foundation cracking, road heave) is what separates a memorized chart from genuine understanding.

questions.prompt: A soil sample has D60 = 6 mm and D10 = 1 mm. What is its uniformity coefficient Cu, and what does that value suggest?

options.text: Cu = 6, suggesting well-graded (wide range of grain sizes)
Cu = 0.17, suggesting poorly-graded
Cu = 5, suggesting the sample is entirely clay
Cu cannot be computed without the D30 value

explanations.a: Correct - Cu = D60/D10 = 6/1 = 6, above the well-graded threshold of about 4-6, indicating a broad spread of grain sizes.
explanations.b: Inverting the ratio (D10/D60) gives 0.17, but Cu is defined as D60/D10, not the reverse.
explanations.c: Cu describes gradation shape, not mineralogy or grain-size class; a Cu of 6 says nothing about clay content.
explanations.d: Cu only requires D60 and D10; the coefficient of curvature Cc is the one that also needs D30.

questions.prompt: A clay has LL = 45% and PI = 22, placing it below the LL = 50 line and just above the A-line (PI_A = 0.73*(45-20) = 18.25) on the Casagrande chart. What USCS classification best fits?

options.text: CH (high-plasticity clay)
CL (low-plasticity clay)
GW (well-graded gravel)
SP (poorly-graded sand)

explanations.a: CH requires LL above 50; this sample's LL of 45% falls in the low-plasticity field instead.
explanations.b: Correct - LL below 50 places it in the low-plasticity field, and a PI of 22 sits above the A-line value of 18.25 at LL=45, supporting a CL designation.
explanations.c: GW and SP labels apply to coarse-grained gravel and sand classified by gradation, not to fine-grained clay described by Atterberg limits.
explanations.d: SP is a poorly-graded sand classification; it has nothing to do with plasticity index or liquid limit.

questions.prompt: Match each clay mineral to its structural behavior.

right.text: Tightly bonded, non-expanding layers; low plasticity, low shrink-swell
Layers bonded by potassium ions; intermediate plasticity
Weakly bonded layers that water forces apart; high shrink-swell, expansive-soil risk

questions.explanation: Clay mineralogy sets engineering behavior directly: kaolinite's tight non-expanding structure gives low plasticity, illite's potassium bonding gives intermediate behavior, and smectite's weak interlayer bonding lets water in, producing high plasticity and dramatic shrink-swell.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to classify a fine-grained soil sample using Atterberg limits and the Casagrande chart.

items.text: Measure liquid limit (LL) and plastic limit (PL) in the lab
Compute plasticity index PI = LL - PL
Plot the point (LL, PI) on the Casagrande chart
Read the classification from position relative to the A-line and the LL = 50 line

questions.explanation: Classification starts with the two lab-measured limits, derives the plasticity index from their difference, plots that pair of values on the chart, and only then reads off the CL/CH/ML/MH classification from where the point falls.

lessons.label: Porosity, Permeability, and Darcy's Law

sections.heading: Porosity Is Not Permeability
sections.body: Porosity (n) is simply the fraction of a material's volume that is void space, and it is easy to assume that more void space means water moves through more easily - but the two properties can point in opposite directions entirely. Clean, well-sorted gravel has porosity of only about 25-40%, yet its hydraulic conductivity K runs from roughly 10^-1 to 10^-3 m/s, letting water drain through it almost as fast as an open channel. Clay, by contrast, can have porosity of 40-70% - more void space than gravel - while its hydraulic conductivity is only about 10^-9 to 10^-11 m/s, six to eight orders of magnitude lower. The reason is that permeability depends on how well the pores are connected and how large the connecting throats are, not on total void volume: clay's pores are individually tiny and tortuously connected by platy mineral grains, choking flow even though the material is mostly space.

sections.heading: Darcy's Experiment and His Law
sections.body: Henry Darcy derived the governing equation for this kind of flow empirically in 1856, running water through vertical sand columns to design the public fountains of Dijon, France. His result, published as an appendix to his water-supply report, is the linear relationship Q = -K * A * (dh/dl), where Q is volumetric flow rate, A is the cross-sectional area the flow passes through, dh/dl is the hydraulic head gradient driving the flow, and K is the hydraulic conductivity - a property of both the material and the fluid moving through it. Darcy's law holds for slow, laminar flow through porous media, which describes the overwhelming majority of natural groundwater flow.

sections.heading: Intrinsic Permeability vs Hydraulic Conductivity, and Measuring K
sections.body: Because hydraulic conductivity K bundles in the properties of water (viscosity, density), it is not a pure material property - the same sand conducts oil differently than it conducts water. Intrinsic permeability, k, strips the fluid out and describes only the pore geometry itself, related to K by K = k * (rho * g)/mu, where mu is fluid viscosity. A student can measure K directly with two standard permeameter setups: the constant-head test, which holds a fixed head difference across a sample (best for permeable materials like sand and gravel, where flow is fast enough to measure directly) and the falling-head test, which lets the head decline through a narrow standpipe over time and works far better for low-K materials like clay and silt, where flow is too slow for a constant-head setup to produce measurable volumes in reasonable time.

lessons.workedExample: A student runs a falling-head permeameter on a silty clay sample: cross-sectional area of the sample A = 20 cm2, standpipe area a = 0.5 cm2, sample length L = 10 cm, head falls from h0 = 40 cm to h1 = 30 cm over t = 3600 seconds. The falling-head formula K = (a*L)/(A*t) * ln(h0/h1) gives K = (0.5*10)/(20*3600) * ln(40/30) = (5/72000) * 0.2877 = 2.0 x 10^-5 cm/s, about 2 x 10^-7 m/s - consistent with a silty clay, intermediate between clean sand and pure clay, and far too slow to measure with a constant-head setup in any reasonable lab period.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask students to distinguish porosity from permeability because it is the single most common groundwater misconception, and clay is the perfect trap: it has the highest porosity of common earth materials yet is essentially an aquitard. A student who can state that clay's high porosity coexists with K as low as 10^-9 to 10^-11 m/s because pore connectivity, not pore volume, controls flow is demonstrating real hydrogeologic reasoning. Naming Darcy's 1856 sand-column work and correctly matching test method (constant-head vs falling-head) to material permeability shows the student has actually run or understood the physical measurement, not just memorized the equation Q = -KA dh/dl.

questions.prompt: Clay has porosity of 40-70% (higher than gravel's 25-40%) yet a hydraulic conductivity K of only 10^-9 to 10^-11 m/s, versus gravel's 10^-1 to 10^-3 m/s. What best explains this?

options.text: Porosity and permeability always increase together, so this data must be an error
Permeability depends on how well pores are connected and how large the connecting throats are, not on total void volume
Clay contains no void space at all, despite its reported porosity
Gravel has lower porosity, so it must have lower permeability too

explanations.a: This is exactly the misconception the clay-gravel contrast disproves: high porosity does not guarantee high permeability.
explanations.b: Correct - clay's pores are individually tiny and tortuously connected by platy grains, choking flow despite abundant void space, while gravel's large, well-connected pores let water move freely with less void space overall.
explanations.c: Clay's porosity is real and measured; the issue is pore connectivity and throat size, not absence of voids.
explanations.d: This inverts the actual relationship - gravel has both lower porosity and dramatically higher permeability than clay.

questions.prompt: In Darcy's law Q = -K * A * (dh/dl), what does K represent?

options.text: Porosity of the material
Hydraulic conductivity, a property of both the material and the fluid
The cross-sectional area flow passes through
The hydraulic head gradient driving flow

explanations.a: Porosity (n) is a separate quantity describing void fraction; it is not what K represents in Darcy's equation.
explanations.b: Correct - K is hydraulic conductivity, bundling both pore geometry and the moving fluid's properties (viscosity, density), distinct from intrinsic permeability k.
explanations.c: Cross-sectional area is represented by A in the equation, a separate term from K.
explanations.d: The head gradient is dh/dl, a separate term multiplied by K and A, not K itself.

questions.prompt: Match each material or concept to its correct value or role.

right.text: About 10^-1 to 10^-3 m/s
About 10^-9 to 10^-11 m/s
Pore-geometry property independent of the fluid, related to K via fluid density/viscosity
Derived Q = -K*A*(dh/dl) from sand-column experiments for the Dijon water supply

questions.explanation: Gravel and clay sit at opposite ends of the hydraulic conductivity range despite clay's higher porosity; intrinsic permeability isolates pore geometry from the fluid; and Darcy's 1856 sand-column work is the empirical origin of the governing flow equation.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a falling-head permeameter test used to measure K for a low-permeability sample like clay.

items.text: Set up the sample with a narrow standpipe attached above it
Record the starting head h0 in the standpipe
Let water flow through the sample as the standpipe head falls over a measured time t
Record the final head h1 and compute K from the falling-head formula

questions.explanation: A falling-head test requires setting up the standpipe, recording the initial head, allowing time to pass as slow flow drains the standpipe, then recording the final head and computing K - this method is chosen over constant-head specifically because it can resolve very slow flow through low-K materials like clay.

units.label: Seismic Waves and Instrumentation

lessons.label: Body Waves: P, S, and What Their Speeds Reveal

sections.heading: Two ways to shake a solid
sections.body: Body waves travel through the Earth's interior in two families. P waves (primary, or compressional) push and pull particles back and forth parallel to the direction of travel, exactly like sound in air — the medium alternately compresses and rarefies. S waves (secondary, or shear/transverse) displace particles perpendicular to travel, like a shaken rope. Their speeds come from elastodynamics: Vp = sqrt((K + 4mu/3)/rho) and Vs = sqrt(mu/rho), where K is the bulk modulus (resistance to volume change), mu is the shear modulus (resistance to shape change), and rho is density. Because the P formula carries an extra restoring term, P always outruns S in the same material — hence 'primary,' the first arrival on any seismogram.

sections.heading: The Poisson-solid ratio and typical crustal numbers
sections.body: For a Poisson solid, an idealization where K and mu are equal (a common crustal approximation), the ratio works out to Vp/Vs = sqrt(3) ~ 1.73. Real rocks cluster near this value: upper continental crust runs roughly 6 km/s for Vp, the upper mantle jumps to roughly 8 km/s at the Mohorovicic discontinuity, and liquid water carries P waves at about 1.5 km/s. Vp/Vs deviates from 1.73 with fluid content, partial melt, or fracturing, which is why seismologists invert for the ratio itself as a rock-physics diagnostic — a locally low Vp/Vs can flag gas-saturated rock; a locally high one can flag partial melt or fluid-filled cracks.

sections.heading: Why the shear modulus is the whole story for the core
sections.body: A fluid, by definition, cannot support shear stress — it has no restoring force for shape distortion, so mu = 0. Plug that into Vs = sqrt(mu/rho): S waves cannot propagate through a liquid at all. Richard Oldham first proposed a fluid-like core region in 1906 from anomalous travel times; Beno Gutenberg refined the core-mantle boundary depth in 1913. The decisive proof came from two independent lines of evidence: S waves are never observed to arrive having passed through the region below about 2900 km depth, and P waves show a shadow zone from roughly 103 to 142 degrees angular distance from an earthquake, where direct P arrivals go missing because the outer core refracts them away like a lens with a lower velocity. Together, these two absences — no S, and a specific P gap — are the classic wave-speed-to-interior-structure inference: seismologists read the Earth's deep material state off which wave types do and do not show up.

lessons.workedExample: A crustal rock sample has K = 52 GPa, mu = 30 GPa, and rho = 2700 kg/m^3. Vp = sqrt((52e9 + 4*30e9/3)/2700) = sqrt(92e9/2700) ~ 5.84 km/s. Vs = sqrt(30e9/2700) ~ 3.33 km/s. The ratio Vp/Vs ~ 1.75, close to the Poisson-solid value of 1.73, consistent with typical upper-crustal granite-gneiss. If the same rock were water-saturated and fractured such that mu dropped to 20 GPa while K stayed near 52 GPa, Vp would fall only slightly (fluid resists compression) but Vs would fall sharply to about 2.72 km/s, pushing Vp/Vs up toward 2.0 (~1.98) — the signature seismologists look for to flag fluid-filled fracture zones in exploration surveys.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about P and S speeds to test whether a student understands that seismology infers unseen material properties from wave behavior rather than measuring them directly. The strong answer explains WHY S waves die in the outer core — mu = 0 in a liquid, not just 'the core blocks them' — and can name the independent P-shadow-zone evidence rather than treating the two clues as one fact. A student who can compute Vp/Vs from K, mu, and rho, and explain what a deviation from 1.73 implies about fluid or melt content, is demonstrating the mechanism, not reciting a memorized number.

questions.prompt: Why can S waves not travel through the Earth's outer core?

options.text: The outer core is too hot for any wave to travel through it
The outer core's shear modulus (mu) is zero because it behaves as a fluid
The outer core's density is too low to support wave propagation
S waves are absorbed entirely by the mantle before reaching the core

explanations.a: Temperature alone does not block wave propagation; it is the mechanical state (fluid vs. solid) that matters.
explanations.b: Correct — a fluid cannot support shear stress, so mu = 0, and Vs = sqrt(mu/rho) becomes zero: no S-wave propagation is possible.
explanations.c: Density affects wave speed but does not prevent propagation outright; density alone would only change the speed, not eliminate the wave.
explanations.d: S waves do travel through the mantle and are recorded up to the core-mantle boundary; the absence begins specifically at the fluid outer core, not before.

questions.prompt: For a Poisson solid, what is the approximate value of Vp/Vs?

explanations.a: A ratio of 1.0 would mean P and S travel at the same speed, which never happens because the P formula always includes the extra 4mu/3 term.
explanations.b: Correct — when K equals mu (the Poisson-solid idealization), the ratio reduces to sqrt(3), about 1.73, matching typical crustal rock.
explanations.c: 2.5 is higher than typical solid crustal rock and would suggest significant fluid or melt content, not a baseline Poisson solid.
explanations.d: 0.58 is the inverse of the correct ratio; P waves are always faster than S waves in the same material, never slower.

questions.prompt: Match each observation to the interior structure conclusion it supports.

left.text: No S-wave arrivals recorded through the deep interior
P-wave shadow zone between 103 and 142 degrees
Vp/Vs near 1.73 in a rock sample
Vp/Vs well above 1.73 in a rock sample

right.text: The outer core has zero shear modulus (is fluid)
The outer core refracts P waves away like a lower-velocity lens
The rock behaves close to an ideal Poisson solid
The rock likely contains fluid, melt, or fractures

questions.explanation: The absence of S waves through the deep Earth directly demonstrates a fluid outer core (mu = 0); the P shadow zone shows the same fluid layer refracting P rays away from that angular band; a Vp/Vs near 1.73 matches the Poisson-solid baseline for ordinary solid rock; and a Vp/Vs well above 1.73 flags fluid, melt, or fracturing that lowers the shear modulus relative to the bulk modulus.

lessons.label: Surface Waves, Amplitude Decay, and Dispersion

sections.heading: Two surface-wave families, two particle motions
sections.body: Body waves (P and S) can combine at a free surface into waves that hug the Earth's outer boundary and decay quickly with depth. Rayleigh waves, predicted mathematically by Lord Rayleigh in 1885, move particles in a retrograde ellipse confined to the vertical plane containing the propagation direction — the surface traces a backward-rolling loop, like the surface of a wave in the ocean. Love waves, described by A.E.H. Love in 1911, move particles horizontally and transverse to propagation, with no vertical component at all; they require a layered medium — specifically a lower-velocity layer over a faster half-space — to exist, because they arise from constructive interference of shear waves trapped and reflecting within that surface layer. A uniform half-space supports Rayleigh waves but cannot support Love waves at all.

sections.heading: Why surface waves dominate distant damage
sections.body: Surface waves are confined to roughly one wavelength of depth, so their energy spreads across a widening ring on essentially a 2-D surface, with geometric-spreading amplitude decay going as 1/sqrt(r). Body waves spread through the full 3-D volume, decaying as 1/r. At large distance r, 1/sqrt(r) shrinks far more slowly than 1/r, so surface-wave amplitude comes to dwarf body-wave amplitude — which is exactly why distant large earthquakes (Mexico City in 1985, hundreds of kilometers from the rupture) do their damage through long-period surface-wave shaking rather than the P or S arrivals that came first but were already small.

sections.heading: Dispersion: group velocity, phase velocity, and crustal structure
sections.body: Because longer-period surface waves sample deeper (faster) material and shorter-period waves stay shallow (slower), surface waves are dispersive: different periods travel at different speeds, so the wave train stretches out over distance instead of arriving as a single pulse. Phase velocity describes the speed of an individual wave crest; group velocity describes the speed of the overall energy envelope, and it is group velocity that a station actually times. Traditional surface-wave magnitude (Ms) uses the roughly 20-second-period Rayleigh wave near a group velocity of about 3.5 km/s as the reference arrival to measure. Seismologists exploit the dispersion itself as data: by measuring group or phase velocity as a function of period across many stations and inverting the resulting dispersion curve, they recover how shear velocity varies with depth — a standard method for mapping crustal and upper-mantle structure without ever drilling.

lessons.workedExample: A magnitude 8 earthquake ruptures at a subduction zone. At a station 300 km away, the P wave (about 6 km/s average) arrives first at roughly 50 seconds; the S wave (about 3.5 km/s) follows around 86 seconds; the surface-wave train, dispersing across a group-velocity range of roughly 3.0-3.5 km/s but carrying most of the radiated energy, arrives around 86-100 seconds after the origin time (essentially overlapping the S arrival at its leading edge, then stretching out) and produces the largest, longest-lasting shaking on the seismogram — often 5-10x the peak amplitude of the S arrival. Because surface-wave amplitude falls off as 1/sqrt(r) versus the body waves' 1/r, doubling the distance to 600 km roughly halves body-wave amplitude but only shrinks surface-wave amplitude by a factor of about 1.41 — explaining why cities far from the epicenter can still suffer serious surface-wave-driven damage.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes surface waves to check that a student can explain WHY distant earthquakes are dangerous, not just that they are. The strong answer connects the geometric-spreading exponent (1/sqrt(r) vs. 1/r) to the physical fact that surface-wave energy is trapped near the surface rather than spread through a volume, and can distinguish Rayleigh from Love motion by describing the actual particle path rather than naming them interchangeably. Being able to explain dispersion — why a surface-wave train stretches out and why that stretching is USED, not just endured, to map crustal structure — separates memorized vocabulary from real understanding of the physics.

questions.prompt: Why can Love waves not exist in a uniform (unlayered) half-space?

options.text: Love waves require a lower-velocity surface layer to trap and interfere shear energy
Love waves are actually just P waves traveling along the surface
Love waves require a liquid layer, and a uniform solid has none
Uniform half-spaces cannot transmit any shear energy at all

explanations.a: Correct — Love waves arise from constructive interference of shear waves reflecting within a slower surface layer over a faster half-space; without that velocity contrast, there is no trapping and no Love wave.
explanations.b: Love waves are horizontally polarized shear (transverse) motion, unrelated to P-wave compressional motion.
explanations.c: The required contrast is a velocity layering (slow over fast), not specifically a liquid layer; solid layered crust supports Love waves fine.
explanations.d: A uniform half-space transmits shear (S) waves normally; it simply lacks the layering needed to trap and interfere them into a Love wave.

questions.prompt: Why do surface waves come to dominate the shaking at large distance from an earthquake, even though P and S waves arrive first?

options.text: Surface waves travel faster than body waves at long range
Surface-wave energy spreads over a 2-D surface (1/sqrt(r) decay) while body-wave energy spreads through a 3-D volume (1/r decay), so surface waves decay more slowly with distance
Body waves are absorbed completely by the crust within the first 50 km
Surface waves are not subject to geometric spreading at all

explanations.a: Surface waves are slower than P and S, which is exactly why they arrive last, not first.
explanations.b: Correct — the difference in spreading geometry (2-D surface ring vs. 3-D expanding sphere) means surface-wave amplitude falls off more slowly with distance, so it overtakes body-wave amplitude at range.
explanations.c: Body waves do lose amplitude with distance but are not fully absorbed within 50 km; they simply decay faster than surface waves per unit distance.
explanations.d: Surface waves do undergo geometric spreading, just at a slower 1/sqrt(r) rate rather than 1/r.

questions.prompt: Match each surface-wave concept to its correct description.

right.text: Retrograde ellipse in the vertical plane
Horizontal, transverse to propagation, no vertical component
Speed of an individual wave crest
Speed of the overall energy envelope, used for Ms at about 3.5 km/s

questions.explanation: Rayleigh waves trace a retrograde ellipse confined to the vertical plane; Love waves move purely horizontally and transverse to travel with no vertical component; phase velocity tracks an individual crest, while group velocity tracks the energy envelope actually timed for surface-wave magnitude near 3.5 km/s.

lessons.label: Ray Paths: Reflection, Refraction, and Phase Names

sections.heading: Snell's law and curving rays
sections.body: At any boundary between two velocity layers, a seismic ray bends according to Snell's law: sin(i1)/V1 = sin(i2)/V2, the same relation that bends light at a lens. As the incidence angle i1 grows, at some point sin(i2) would need to exceed 1 — the physically impossible limit — and the ray instead travels along the boundary itself as a head wave, radiating energy back up into the upper layer at the critical angle ic = arcsin(V1/V2). Because seismic velocity generally increases with depth inside the Earth (compaction, phase changes, decreasing porosity), rays continuously refract toward the boundary-parallel direction and curve upward, eventually returning to the surface even without any discrete layer boundary — this is why a P wave sent steeply downward still comes back up hundreds of kilometers away instead of diving forever.

sections.heading: The refraction crossover distance and Mohorovicic's 1909 discovery
sections.body: A direct wave through a slow upper layer of thickness h and velocity V1 arrives at time t = x/V1. A head wave critically refracted along a faster layer below (velocity V2) arrives later at short range but, because it travels the deep leg at V2, catches up at long range; its travel time is t = x/V2 + 2h*cos(ic)/V1. Setting the two travel-time equations equal and solving gives the crossover distance xcross — beyond which the refracted head wave becomes the first arrival — and inverting that relation gives the layer thickness h. Andrija Mohorovicic used exactly this method in 1909, reading a Croatian earthquake's seismograms and noticing two distinct P arrivals with a crossover near 200 km, to infer a sharp velocity jump from about 6 km/s to about 8 km/s at roughly 30-50 km depth — the boundary now named for him, the Moho, marking the crust-mantle transition.

sections.heading: Decoding the phase alphabet
sections.body: Seismologists name each distinct ray path with a letter code so a single arrival tells you what it sampled. P and S are direct through-mantle paths; PP is a P wave that reflects once off the free surface partway and continues as P; PcP reflects off the core-mantle boundary (c) and returns as P without entering the core; PKIKP dives through the mantle as P, crosses the outer core as K (a compressional wave in fluid, since only P-type waves survive there), continues through the inner core as I, exits the outer core again as K, and returns through the mantle as P — a full round trip to the inner core and back. A lowercase leading letter denotes a depth phase: pP leaves the source traveling upward as P, reflects off the free surface just above the hypocenter, and then follows a normal P path — the pP minus P arrival-time gap is a standard way to estimate focal depth independent of the location solution itself.

lessons.workedExample: A refraction line records a direct P wave with slope corresponding to V1 = 5 km/s and a head wave with slope corresponding to V2 = 7 km/s, crossing over at xcross = 40 km. The critical angle is ic = arcsin(5/7) = 45.6 degrees. Using the crossover relation h = (xcross/2) * sqrt((V2-V1)/(V2+V1)) gives h = 20 * sqrt(2/12) = 20 * 0.408 ~ 8.2 km — a plausible upper-crustal layer thickness. This is the same style of calculation, scaled up, that Mohorovicic performed in 1909 with a crossover near 200 km and velocities near 6 and 8 km/s to place the crust-mantle boundary at roughly 30-50 km beneath the Balkans.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about ray bending and phase names to test whether a student sees seismic phases as engineered diagnostics rather than arbitrary labels. The strong answer explains that a crossover distance is not just a graph feature but algebraically encodes a layer thickness, and can trace what PKIKP actually samples (mantle, outer core, inner core, outer core, mantle) rather than reciting the letters. Explaining why velocity increasing with depth alone — with no sharp boundary — still curves a ray back to the surface shows genuine grasp of Snell's law as a continuous, not just discrete, phenomenon.

questions.prompt: What physical quantity does Andrija Mohorovicic infer from the 1909 refraction crossover-distance method?

options.text: The Earth's total radius
The thickness of the upper layer above a velocity discontinuity
The earthquake's moment magnitude
The density of the outer core

explanations.a: The method uses local crustal refraction data, not global geometry, and says nothing about Earth's radius.
explanations.b: Correct — solving the crossover-distance equation for h yields the thickness of the upper (slower) layer above the velocity jump, which is how Mohorovicic located the crust-mantle boundary.
explanations.c: Magnitude requires amplitude and distance calibration, not travel-time crossover geometry.
explanations.d: The outer core lies thousands of kilometers deeper than any near-source crustal refraction survey can sample.

questions.prompt: Why does a seismic ray sent steeply downward eventually curve back up to the surface even without a sharp layer boundary?

options.text: Gravity pulls the ray back toward the surface
Velocity generally increases with depth, so Snell's law continuously refracts the ray toward horizontal until it turns upward
The ray loses energy and stops descending
Earth's rotation deflects the ray via the Coriolis effect

explanations.a: Seismic ray paths are governed by elastic wave propagation and Snell's law, not gravitational attraction on the wave itself.
explanations.b: Correct — as velocity increases continuously with depth, Snell's law bends the ray progressively toward the horizontal at each infinitesimal boundary until it turns over and heads back up, exactly like light bending in a graded-index medium.
explanations.c: Energy loss (attenuation) reduces amplitude but does not by itself reverse the direction of travel.
explanations.d: The Coriolis effect is negligible at seismic wave speeds and does not explain ray curvature.

questions.prompt: Match each seismic phase name to what its ray path actually does.

right.text: P wave reflecting once off the free surface, then continuing as P
P wave reflecting off the core-mantle boundary without entering the core
P wave crossing the outer core (K), inner core (I), and outer core (K) again
Upward P leg from the source that reflects off the surface near the hypocenter before following a normal P path, used to estimate focal depth

questions.explanation: PP reflects once off the free surface partway along a P path; PcP reflects off the core-mantle boundary and stays outside the core; PKIKP tunnels through the outer core (K), inner core (I), and outer core (K) again; pP is the depth phase whose upward-then-reflected leg lets seismologists estimate hypocenter depth from its time offset relative to P.

lessons.label: The Seismometer: Inertial Sensing, Response, and Noise

sections.heading: The mass-spring-damper as an inertial sensor
sections.body: A seismometer's core is a mass suspended by a spring inside a frame bolted to the ground, with a damper controlling how the mass responds to sudden motion. When the ground jerks, inertia makes the mass lag momentarily behind the frame, and that relative displacement — recorded optically, electromagnetically, or via force feedback — becomes the signal. This is a damped harmonic oscillator with a natural period T0 (how fast the mass would ring if displaced and released) and a damping ratio (how quickly ringing dies out, typically set near 0.7 of critical damping to flatten the response without excessive ringing or excessive sluggishness). Below its natural frequency the instrument is displacement-sensitive; above it, roughly velocity- or acceleration-sensitive — meaning every raw record is the true ground motion convolved with (multiplied through, in frequency terms) the instrument's own response, and recovering true ground motion requires deconvolving that instrument response back out.

sections.heading: From torsion pendulums to broadband force-balance sensors
sections.body: The Wood-Anderson torsion seismometer was built and described by Anderson and Wood in 1925; a decade later, Charles Richter calibrated his 1935 local-magnitude scale against the network of these instruments already operating in Southern California, so the instrument predates the scale rather than arriving with it. The Wood-Anderson used a small copper cylinder on a fine wire with T0 = 0.8 seconds and damping near 0.8 of critical, and a nominal static magnification of 2800 — a figure later shown by Uhrhammer and Collins (1990) to be closer to 2080 once the wire's actual mechanical behavior was properly measured, a correction still cited whenever historical Wood-Anderson magnitudes are recalibrated. Modern research seismometers replaced torsion mechanics with force-balance feedback: a sensor detects mass displacement and a servo loop drives current through a coil to null it, with the current itself becoming the output signal. The Streckeisen STS-2, a standard broadband instrument, is engineered flat in velocity response from 120 seconds period out to 50 Hz — a bandwidth wide enough to capture both slow, long-period surface waves and fast, high-frequency P onsets on the same channel. Strong-motion accelerometers use a separate, stiffer design tuned to stay on-scale (not clip) for the large accelerations recorded very close to a rupture, where a broadband velocity sensor would saturate.

sections.heading: Noise floors and the networks that host them
sections.body: Every site has an ambient noise floor from microseisms (ocean-wave-driven ground hum), wind, traffic, and thermal effects in the electronics. Peterson (1993) compiled global station data into the New High Noise Model and New Low Noise Model (NHNM and NLNM), power-spectral-density envelopes that define the realistic bounds within which any real station's noise should fall — a station significantly above the NHNM at some frequency signals a siting or instrument problem. Careful siting (bedrock vaults, boreholes, isolation from cultural noise) pushes stations toward the NLNM. These principles underlie global seismic networks: the Global Seismographic Network (GSN), the Federation of Digital Seismograph Networks (FDSN) that coordinates data exchange internationally, and the EarthScope Transportable Array that swept broadband stations across the contiguous United States.

lessons.workedExample: A Wood-Anderson instrument records a peak trace amplitude of 20 mm for a nearby small earthquake. Using the corrected static magnification of 2080 (Uhrhammer and Collins, 1990) rather than the nominal 2800, the true ground displacement is 20 mm / 2080 ~ 0.0096 mm, about 2.5 micrometers more than the 0.0071 mm one would infer using the old 2800 figure. That roughly 35% discrepancy in inferred ground motion — traced to the wire's real mechanical stiffness rather than the idealized behavior assumed when Anderson and Wood specified the instrument in 1925 — means historical Wood-Anderson ground-motion estimates that used the nominal 2800 figure were systematically too small, which is why modern re-analyses of historical Richter magnitudes apply the Uhrhammer-Collins correction rather than trusting the original nominal specification.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes seismometer design to see whether a student understands that a seismogram is never raw ground motion — it is ground motion filtered through a specific instrument response, and any comparison across instruments or eras requires accounting for that. The strong answer names the mass-spring-damper mechanism, states why frequency response has upper and lower bounds (STS-2's 120s-to-50Hz window is a deliberate engineering choice, not a law of nature), and can explain a concrete historical correction like the Wood-Anderson magnification revision rather than treating instrument specifications as immutable trivia.

questions.prompt: Why must a raw seismogram be deconvolved to recover true ground motion?

options.text: Because the recorded signal is the true ground motion convolved with the instrument's own frequency response
Because seismometers only record noise, never real signal
Because deconvolution removes earthquakes that are too small to matter
Because raw seismograms are always upside down

explanations.a: Correct — a seismometer is a damped oscillator whose own natural period and damping shape the output, so the recorded trace equals ground motion convolved with instrument response, and deconvolution reverses that shaping.
explanations.b: Seismometers record real ground motion combined with noise; they do not record only noise.
explanations.c: Deconvolution corrects for instrument response; it has nothing to do with filtering out small events.
explanations.d: Instrument polarity conventions exist but are not the reason deconvolution is needed; the core issue is the frequency-dependent response of the sensor.

questions.prompt: The Uhrhammer and Collins (1990) remeasurement of the Wood-Anderson seismometer found its true static magnification to be closer to which value, versus the long-used nominal figure of 2800?

options.text: 3500, higher than nominal
2080, lower than nominal
2800, exactly matching the nominal value
800, far lower than nominal

explanations.a: The correction lowered the figure, it did not raise it.
explanations.b: Correct — Uhrhammer and Collins (1990) found a static magnification near 2080, roughly 25-30% lower than the nominal 2800 Anderson and Wood had assumed, once the suspension wire's real mechanical behavior was measured.
explanations.c: The whole point of the remeasurement was that the long-used 2800 figure was inaccurate, not confirmed.
explanations.d: 800 overstates the correction; the remeasured value is 2080, not that much lower.

questions.prompt: Order these events in the history and design of seismic instrumentation, earliest to most recent.

items.text: Wood-Anderson torsion seismometer built with nominal magnification 2800
Richter defines the local-magnitude scale calibrated against Wood-Anderson records
Uhrhammer and Collins remeasure Wood-Anderson magnification as closer to 2080
Peterson compiles the NHNM and NLNM global noise models

questions.explanation: Anderson and Wood built and described the torsion seismometer in 1925, so the instrument itself dates to 1925. Richter's local-magnitude scale came a decade later, in 1935, calibrated against the Wood-Anderson instruments already in the field — the 1935 date belongs to the scale, not to the instrument. Uhrhammer and Collins published their magnification remeasurement in 1990, and Peterson's global noise-model compilation followed in 1993, giving the order 1925, 1935, 1990, 1993.

lessons.label: Reading a Seismogram

sections.heading: Three components, three jobs
sections.body: A modern station records three orthogonal channels: vertical (Z), north-south (N), and east-west (E). The P wave, being compressional, arrives first and shows up on all three components but often most crisply on Z, since near-vertical incidence pushes straight up-down. The S wave arrives second, typically largest on the horizontal N and E channels because shear motion transverse to a near-vertical ray path is mostly horizontal. Picking the P onset means finding the first clear break from background noise — a sudden, sharp deflection — not the first big wiggle; picking S means finding the second such onset, usually where horizontal amplitude jumps and the character of the wiggle changes. Particle motion confirms both picks: plotting horizontal-vs-vertical or the two horizontal components against each other over a short window should show P motion aligned along the source-to-station azimuth (radial) and S motion transverse to it, which is a genuine physical check, not a guess.

sections.heading: Amplitude, period, and the S-P rule of thumb
sections.body: Reading amplitude and period correctly means measuring peak-to-peak or zero-to-peak displacement in real units (using the instrument's calibration, never raw counts) and measuring period as the time between two like-phase zero crossings, not an eyeballed wiggle width. A simple and genuinely useful field rule: the S-P time interval (seconds between S and P arrival) times roughly 8 km/second gives a rough distance to the source, because P and S travel at different speeds and their separation grows linearly with distance for a given crustal velocity structure — a shortcut usable well before any formal location is computed.

sections.heading: Local, regional, teleseismic character, and telling signals apart
sections.body: A local earthquake (under about 100-150 km) shows a short S-P gap, high-frequency content, and rapid decay. A regional event (out to about 1000-2000 km) shows more separation, includes efficient regional phases like Pn and Sn refracted along the Moho, and a longer coda (the scattered wave train tapering after the main arrivals, whose duration itself correlates with magnitude in coda-magnitude methods). A teleseismic event (beyond about 2000-3000 km, arriving from another continent) shows a long, quiet gap between weak, sharp P and the far larger surface-wave train, with distinctly lower dominant frequency because high frequencies attenuate over global travel paths. Distinguishing a real earthquake from a quarry blast or explosion is aided by source depth (blasts are always at the surface, so no depth phase like pP separates from P) and by a weaker or absent S wave relative to P, since explosions radiate mostly compressional energy; a station glitch, by contrast, is recognizable as an instantaneous spike or step with no coherent moveout across nearby stations and no plausible travel-time relationship to any real source.

lessons.workedExample: A three-component station records a sharp vertical-channel onset at 14:22:05.0, a larger horizontal-channel onset at 14:22:11.8, and a broad, high-amplitude wave train peaking around 14:22:45. The S-P interval is 11.8 - 5.0 = 6.8 seconds; multiplying by roughly 8 km/s gives an estimated distance of about 54 km, consistent with a local event. Particle-motion analysis on the first 2 seconds after the P pick shows motion aligned along the back-azimuth to a known regional fault, confirming the P pick is genuine and not a glitch. The high-frequency content and rapid decay after the surface-wave peak (short coda, back to background within 20-30 seconds) further support a small local tectonic earthquake rather than a distant teleseism, which would show a much longer, lower-frequency wave train.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge tests seismogram-reading skill because it is the single most concrete, falsifiable skill in the unit: either the P and S picks are defensible from real waveform features and confirmed by particle motion, or they are not. The strong answer explains why particle motion is a genuine cross-check (radial alignment for P, transverse for S) rather than just naming it, and can apply the S-P rule of thumb correctly while also stating its limits — it is a rough estimate, not a substitute for a proper multi-station location. A student who can tell a quarry blast from a teleseism using specific waveform evidence (depth phase absence, S/P amplitude ratio, frequency content) shows they understand what the wiggles physically encode.

questions.prompt: A station records an S-P interval of 6.8 seconds. Using the roughly 8 km/s rule of thumb, what is the approximate distance to the source?

options.text: About 0.85 km
About 54 km
About 8 km
About 544 km

explanations.a: This divides instead of multiplying the S-P interval by the rule-of-thumb factor.
explanations.b: Correct — 6.8 seconds times roughly 8 km/second gives approximately 54 km, a plausible local-event distance.
explanations.c: This uses only the conversion factor itself, ignoring the measured S-P interval.
explanations.d: This is off by roughly a factor of 10 from the correct multiplication.

questions.prompt: Why is particle motion a genuine confirmation of a P-wave pick, rather than just a formality?

options.text: Because P-wave particle motion should align along the radial direction (source-to-station azimuth), a physically predicted signature that a glitch or noise spike would not reproduce
Because particle motion always points due north regardless of source location
Because particle motion analysis directly gives the earthquake's magnitude
Because particle motion is only meaningful for surface waves, not P waves

explanations.a: Correct — P waves are compressional, so genuine P motion should align with the direction back to the source; a spurious pick or instrument glitch has no reason to show this specific, physically predicted alignment.
explanations.b: Particle motion direction depends on the actual source-to-station azimuth, not a fixed compass direction.
explanations.c: Particle motion helps confirm phase identity and source direction; magnitude requires amplitude and distance calibration separately.
explanations.d: Particle motion analysis applies to P and S body waves as well as surface waves — it is a general tool for confirming wave type and direction.

questions.prompt: Match each seismogram character to the source-distance category it indicates.

left.text: Short S-P gap, high frequency, rapid decay
Pn/Sn refracted phases, moderate S-P gap, longer coda
Long quiet gap before a large, low-frequency surface-wave train
Weak or absent S wave, no depth phase separation from P

right.text: Local earthquake (under about 100-150 km)
Regional earthquake (out to about 1000-2000 km)
Teleseismic earthquake (beyond about 2000-3000 km)
Surface explosion or quarry blast, not a tectonic earthquake

questions.explanation: A short S-P gap with high-frequency, rapidly decaying signal indicates a local event; Pn/Sn moveout with a longer coda indicates a regional event; a long quiet gap before a dominant low-frequency surface-wave train indicates a teleseism; and a weak S relative to P with no depth-phase separation (because the source is at the surface) indicates an explosion rather than a tectonic earthquake.

lessons.label: Locating an Earthquake: Travel-Time Curves, Triangulation, and Wadati

sections.heading: Travel-time tables and the three-station circle method
sections.body: A travel-time table gives the expected arrival time of each phase as a function of source-station distance and depth, built from a reference Earth velocity model. Harold Jeffreys and Keith Bullen published the standard global tables in 1940 (JB40), refined by decades of instrumental data into IASP91, published by Brian Kennett and Eric Engdahl in 1991 — systematically faster than JB40 for teleseismic P, by roughly one to a few seconds depending on distance, reflecting improved velocity models. Given one station's S-P interval, the travel-time table converts that into a distance (not a direction), so the possible source lies anywhere on a circle centered at that station. A second station's circle intersects the first at two points; a third station's circle resolves the ambiguity to one location — which is why three stations, at minimum, are needed for basic triangulation, and why sparse networks with only one or two live stations cannot locate an event uniquely on their own.

sections.heading: Geiger's method: solving for x, y, z, and origin time together
sections.body: Real location is not done by literally drawing circles; it is solved as an inverse problem. Geiger's method (Geiger, 1910) starts from a trial hypocenter (x, y, z) and origin time t0, computes predicted arrival times at every station from the travel-time table, compares them to observed picks, and linearizes the residuals via a Taylor expansion to get a system of equations relating small location and time corrections to the observed misfits. Solving that system by least squares (typically via matrix inversion or an iterative Gauss-Newton scheme) yields an updated (x, y, z, t0); the process repeats until the residuals stop shrinking. All four unknowns are solved simultaneously because they are coupled — a wrong depth can be partly compensated by a wrong origin time while still fitting arrival times reasonably well at some stations, which is exactly why depth and origin time trade off against each other in poorly constrained solutions.

sections.heading: The Wadati diagram and azimuthal gap
sections.body: Kiyoo Wadati's 1933 diagram plots the S-P interval on the vertical axis against the P arrival time on the horizontal axis, using picks from several stations for one earthquake. Because both S-P and P-arrival time grow together with distance in a predictable way, the points fall on a line whose slope equals Vp/Vs - 1 (recoverable algebraically from the P and S travel-time relations) and whose horizontal-axis intercept, extrapolated back to where the S-P interval reaches zero, gives the earthquake's origin time directly — without needing a full location solution first. Beyond the math, station geometry matters enormously: the azimuthal gap is the largest angular gap, as seen from the hypocenter, between azimuths to any two adjacent recording stations. A large gap (stations clustered on one side of the event) leaves depth and the far-side location poorly constrained, since no station samples rays leaving in that empty direction — a standard reason agencies flag certain locations, especially offshore or borderland events, as having larger depth uncertainty.

lessons.workedExample: Four stations report P arrival times of 10.0 s, 10.0 s, 15.0 s, and 22.0 s (relative to some reference), with corresponding S-P intervals of 4.0 s, 6.0 s, 9.0 s, and 13.0 s. Plotting S-P against P arrival time on a Wadati diagram, the best-fit line has a slope of about 0.672 and extrapolates back to an origin time near t = 2.34 s (where S-P would reach 0), giving both Vp/Vs = 1 + slope ~ 1.67 and the earthquake's origin time without yet knowing station distances or a hypocenter. A subsequent Geiger's-method inversion using these same four stations, but with them clustered within a 90-degree azimuthal wedge, converges to a location with well-constrained horizontal position but a poorly resolved depth, precisely because the 270-degree azimuthal gap on the empty side leaves no ray coverage to pin down how deep the source sits.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about earthquake location to check whether a student understands that location is an inverse problem with real failure modes, not a lookup. The strong answer explains why three stations are the geometric minimum for triangulation, why Geiger's method solves for depth and origin time jointly rather than separately (and why that coupling causes trade-offs), and can read a Wadati diagram's slope and intercept as Vp/Vs and origin time respectively rather than treating it as an arbitrary plot. Naming the azimuthal gap and explaining concretely why a lopsided network degrades depth resolution — not just 'more stations are better' — is the mark of someone who has actually located an event, not read about it.

questions.prompt: On a Wadati diagram, what does the horizontal-axis intercept (where S-P extrapolates to zero) represent?

options.text: The earthquake's magnitude
The earthquake's origin time
The station's azimuthal gap
The depth of the earthquake

explanations.a: Magnitude is derived from amplitude and distance calibration, not from the Wadati diagram's intercept.
explanations.b: Correct — extrapolating the S-P vs. P-arrival-time line back to where S-P equals zero gives the origin time, since at the source itself P and S have not yet separated.
explanations.c: Azimuthal gap is a network-geometry property unrelated to the Wadati diagram's axes.
explanations.d: Depth is not directly read from a Wadati diagram; it typically requires a full Geiger-style location inversion.

questions.prompt: Why does Geiger's method solve for hypocenter location (x, y, z) and origin time (t0) simultaneously rather than one at a time?

options.text: Because solving them separately is computationally faster
Because the four unknowns are coupled — errors in depth and origin time can partially cancel in the arrival-time residuals, so they must be fit jointly to converge on a consistent solution
Because origin time has no effect on predicted arrival times
Because only depth needs to be solved; x, y, and t0 are always known in advance

explanations.a: Joint solution is not chosen for speed; it is required by the physics of how the unknowns interact in the residuals.
explanations.b: Correct — a trade-off exists where a deeper source paired with an earlier origin time can produce similar predicted arrival times to a shallower source with a later origin time, so all four unknowns must be solved together via least squares to avoid a biased fit.
explanations.c: Origin time directly shifts every predicted arrival time and is central to computing residuals.
explanations.d: None of x, y, or t0 are known in advance; all four unknowns are solved for from the station data.

questions.prompt: Order these historical developments in earthquake travel-time modeling and location, earliest to most recent.

items.text: Geiger publishes the iterative least-squares hypocenter location method
Wadati introduces the S-P vs. P-arrival-time diagram
Jeffreys and Bullen publish the JB40 global travel-time tables
Kennett and Engdahl publish the IASP91 travel-time model

questions.explanation: Geiger's method was published in 1910, Wadati's diagram in 1933, the Jeffreys-Bullen tables in 1940, and the IASP91 model by Kennett and Engdahl in 1991 as a modern update superseding JB40.

lessons.label: Sizing an Earthquake: Magnitude Scales and Intensity

sections.heading: Richter's local magnitude and its baggage
sections.body: Charles Richter defined local magnitude in 1935 as ML = log10(A) - log10(A0), where A is the peak trace amplitude in millimeters on a standard Wood-Anderson torsion seismometer and log10(A0) is an empirical correction table accounting for how amplitude decays with distance, calibrated for Southern California events recorded at 100 km. Every piece of that definition carries historical baggage: it presumes a specific instrument (Wood-Anderson, T0 = 0.8 s), a specific region's attenuation behavior, and a reference distance, so ML computed elsewhere requires re-deriving the A0 correction table for local geology. Body-wave magnitude (mb) uses short-period P-wave amplitude and works globally at teleseismic distances, while surface-wave magnitude (Ms) uses roughly 20-second-period surface waves. Both saturate at large size: for very large ruptures, the specific wave periods each scale measures stop growing in amplitude even as the fault keeps growing, so mb saturates around magnitude 6-6.5 and Ms around 8-8.5 — the scales run out of dynamic range before the earthquake does.

sections.heading: Seismic moment and moment magnitude
sections.body: Seismic moment sidesteps saturation entirely by measuring the physical cause of the earthquake rather than a filtered wave amplitude: M0 = mu * A * D, where mu is the shear modulus of the rock, A is the ruptured fault area, and D is the average slip (displacement) across that area. Because M0 scales directly with how much rock moved and how far, it keeps growing without limit as ruptures get bigger. Hanks and Kanamori (1979) converted moment into a magnitude-like number with Mw = (2/3) * log10(M0) - 10.7, with M0 in dyne-cm, deliberately built so Mw matches ML and Ms in the unsaturated mid-range while remaining accurate for the largest earthquakes ever recorded. Because each whole magnitude unit represents a 10^1.5 jump in radiated energy — about 31.6 times more energy per unit, since energy scales as M0^1 while the magnitude formula uses log M0 with a 2/3 exponent — a magnitude 9 earthquake releases roughly 31.6^2 ~ 1000 times the energy of a magnitude 7.

sections.heading: The separate axis: shaking intensity
sections.body: Magnitude describes the earthquake's total size at its source; intensity describes what a specific location experienced, and the two are related but distinct measurements — the same magnitude 7 event produces very different shaking at 10 km versus 300 km. The Modified Mercalli Intensity (MMI) scale ranks felt and observed effects (I, not felt, through XII, total destruction) from eyewitness reports and damage surveys, without instruments. Instrumental measures — peak ground acceleration (PGA) and peak ground velocity (PGV) — quantify shaking directly from accelerometer records and correlate empirically with MMI and with damage potential. The USGS ShakeMap system combines instrumental recordings with ground-motion prediction equations to produce near-real-time shaking maps across a whole region within minutes of an event, while the crowdsourced Did You Feel It (DYFI) system collects felt reports from residents to fill in intensity where instruments are sparse — together giving both a rapid instrumental picture and a dense, citizen-reported one.

lessons.workedExample: The 2011 Tohoku, Japan earthquake had an estimated seismic moment M0 ~ 3.9 x 10^22 N*m (published estimates span roughly 3.9 to 5.3 x 10^22 N*m depending on the inversion and data used, which is why Tohoku is quoted as both Mw 9.0 and Mw 9.1), equal to 3.9 x 10^29 dyne-cm (1 N*m = 10^7 dyne-cm). Applying Mw = (2/3) * log10(M0) - 10.7 with M0 in dyne-cm: log10(3.9 x 10^29) ~ 29.59, so Mw = (2/3)(29.59) - 10.7 ~ 19.73 - 10.7 ~ 9.0, matching the widely reported Mw 9.0-9.1. Because each unit is a 31.6x jump in energy, this event released roughly 31.6 times the energy of a hypothetical Mw 8.0 rupture nearby, and its Ms would have saturated well below its true size — a clear illustration of why moment magnitude, not Ms or mb, is the standard for characterizing the largest earthquakes.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes magnitude scales because 'how big was the earthquake' has more than one correct answer depending on which scale is used, and a fair project should say which one and why. The strong answer explains WHY mb and Ms saturate (a physical wave-period limitation, not a measurement error) and can walk through converting a stated seismic moment into Mw using the Hanks-Kanamori (1979) formula rather than quoting a magnitude from memory. Distinguishing magnitude (source size) from intensity (local shaking, via MMI, PGA/PGV, ShakeMap, or DYFI) shows the student understands that 'how big' and 'how bad here' are answered by entirely different instruments and scales.

questions.prompt: Why do mb and Ms magnitude scales saturate for very large earthquakes, while moment magnitude (Mw) does not?

options.text: mb and Ms measure wave amplitude at fixed periods that stop growing once the rupture exceeds a certain size, while Mw is derived from seismic moment (M0 = mu * A * D), which keeps scaling with fault area and slip
mb and Ms are only usable for earthquakes below magnitude 3
Mw does not saturate because it ignores fault rupture size entirely
mb and Ms saturate because seismometers physically break during large earthquakes

explanations.a: Correct — mb and Ms rely on wave amplitude at specific periods that stop increasing once the rupture's characteristic dimensions exceed those periods' sensitivity, while Mw is built directly from the physical rupture parameters in M0, which have no such ceiling.
explanations.b: mb and Ms are used across a wide range including large earthquakes; their limitation is a ceiling at the high end, not restriction to small events.
explanations.c: Mw is explicitly derived from fault area and slip via seismic moment, not by ignoring rupture size.
explanations.d: Saturation is a property of the amplitude-period relationship in the scale's definition, not instrument damage.

questions.prompt: Approximately how many times more energy does a magnitude 9 earthquake release compared to a magnitude 7 earthquake?

options.text: About 2 times
About 63 times
About 1000 times
About 100,000 times

explanations.a: This drastically understates the energy scaling, which is logarithmic and steep between magnitude units.
explanations.b: 63 times is roughly two units' worth counted as a single 31.6x step rather than compounding across the two-unit gap.
explanations.c: Correct — each whole magnitude unit is about a 31.6x energy increase, so two units apart is 31.6 x 31.6 ~ 1000 times the energy.
explanations.d: This overstates the scaling; 100,000x would correspond to roughly three magnitude units, not two.

questions.prompt: Match each earthquake-sizing concept to what it actually measures.

right.text: Peak Wood-Anderson trace amplitude at a reference distance
Seismic moment M0 = mu * A * D via the Hanks-Kanamori (1979) formula
Felt effects and observed damage at a specific location, ranked I to XII
Near-real-time regional shaking map from instrumental recordings and ground-motion prediction

questions.explanation: ML is defined directly from Wood-Anderson peak trace amplitude at a calibrated reference distance; Mw is derived from the physical seismic moment M0 = mu * A * D via the Hanks-Kanamori (1979) conversion; Modified Mercalli Intensity ranks felt effects and damage observations at a location on a I-to-XII scale; and ShakeMap combines instrumental data with ground-motion prediction equations to generate a near-real-time regional shaking map.

units.label: Field and Lab Methods, and Interpretation

lessons.label: Sampling Design: Getting Data That Can Support a Claim

sections.heading: Match the sampling pattern to the question
sections.body: A rock outcrop is not a sample; it is where you are allowed to collect one. The pattern you walk decides what claim your data can later support. Targeted (judgmental) sampling — picking the freshest, most representative-looking exposure of each unit — is right for building a stratigraphic column or answering "what units are present." It is wrong for quantifying variability, because a geologist's eye is drawn to the cleanest rock, which biases the sample toward whatever looks least weathered. A transect (a line of stations at fixed spacing, e.g. every 2 m up a section) is the standard for measuring how a property changes with position — grain size fining upward, clast counts across a fault zone. A grid imposes a regular 2D spacing over an area, useful for contour-mapping a property like soil pH or magnetic anomaly. Stratified random sampling divides the area into zones (by unit, slope, or facies) first, then samples randomly within each zone — this is the only pattern that supports a statistical claim like a mean or a confidence interval, because random placement is what lets you invoke the sampling theory behind a standard error.

sections.heading: How much is enough, and what heterogeneity does to it
sections.body: Required sample count rises with how variable the material is and falls as your tolerance for error grows, roughly n proportional to variance over the square of the allowed margin — a formalization of the intuition that a heterogeneous unit (rounded gravel with cobbles to sand) needs many more measurements to characterize than a homogeneous one (a massive shale bed). Geologic practice for grain-size and clast counts commonly targets 100 counted clasts or grains per station as a floor, following long-standing pebble-count conventions (Wolman, 1954), because below that the count is dominated by which handful you happened to grab rather than the deposit.

sections.heading: Field discipline: chain of custody and honest location
sections.body: A sample is only as good as its provenance record: a unique label written on the bag AND on the rock with a paint marker, a field-notebook entry logging unit, station, and collector before the sample leaves your hand, and a photograph including a scale bar (a card, coin, or Jacob's staff) and a compass direction so orientation is recoverable later. Consumer GPS/GNSS is accurate to roughly 3-5 m; real-time kinematic (RTK) GPS, using a fixed base station broadcasting corrections, resolves to centimeters and is required when station spacing is itself only a few meters. Collecting on public or private land requires permission or a permit — many U.S. national parks and monuments prohibit collecting entirely — and contamination is avoided by cleaning tools between samples and bagging separately, since one stray fragment can invalidate an entire provenance claim.

lessons.workedExample: A team wants to test whether clast roundness increases downstream in a gravel-bed river, a question about a trend with distance. They lay a transect of nine stations at 200 m spacing along 1.6 km of channel, and at each station count and measure roundness on 100 clasts picked by a blind grid-intercept method (not by eye) following Wolman (1954) conventions, logging station GPS (consumer-grade, +/-4 m, adequate at this spacing), a photo with a coin for scale, and a unique station-clast ID on every bag. A targeted "grab the best-looking clasts" approach would have biased the sample toward whichever rocks looked roundest, destroying the very trend being tested.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks "how did you decide where and how many to sample?" because the answer reveals whether the data can bear the statistical weight of the claim in the abstract. A student who says "I picked good-looking rocks" has judgmental sampling, which cannot support a quantitative trend or a confidence interval. A student who names the pattern (transect, grid, or stratified random), states the station spacing and count-per-station, and can justify both against the specific question being asked has shown the sampling design was chosen on purpose, not by convenience — the single biggest predictor of whether a project's conclusion is actually supported by its data.

questions.prompt: A student wants to compute a mean grain size with a defensible confidence interval for a sand unit. Which sampling pattern should they use?

options.text: Targeted sampling of the freshest-looking exposure
Stratified random sampling within the unit
Whatever clasts are easiest to reach
A single sample from the thickest part of the bed

explanations.a: Targeted sampling is biased toward whatever looks cleanest or most typical to the collector's eye, which distorts a variability estimate.
explanations.b: Correct — stratified random sampling places samples randomly within a defined zone, which is what justifies applying standard statistical formulas (mean, standard error, confidence interval) to the result.
explanations.c: Convenience sampling introduces uncontrolled bias (e.g., toward accessible, less weathered material) and cannot support a statistical claim.
explanations.d: One sample gives no estimate of variability at all, so no confidence interval can be computed.

questions.prompt: Why does required sample size increase for a heterogeneous deposit (mixed gravel and cobbles) compared to a homogeneous one (massive shale)?

options.text: Heterogeneous deposits are always larger in area
Required n scales with the variance of the property being measured
GPS accuracy is worse on heterogeneous deposits
Heterogeneous deposits require fewer samples because they are more interesting

explanations.a: Deposit area is unrelated to how many samples are needed to characterize a property's variability.
explanations.b: Correct — the sample size needed to pin down a mean to a given precision rises with the underlying variance; a mixed gravel/cobble unit has far more grain-size variance than a massive shale, so it needs many more measurements to characterize.
explanations.c: GPS accuracy depends on satellite geometry and receiver type, not deposit texture.
explanations.d: Sample size requirements are about statistical precision, not interest level.

questions.prompt: Match each field-discipline practice to what it protects against.

left.text: RTK GPS instead of consumer GPS
Photo with scale bar and compass direction

right.text: Sample mix-up / lost provenance
Position error too large relative to station spacing
Inability to recover scale and orientation later
Cross-contamination between samples

questions.explanation: Labeling prevents provenance mix-ups; RTK GPS (centimeter-level) is needed when consumer GPS's 3-5 m error would swamp close station spacing; a scaled, oriented photo lets later analysis recover size and direction; cleaning tools prevents one sample's material contaminating the next.

lessons.label: Measuring Orientation: Strike, Dip, and the Field Notebook

sections.heading: Strike, dip, and two ways to write them down
