Applying Mw = (2/3) log10(M0) - 6.03: log10(9 x 10^19) is approximately 19.95, so Mw = (2/3)(19.95) - 6.03 = 13.3 - 6.03, giving Mw approximately 7.3. This is a realistic magnitude for a rupture of this size — comparable to the 1992 Landers, California earthquake — and shows how a few field-measurable quantities (rupture length, width, and average offset) translate directly into the moment magnitude reported on a catalog.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking a student to justify a reported magnitude wants to see M0 = mu x A x D used as a derivation, not just quoted from a catalog. The strong answer plugs in the rigidity, ruptured area, and slip actually estimated for the event, shows the log10 conversion to Mw, and can explain in one sentence why moment-based magnitude does not saturate the way amplitude-based scales do for great earthquakes. Naming the double-couple representation, or recognizing when a non-double-couple component (isotropic or CLVD) signals an explosion or a volcanic source rather than tectonic slip, shows the student understands what the moment tensor is actually encoding.

questions.prompt: A rupture has A = 1.5 x 10^9 m^2, D = 2 m, and mu = 3 x 10^10 Pa. What is M0?

explanations.b: This drops nine orders of magnitude; multiplying three quantities each around 10^9-10^10 in size cannot land at 10^9 overall.
explanations.c: This is exactly half the correct product, as if slip D = 2 m were entered as D = 1 m instead.
explanations.d: This overshoots by a factor of 10, likely from mis-multiplying the exponents (10^10 x 10^9 x 10^0 should combine to 10^19, not 10^20).

questions.prompt: Using Mw = (2/3) log10(M0) - 6.03 with M0 = 9 x 10^19 N*m, what moment magnitude results?

options.text: Mw approximately 7.3
Mw approximately 9.0
Mw approximately 5.0
Mw approximately 19.95

explanations.a: Correct — log10(9 x 10^19) is about 19.95; (2/3)(19.95) - 6.03 is about 13.3 - 6.03, giving Mw approximately 7.3.
explanations.b: Mw 9.0 corresponds to a moment roughly four orders of magnitude larger than 9 x 10^19 N*m, the size of a great subduction earthquake, not this rupture.
explanations.c: Mw 5.0 corresponds to a moment thousands of times smaller than 9 x 10^19 N*m; this rupture's area and slip are far too large for that magnitude.
explanations.d: 19.95 is log10(M0) itself, an intermediate step, not the final magnitude after applying the (2/3) scaling and the -6.03 offset.

questions.prompt: Match each moment-tensor source signature to the physical process it indicates.

left.text: Pure double couple (zero trace, zero isotropic part)

right.text: Shear slip on a single planar fault
Volume change, e.g. an underground nuclear explosion
Tensile cracking or magma/fluid movement in volcanic or geothermal settings

questions.explanation: A pure double couple is what shear slip on a planar fault produces; an isotropic component signals volume change such as an explosion, which is why it is used to discriminate explosions from earthquakes in test-ban monitoring; a CLVD component appears in volcanic and geothermal source inversions where tensile opening or fluid movement accompanies the faulting.

lessons.label: Focal Mechanisms: Reading a Beach Ball

sections.heading: Building the beach ball from first motions
sections.body: The first thing a seismic wave does at a distant station is push the ground either away from the source (compression, recorded as an initial upward P-wave motion) or pull it toward the source (dilatation, initial downward motion). Plotting each station's first-motion polarity at the point where its ray path leaves the source, projected onto a lower-hemisphere stereographic net (the same projection used for structural geology), sorts stations into four quadrants: two compressional and two dilatational, arranged like the shaded and unshaded panels of a beach ball. The boundary between quadrants traces two perpendicular great circles, called nodal planes, along which theoretical first-motion amplitude is zero — stations exactly on a nodal plane show no clear polarity at all, which is why dense station coverage matters for a clean solution.

sections.heading: Two planes, one ambiguity
sections.body: Here is the catch: the double-couple radiation pattern is perfectly symmetric between its two nodal planes, so the beach ball alone cannot tell you which plane is the actual fault and which is the geometrically required but physically fictitious auxiliary plane. This is the fundamental fault-plane ambiguity, and it is not solved by better data on the beach ball itself — every double-couple solution has exactly this problem. Seismologists resolve it with independent evidence: aftershocks, which cluster along and illuminate the true rupture surface far more clearly than the auxiliary plane; mapped surface rupture, where a trace of fresh offset on the ground settles the question directly; or prior geological knowledge of which plane corresponds to a known, mapped fault in the area.

sections.heading: P and T axes, and reading a Global CMT solution
sections.body: Beyond the two nodal planes, a focal mechanism defines a P axis (the direction of maximum compressive stress inferred from the mechanism, bisecting the two dilatational quadrants) and a T axis (maximum tensile/extensional direction, bisecting the two compressional quadrants), both plotted on the same diagram. The Global CMT (Centroid Moment Tensor) project publishes, for every earthquake above about M5, the strike/dip/rake of both nodal planes, the scalar moment, and the P/T/null axes, derived from waveform modeling rather than first motions alone. Reading one means checking the dip of each candidate plane (steep and near-vertical suggests strike-slip; shallow suggests thrust) and the rake (near 0/180 for strike-slip, near +90 for normal, near -90 for reverse), then naming the faulting style once independent evidence picks the real plane.

lessons.workedExample: A Global CMT solution lists nodal plane 1 as strike 10, dip 85, rake 175, and nodal plane 2 as strike 280, dip 85, rake 5. Both planes are nearly vertical with rakes near 0/180, so the mechanism is strike-slip regardless of which plane is real — that part of the ambiguity does not affect the faulting style here. To find which plane is the true fault, a seismologist plots the following week's aftershocks and finds they align in a tight, roughly east-west band along strike 280, matching nodal plane 2 (rake 5, meaning left-lateral motion) rather than the north-south trend of plane 1. The aftershock geometry — not the beach ball alone — resolves the ambiguity and identifies the true rupture as an east-west-striking, left-lateral strike-slip fault.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'which of the two nodal planes is the real fault?' is testing whether a student understands that the fault-plane ambiguity is mathematically built into every double-couple solution, not a data-quality problem to be fixed with more stations. The strong answer names at least one independent line of evidence — aftershock alignment, mapped surface rupture, or known regional fault geology — that breaks the symmetry, rather than claiming the beach ball itself picks the answer. This distinguishes a student who has actually worked with focal mechanisms from one who has only memorized what a beach ball looks like.

questions.prompt: Why can't a focal mechanism's beach ball diagram, by itself, tell you which of its two nodal planes is the true fault?

options.text: Because the double-couple radiation pattern is symmetric between the two planes, so both fit the recorded first motions equally well
Because seismic stations never record enough first-motion data to constrain either plane
Because the P and T axes are always misplotted on modern beach ball diagrams
Because nodal planes only exist for reverse faults, not for strike-slip or normal faults

explanations.a: Correct — a double couple produces radiation symmetric between its two nodal planes, so both the true fault plane and the auxiliary plane fit the observed first motions equally well; only outside evidence breaks the tie.
explanations.b: With enough well-distributed stations the first motions can constrain both nodal planes precisely; the ambiguity persists even with excellent data because it is inherent to the double-couple model, not a data-quantity issue.
explanations.c: P and T axes are computed correctly from the mechanism itself; they do not resolve which nodal plane is the true fault, but that is a separate issue from being 'misplotted.'
explanations.d: Every double-couple focal mechanism, regardless of faulting style, has exactly two nodal planes and the same ambiguity; it is not specific to reverse faults.

questions.prompt: In the worked example, what independent evidence identified nodal plane 2 (strike 280) as the true fault rather than nodal plane 1 (strike 10)?

options.text: The aftershocks aligned along strike 280, matching nodal plane 2
Nodal plane 2 had a steeper dip than nodal plane 1
The P axis pointed directly along nodal plane 2
The scalar moment was larger for nodal plane 2

explanations.a: Correct — the aftershock locations clustered along an east-west trend matching strike 280, the classic form of independent evidence used to resolve the fault-plane ambiguity.
explanations.b: Both planes had the same dip (85 degrees) in this example, so dip could not distinguish between them.
explanations.c: The P axis describes inferred stress direction, common to both candidate planes; it does not by itself identify which plane slipped.
explanations.d: Scalar moment is a single value describing the whole earthquake's size, not something that differs between the two candidate nodal planes of one mechanism.

questions.prompt: Match each focal-mechanism feature to what it represents.

right.text: A great circle on the beach ball where theoretical first-motion amplitude is zero
Inferred direction of maximum compressive stress, bisecting the dilatational quadrants
Inferred direction of maximum tensile/extensional stress, bisecting the compressional quadrants
A published waveform-derived moment tensor giving both nodal planes, moment, and P/T axes for a cataloged earthquake

questions.explanation: Nodal planes are the zero-amplitude boundaries between the beach ball's quadrants; the P axis bisects the dilatational quadrants as the inferred compression direction; the T axis bisects the compressional quadrants as the inferred tension direction; and a Global CMT solution is the published, waveform-derived record of all of these quantities for a given earthquake.

lessons.label: Stress Drop, Rupture Area, and Self-Similar Scaling

sections.heading: Stress drop: a stubbornly constant number
sections.body: Stress drop is the difference between the shear stress acting on a fault just before it slips and just after, the portion of stored strain actually released by that rupture. James Brune's 1970 model treated a rupture as an instantaneously stopping circular crack and related the stress drop directly to seismic moment and source radius, giving seismologists a way to estimate it from a recorded waveform's corner frequency. The striking empirical result, confirmed across roughly ten orders of magnitude of seismic moment from small M2 events to great M9 subduction earthquakes, is that stress drop stays in a narrow band of about 1 to 10 MPa regardless of earthquake size. A fault does not fail at a size-dependent stress threshold; it fails at roughly the same few megapascals of accumulated stress whether the rupture ends up 1 km or 1000 km long.

sections.heading: Self-similarity: why constant stress drop forces D to scale with L
sections.body: If stress drop is approximately constant regardless of size, then average slip D must scale up in proportion to rupture length L (Delta-sigma is proportional to mu x D / L, so holding Delta-sigma fixed means D/L stays fixed too). Because seismic moment is M0 = mu x A x D, and area A scales as L^2 for a roughly self-similar rupture shape, moment ends up scaling as M0 proportional to L^3. Since Mw is built from log10(M0), each unit increase in Mw corresponds to roughly a 32-fold increase in moment (10^1.5), which in turn requires rupture length to grow by roughly the cube root of 32, about 3-fold, for every unit of magnitude. This single scaling relationship is why earthquake source dimensions span such an enormous range — three magnitude units apart implies roughly 30-fold longer ruptures.

sections.heading: Wells and Coppersmith: putting numbers on the relationship
sections.body: Wells and Coppersmith's widely used 1994 compilation of worldwide historical earthquakes turned this scaling into practical regressions relating moment magnitude to surface rupture length, subsurface rupture length, rupture width, rupture area, and average and maximum displacement, fit separately for strike-slip, normal, and reverse-faulting earthquakes because the relationships differ somewhat by faulting style. Real earthquakes bear this out: a strike-slip event around M6 typically ruptures only about 10-15 km of fault, while the largest subduction earthquakes on record — the 2004 Sumatra-Andaman M9.1 and 2011 Tohoku M9.0 — ruptured roughly 1300 km and 500 km of fault respectively, requiring correspondingly enormous plate boundary segments to host them.

lessons.workedExample: Compare an M6.0 strike-slip earthquake to an M9.0 subduction earthquake using self-similar scaling. Three magnitude units separate them, and moment scales as M0 proportional to L^3, so a 3-unit magnitude gap gives a moment ratio of 10^(1.5x3) = 10^4.5, and a linear rupture-dimension ratio of (10^4.5)^(1/3) = 10^1.5, or roughly 32-fold longer rupture. If the M6.0 event ruptures about 12 km of fault, the M9.0 event should require on the order of 12 x 32, or roughly 380 km of fault length just from this simple scaling law. Real M9 ruptures run somewhat longer than this simple estimate — Tohoku's roughly 500 km and Sumatra 2004's roughly 1300 km — because real fault segments, aspect-ratio limits on rupture width, and multi-segment cascading aren't captured by the L^3 scaling alone.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking 'why does a bigger earthquake need a bigger fault?' wants to see the mechanism, not just a memorized fact. The strong answer starts from the empirical constancy of stress drop across magnitude, shows how that constancy forces slip to scale with rupture length, and derives from there why moment scales as length cubed — landing on the real conclusion that each added magnitude unit demands a roughly three-fold longer rupture. A student who can only say 'bigger earthquakes have bigger faults' without the stress-drop mechanism underneath has not engaged with the actual physics being tested.

questions.prompt: Brune's circular-crack model and subsequent observations show that typical earthquake stress drop:

options.text: Stays roughly constant, around 1-10 MPa, across about ten orders of magnitude of seismic moment
Increases linearly with rupture length, from under 1 MPa for small events to over 1000 MPa for M9 events
Is essentially random and shows no relationship to any other source parameter
Only applies to strike-slip earthquakes and has no defined value for reverse or normal faults

explanations.a: Correct — stress drop holds in a narrow band of roughly 1-10 MPa across roughly ten orders of magnitude of seismic moment, from small to great earthquakes, which is the empirical basis for self-similar scaling.
explanations.b: Stress drop does not scale up with rupture size; if it did, self-similar scaling (moment proportional to length cubed) would not hold, and it demonstrably does across a huge magnitude range.
explanations.c: Stress drop is tightly constrained to a narrow range rather than random; this constancy is exactly what makes the self-similar scaling laws work.
explanations.d: Stress drop is estimated for all faulting styles from corner-frequency analysis of recorded waveforms; it is not restricted to strike-slip earthquakes.

questions.prompt: If stress drop stays roughly constant as rupture length L increases, why does seismic moment M0 scale as roughly L^3 rather than just L^2 (area alone)?

options.text: Because holding stress drop fixed forces average slip D to also scale with L, and M0 = mu x A x D adds that extra factor of L on top of area's L^2
Because rigidity mu increases with rupture length in most crustal rock
Because rupture width stops scaling with length past a certain magnitude
Because M0 is defined independently of both area and slip for large earthquakes

explanations.a: Correct — since Delta-sigma is proportional to mu x D/L, a constant stress drop requires D to grow in proportion to L; combined with area A proportional to L^2, M0 = mu x A x D then scales as L^3.
explanations.b: Rigidity mu is a material property of the host rock and is treated as roughly constant for a given crustal setting, not something that grows with rupture length.
explanations.c: Width does saturate at the seismogenic thickness for very long ruptures, which is a real complication, but the core L^3 scaling in the worked reasoning comes from slip tracking length, not from width behavior.
explanations.d: M0 = mu x A x D by definition, directly built from area and slip; it is never defined independently of them.

questions.prompt: Order these earthquakes from shortest to longest rupture length, based on the figures given in this lesson.

items.text: M6.0 strike-slip earthquake (~10-15 km rupture)
2011 Tohoku M9.0 (~500 km rupture)
2004 Sumatra-Andaman M9.1 (~1300 km rupture)

questions.explanation: The M6.0 strike-slip event ruptures only about 10-15 km of fault, Tohoku's M9.0 subduction rupture extended roughly 500 km, and the cascading, multi-segment 2004 Sumatra-Andaman M9.1 rupture reached roughly 1300 km, the longest of the three.

lessons.label: Nucleation, Rupture Velocity, and Supershear

sections.heading: Starting small: nucleation
sections.body: Every earthquake begins in a patch far smaller than the eventual rupture, typically tens to a few hundred meters across, where accumulated stress first exceeds the local frictional strength of the fault. In that nucleation zone, slip starts slowly and stably rather than instantly at full rupture speed; laboratory friction experiments and dynamic rupture models both show a brief, quasi-static phase during which slip accelerates before the rupture reaches the fast, self-sustaining propagation that radiates the strong seismic waves we record. What determines whether a nucleating patch stalls out as a small event or cascades into a large rupture is an active research question, tied to local stress heterogeneity and fault-surface properties rather than anything visible from outside — which is a core reason large-earthquake prediction remains unsolved even where nucleation zones can be located after the fact.

sections.heading: The rupture front as a propagating crack tip
sections.body: Once nucleation succeeds, the rupture front behaves like the tip of a rapidly propagating shear crack, advancing outward from the nucleation point at a speed set by the fault's frictional and elastic properties. For an ordinary, sub-shear rupture this speed is typically about 0.7 to 0.9 times the local shear-wave velocity (Vs), commonly around 2.5-3.1 km/s in continental crust where Vs is roughly 3.5 km/s. A rupture that expands outward from nucleation in both directions along the fault is bilateral; one that propagates predominantly one way, because nucleation sat near one end of the eventual rupture or because of some barrier on the other side, is unilateral. Both patterns are common and are read directly from where and how fast slip appears at different points along the fault in kinematic rupture models.

sections.heading: Supershear: crossing the shear-wave speed limit
sections.body: Under the right conditions — strong prestress, a favorably oriented and smooth fault segment, and often after an initial sub-shear phase — a rupture front can accelerate past the shear-wave speed entirely, becoming supershear, with propagation velocities approaching or exceeding the P-wave speed. This was long predicted theoretically (the Burridge-Andrews mechanism describes a secondary rupture front outrunning the main one) before being confirmed observationally. Documented supershear earthquakes include the 1999 Mw7.4 Izmit earthquake in Turkey (mean rupture velocity of roughly 4.8 km/s along parts of the North Anatolian Fault), the 2002 Mw7.9 Denali earthquake in Alaska, and the 2018 Mw7.5 Palu earthquake in Indonesia, which sustained a supershear speed of roughly 4.1 km/s from very early in the rupture despite propagating around sharp bends in the fault.

lessons.workedExample: Compare two ruptures on faults with the same shear-wave velocity, Vs = 3.5 km/s. An ordinary sub-shear rupture propagating at 0.85 x Vs travels at about 3.0 km/s. The 1999 Izmit rupture, by contrast, is documented at a mean velocity of about 4.8 km/s along the North Anatolian Fault — roughly 1.37 times Vs, well into supershear territory and approaching typical crustal P-wave speeds of around 6 km/s. The physical distinction matters: a sub-shear crack tip stays subsonic relative to the shear waves it generates, while a supershear rupture outruns its own shear wavefront, a fundamentally different propagation regime first predicted theoretically through the Burridge-Andrews mechanism before Izmit and later events like Denali (2002) and Palu (2018) confirmed it seismologically.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking 'how fast does a rupture actually travel, and can it ever exceed the shear-wave speed?' is testing whether a student distinguishes rupture propagation (a crack tip moving through already-stressed rock) from wave propagation (the seismic energy radiating outward), two related but distinct speeds that are easy to conflate. The strong answer gives the typical sub-shear range (0.7-0.9 Vs) as the default, then names supershear as the documented exception with at least one real, dated event — Izmit 1999, Denali 2002, or Palu 2018 — rather than treating supershear as a hypothetical curiosity.

questions.prompt: For an ordinary (sub-shear) earthquake rupture, propagation velocity typically falls in what range relative to the local shear-wave velocity (Vs)?

options.text: About 0.7 to 0.9 times Vs
About 2 to 3 times Vs
Exactly equal to Vs, always
About 0.01 to 0.05 times Vs

explanations.a: Correct — an ordinary sub-shear rupture front propagates at roughly 0.7 to 0.9 times the local shear-wave velocity, staying below Vs.
explanations.b: Speeds several times Vs would exceed even documented supershear ruptures like Izmit's roughly 1.37xVs; this range is unrealistically fast.
explanations.c: Rupture velocity approaches but characteristically stays below Vs for sub-shear ruptures; treating it as always exactly equal to Vs ignores the physical distinction between rupture speed and wave speed.
explanations.d: This range is far too slow for propagating rupture; it is closer to nucleation-phase slip acceleration than to the sustained crack-tip propagation speed of an ongoing rupture.

questions.prompt: Match each documented supershear earthquake to its approximate rupture velocity or key detail from this lesson.

right.text: Mean rupture velocity of about 4.8 km/s on the North Anatolian Fault
Inferred as a supershear event on the Denali Fault system
Sustained supershear speed of about 4.1 km/s despite sharp fault bends

questions.explanation: The 1999 Izmit earthquake showed a mean rupture velocity of about 4.8 km/s on the North Anatolian Fault; the 2002 Denali earthquake has been inferred as a supershear event on the Denali Fault system; the 2018 Palu earthquake sustained a rupture velocity of about 4.1 km/s from early on despite propagating through sharp fault bends.

questions.prompt: What happens during earthquake nucleation, before the main rupture reaches its sustained propagation speed?

options.text: Slip begins slowly and stably in a small patch, accelerating before transitioning to fast, self-sustaining rupture propagation
The entire eventual rupture area slips simultaneously at full speed from the first instant
Nucleation only occurs in supershear earthquakes, never in ordinary sub-shear ruptures
Nucleation is identical in size to the final rupture area, just slower

explanations.a: Correct — nucleation starts in a small patch (tens to a few hundred meters) with a brief, quasi-static phase of slowly accelerating slip before transitioning into fast, self-sustaining crack-tip propagation.
explanations.b: This describes the opposite of nucleation; the whole rupture area does not slip at once from the start, it grows outward from a small initiating patch.
explanations.c: Nucleation precedes every earthquake, sub-shear or supershear; supershear is a later transition in propagation speed, not a feature exclusive to how ruptures start.
explanations.d: Nucleation patches are typically far smaller than the eventual rupture area, not comparable in size to it.

lessons.label: Where Earthquakes Nucleate, and How Deep

sections.heading: The seismogenic layer and the brittle-ductile transition
sections.body: In continental crust, most tectonic earthquakes nucleate within a relatively thin seismogenic layer extending from the surface down to roughly 15 km, below which rock behaves too ductile to store the elastic strain that produces brittle rupture. This limit is set largely by temperature: quartz-rich crustal rock transitions from frictional (stick-slip, brittle) behavior to plastic, creeping flow at roughly 300 degrees Celsius, a temperature reached around 10-20 km depth depending on the local geothermal gradient. Above that transition rock is cool and strong enough to lock and store strain; below it, rock deforms by slow crystal-plastic flow that dissipates stress aseismically rather than storing it for sudden release, which is why the deepest crustal earthquakes cluster close to this brittle-ductile boundary rather than well below it.

sections.heading: Locked and creeping segments side by side
sections.body: Even within the seismogenic layer, fault behavior varies along strike. The central San Andreas Fault's creeping section slips steadily aseismically at roughly 25-30 mm/yr, releasing plate-motion strain continuously rather than storing it for a large rupture, while the adjacent locked segments to the north and south — including the segment that produced the M7.9 1857 Fort Tejon earthquake — store strain until failing in large, infrequent events. The Parkfield segment sits at the transition between the creeping section and the locked Cholame segment, which is part of why it has hosted the unusually regular sequence of moderate M6 earthquakes discussed elsewhere in this unit. Intraplate settings produce large earthquakes too, even far from any plate boundary: the New Madrid Seismic Zone in the central United States, reactivating an ancient buried rift structure, produced a sequence of major earthquakes in 1811-1812 despite sitting deep within the stable North American plate interior.

sections.heading: The deep-focus puzzle: quakes where brittle failure shouldn't work
sections.body: Above roughly 50-100 km, rising confining pressure should suppress ordinary frictional sliding entirely, yet earthquakes are reliably recorded down to about 700 km, concentrated along subducting slabs (Wadati-Benioff zones), with activity peaking near 600 km before dropping sharply toward near-zero by about 680 km. Two competing mechanisms are proposed and neither is fully settled. Dehydration embrittlement holds that hydrous minerals in the subducting slab break down under heat and pressure, releasing fluid that raises pore pressure, weakens the fault, and enables brittle-style failure — most plausible at intermediate depths of roughly 70-300 km where hydrous phases are still present. Transformational faulting proposes that the olivine-to-spinel phase transition in the mantle transition zone (roughly 410-660 km) creates dense, weak lens-shaped 'anticracks' whose coalescence triggers shear failure without any fluid involved. Since dehydration becomes implausible at the greatest depths where hydrous minerals should already be exhausted, the deepest recorded earthquakes remain the least well explained by either mechanism.

lessons.workedExample: Contrast three earthquakes by depth and mechanism. A M4 earthquake at 8 km depth on an ordinary continental fault nucleates comfortably within the brittle seismogenic layer, well above the roughly 15 km brittle-ductile transition. A M6 intraplate earthquake in the New Madrid Seismic Zone, at a similar shallow depth but hundreds of kilometers from any plate boundary, shows that large ruptures do not require proximity to a plate edge, only an ancient weak structure (here, a buried rift) and enough accumulated regional stress. A M7 earthquake at 600 km depth within a subducting slab cannot be explained by ordinary frictional failure at all, since confining pressure at that depth should lock any fault shut; it must instead be attributed to either dehydration embrittlement or transformational faulting in the olivine-spinel system, and seismologists studying that specific event cannot yet say with confidence which mechanism actually operated.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking 'why do earthquakes stop happening below about 15-20 km in continental crust, yet somehow still occur near 600 km in subduction zones?' is testing whether a student can hold two different depth-limiting mechanisms in mind at once rather than applying one universal rule. The strong answer explains the shallow limit through the brittle-ductile transition and temperature-controlled rock rheology, then explains the deep-focus exception as a genuinely different, still-debated physical process (dehydration embrittlement versus transformational faulting), naming both candidate mechanisms rather than treating deep earthquakes as a minor footnote to shallow seismology.

questions.prompt: What primarily limits the base of the seismogenic layer in continental crust to roughly 15 km?

options.text: The brittle-ductile transition, where quartz-rich rock shifts from frictional, brittle behavior to plastic, ductile flow at around 300 degrees Celsius
A hard physical floor of solid rock beneath which no earthquakes are physically possible at any depth
The exact depth of the Moho beneath all continental crust
A universal pressure limit that is identical everywhere on Earth regardless of local temperature

explanations.a: Correct — rock transitions from brittle, stick-slip behavior to ductile, plastic flow at roughly 300 degrees Celsius, a temperature reached around 10-20 km depending on local geothermal gradient, which sets the seismogenic layer's base.
explanations.b: There is no impenetrable rock floor; the limit is a temperature-controlled rheological transition, and deep-focus earthquakes below 300 km show brittle-style failure can still occur under very different conditions.
explanations.c: The Moho (crust-mantle boundary) is a compositional boundary, not the mechanism controlling the brittle-ductile transition depth, and the two do not coincide everywhere.
explanations.d: The transition depth varies with local geothermal gradient, so it is not a fixed, universal pressure limit independent of temperature.

questions.prompt: Match each seismicity example to its description from this lesson.

right.text: Sits at the transition between the creeping section and the locked Cholame segment
Slips steadily aseismically at roughly 25-30 mm/yr
Large earthquakes on an ancient reactivated rift, far from any plate boundary
Explained by either dehydration embrittlement or transformational faulting, with no consensus

questions.explanation: Parkfield sits at the boundary between the creeping and locked sections of the San Andreas; the creeping section itself slips aseismically at roughly 25-30 mm/yr; the New Madrid Seismic Zone shows large intraplate earthquakes on an ancient rift far from any plate edge; and deep-focus earthquakes near 600 km remain explained by competing, unresolved mechanisms.

questions.prompt: Why is dehydration embrittlement considered less plausible as an explanation for the very deepest recorded earthquakes (approaching 700 km) compared to intermediate-depth events (roughly 70-300 km)?

options.text: Because hydrous minerals capable of releasing fluid should already be exhausted or transformed by the time a slab reaches such extreme depths
Because confining pressure disappears entirely below 300 km, making any failure mechanism unnecessary
Because subducting slabs never reach depths greater than 300 km
Because dehydration embrittlement has never been observed at any depth and is purely hypothetical

explanations.a: Correct — dehydration embrittlement depends on hydrous mineral phases releasing fluid; at the greatest slab depths those phases should already be exhausted, making the mechanism less plausible there than transformational faulting.
explanations.b: Confining pressure increases with depth, it does not disappear; high confining pressure is exactly why ordinary frictional failure is otherwise expected to be suppressed at these depths.
explanations.c: Subducting slabs are tracked seismically to roughly 700 km via Wadati-Benioff zone earthquakes, well beyond 300 km.
explanations.d: Dehydration embrittlement is a well-studied, evidence-supported mechanism at intermediate depths; it is considered less applicable only at the greatest depths, not unobserved altogether.

units.label: Recording the Ground: Seismometers, Response, and Networks

lessons.label: How a Seismometer Actually Works

sections.heading: A mass that refuses to move
sections.body: Every mechanical seismometer is built around the same trick: a mass hung from a spring inside a frame that is bolted to the ground. When the ground shakes, the frame moves with it, but the mass's inertia makes it lag behind — and a sensor reads the relative motion between mass and frame as a proxy for ground motion. The system behaves as a damped harmonic oscillator with its own natural period T0 (set by the mass and spring stiffness) and a damping ratio that controls how fast oscillations die out. Seismometer designers target damping near 0.7 of critical: underdamped, the pendulum rings at every jolt and smears the record; overdamped, it responds sluggishly. A damping ratio near 0.7 gives the flattest, most faithful amplitude response across the widest band of frequencies without either problem dominating. Real instruments hit that target with electromagnetic damping: a coil attached to the mass moves through a magnetic field and is shorted through a resistor, so the induced eddy currents themselves brake the motion, with proportionally more braking as the mass moves faster (older designs instead used an oil-filled dashpot for the same purpose).

sections.heading: Why the mass only 'sees' fast shaking
sections.body: The physics of the mass-spring-damper means the instrument only tracks true ground displacement for motions faster (shorter-period) than its own natural period; for motions slower than T0, the mass simply moves along with the frame and the instrument goes blind. This is why the historic Wood-Anderson torsion seismograph, with T0 = 0.8 s and damping near 0.8 of critical, could only ever resolve local, high-frequency shaking — exactly the band Charles Richter needed in 1935 to define local magnitude (ML) from Southern California quakes. Its fixed static magnification of 2800x turned microscopic torsion into a readable photographic trace, but it was mechanically incapable of recording the long-period motion from a distant or very large earthquake.

sections.heading: From springs to feedback: the broadband era
sections.body: Modern broadband instruments such as the Streckeisen STS-2 and the Nanometrics Trillium family solve the short-period-only problem with force-balance feedback: a small mass is kept almost motionless by an electromagnetic coil driven by a servo loop, and the feedback current itself — not the mass's displacement — becomes the recorded signal. Because the loop actively cancels the mass's own resonance, the effective flat response stretches the passband enormously. The STS-2, for example, is flat to ground velocity from 120 seconds up past 50 Hz, letting one instrument capture everything from teleseismic surface waves to local high-frequency P-wave arrivals that a Wood-Anderson could never touch.

lessons.workedExample: A M 8.5 earthquake generates surface waves with periods of 100-200 seconds. A Wood-Anderson instrument (T0 = 0.8 s) is essentially deaf to this signal — the mass simply rides along with the 150-second-period ground swell, producing almost no relative motion to record. An STS-2, flat to velocity from 120 s to 50 Hz, faithfully records the same surface wave train as a large, clean oscillation, because its force-balance feedback actively holds the mass still regardless of how slowly the ground moves beneath it.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'why not just use one universal seismometer' is testing whether a student understands that instrument response is a physical constraint, not a settings dial. The strong answer names the natural period T0 as the boundary between what an instrument can and cannot see, and explains that force-balance feedback — not a bigger spring — is what let modern broadbands escape that boundary. A student who can trace Wood-Anderson's 0.8 s period to why Richter's ML scale saturates for big, distant quakes has grasped the mechanism, not just the vocabulary.

questions.prompt: A seismometer's mass-spring system has natural period T0. For ground motion with a period much LONGER than T0, what does the instrument do?

options.text: It amplifies the motion far beyond its true amplitude
The mass moves along with the frame, so little relative motion is recorded
It records the motion perfectly regardless of period
It inverts the polarity of the signal

explanations.a: Amplification near resonance can occur close to T0 in an underdamped system, but for periods much longer than T0 the mass tracks the frame, not the opposite.
explanations.b: Correct — below the instrument's resonance (motion slower than T0), the inertial mass has no reason to lag behind the moving frame, so the relative displacement the sensor reads goes toward zero.
explanations.c: A mechanical mass-spring pendulum is fundamentally band-limited; it cannot record faithfully outside its passband without feedback correction.
explanations.d: Polarity inversion is not a consequence of period relative to T0; it would be a wiring or convention issue, not a physical limitation of the pendulum.

questions.prompt: Why do seismometer designers target a damping ratio near 0.7 of critical rather than 0 (undamped) or 1.5 (heavily overdamped)?

options.text: 0.7 critical gives the flattest amplitude response across the widest frequency band without ringing or sluggishness
0.7 critical is required by international calibration law
Undamped systems record no signal at all
Overdamped systems oscillate indefinitely after a jolt

explanations.a: Correct — near 0.7 of critical damping balances two failure modes: an underdamped pendulum rings at every impulse and smears the trace, while an overdamped one responds too sluggishly; 0.7 is the classic engineering sweet spot.
explanations.b: There is no such regulatory requirement; 0.7 is an engineering optimum, not a legal standard.
explanations.c: An undamped system still records a signal, but it rings continuously at its natural period after any impulse, corrupting the trace.
explanations.d: This describes underdamping, not overdamping — an overdamped system is sluggish and settles without oscillating, the opposite of ringing indefinitely.

questions.prompt: Match each instrument to its defining characteristic.

right.text: T0 = 0.8 s, static magnification 2800x, basis of Richter's ML scale
Flat velocity response from 120 s to beyond 50 Hz
Drives a coil current to hold the mass nearly motionless, extending the usable passband

questions.explanation: The Wood-Anderson's fixed short period and 2800x gain made it the instrument behind Richter's original local magnitude scale; the STS-2 is a modern broadband flat from 120 s to over 50 Hz; and the force-balance feedback loop is the mechanism — an actively held-still mass — that makes such a wide passband possible.

questions.prompt: Order these developments in seismometer design from earliest to most recent.

items.text: Wood-Anderson torsion seismograph (T0 = 0.8 s, purely mechanical)
Richter defines local magnitude (ML) using Wood-Anderson records
Force-balance feedback broadbands (e.g., STS-2) flat from 120 s to 50 Hz

questions.explanation: The Wood-Anderson instrument (1925) came first; Richter then built his 1935 ML scale directly on its short-period, fixed-gain records; force-balance broadband feedback instruments emerged decades later, extending the recordable band far beyond what any purely mechanical pendulum could reach.

lessons.label: Instrument Response and Why You Must Remove It

sections.heading: The raw trace is not ground motion — it is counts
sections.body: A digital seismograph does not output meters per second; it outputs digitizer counts, an arbitrary integer proportional to the voltage the sensor produced. To recover physical units, you must know the instrument response: the transfer function describing how the sensor and digitizer together distort true ground motion into that voltage, frequency by frequency. Seismologists express this transfer function as a set of poles and zeros in the Laplace domain (plus an overall gain), a compact description inherited from control theory. Zeros suppress response at certain frequencies (typically at zero frequency, since a seismometer cannot see permanent ground offset); poles set resonances and roll-offs, including the mass-spring corner discussed in force-balance design. Multiplying by this function's inverse in the frequency domain — deconvolution — is the only rigorous way to turn counts back into displacement, velocity, or acceleration.

sections.heading: Two passbands, two purposes
sections.body: Instruments are typically calibrated 'flat' over one of two ranges: flat-to-velocity (output proportional to ground velocity across the passband, the standard for broadband seismometers like the STS-2) or flat-to-acceleration (used for strong-motion accelerometers, since acceleration is what matters for engineering shaking hazard, typically flat from near 0 Hz (DC) up to roughly 50-100 Hz, so it stays faithful all the way down to a fixed offset rather than only over a mid-band window — the opposite low-frequency corner from a broadband's flat-to-velocity band, which by contrast rolls off below its long-period limit). Removing the response means dividing out the appropriate poles-and-zeros model to recover the physical quantity you actually want — and outside the flat passband, the correction can amplify noise disastrously, since it divides by a response that is near zero.

sections.heading: Why nothing is meaningful before this step
sections.body: Every downstream seismological product depends on response-corrected data. A magnitude estimate needs true displacement or velocity amplitude, not raw counts scaled by whatever gain that particular digitizer happened to have. A spectrum used to study source properties or site amplification is meaningless if it still contains the instrument's own resonant peaks. Even comparing two stations' waveforms by eye is misleading if one runs a different digitizer gain than the other. This is why every properly archived station publishes its response as metadata — in StationXML (the modern FDSN standard, an XML schema) or the older RESP text format — alongside the waveform data itself, so anyone downloading a seismogram can deconvolve it correctly.

lessons.workedExample: A station records a local quake at 800,000 counts peak on its vertical channel. Its StationXML metadata lists an overall sensitivity (gain) of 4 x 10^8 counts per m/s within its flat passband. Dividing, 800,000 / (4 x 10^8) = 0.002 m/s = 2 mm/s peak ground velocity — a physically meaningful number a seismologist can compare across stations or plug into a magnitude formula. Skipping this step and reporting '800,000 counts' as if it were the shaking intensity would be comparing apples to a completely different station's oranges, since gain varies by digitizer and sensor model.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'what units is your seismic data in, and how did you get there' is checking whether a student blindly plotted raw counts and called it ground motion. The strong answer names the instrument response (poles and zeros) as the thing standing between counts and physics, states which passband their station is flat over (velocity or acceleration), and points to where the response metadata came from (StationXML or RESP). Reporting a magnitude, PGA, or spectrum from undeconvolved counts is the single most common error a fair judge is trained to catch.

questions.prompt: What does a digital seismograph actually output before any correction is applied?

options.text: Ground displacement in meters
Digitizer counts, proportional to sensor voltage
Peak ground acceleration in g
Local magnitude directly

explanations.a: Displacement in meters is a derived, response-corrected physical quantity, not the raw instrument output.
explanations.b: Correct — the raw record is digitizer counts, an arbitrary integer proportional to voltage, which must be corrected using the instrument response to become a physical unit.
explanations.c: Acceleration in g is likewise a derived quantity that requires deconvolving the instrument's transfer function first.
explanations.d: Magnitude is calculated from response-corrected amplitude measurements, several processing steps removed from the raw count stream.

questions.prompt: Why is deconvolving the response especially risky OUTSIDE an instrument's flat passband?

options.text: Because the response there is near zero, so dividing by it amplifies noise disastrously
Because StationXML files do not cover frequencies outside the passband
Because poles and zeros only exist inside the flat band
Because outside the passband the sensitivity value changes sign

explanations.a: Correct — removing the response is a division by the instrument's transfer function; where that function is near zero (outside the flat band), the correction blows up and amplifies whatever noise is present.
explanations.b: StationXML describes the full poles-and-zeros model across all frequencies, not just the flat band; the danger is mathematical, not a metadata gap.
explanations.c: The poles and zeros describe the response across the entire frequency range, including the roll-offs outside the flat band — that is precisely where they matter most.
explanations.d: Sensitivity does not flip sign outside the passband; the issue is that the response magnitude drops toward zero, not that it becomes negative.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its role in instrument response.

right.text: The Laplace-domain transfer function describing how the instrument distorts true ground motion
The calibrated range where output is proportional to ground velocity, standard for broadband seismometers
The metadata format(s) that publish a station's response so users can deconvolve it

questions.explanation: Poles and zeros mathematically define the transfer function; a flat-to-velocity passband is the calibrated range where broadband sensors output signal proportional to ground velocity; StationXML (modern) and RESP (legacy) are the formats that carry this response information alongside the waveform.

questions.prompt: Order the steps needed to turn a raw seismogram into a usable ground-velocity waveform.

items.text: Digitizer records raw counts from sensor voltage
Retrieve the station's response metadata (StationXML or RESP)
Deconvolve the poles-and-zeros transfer function from the counts
Use the resulting velocity waveform for magnitude, spectra, or comparison

questions.explanation: Raw counts come first from the digitizer; you then obtain the matching response metadata; deconvolving that response from the counts yields physically meaningful ground motion; only then is the waveform valid for magnitude estimation, spectral analysis, or cross-station comparison.

lessons.label: Strong Motion vs Weak Motion Instruments

sections.heading: Two instruments for two ends of the shaking spectrum
sections.body: Broadband seismometers like the STS-2 are exquisitely sensitive — that sensitivity is exactly what makes them saturate, or 'clip,' near a large, nearby earthquake, where the true shaking swings far past what the sensor's mechanical range or electronics can track. Strong-motion accelerometers solve this by trading sensitivity for range: force-balance accelerometers (FBAs) — the Kinemetrics Episensor is a widely deployed real-world example — typically span roughly plus or minus 2 g of acceleration, staying on-scale through the violent shaking a broadband would clip on. Paired with a 24-bit digitizer, an FBA still resolves fine detail even at that wide range, because 24 bits of resolution (about 16.7 million discrete levels) gives a theoretical dynamic range near 144 decibels, and real digitizers still deliver an effective dynamic range in the 130s after accounting for self-noise — from faint shaking up to the full plus or minus 2 g limit. This is why a well-instrumented station co-locates both instrument types: the broadband captures small and distant events with high fidelity, and the accelerometer stays faithful exactly where the broadband would fail.

sections.heading: Integrating acceleration invites drift
sections.body: Strong-motion records are acceleration; getting velocity or displacement requires integrating once or twice, and integration is unforgiving of any tiny, uncorrected offset in the raw trace. A baseline offset — a small DC bias from tilt, sensor imperfection, or clipping — that looks negligible in acceleration becomes a linear drift once integrated to velocity and a parabolic runaway once integrated again to displacement. A record that should return to zero after the shaking stops can instead show a spurious, ever-growing residual displacement of meters, swamping the real ground motion.

sections.heading: High-pass filtering as the fix — and the tradeoff
sections.body: Processors correct this by applying a high-pass filter before or during integration, removing the low-frequency baseline drift while preserving the higher-frequency shaking that matters for engineering. But the filter's corner frequency is a genuine choice, not a formality: setting it too high strips real long-period content (important for tall buildings and long-span structures), while too low lets residual drift back in. Processors also routinely apply a pre-event baseline correction — subtracting the mean level measured in the quiet seconds before the shaking starts — as a first, simpler pass at removing the same kind of DC offset before any filtering is applied. That choice directly shapes the reported peak ground velocity (PGV), since PGV is measured from the very velocity trace the filter and integration produced — two analysts filtering the same acceleration record differently can report different PGVs from identical raw data.

lessons.workedExample: A strong-motion station 5 km from an M6.5 rupture records acceleration on its FBA (range plus or minus 2 g), while its co-located broadband clips within the first two seconds of the S-wave arrival — its huge gain drives the recording electronics past their limit. Processing the FBA data, a small 0.001 g baseline offset left uncorrected would integrate over 20 seconds of shaking into a spurious velocity drift of roughly 0.2 m/s and a wildly unrealistic displacement trend. Applying a 0.1 Hz high-pass filter before integration removes that drift, yielding a clean velocity trace from which the analyst reads a physically sensible peak ground velocity.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'why do you need two different instruments at the same site' is probing whether a student understands that sensitivity and range trade off against each other, not that one instrument is simply 'better.' The strong answer names accelerometer clipping range and broadband saturation as complementary failure modes, and can explain that a reported PGV is not a raw physical constant but the output of a specific high-pass filter choice — a detail that separates a student who processed real strong-motion data from one who quoted a number off a website.

questions.prompt: Why does a network need both a broadband seismometer and an accelerometer at the same strong-motion site?

options.text: The accelerometer measures temperature while the broadband measures shaking
The broadband is more sensitive but clips near large nearby shaking; the accelerometer's wider range (about plus or minus 2 g) stays on-scale
Both instruments are identical and redundancy is the only reason
The accelerometer replaces the need for any digitizer

explanations.a: Accelerometers measure ground acceleration, not temperature; this describes an unrelated sensor type.
explanations.b: Correct — the broadband's high sensitivity is exactly why it saturates near strong local shaking, while the accelerometer trades sensitivity for a much wider dynamic range so it stays on-scale precisely when the broadband fails.
explanations.c: The two instrument types have fundamentally different sensitivity and range specifications; they are not identical, and co-location is functional, not merely redundant.
explanations.d: A digitizer is still required to convert the accelerometer's analog signal to digital counts; the accelerometer does not replace it.

questions.prompt: A small, uncorrected baseline offset in an acceleration record has what effect after integrating twice to displacement?

options.text: No effect, since integration averages out small errors
A parabolic runaway that swamps the real displacement signal
The offset appears only as a high-frequency oscillation
The offset cancels the true signal exactly

explanations.a: Integration does not average away a constant offset — it accumulates it, growing the error rather than canceling it.
explanations.b: Correct — a constant baseline offset in acceleration integrates once into a linear drift in velocity, then again into a parabolic (quadratic-in-time) runaway in displacement, which can dwarf the true ground motion.
explanations.c: A constant baseline offset is a low-frequency (effectively zero-frequency) error, not a high-frequency oscillation.
explanations.d: There is no mechanism by which a baseline offset would exactly cancel the true signal; it adds a spurious trend on top of it.

questions.prompt: Why can two analysts report different peak ground velocities (PGV) from the identical raw acceleration record?

options.text: PGV is a fixed physical constant that cannot vary by processing
Different high-pass filter corner-frequency choices before/during integration change the resulting velocity trace
PGV is read directly off the raw acceleration counts without any processing
Only the digitizer bit-depth affects PGV, never the filter

explanations.a: PGV is derived through processing choices, not a fixed constant independent of how the record was handled.
explanations.b: Correct — the high-pass filter's corner frequency is a genuine analyst choice that trades off removing drift versus preserving real long-period content, and PGV is measured from the velocity trace that choice produces.
explanations.c: PGV is a velocity quantity, obtained only after integrating the acceleration record and filtering it, not read directly from raw acceleration counts.
explanations.d: Bit-depth affects resolution and dynamic range, but the filter's corner-frequency choice is what directly shapes the reported PGV here.

questions.prompt: Order the steps in turning a raw strong-motion acceleration record into a reported peak ground velocity.

items.text: FBA records raw acceleration on-scale through strong shaking
Apply a high-pass filter to remove baseline drift
Integrate the filtered acceleration to velocity
Read the peak value off the resulting velocity trace as PGV

questions.explanation: The accelerometer first records raw acceleration without clipping; the high-pass filter removes the baseline offset that would otherwise cause drift; integrating the filtered record produces velocity; only then is the peak read off as the reported PGV.

lessons.label: Seismic Noise and Station Siting

sections.heading: The ground is never silent — Peterson's noise models
sections.body: Even with no earthquake occurring, seismometers record continuous ambient vibration: seismic noise from oceans, wind, traffic, and the atmosphere. Jon Peterson's 1993 USGS report (Open-File Report 93-322) compiled power spectral density (PSD) measurements from a worldwide network of stations and distilled them into two reference curves still used today: the New Low Noise Model (NLNM) and New High Noise Model (NHNM). Together they bracket the envelope within which essentially all real station noise falls, at every period from roughly 0.01 to 10,000 seconds. A station's own PSD is judged against this envelope — sitting near the NLNM means an exceptionally quiet, well-sited station capable of detecting the smallest signals; drifting toward the NHNM flags a noisy site or an instrument problem.

sections.heading: The ocean's fingerprint: microseism peaks
sections.body: The dominant natural noise source on Earth is the ocean, and it leaves two signature peaks in every noise spectrum. The primary microseism peak sits near a 14-second period, generated directly as ocean swell pushes on the shoreline and seafloor at the wave period itself. The secondary (double-frequency) microseism peak sits near a 7-second period — roughly half the primary's period — produced when opposing ocean swells of similar frequency interfere and generate a pressure signal at twice the wave frequency, a mechanism traceable to Longuet-Higgins' 1950s theoretical work. Above roughly 1 Hz, a different noise regime takes over: cultural noise from traffic, machinery, and human activity, which is why quiet siting matters far more for high-frequency local-earthquake detection than the microseism band does.

sections.heading: Choosing where and how to bury the sensor
sections.body: Because noise varies so much by location and installation, siting is an active design problem. A concrete vault, isolated from wind loading and temperature swings, is the traditional standard; a borehole installation buries the sensor tens to hundreds of meters down, escaping near-surface wind and cultural noise entirely for a substantially quieter high-frequency floor. Ocean-bottom seismometers push further, placing sensors directly on the seafloor to fill in oceanic gaps in coverage, though they trade quiet siting for harsh installation and recovery logistics. Routine quality control at any station relies on the probabilistic power spectral density (PPSD) plot — a histogram of PSDs computed over many time windows — letting an analyst see at a glance whether a station sits consistently between the Peterson bounds or has degraded.

lessons.workedExample: A station operator compares two candidate sites for a new broadband instrument: a surface vault 200 m from a highway, and a borehole 100 m deep in the same area. PPSD plots at the surface vault show elevated power above 1 Hz that tracks daytime traffic and disappears at night — classic cultural noise pushing the station toward the Peterson NHNM during the day. The borehole's PPSD, computed over the same weeks, sits close to the NLNM at all periods, including through the daytime hours, because 100 m of overburden attenuates the traffic-generated high-frequency energy that never reaches that depth.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking 'how do you know your station's data is any good' is testing whether a student treats noise as something to characterize rather than ignore. The strong answer names Peterson's NLNM/NHNM as the actual yardstick, identifies whether their signal of interest falls near the ocean microseism peaks (14 s primary, 7 s secondary) or in the cultural-noise band above 1 Hz, and describes checking a PPSD plot rather than assuming a clean-looking waveform means a clean station.

questions.prompt: What do Peterson's (1993) New Low Noise Model and New High Noise Model together represent?

options.text: The exact noise level every seismic station must match
An envelope bracketing the range within which nearly all real station noise falls, used to judge station quality
The theoretical minimum and maximum magnitude an instrument can detect
A single average noise curve with no upper or lower bound

explanations.a: Stations are not required to match a single value; the models define a bracketing range, and real stations fall at different points within it depending on siting.
explanations.b: Correct — Peterson's 1993 NLNM and NHNM together define the envelope within which almost all real seismic station noise spectra fall, letting an analyst judge whether a given station is quiet or noisy relative to that envelope.
explanations.c: The models describe ambient background noise power spectral density, not earthquake magnitude detection limits directly, though quieter noise does improve detection thresholds.
explanations.d: There are explicitly two separate curves, a low bound and a high bound, not one average curve.

questions.prompt: What generates the secondary (double-frequency) microseism peak near a 7-second period?

options.text: Direct ocean swell pressure on the seafloor at the swell's own period
Interference between opposing ocean swells of similar frequency, producing a signal at twice the wave frequency
Traffic and human cultural activity near the coast
Atmospheric pressure changes unrelated to the ocean

explanations.a: This describes the primary microseism mechanism (near 14 s), where the swell's own period produces the peak directly, not the secondary peak.
explanations.b: Correct — the secondary, double-frequency microseism arises when opposing ocean swells of similar frequency interfere, generating a pressure signal at twice the swell frequency, appearing near half the primary period.
explanations.c: Cultural noise from traffic and machinery dominates a much higher frequency band (above roughly 1 Hz), not the microseism band.
explanations.d: The double-frequency microseism mechanism is specifically tied to ocean wave-wave interaction, not general atmospheric pressure fluctuation.

questions.prompt: Match each siting strategy to its main noise-reduction benefit.

left.text: Borehole installation (tens to hundreds of meters deep)

right.text: Isolates the sensor from wind loading and surface temperature swings
Escapes near-surface wind and cultural (traffic) noise for a quieter high-frequency floor
Fills oceanic gaps in station coverage at the cost of harsh installation and recovery

questions.explanation: A vault primarily buffers wind and temperature; a borehole goes further by physically escaping the near-surface layer where wind and cultural noise couple into the ground; an ocean-bottom seismometer trades installation difficulty for coverage where no land station could otherwise sit.

questions.prompt: Order these periods from shortest to longest: cultural noise band onset, secondary microseism peak, primary microseism peak.

items.text: Cultural noise onset (~1 Hz, i.e., ~1 second period)
Secondary microseism peak (~7 second period)
Primary microseism peak (~14 second period)

questions.explanation: Cultural noise from traffic and machinery dominates above about 1 Hz, i.e., at periods around 1 second or shorter; the secondary (double-frequency) microseism sits near 7 seconds; the primary microseism sits at roughly double that, near 14 seconds — so ordered by period they run cultural noise, secondary microseism, primary microseism.

lessons.label: Networks, Data Formats, and Getting Real Waveforms

sections.heading: A federation of networks, not one system
sections.body: No single organization runs the world's seismometers. The Global Seismographic Network (GSN), operated jointly by IRIS/EarthScope, the USGS, and university partners, provides roughly 150 permanent broadband stations spread across the globe for a uniform baseline of Earth's largest events. The Advanced National Seismic System (ANSS) federates seismic networks specifically across the United States for rapid hazard response. Both plug into the International Federation of Digital Seismograph Networks (FDSN), a coordinating body that standardizes network codes, data formats, and web-service access so a researcher can query any member network's data through one consistent interface, regardless of who actually owns the instrument. The EarthScope USArray Transportable Array (TA) exemplified this scale: roughly 400 broadband stations at any moment, rolled in a uniform grid across the contiguous United States from 2004 to 2013, systematically imaging crust and mantle structure beneath the whole country one region at a time before moving on.

sections.heading: Reading a channel code
sections.body: FDSN's SEED convention names every data stream with a network, station, location, and three-letter channel code, and that channel code encodes real physical meaning. The first letter is the band code, describing sample rate and corner period: B for broadband (sample rate 10-80 samples per second, commonly around 20-40, with a long-period corner at 10 s or longer — a low-frequency, not high-frequency, corner) versus H for high-broadband (sampled around 100+ samples per second, with that same long-period corner). The second letter is the instrument code: H for a high-gain seismometer versus N for an accelerometer. The third letter is orientation: Z, N, or E for vertical, north, and east. So BHZ is a broadband seismometer's vertical component at a modest sample rate; HHZ is the same physical seismometer's vertical component sampled much faster; HNZ is an accelerometer's vertical component at that same fast rate — three different codes can describe two different sensors at one site.

sections.heading: From a raw file to a usable waveform
sections.body: The actual waveform samples travel in miniSEED, a compact binary format built for the huge volumes continuous seismic recording produces. For a real project, the practical path is FDSN web services: a researcher specifies a network, station, time window, and channel in a URL request to a data center (IRIS/EarthScope's is the most widely used), and receives back miniSEED waveform data plus, on request, the matching StationXML response metadata needed to deconvolve it — turning a specific historical earthquake into downloadable, science-fair-usable data with no special hardware required.

lessons.workedExample: A student wants a real record of a 2011 M5 earthquake from a station in California. They query an FDSN web service for network code 'CI' (Caltech/USGS Southern California network), a station near the epicenter, channel 'BHZ', and a time window spanning the origin time plus ten minutes. The service returns a miniSEED file of vertical-component broadband velocity counts and a StationXML file with the instrument's poles and zeros. Reading BHZ tells them immediately what they have: a broadband seismometer's vertical component at a lower (20-40 Hz range) sample rate — appropriate for measuring surface waves, though a fast-sampled HHZ or HNZ channel would be preferable if they instead wanted to resolve high-frequency P-wave detail.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'where did your waveform data actually come from' is checking whether a student sourced real, traceable seismic data or fabricated a plot. The strong answer names the specific network (GSN, ANSS, or a regional network under FDSN), states which channel code they pulled and why (BHZ vs HHZ vs HNZ each imply a different sample rate or sensor type suited to different signals), and can describe requesting it through FDSN web services rather than gesturing at 'a database.' That level of specificity is the difference between a real dataset and an invented one.

questions.prompt: What does the channel code 'HNZ' tell you about a station's instrument?

options.text: A broadband seismometer's vertical component at a lower sample rate
An accelerometer's vertical component at a high sample rate
A broadband seismometer's north-south component
A low-gain seismometer's east component

explanations.a: That describes 'BHZ' — the B band code indicates the lower (broadband, ~20-40 sps) sample rate, and H as the second letter indicates a high-gain seismometer, not an accelerometer.
explanations.b: Correct — H as the first letter (high broadband) indicates a fast sample rate, N as the second letter indicates an accelerometer, and Z indicates the vertical component.
explanations.c: The third letter Z specifically denotes the vertical component, not north-south, which would be coded N.
explanations.d: N as the second letter denotes an accelerometer (not a low-gain seismometer), and Z denotes vertical, not east, which would be coded E.

questions.prompt: What is the primary role of the FDSN in global seismology?

options.text: It manufactures all seismometers used worldwide
It coordinates standardized codes, formats, and web-service access so data from many independently-owned networks can be queried uniformly
It is a single physical seismic network covering the whole planet
It only handles data from the USArray Transportable Array

explanations.a: The FDSN is a coordinating body, not an instrument manufacturer; it standardizes practice across networks that each operate their own hardware.
explanations.b: Correct — the FDSN's role is standardizing network/channel codes, data formats like miniSEED, and web-service access across member networks like the GSN and ANSS, so users query diverse, independently-owned instruments through one consistent interface.
explanations.c: The FDSN is a federation of many separately-operated networks (GSN, ANSS, regional networks, etc.), not one unified physical network.
explanations.d: USArray is just one deployment among many networks the FDSN framework federates; it is not the FDSN's sole scope.

questions.prompt: Match each network or format to its description.

right.text: Roughly 150 permanent global broadband stations providing a uniform worldwide baseline
~400 stations rolled in a uniform grid across the contiguous US, 2004-2013
Compact binary format carrying the actual continuous waveform samples

questions.explanation: The GSN is the permanent global backbone network; the Transportable Array was a temporary, migrating deployment that imaged the contiguous US from 2004 to 2013 before redeploying to Alaska; miniSEED is simply the data container format the waveform samples travel in, regardless of which network recorded them.

questions.prompt: Order the steps in obtaining a usable, response-correctable waveform for a real earthquake through FDSN web services.

items.text: Identify the event's origin time and a nearby station/network code
Choose an appropriate channel code (e.g., BHZ vs HHZ vs HNZ) for the signal of interest
Submit an FDSN web-service request for that network/station/channel/time window
Receive miniSEED waveform data plus StationXML response metadata

questions.explanation: You first need the event and a candidate station; then decide which channel code fits the signal you want to study; then submit the actual FDSN request specifying network, station, channel, and time window; and finally you receive the miniSEED waveform together with the StationXML metadata needed to remove the instrument response.

lessons.label: Arrays and Beamforming

sections.heading: Two numbers describe where a wave came from
sections.body: A seismic array — many sensors packed close together, tens of meters to a few kilometers apart, rather than spread across a continent — measures a wavefront in a fundamentally different way than a single station does. As a wave sweeps across the array, it arrives at each sensor at a slightly different time, and those tiny time differences encode exactly two quantities: back-azimuth, the compass direction the wave arrived from, and slowness, the inverse of the apparent horizontal velocity the wavefront sweeps across the array's surface. Together, back-azimuth and slowness let an array locate and characterize a distant source using only its own footprint, without needing a network of stations spread over hundreds of kilometers.

sections.heading: Delay-and-sum: turning timing differences into a pointed ear
sections.body: The core array technique is delay-and-sum beamforming: for an assumed back-azimuth and slowness, the processor computes the exact time delay a plane wave from that direction would produce at each sensor, shifts every trace by its corresponding delay, and sums the aligned traces. If the assumed direction and slowness are correct, real coherent signal adds constructively across all sensors while incoherent noise — uncorrelated from sensor to sensor — tends to cancel. Sweeping this process across a grid of candidate back-azimuths and slownesses and looking for the combination that maximizes summed energy is exactly how an array locates an unknown arrival; the frequency-domain version of this same search, f-k (frequency-wavenumber) analysis, separates coherent signal from background noise directly in frequency-wavenumber space, making it a standard tool for both signal detection and noise characterization.

sections.heading: Why N sensors beat one, and by how much
sections.body: Because incoherent noise at N independent sensors partially cancels while coherent signal from a common source adds up directly, beamforming's detection gain over a single sensor scales roughly as the square root of N — doubling detectable sensitivity requires quadrupling the number of elements. This sqrt(N) gain is precisely why Cold War-era arrays like LASA (Large Aperture Seismic Array, built in Montana in 1965 under the VELA UNIFORM nuclear-monitoring program) and NORSAR (established in Norway in the late 1960s under the same program) packed hundreds of seismometers into subarrays: dense instrumentation bought detection sensitivity for distant, weak nuclear-test signals that no single high-quality station could match. An array wins over a distributed network specifically when the goal is detecting and characterizing a single distant, coherent arrival; a distributed network wins when the goal is instead resolving how ground motion varies across a broad region.

lessons.workedExample: An array of 25 sensors detects a faint arrival. Sweeping delay-and-sum beamforming across candidate slowness and back-azimuth values, the summed energy peaks sharply at a back-azimuth of 305 degrees and a slowness corresponding to a P-wave from roughly 60 degrees epicentral distance — information a single sensor's waveform alone could never extract, since one sensor records only amplitude and timing at one point, not a wavefront's direction of travel. With 25 elements, the array's detection threshold improves by roughly sqrt(25) = 5x over a single comparable sensor, pulling the arrival above the noise floor.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking 'why use an array instead of just more separate stations' is testing whether a student understands that arrays exploit coherence, not just raw sensor count. The strong answer names back-azimuth and slowness as the two quantities an array actually measures, explains delay-and-sum (or f-k) beamforming as the mechanism that turns timing differences into a pointed detector, and can state the sqrt(N) detection-gain scaling rather than vaguely claiming 'more sensors is better.'

questions.prompt: What two quantities does a seismic array directly measure from the timing differences across its sensors?

options.text: Magnitude and depth
Back-azimuth and slowness
P-wave and S-wave arrival times only
Static gain and damping ratio

explanations.a: Magnitude and depth are properties of the source typically estimated from amplitude and travel-time modeling, not directly from an array's cross-sensor timing differences.
explanations.b: Correct — the tiny arrival-time differences across a densely packed array's sensors directly encode back-azimuth (direction of arrival) and slowness (inverse apparent velocity across the array).
explanations.c: P- and S-wave arrival times are properties any single station can also measure; they are not the array-specific quantities extracted from cross-sensor timing.
explanations.d: Static gain and damping ratio are properties of an individual seismometer's mechanical design, unrelated to array geometry or beamforming.

questions.prompt: In delay-and-sum beamforming, why does the correct assumed back-azimuth and slowness produce a peak in summed energy?

options.text: Because shifting traces by the correct delays aligns coherent signal so it adds constructively while incoherent noise tends to cancel
Because it amplifies noise at every sensor equally
Because it removes the need for any instrument response correction
Because it converts velocity records into displacement records

explanations.a: Correct — when the assumed direction and slowness match the true wavefront, the applied time shifts align the real, coherent signal across sensors so it sums constructively, while noise that is uncorrelated sensor-to-sensor tends to cancel out.
explanations.b: Noise amplification equally at every sensor would not produce a distinguishing peak; the technique specifically relies on noise NOT being coherent, so it partially cancels rather than adds.
explanations.c: Beamforming is a spatial timing-alignment technique across sensors; it does not address instrument response, which is a separate frequency-domain correction per sensor.
explanations.d: Beamforming combines already-recorded traces in time; it does not itself convert between velocity and displacement units.

questions.prompt: Match each array-related term to its description.

right.text: Frequency-wavenumber domain method separating coherent signal from noise
Montana array built 1965 under VELA UNIFORM for nuclear-test monitoring
Detection sensitivity improvement scaling with the square root of the number of array elements

questions.explanation: f-k analysis is the frequency-domain counterpart to delay-and-sum beamforming, used to separate signal from noise; LASA was a Cold War-era nuclear-monitoring array built in Montana in 1965; and the sqrt(N) scaling describes how much detection sensitivity an array gains as more coherent-summing elements are added.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a delay-and-sum beamforming search for an unknown arrival's direction and slowness.

items.text: Choose a candidate back-azimuth and slowness
Compute the time delay that direction/slowness would produce at each sensor
Shift each trace by its computed delay and sum across all sensors
Repeat across a grid of candidates and take the combination that maximizes summed energy

questions.explanation: Beamforming tests one candidate direction/slowness at a time: it computes what delay that assumption implies at each sensor, applies those delays and sums the traces, and then repeats this across many candidates, with the true back-azimuth and slowness revealed as whichever combination produces the largest constructive sum.
