lessons.label: New Sensing: Fiber, MEMS, and Citizen Networks

sections.heading: Turning ordinary fiber-optic cable into thousands of sensors
sections.body: Distributed Acoustic Sensing (DAS) repurposes existing 'dark' (unused) telecommunications fiber as a dense seismic array by sending laser pulses down the cable and analyzing the tiny Rayleigh backscatter that reflects from microscopic imperfections along its length. As the fiber stretches or compresses with passing seismic waves, the backscatter's phase shifts measurably, and by timing the returning light, a single interrogator unit converts one fiber into a virtual array of channels spaced roughly every meter to a few meters along its entire length — potentially tens of kilometers of channels from one instrument. Critically, DAS measures strain rate along the fiber's axis, not particle velocity the way a conventional seismometer does, so DAS data requires different processing and is most directly comparable to strain-sensitive measurements rather than a drop-in replacement for a three-component seismometer's output.

sections.heading: MEMS: cheap accelerometers, real tradeoffs
sections.body: Micro-electromechanical systems (MEMS) accelerometers — the same class of chip that detects phone orientation — have been repurposed for seismology at a fraction of a research-grade instrument's cost. MyShake, developed at UC Berkeley and launched in 2016, uses a smartphone's built-in MEMS accelerometer paired with a phone app to detect earthquake shaking as part of an early-warning network. The Quake-Catcher Network, a Stanford/USGS collaboration founded in 2008, distributed low-cost USB MEMS sensors to volunteers' homes and offices. Raspberry Shake packages a MEMS or geophone sensor with a Raspberry Pi single-board computer as an affordable, plug-in seismograph for schools and hobbyists. All three trade the research-grade sensitivity and low self-noise of an STS-2 or FBA for extremely low cost and massive numbers, useful specifically for detecting strong, nearby shaking rather than resolving faint distant earthquakes.

sections.heading: What density buys, and what it cannot
sections.body: Dense nodal deployments — hundreds to thousands of compact, self-contained geophone nodes rented and laid out temporarily across a small area — apply the same 'more, cheaper sensors' logic for short-duration research surveys, imaging subsurface structure at a spatial resolution a sparse permanent network could never achieve. Judging any of these newer approaches means asking the same three questions every time: what bandwidth can it actually record, how much self-noise does it add on top of true signal, and what specific science does that combination support. A MEMS network can detect and rapidly locate a damaging M5+ earthquake but cannot resolve the faint long-period signals a broadband array reads; DAS can image structure at meter-scale spatial density along a fiber's path but cannot easily replace a three-component broadband station's fidelity.

lessons.workedExample: A city wants earthquake early warning but cannot afford broadband stations every few blocks. It deploys 2,000 MyShake-enabled phones and 50 Raspberry Shake units across neighborhoods. When an M5.5 strikes 10 km away, the dense MEMS network detects strong shaking at dozens of points within seconds, cheaply triangulating the source region — something a sparse network of three expensive broadbands 20 km apart could do more precisely but far more slowly to canvas. However, none of those MEMS units could resolve the same quake's fainter aftershocks or teleseismic surface waves days later, exactly the higher-fidelity, low-self-noise task an STS-2 broadband is built for.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'why not just use cheap sensors everywhere' is testing whether a student can weigh bandwidth, self-noise, and cost against each other rather than treating 'more data' as automatically better. The strong answer names a specific new-sensing technology (DAS, MEMS via MyShake/Quake-Catcher/Raspberry Shake, or nodal arrays), states what it measures (strain rate versus particle velocity, for instance) and its self-noise limitation, and identifies one concrete task it is suited for and one it is not — showing the tradeoff was reasoned through, not assumed away.

questions.prompt: What physical quantity does Distributed Acoustic Sensing (DAS) actually measure along a fiber-optic cable?

options.text: Particle velocity, identical to a conventional seismometer
Strain rate along the fiber's axis, via changes in Rayleigh backscatter phase
Ground acceleration in units of g, directly
Magnetic field fluctuations along the cable

explanations.a: DAS is explicitly not equivalent to a conventional seismometer's particle-velocity measurement; it measures a different physical quantity requiring different processing.
explanations.b: Correct — DAS sends laser pulses down the fiber and measures the phase shift of Rayleigh backscatter as the fiber strains with passing seismic waves, yielding strain rate along the fiber's axis at each channel.
explanations.c: DAS does not output acceleration directly; its native measurement is strain rate, a distinct quantity from acceleration.
explanations.d: DAS relies on optical backscatter phase changes from mechanical strain, not on any magnetic sensing principle.

questions.prompt: MyShake, Quake-Catcher Network, and Raspberry Shake are best described as sharing which core tradeoff relative to research-grade broadbands like the STS-2?

options.text: Lower cost and larger numbers, at the price of higher self-noise and lower sensitivity to faint signals
Higher cost but identical sensitivity to an STS-2
They eliminate the need for any digitizer
They measure strain rate instead of acceleration

explanations.a: Correct — MEMS-based sensors in MyShake, Quake-Catcher Network, and Raspberry Shake are cheap and deployable in large numbers, but the MEMS chips themselves have higher self-noise and lower sensitivity than a research-grade broadband, making them suited to strong nearby shaking rather than faint distant signals.
explanations.b: The entire appeal of these systems is low cost; they are not comparable in cost, and they do not match an STS-2's sensitivity or low self-noise.
explanations.c: These systems still require a digitizer (built into the phone or the MEMS sensor board) to convert the analog signal to digital samples.
explanations.d: MEMS accelerometers measure acceleration, not strain rate; strain rate is the DAS measurement, a different technology described elsewhere in this lesson.

questions.prompt: Match each new-sensing approach to its description.

right.text: Repurposes dark fiber-optic cable as a meter-spaced virtual array measuring strain rate
UC Berkeley smartphone-app earthquake detection network launched in 2016
Hundreds to thousands of temporary geophone nodes for high-resolution short-duration subsurface imaging

questions.explanation: DAS turns fiber-optic cable itself into a dense strain-rate-sensing array; MyShake is the Berkeley-built smartphone MEMS app for earthquake early warning, launched in 2016; dense nodal deployments rent out large numbers of compact geophone nodes for temporary, high-resolution research surveys.

questions.prompt: Order these historically, from earliest to most recent: Quake-Catcher Network, MyShake, DAS on telecommunications dark fiber for seismology.

items.text: Quake-Catcher Network (Stanford/USGS, founded 2008)
MyShake (UC Berkeley, launched 2016)
DAS on repurposed telecom dark fiber for seismic monitoring (broad adoption in the following years)

questions.explanation: The Quake-Catcher Network was founded in 2008, distributing low-cost USB MEMS sensors; MyShake followed as a Berkeley smartphone-app network launched in 2016; distributed acoustic sensing on repurposed dark fiber for seismic monitoring saw its broad seismological adoption afterward, as an even newer sensing approach.

units.label: Locating Earthquakes from Arrival Times

lessons.label: Picking Arrivals and the Wadati Diagram in Practice

sections.heading: Reading a seismogram: impulsive versus emergent onsets
sections.body: Every location starts with a human or algorithm deciding exactly when an arrival begins, and that decision is harder than it sounds. A P-wave onset is impulsive when the trace jumps from background noise to a sharp, high-frequency first motion within a sample or two - typical of nearby, well-recorded events with a clean path. An emergent onset instead ramps up gradually over a second or more, common for weak, distant, or attenuated arrivals, or when the wave has crossed a low-velocity zone that disperses its high frequencies. Analysts (and automated pickers) assign each pick a quality weight - codes 0 through 4, corresponding to roughly less than 0.05, 0.05-0.1, 0.1-0.2, 0.2-0.4, and greater than 0.4 second uncertainty, with weight 4 conventionally excluded from the fit entirely - and that weight later controls how much the pick influences the location.

sections.heading: Finding S on the horizontal components
sections.body: P arrives first because it is a compressional wave that travels faster through the same rock, but S is the harder pick: it is not a new arrival from silence but a change in character partway through the P and P-coda energy, so it is best identified on the horizontal components (P energy is strongest on vertical; S energy is strongest horizontal, and shows as a shift in frequency content and particle motion). S picks routinely carry 2-3 times the timing uncertainty of P picks on the same station, simply because the onset is buried in coda.

sections.heading: The Wadati diagram: turning two picks into velocity and origin time
sections.body: Kiyoo Wadati showed in 1933 that plotting the S-minus-P time against the P arrival time, across several stations for one earthquake, produces a straight line whose slope is (Vp/Vs) - 1 and whose x-intercept, extrapolated back to S-P = 0, is the origin time. This works without knowing the hypocentral distance at all, because S-P time scales with distance the same way P time does. For a Poisson solid (Poisson's ratio 0.25), Vp/Vs works out to exactly the square root of 3, about 1.73 - the textbook crustal value - though real crust commonly ranges 1.6-1.9 depending on fluid content and fracturing, and a Wadati slope far from 1.73 is itself a clue about the rock the waves crossed. Wadati's same 1930s arrival-time work also uncovered something beyond this diagram: deep-focus earthquakes beneath island arcs define an inclined zone of seismicity dipping from the trench down into the mantle, now called the Wadati-Benioff zone, marking the subducting slab. An off-nominal Wadati slope is itself worth flagging before the arrival times ever reach Geiger's method for a full hypocenter solution - a bad velocity ratio at this stage propagates into every iteration downstream.

lessons.workedExample: Five stations record S-P times of 1.46, 3.29, 5.04, 7.01, and 8.76 s at P arrival times of 10.0, 12.5, 14.9, 17.6, and 20.0 s after a reference clock. A least-squares line through these five (P, S-P) points gives a slope of about 0.73 and an x-intercept near 8.0 s, so Vp/Vs = 1.73 and origin time = 8.0 s. Now suppose the fourth station's S pick was mistakenly read 2 s too late (S-P = 9.01 instead of 7.01): the regression slope steepens to about 0.81 (implying Vp/Vs near 1.81) and the origin time shifts later by roughly 0.2 s - one bad S pick biases both the velocity ratio and the origin time, not just the one station's residual.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks "how did you pick your arrivals, and how sure are you" is testing whether a student treats seismogram reading as a measurement with error bars rather than a single confident click. The strong answer names impulsive versus emergent onsets, explains why S is picked on horizontal components with larger uncertainty than P, and can show a Wadati plot where removing or correcting one suspect pick changes the fitted Vp/Vs and origin time - demonstrating that the student understands picks are inputs to a regression, not ground truth, and that a single bad S reading contaminates results derived from the whole station set.

questions.prompt: On a Wadati diagram (S-P time plotted against P time), what does the slope of the best-fit line represent?

options.text: The earthquake's origin time
Vp/Vs minus 1
The hypocentral distance in kilometers
The focal depth

explanations.a: Origin time comes from the x-intercept (where S-P extrapolates to zero), not the slope.
explanations.b: Correct - Wadati (1933) showed the slope of S-P versus P time equals (Vp/Vs) - 1, letting the ratio be read off without knowing distance.
explanations.c: Distance is not read directly from a Wadati plot; the plot uses S-P and P times, not distance.
explanations.d: Focal depth requires additional information (like depth phases or a full location); it is not given by the Wadati slope.

questions.prompt: Why is the S-wave arrival typically picked with larger timing uncertainty than the P-wave arrival at the same station?

options.text: S waves travel faster and arrive before background noise begins
S arrives as a gradual character change within the P coda rather than a fresh onset from silence
S waves are always emergent while P waves are always impulsive
S waves cannot be recorded on horizontal components

explanations.a: S waves travel slower than P, not faster, and this is not why the pick is harder.
explanations.b: Correct - S has to be identified as a shift in frequency content and particle motion buried inside ongoing P-coda energy, not a clean onset from a quiet trace, so its timing is inherently less certain.
explanations.c: Onset character (impulsive vs. emergent) depends on signal quality and path, not a fixed rule tied to phase type.
explanations.d: S energy is strongest on the horizontal components; that is where analysts look for it, not evidence it cannot be recorded there.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of building a Wadati diagram for one earthquake.

items.text: Pick the P and S arrival times at each recording station
Compute S-P time for each station
Plot S-P time (y-axis) against P time (x-axis) for all stations
Fit a line and read Vp/Vs from the slope and origin time from the intercept

questions.explanation: You must first read both phase arrivals at each station, subtract to get S-P, plot those pairs, and only then fit the line whose slope gives Vp/Vs and whose intercept gives origin time.

questions.prompt: Match each onset description to what it implies about the pick.

left.text: One S pick 2 s too late

right.text: Sharp jump from noise to signal within a sample or two, low timing uncertainty
Gradual ramp-up over roughly a second, higher timing uncertainty
Consistent with a Poisson solid (Poisson's ratio 0.25)
Biases the fitted slope and intercept for every station in the regression

questions.explanation: Impulsive onsets are sharp and precise; emergent onsets ramp up and carry more uncertainty; a Vp/Vs of about 1.73 matches the classic Poisson-solid value; and because the Wadati fit uses all stations together, a single bad pick shifts the whole line, not just its own point.

lessons.label: Geiger's Method: Solving for Four Unknowns

sections.heading: Four unknowns, one nonlinear problem
sections.body: Locating an earthquake means solving for four numbers at once: latitude, longitude, depth, and origin time. The observations are arrival times at a set of stations, and travel time is a nonlinear function of hypocenter position through the velocity model, so there is no direct algebra that inverts observed times into a location. Geiger published the linearized least-squares solution in 1910-1912: start from a guess of the hypocenter and origin time, compute the travel-time residual (observed minus predicted arrival) at every station, and use the local derivative of travel time with respect to each of the four unknowns to solve for a correction step. This is Gauss-Newton iteration applied to seismology, and it remains the mathematical core of essentially every routine earthquake location program in use today, including HYPOINVERSE and HYPOCENTER.

sections.heading: Iterating to convergence
sections.body: Each Geiger iteration linearizes the travel-time curve around the current guess, builds a matrix of partial derivatives (how much each station's predicted time changes per kilometer of latitude, longitude, depth shift, and per second of origin-time shift), and solves the resulting linear system by least squares to get a correction. The hypocenter guess is updated, residuals recomputed, and the process repeats until the corrections shrink below a threshold - typically a handful of iterations for a well-behaved dataset, though a poor starting guess or sparse station coverage can make it diverge or converge to the wrong local minimum.

sections.heading: The depth-origin time trade-off and what RMS actually measures
sections.body: The single most persistent instability in Geiger-style inversion is the trade-off between focal depth and origin time: moving the hypocenter deeper delays every predicted arrival almost uniformly, and shifting origin time later does almost the same thing, so the two parameters are nearly degenerate whenever stations are far from directly above the earthquake (teleseismic distances, or any network with a poor azimuthal wrap). This is why many routine locations fix depth at a default (often 10 km) rather than let it float. It is also critical to remember that the final RMS residual measures how well the chosen velocity model and station picks fit each other - a low RMS can result from a systematically wrong velocity model fitting consistently wrong picks just as well as it results from an accurate location; RMS is a self-consistency check, not proof of accuracy.

lessons.workedExample: A network of six stations reports P arrivals for an earthquake with residuals of +0.3, -0.2, +0.1, +0.4, -0.3, and +0.2 s against a first location guess with hypocenter fixed at 10 km depth. Geiger's method computes the derivative of travel time with respect to latitude, longitude, depth, and origin time at each station, forming a 6x4 matrix, and solves for the correction that best explains those residuals - moving the epicenter 3 km northeast and origin time 0.15 s earlier, which drops the RMS from 0.27 s to 0.09 s after two iterations. If depth is allowed to float instead of staying fixed at 10 km, the same residuals can equally be explained by a hypocenter 4 km shallower and origin time 0.4 s later - the depth and origin-time corrections trade off against each other almost one-for-one because no station lies close to overhead.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes Geiger's method because it exposes whether a student understands that a location is an iterative best-fit, not a lookup. The sharp answer explains why depth and origin time trade off (near-degenerate sensitivity when no station is near the epicenter or the network lacks close-in azimuthal coverage), and why a small final RMS is not evidence the depth is correct - it only shows the model and the picks are mutually consistent. A student who quotes RMS as "how accurate the location is" without that caveat has not understood what the number measures.

questions.prompt: What does Geiger's method actually solve for in each iteration?

options.text: The exact hypocenter directly from a closed-form algebraic formula
A least-squares correction to the current hypocenter guess, using linearized travel-time derivatives
The station azimuths only, ignoring travel time
The magnitude of the earthquake

explanations.a: Travel time is a nonlinear function of hypocenter position, so there is no direct closed-form inversion; that is exactly why iteration is needed.
explanations.b: Correct - Geiger's 1910-1912 method linearizes travel time around a current guess and solves the resulting least-squares system for a correction, repeating until it converges.
explanations.c: Geiger's method uses arrival-time residuals at stations, not azimuth alone.
explanations.d: Magnitude is a separate calculation unrelated to the location's least-squares travel-time fit.

questions.prompt: Why do focal depth and origin time trade off against each other in Geiger-style location?

options.text: Because deepening the hypocenter and delaying origin time both shift nearly all predicted arrivals in a similar way when no station sits near the epicenter
Because depth and origin time are mathematically identical variables
Because deeper earthquakes always have later origin times by definition
Because RMS residual cannot be computed when depth is unknown

explanations.a: Correct - without a station close to overhead to break the degeneracy, deepening the source and delaying the clock produce nearly the same shift in every predicted arrival time, so the inversion cannot cleanly separate the two.
explanations.b: They are distinct physical unknowns; the issue is that their effects on predicted arrivals are hard to distinguish given the data, not that they are the same variable.
explanations.c: There is no such definitional relationship between depth and origin time.
explanations.d: RMS can be computed regardless of whether depth is fixed or free; the trade-off is about parameter resolvability, not about RMS computability.

questions.prompt: A location result reports a very low RMS residual (0.05 s). What does this most directly demonstrate?

options.text: The hypocenter is accurate to within a few hundred meters
The chosen velocity model and the arrival-time picks are mutually consistent with the fitted hypocenter
The station network has no azimuthal gap
The earthquake's depth was measured directly, not inferred

explanations.a: A low RMS does not guarantee physical accuracy - a systematically wrong velocity model can still fit consistently wrong picks well.
explanations.b: Correct - RMS is a self-consistency measure between the model, the picks, and the fitted location; it says the fit is good, not that the true location is close to the reported one.
explanations.c: Azimuthal gap is a separate geometric property of the station distribution, not something RMS reports on.
explanations.d: Depth in Geiger-style location is always inferred through the inversion, never measured directly, regardless of the RMS value.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of one Geiger iteration.

items.text: Start from a current hypocenter and origin-time guess
Compute predicted arrival times and residuals (observed minus predicted) at each station
Build the matrix of travel-time derivatives with respect to the four unknowns
Solve the least-squares system for a correction and update the hypocenter/origin time

questions.explanation: Each iteration begins from the current guess, computes how far off the predictions are, builds the local sensitivity (derivative) matrix, and then solves for and applies the correction before repeating.

lessons.label: Velocity Models, Station Geometry, and Depth

sections.heading: 1D layered models and the global standards
sections.body: Every location needs a velocity model to turn hypocentral distance into predicted travel time, and the simplest useful choice is a 1D layered model - velocity as a function of depth only, ignoring lateral variation. For teleseismic and regional work, seismologists lean on standard global tables built from decades of arrival-time data worldwide: IASP91 (Kennett and Engdahl, 1991) and its refinement ak135 (Kennett, Engdahl, and Buland, 1995), both derived by fitting smooth velocity-depth profiles to millions of reported travel times. These global models work well for average Earth structure but systematically mislocate events in regions with real 3D heterogeneity - subduction zones, thick sedimentary basins, or continental roots - because a 1D model cannot represent a fast slab or a slow basin sitting off to one side of the raypath. Local networks instead build custom 1D or fully 3D velocity models from controlled-source seismic surveys or tomographic inversion to correct for exactly that heterogeneity.

sections.heading: Station geometry: azimuthal gap and depth control
sections.body: Even a perfect velocity model cannot compensate for bad station geometry. The azimuthal gap - the largest angular gap, viewed from the epicenter, between two adjacent stations - is the standard geometric health check: a gap under 180 degrees is the common rule of thumb for a location judged reliable, since a gap approaching or exceeding that means the earthquake is effectively outside the network, with all stations bunched on one side. Depth control has its own separate geometric requirement: resolving depth well generally needs at least one station within roughly one focal-depth distance of the epicenter, because only a station nearly overhead has arrival times sensitive to small changes in depth rather than dominated by horizontal distance.

sections.heading: Depth phases: pP and sP for teleseismic control
sections.body: For earthquakes recorded only teleseismically, where no station sits close enough for direct depth sensitivity, depth phases fill the gap. pP is a P wave that first travels upward from the source, reflects off the free surface near the epicenter, and then travels down and out as a second P arrival; sP does the same starting as an S leg. The time delay between P and pP (or P and sP) at a single distant station depends almost entirely on focal depth, nearly independent of the uncertain deep-Earth velocity structure the direct P wave crossed, making depth phases one of the most reliable single-station depth estimators available. This is precisely why catalog depth is often flagged as the least trustworthy number in an event listing: without a close station or clearly identified depth phases, depth is fixed by convention or poorly resolved by the depth-origin time trade-off, while epicenter and magnitude rest on much stronger geometric and amplitude constraints.

lessons.workedExample: A magnitude 6.5 earthquake occurs offshore with the nearest station 220 km away and a focal depth later determined to be 15 km - meaning no station is anywhere near the roughly-one-focal-depth range needed for direct depth control, so the routine catalog solution fixes depth at a default 10 km. A later teleseismic study identifies pP and sP arrivals 8.2 s and 11.5 s respectively after the direct P at a station 6000 km away; converting those delays through the ak135 travel-time tables for near-vertical near-surface reflection paths gives a depth of 14-16 km, confirming the routine catalog's fixed-depth value was coincidentally close, but for a different, unverified reason - the fixed value was an assumption, while the depth-phase result is an actual measurement.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks "how confident are you in the depth you're citing" is checking whether a student knows depth is the weak link in any catalog row. The strong answer distinguishes a resolved depth (a station within about one focal depth, or a clear teleseismic pP/sP reading) from a fixed or assumed depth, and can explain the azimuthal-gap rule of thumb (under 180 degrees) as the geometric precondition for trusting the epicenter itself. Citing IASP91 or ak135 by name, and knowing they are global averages that can be locally wrong in a subduction zone or basin, signals the student understands velocity-model choice is itself a source of systematic error, not a settled input.

questions.prompt: What geometric condition is generally needed to resolve focal depth well from local/regional station data?

options.text: An azimuthal gap greater than 180 degrees
At least one station located within roughly one focal-depth distance of the epicenter
All stations recording only P waves, no S waves
A velocity model with more than ten layers

explanations.a: A gap greater than 180 degrees is the opposite of good geometry - it signals the earthquake lies effectively outside the network.
explanations.b: Correct - a station nearly overhead (within about one focal depth) has arrival times sensitive to depth changes rather than dominated by horizontal distance, which is what actually constrains depth.
explanations.c: Depth resolution is about station-source geometry, not which phase types are recorded.
explanations.d: Layer count in the velocity model does not substitute for having a station close enough to be depth-sensitive.

questions.prompt: Why do depth phases like pP and sP give reliable depth estimates even for teleseismic earthquakes with no nearby stations?

options.text: Their delay relative to direct P depends mainly on focal depth and is largely insensitive to the deep-Earth velocity structure crossed en route
They always arrive before the direct P wave, simplifying the calculation
They eliminate the need for any velocity model
They are only observable when the azimuthal gap is under 180 degrees

explanations.a: Correct - pP and sP reflect near the epicenter before traveling the same long path as the direct P, so their delay isolates the near-source depth effect from the shared, uncertain deep-Earth path.
explanations.b: pP and sP travel a longer path (up, then down, then across) than the direct P, so they arrive after it, not before.
explanations.c: Converting the P-to-pP delay into a depth still requires a velocity model (e.g., ak135) for the near-surface reflection geometry.
explanations.d: Depth phases are a teleseismic single-station technique and are unrelated to the local network's azimuthal gap.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its role in earthquake location.

right.text: Global 1D average velocity-depth tables built from worldwide travel-time data
Geometric health check on station coverage around the epicenter
Surface-reflected phases that give single-station teleseismic depth control
Corrects for real lateral heterogeneity a global 1D model cannot represent

questions.explanation: IASP91 and ak135 are global 1D reference models from worldwide data; azimuthal gap checks whether stations surround the epicenter; pP/sP delays give depth from a single distant station; and local/3D models correct for the lateral structure (slabs, basins) a global 1D average misses.

questions.prompt: Why is catalog depth commonly flagged as the least reliable number in an earthquake location, compared to epicenter or magnitude?

options.text: Depth cannot be measured by any known seismic method
Without a nearby station or identified depth phases, depth is often fixed by convention or weakly resolved due to the depth-origin time trade-off
Magnitude and epicenter do not depend on the velocity model at all
Depth is only reported for earthquakes below magnitude 4

explanations.a: Depth phases and near-source stations do measure depth; the issue is these conditions are often absent, not that depth is unmeasurable in principle.
explanations.b: Correct - lacking a close station or clean pP/sP readings, routine solutions often fix depth at a default and it remains poorly separated from origin time, unlike epicenter and magnitude which rest on stronger constraints.
explanations.c: Epicenter location does depend on the velocity model too; the claim that it is independent is false.
explanations.d: Depth is reported for earthquakes of all magnitudes; there is no such magnitude cutoff.

lessons.label: Relative Relocation and Double-Difference

sections.heading: Why relative location beats absolute location for clusters
sections.body: Absolute location (Geiger's method against a 1D velocity model) has an error budget dominated by the velocity model being wrong along the shared part of the raypath. For a single isolated earthquake that error is unavoidable. But for a cluster of nearby earthquakes, the unknown velocity structure along the shared portion of each pair's raypaths is nearly identical, so if you difference the arrival times of two nearby events at the same station, the shared-path error cancels almost completely. Master-event relocation exploits this crudely: pick one well-located reference event and relocate every other event in the cluster relative to it using the differenced residuals. Double-difference relocation, introduced by Waldhauser and Ellsworth (2000), generalizes this to every pair of events in a cluster simultaneously, solving a joint linear system that minimizes the difference between observed and predicted differential travel times for all event pairs sharing common stations.

sections.heading: Cross-correlation: getting differential times to sub-sample precision
sections.body: The real power of the method comes from combining catalog phase picks with waveform cross-correlation: when two earthquakes are close enough that their waveforms at a shared station look nearly identical (similar mechanism, similar path), cross-correlating the waveforms yields a differential arrival time far more precise than two independent human or automated picks - often to a few milliseconds, far below one sample interval at typical 100 Hz sampling. hypoDD, the software Waldhauser released alongside the method, became the standard implementation, feeding both catalog differential times and cross-correlation differential times into one weighted least-squares (or conjugate-gradient) solve for relative event positions.

sections.heading: From clouds to streaks - and the temptation to over-read them
sections.body: The visible result of double-difference relocation is often dramatic: a diffuse cloud of hypocenters spanning several kilometers in the routine catalog collapses into a thin streak or planar sheet just tens to hundreds of meters wide, because most of the routine catalog's scatter was velocity-model noise rather than real earthquake dispersion. This is genuinely valuable - relocated seismicity has revealed previously unmapped fault planes and illuminated aftershock sequences and swarm migration paths that active-source geology missed. But the collapse invites a specific overreach: a tight planar alignment of relocated hypocenters is consistent with slip on a single fault surface, but it is not proof of one, since events can align along a genuine structural feature that is fractured or segmented rather than a continuous plane, or an alignment can partly reflect the geometry of common stations and correlated waveform families rather than the true rupture surface. Relocated streaks are strong evidence to be combined with focal mechanisms and independent geologic mapping, not treated as a direct photograph of a fault.

lessons.workedExample: A routine catalog locates 200 aftershocks of a mainshock scattered through a roughly 5 km by 3 km by 4 km volume, with RMS residuals near 0.3 s each - typical 1D-model noise. Applying hypoDD with catalog phase data plus waveform cross-correlation for the 140 event pairs with correlation coefficients above 0.8 collapses the cloud into a near-planar sheet about 300 m thick, dipping 70 degrees, that aligns with the mainshock's focal-mechanism nodal plane. A student concludes this proves the fault dips exactly 70 degrees and is a single unbroken surface; a more careful reading notes that the cross-correlated pairs are drawn from the subset of aftershocks similar enough to correlate well, so the sheet may under-represent structurally distinct sub-events that correlate poorly and were excluded from the tightest cluster.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks "why does relocated seismicity look so much tighter than the catalog" is testing whether a student understands double-difference cancels shared-path velocity error rather than magically sharpening the raw data. The strong answer names Waldhauser and Ellsworth (2000), explains that differencing arrival times between nearby event pairs removes the common unknown velocity structure, and describes cross-correlation's role in pushing differential-time precision below a sample interval. Equally important is the caution: a judge is impressed by a student who resists calling a tight relocated streak definitive proof of a single fault plane, and instead treats it as strong but partial evidence requiring corroboration from focal mechanisms or field mapping.

questions.prompt: Why does double-difference relocation reduce location error for a cluster of nearby earthquakes?

options.text: It uses a completely different, more accurate velocity model than absolute location
Differencing arrival times between nearby event pairs cancels the shared, unknown velocity-model error along their common raypath
It ignores waveform data entirely and relies only on station azimuths
It requires no velocity model at all

explanations.a: Double-difference still uses a velocity model to predict travel times; the improvement comes from differencing, not from a fundamentally different model.
explanations.b: Correct - nearby events share most of their raypath, so their common velocity-model error is nearly identical and cancels when arrival times are differenced, as Waldhauser and Ellsworth (2000) formalized.
explanations.c: The method incorporates waveform cross-correlation precisely because waveform data (not azimuth alone) sharpens differential timing.
explanations.d: A velocity model is still needed to predict travel times and their derivatives; only the shared-path error is what cancels.

questions.prompt: What advantage does waveform cross-correlation add over catalog phase picks alone in double-difference relocation?

options.text: It removes the need to identify P and S phases at all
It yields differential arrival times precise to a few milliseconds, well below a typical sample interval, for waveform pairs similar enough to correlate well
It works equally well regardless of how similar the two earthquakes' waveforms are
It eliminates the need for a master event or reference location

explanations.a: Cross-correlation still operates on identified phase windows; it refines timing, it does not remove the need for phase identification.
explanations.b: Correct - for similar waveforms from nearby, similarly-mechanism events, cross-correlation resolves differential timing to a few milliseconds, sub-sample precision far tighter than independent picks.
explanations.c: Cross-correlation quality depends heavily on waveform similarity; dissimilar events give poor or unusable correlation-based differential times.
explanations.d: Double-difference relocates the whole cluster jointly and does not strictly require a single master event, but cross-correlation itself is a separate benefit about timing precision, not about removing a master event requirement.

questions.prompt: A relocated aftershock sequence collapses from a scattered cloud into a thin, planar streak. What is the most defensible conclusion?

options.text: The streak is definitive proof of a single continuous, unbroken fault surface

The streak is strong evidence consistent with slip localized on or near a fault structure, but should be corroborated with focal mechanisms or geologic mapping before treating it as a direct image of one continuous surface
The collapse proves the original catalog locations were fabricated
The streak has no relationship to the underlying fault geometry

explanations.a: A tight planar alignment is consistent with a single fault surface but does not rule out a segmented or fractured structure, or bias from which event pairs correlated well enough to be included.
explanations.b: Correct - relocated streaks are valuable, strong evidence, but the alignment can partly reflect which events had correlatable waveforms, so independent corroboration is the responsible next step.
explanations.c: The scatter in routine catalogs reflects real velocity-model limitations, not fabrication; double-difference does not expose fraud, it removes shared-path error.
explanations.d: Relocated streaks are generally understood to relate meaningfully to fault structure - the caution is about over-interpreting them as a complete, definitive picture, not dismissing them entirely.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a double-difference relocation workflow.

items.text: Start from a routine catalog of scattered absolute locations for a cluster
Identify event pairs sharing common stations and compute catalog differential times
Refine differential times for similar waveform pairs using cross-correlation
Jointly solve the linear system minimizing differential travel-time residuals across all pairs

questions.explanation: Double-difference relocation begins from a routine catalog, forms differential times between event pairs at shared stations, sharpens those differences with cross-correlation where waveforms are similar, and then solves the joint system (as in hypoDD) to produce relative locations.

lessons.label: Detection, Templates, and Catalog Completeness

sections.heading: STA/LTA: the classic energy trigger
sections.body: Before any arrival can be picked or any hypocenter located, an earthquake has to be detected in continuous data, and the workhorse algorithm since the 1970s-80s is STA/LTA - short-term average over long-term average. A short window (seconds) tracks recent signal energy while a long window (tens of seconds to minutes) tracks the background level; when the ratio crosses a threshold (commonly 3 to 5), the algorithm declares a trigger. STA/LTA is cheap, real-time capable, and still runs at the front end of most seismic networks, but it fundamentally misses signals below the noise floor - anything too small or too far away to raise short-term energy clearly above background never triggers, no matter how real the earthquake is.

sections.heading: Matched filtering and template detection
sections.body: Matched-filter (template) detection takes a different approach: instead of watching for a generic energy spike, it cross-correlates continuous data against the waveform of a known, previously located earthquake (the template), scanning for any window in continuous data that matches the template's waveform shape closely, even at amplitudes buried well below the STA/LTA noise floor - because correlation exploits waveform similarity rather than raw amplitude. Studies applying template matching to aftershock sequences and swarms have repeatedly found detections increasing catalog event counts by roughly an order of magnitude over the STA/LTA-based routine catalog for the same time period and region, revealing enormous populations of small earthquakes that were physically present in the continuous waveform data all along but never crossed a simple energy trigger.

sections.heading: Deep-learning pickers and the completeness problem
sections.body: The newest generation of detectors - PhaseNet (Zhu and Beroza, 2018) and EQTransformer (Mousavi et al., 2020) - use deep neural networks trained on large labeled waveform datasets to pick P and S phases directly from raw seismograms, often matching or exceeding analyst pick quality while running fast enough for continuous, network-wide processing, pushing detection thresholds down further still. Every detection-threshold advance changes what magnitude of completeness (Mc) a catalog achieves - Mc is the magnitude above which the catalog is believed to include essentially all earthquakes that occurred, below which smaller events are increasingly missed. Because detection capability depends on network density, noise conditions, and algorithm choice, Mc is not a fixed property of a region; it shifts whenever the detection method changes. This creates a serious pitfall for seismicity-rate studies: if a network upgrades its picker, adds stations, or a study switches from STA/LTA to template matching partway through a time series, the earthquake rate can appear to jump even though the true underlying rate of ground rupture never changed - only the number of small earthquakes the network could see did.

lessons.workedExample: A seismic network's STA/LTA-based catalog for a six-month aftershock sequence lists 800 earthquakes with Mc = 2.0. Researchers build waveform templates from 50 well-located events and run matched-filter detection on the same continuous data, recovering 7,200 events over the identical period - roughly a ninefold increase - and pushing Mc down to about 0.5, because correlation detects small, template-similar events the energy trigger never flagged. If a student instead plotted only the original STA/LTA catalog's event count per week and it happened to include a mid-sequence switch to template detection, the count would show an artificial jump at the switchover date that has nothing to do with the earthquakes actually slowing down or speeding up - only the detector changed.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking "is this change in earthquake rate real" is testing whether a student can separate a genuine physical process from a detection-threshold artifact. The strong answer names Mc, explains that STA/LTA, template matching, and deep-learning pickers (PhaseNet, EQTransformer) have systematically different, and improving, detection floors, and states plainly that any seismicity-rate comparison across a period where the detection method or network changed must either hold Mc fixed or explicitly correct for the completeness shift - otherwise an apparent rate increase may simply be a smaller Mc, not more earthquakes.

questions.prompt: Why can matched-filter (template) detection find earthquakes that STA/LTA triggering misses entirely?

options.text: It requires the signal to exceed a fixed absolute amplitude threshold, which is more sensitive than STA/LTA
It cross-correlates continuous data against a known template waveform, detecting shape similarity even at amplitudes well below the STA/LTA noise floor
It only works on earthquakes larger than the largest event in the catalog
It replaces the need for any velocity model or station network

explanations.a: Matched filtering is not simply a different amplitude threshold - it detects waveform similarity via correlation, which can succeed at amplitudes an energy-ratio trigger would never flag.
explanations.b: Correct - by correlating against a known template's waveform shape, matched filtering exploits similarity rather than raw energy, letting it detect events buried well below the noise floor that STA/LTA requires signal to clear.
explanations.c: Matched filtering typically finds smaller events similar to the template, not exclusively larger ones.
explanations.d: Matched filtering still needs continuous station data and, for any resulting location, a velocity model; it does not remove those requirements.

questions.prompt: What does the magnitude of completeness (Mc) represent for a seismicity catalog?

options.text: The largest magnitude ever recorded in the catalog
The magnitude above which the catalog is believed to include essentially all earthquakes that occurred
The average magnitude of all events in the catalog
A fixed physical property of a region that never changes

explanations.a: Mc is not the maximum magnitude; it is a completeness threshold, unrelated to the single largest event.
explanations.b: Correct - Mc is the magnitude threshold above which detection is assumed essentially complete, with smaller events increasingly under-detected below it.
explanations.c: Mc is not an average; it is a threshold defining where completeness begins.
explanations.d: Mc depends on network density, noise, and detection method, so it shifts whenever those change - it is not a fixed property of the region itself.

questions.prompt: A seismicity-rate time series shows a sudden jump in weekly earthquake counts exactly at the date a network switched from STA/LTA to template-matching detection. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: The true rate of fault rupture genuinely doubled at that exact date
The detection threshold dropped (Mc decreased) at the switchover, revealing smaller events that were always occurring but previously undetected
Template matching can only detect earthquakes larger than magnitude 5
The velocity model must have changed at the same time

explanations.a: Attributing the jump to a real doubling of physical rupture rate ignores the far simpler, well-documented explanation tied to the detector change happening on the same date.
explanations.b: Correct - template matching (and similarly, deep-learning pickers) systematically lowers Mc relative to STA/LTA, so a count jump coinciding with a detector switch is a classic completeness artifact, not necessarily a real rate change.
explanations.c: Template matching typically detects smaller events than STA/LTA, the opposite of being restricted to only large ones.
explanations.d: A velocity-model change is unrelated to a detection-method switch and is not implied by this scenario.

questions.prompt: Match each detection method to its defining characteristic.

right.text: Energy-ratio trigger; cheap, real-time, but misses signals below the noise floor
Cross-correlates continuous data against known template waveforms; finds sub-noise-floor events, multiplying catalog counts
Deep neural networks trained to pick P/S phases directly from raw waveforms at network scale
Threshold above which a catalog is believed essentially complete; shifts with detection method

questions.explanation: STA/LTA is the classic cheap energy trigger with a noise-floor limit; matched-filter/template detection uses waveform correlation to reach below that floor; PhaseNet and EQTransformer are deep-learning pickers operating at network scale; and Mc is the completeness threshold that moves whenever detection capability changes.

lessons.label: Uncertainty, Quality Flags, and Disagreeing Catalogs

sections.heading: Error ellipses, ERH/ERZ, and what a quality flag actually encodes
sections.body: A location is never a bare latitude-longitude-depth triple; every routine solution comes with a formal uncertainty derived from the same least-squares fit that produced the hypocenter. The horizontal uncertainty is usually reported as an error ellipse (major and minor axis, orientation) or condensed into a single number, ERH (standard error of the horizontal position, typically the semi-major axis or an RMS-combined horizontal error), while ERZ is the analogous vertical (depth) error. These numbers come directly out of the covariance matrix of the Geiger-style inversion - they describe how sensitive the fit is to the picks and geometry given, not an independent check on truth. A location can carry a small ERH purely because many stations agree, even if every station shares the same wrong velocity model; conversely a large ERZ is the routine, expected signature of the depth-origin time trade-off discussed earlier, not evidence of unusually sloppy work.

sections.heading: Station residuals and fixed-depth flags
sections.body: Per-station residuals (observed minus predicted arrival time after the final fit) are the diagnostic layer beneath the summary ERH/ERZ: a station with a residual several times larger than the rest usually signals a bad pick, an unmodeled local velocity anomaly under that station, or a misidentified phase, and catalogs commonly let analysts down-weight or exclude such outliers. A depth entry flagged as fixed (rather than free) is a specific, important quality flag: it means the inversion could not resolve depth from the data (no near station, no depth phases) and a default was imposed, so the reported depth carries essentially no data-derived uncertainty of its own - the absence of an error bar on a fixed depth is not a sign of confidence, it is a sign the value was never really solved for.

sections.heading: Why USGS/NEIC, ISC, and Global CMT disagree on the same event
sections.body: Three major agencies routinely report different numbers for the identical earthquake, and the differences are traceable to real methodological choices, not error: the USGS National Earthquake Information Center produces fast, near-real-time locations (minutes to hours) using a global station subset and standard velocity model, prioritizing speed for hazard response; the International Seismological Centre (ISC) reprocesses events months to years later using a far larger, more complete global station dataset and includes more careful phase re-picking, typically improving station coverage and reducing azimuthal gap over the initial NEIC solution; and Global CMT (Dziewonski, Ekstrom, and collaborators, building on Dziewonski et al., 1981, and running continuously since as Ekstrom et al., 2012 describes) does not relocate the point hypocenter at all - it inverts long-period waveforms for the best-fitting moment tensor and centroid location and depth, which represents the center of the rupture's moment release rather than the epicenter where rupture initiated, so CMT depth and location can differ from NEIC's by tens of kilometers for a large event by definition, not by mistake. For a science-fair project, the practical rule is to cite the source matched to the claim: USGS/NEIC for a fast, well-documented public-facing epicenter and magnitude, ISC for the most complete reprocessed catalog for statistical or completeness work, and Global CMT for focal mechanism and moment magnitude.

lessons.workedExample: For one magnitude 6.8 earthquake, USGS/NEIC reports an epicenter with ERH = 5 km, depth fixed at 10 km (flagged, no ERZ reported), released 18 minutes after the event. Months later, ISC reprocesses using triple the station count, resolving an epicenter 8 km from NEIC's with ERH = 2 km and a free depth of 14 km with ERZ = 3 km. Global CMT separately reports a centroid depth of 22 km, because the moment-tensor centroid represents the weighted center of a rupture that nucleated at 14 km and propagated updip, not the hypocenter itself. A student citing only the CMT depth of 22 km as "the earthquake's depth" without noting it is a centroid, not a hypocenter, would be conflating two physically different quantities that happen to share the word "depth."
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks "why do your sources disagree" is testing whether a student understands that disagreement between USGS, ISC, and Global CMT reflects different methods and different physical quantities, not sloppy data. The strong answer distinguishes ERH/ERZ (fit uncertainty from the inversion's own covariance, not an external accuracy check) from a fixed-depth flag (no depth was actually resolved), and explains that CMT centroid depth is not the same physical quantity as a hypocentral depth, so a several-kilometer or greater mismatch across agencies for the same event is expected and explainable, not a red flag requiring the student to pick the "right" number and discard the rest.

questions.prompt: What does a location's reported ERH (horizontal error) most directly represent?

options.text: An independently verified measurement of true location accuracy
The standard error of the horizontal position derived from the least-squares inversion's own covariance matrix
The distance between the epicenter and the nearest station
The magnitude uncertainty of the event

explanations.a: ERH comes from the fit's internal statistics, not from an independent ground-truth check - a small ERH can still coexist with a systematically wrong location if all stations share the same velocity-model bias.
explanations.b: Correct - ERH is derived from the covariance matrix of the Geiger-style least-squares solution, describing the fit's sensitivity given the picks and geometry, not an external accuracy guarantee.
explanations.c: ERH is a statistical error estimate, not simply a station-distance measurement.
explanations.d: ERH describes horizontal position uncertainty, unrelated to magnitude uncertainty.

questions.prompt: A catalog entry lists depth as "fixed" with no ERZ reported. What does this flag mean?

options.text: The depth was measured with unusually high precision, so no error bar is needed
The inversion could not resolve depth from the available data, so a default value was imposed rather than solved for
The earthquake occurred exactly at the surface
ERZ was accidentally omitted from the report by clerical error

explanations.a: The absence of an error bar on a fixed depth is not a sign of precision - it signals the value was never data-derived in the first place.
explanations.b: Correct - a fixed-depth flag means no nearby station or depth phase resolved the depth, so a default was assigned, and it carries essentially no data-derived uncertainty.
explanations.c: A fixed depth is an assumed default value (often around 10 km), not necessarily zero or surface depth.
explanations.d: The missing ERZ is the expected, meaningful consequence of fixing depth, not a clerical omission.

questions.prompt: Why can Global CMT's reported depth for a large earthquake differ from USGS/NEIC's hypocentral depth by tens of kilometers, without either being wrong?

options.text: CMT reports the centroid depth (the moment-weighted center of the rupture), a physically different quantity from the hypocenter where rupture initiated
CMT and NEIC use identical methods, so any difference must be a data-entry error
CMT never reports depth, only magnitude
NEIC depths are always more accurate than CMT depths

explanations.a: Correct - CMT inverts long-period waveforms for a moment tensor and centroid location representing the rupture's moment-weighted center, which can sit well away from the initiation point (hypocenter) NEIC locates, especially for a rupture that propagated updip or along-strike.
explanations.b: CMT and NEIC use fundamentally different methods (moment-tensor waveform inversion versus arrival-time hypocenter location), so the difference is expected from the methodology, not a data-entry mistake.
explanations.c: Global CMT does report a centroid depth as part of its standard solution.
explanations.d: Neither is universally "more accurate" - they measure different physical quantities (initiation point versus moment-release center), so ranking one as always better is a category error.

questions.prompt: Match each agency/product to what it is best suited to be cited for.

right.text: Fast, near-real-time public epicenter and magnitude for hazard response
Later, more complete reprocessed catalog with larger station sets, best for statistical/completeness work
Focal mechanism and centroid moment magnitude from long-period waveform inversion

questions.explanation: USGS/NEIC prioritizes speed for immediate public and hazard use, ISC reprocesses months to years later with far more stations for the most complete catalog, and Global CMT specializes in moment-tensor and centroid solutions rather than fast hypocenters.

units.label: Magnitude, Energy, and Earthquake Statistics

lessons.label: Richter's Local Magnitude

sections.heading: A scale built around one specific instrument
sections.body: In 1935, Charles Richter, working at Caltech and leaning heavily on Beno Gutenberg for the distance calibration, needed a way to compare Southern California earthquakes without arguing about felt intensity, which depends on soil, building type, and who happened to be awake. His solution, local magnitude ML, was defined entirely around one instrument: the Wood-Anderson torsion seismometer, with a natural period of 0.8 s, damping of 0.8, and a nominal magnification near 2800 (later recalculated closer to 2080 by Uhrhammer and Collins in 1990, once errors in the instrument's assumed torsion-pendulum geometry were traced through the response equations). ML is the base-10 logarithm of the maximum trace amplitude A that instrument would record, minus a correction term log A0(delta) that accounts for how amplitude shrinks with epicentral distance delta as waves spread and attenuate.

sections.heading: Why the log and why the zero point
sections.body: Richter anchored the scale so a magnitude-3 earthquake produces a 1 mm trace amplitude at 100 km on a standard Wood-Anderson instrument in Southern California; A0(delta) is simply the empirical table of what amplitude a magnitude-zero shock would produce at each distance, built partly from Kiyoo Wadati's earlier practice of plotting log amplitude against distance for Japanese earthquakes. The table is not a straight line: at 200 km, Richter's original A0 correction runs roughly 3.4 to 3.5, up from 3.0 at 100 km, because amplitude falls off faster than a simple inverse-distance law once geometric spreading and anelastic attenuation both contribute. Because ML is a base-10 log of amplitude, each whole unit means a tenfold jump in ground-motion amplitude at the seismometer -- a magnitude 5 writes ten times the trace of a magnitude 4 and a hundred times a magnitude 3. That compression is the entire point: it turns amplitudes spanning many orders of magnitude into a manageable, roughly one-to-two-digit number.

sections.heading: A regional recipe, not a universal law
sections.body: The A0(delta) attenuation table was fit to the specific crust, attenuation structure, and typical hypocentral depths of Southern California in the 1930s. Ship that same table to the Pacific Northwest, the Andes, or a region with very different Q (attenuation) structure and it silently mis-estimates magnitude, because waves lose energy at different rates over different rock. Consequently, essentially every seismic network now runs its own regionally recalibrated ML, sometimes using digital broadband records with a simulated Wood-Anderson response rather than an actual torsion instrument, but every version amounts to refitting Richter's original method locally rather than importing his 1935 numbers wholesale.

lessons.workedExample: A Wood-Anderson seismometer 100 km from an epicenter records a maximum trace amplitude of 10 mm. Richter's calibration fixes A0(100 km) so that a 1 mm amplitude there corresponds to ML 3.0. Since ML = log10(A) - log10(A0), and A0 at 100 km is defined as 0.001 mm on this log scale (giving log A0 = -3 so that ML = log10(1) - (-3) = 3 when A = 1 mm), a 10 mm amplitude gives log10(10) - (-3) = 1 + 3 = 4.0. Ten times the amplitude at the same distance means exactly one more magnitude unit -- ML 4.0.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'what does magnitude actually measure' is testing whether a student knows ML is not a direct physical quantity like force or energy -- it is a calibrated logarithm of a specific instrument's trace amplitude, corrected for distance. The strong answer names the Wood-Anderson seismometer, the log-amplitude structure, and the crucial caveat that the distance correction is regionally fit, so a network's ML values are only comparable to other networks that used a compatible calibration. A student who treats magnitude as a universal, instrument-free number has missed why moment magnitude was later needed at all.

questions.prompt: Richter's local magnitude ML is defined using amplitude measured on which instrument?

options.text: A broadband digital seismometer with no fixed response
The Wood-Anderson torsion seismometer
A strong-motion accelerometer
A tide gauge

explanations.a: ML was defined around one specific fixed-response instrument, not a generic broadband sensor.
explanations.b: Correct -- Richter (1935) defined ML around the Wood-Anderson torsion seismometer's trace amplitude, with its characteristic 0.8 s period and damping.
explanations.c: Accelerometers record acceleration for strong-motion engineering purposes, not the displacement trace Richter used.
explanations.d: Tide gauges measure sea level and are unrelated to Richter's magnitude definition.

questions.prompt: If earthquake B produces a Wood-Anderson trace amplitude exactly 100 times larger than earthquake A at the same distance, how do their ML values compare?

options.text: B is 100 units higher
B is 10 units higher
B is 2 units higher
B is the same magnitude

explanations.a: That would treat magnitude as linear in amplitude; it is logarithmic, so 100x amplitude is not 100 units.
explanations.b: Ten units would correspond to a 10-billion-fold amplitude ratio, far more than 100x.
explanations.c: Correct -- since ML is a base-10 log of amplitude, a 100x amplitude ratio is log10(100) = 2 magnitude units.
explanations.d: Equal magnitude would require equal amplitude at the same distance; a 100x difference is far from equal.

questions.prompt: Match each term from Richter's local magnitude scale to what it represents.

left.text: The 1 mm at 100 km calibration point

right.text: Empirical distance-attenuation correction table
The fixed anchor defining ML = 3.0
0.8 s natural period, 0.8 damping, ~2800 (later ~2080) magnification
Refitting the attenuation table to local crust/Q structure

questions.explanation: A0(delta) is the attenuation table; the 1 mm-at-100 km point anchors the zero of the scale; the Wood-Anderson response defines what 'amplitude' physically means; and modern networks refit A0(delta) locally because attenuation structure varies by region.

questions.prompt: Why can Richter's original 1935 A0(delta) attenuation table give wrong magnitudes if applied unmodified outside Southern California?

options.text: Because it was fit to that region's specific crustal attenuation, and other regions attenuate seismic waves differently
Because the Wood-Anderson instrument only exists in California
Because ML cannot be computed for any earthquake outside California
Because the logarithm only works for base-10 numbers in California

explanations.a: Correct -- the distance correction encodes how fast amplitude decays with distance in a specific crust, which varies region to region.
explanations.b: Wood-Anderson-type instruments and their simulated digital equivalents are used worldwide; the instrument itself is not the limiting factor.
explanations.c: ML is computed globally, just with regionally refit attenuation tables -- it is not restricted to California.
explanations.d: Logarithms are a universal mathematical operation with no geographic dependence; the issue is the empirical calibration data, not the math.

lessons.label: Body-Wave, Surface-Wave, and the Saturation Problem

sections.heading: Two more scales, tuned to two more waves
sections.body: Richter's ML worked only for shallow, nearby Southern California events, so Beno Gutenberg extended magnitude to earthquakes recorded globally by building two more scales around two different wave types. Body-wave magnitude mb measures the amplitude A and dominant period T of the first few seconds of P waves -- in the modern short-period band, typically around a 1-second period -- through a formula of the general form mb = log10(A/T) + Q(delta, depth), where Q is an empirical correction for distance and focal depth. Surface-wave magnitude Ms instead measures the amplitude of roughly 20-second-period Rayleigh waves; the standard modern version, the Prague formula adopted by IASPEI, is Ms = log10(A/T) + 1.66 log10(delta) + 3.3, calibrated for shallow teleseismic events. Both scales inherit Richter's logic -- log of an amplitude, plus a distance correction -- and differ mainly in which wave, and therefore which period, they read.

sections.heading: The bandwidth problem: a stopwatch that only reads one tick
sections.body: Both scales share a hidden assumption: that the amplitude of a wave measured near one fixed period is a reliable proxy for the earthquake's total size. That assumption breaks down as ruptures grow. A magnitude-8 or -9 rupture is not a bigger version of a magnitude-5 rupture radiating faster -- it is a fault tens to hundreds of kilometers long that takes tens of seconds to minutes to slip, radiating most of its energy at periods much longer than 1 or even 20 seconds. Measuring such a rupture with a 1-second P-wave amplitude is like trying to weigh a truck with a bathroom scale: past some size, the needle stops climbing, even though the truck keeps getting heavier. This is saturation.

sections.heading: Where each scale runs out of headroom
sections.body: In practice mb saturates around magnitude 6.5 -- beyond that point, larger true earthquakes barely raise the measured 1-second P-wave amplitude, because the rupture radiates so much of its energy at long periods that the short-period band no longer tracks total moment. Ms, built on a longer 20-second period, has more headroom and holds up better, but even it saturates in the range of about Ms 8.3 to 8.5. The classic demonstration is the pair Kanamori used in 1977 when he introduced moment magnitude: the 1960 Chile earthquake and the 1964 Alaska earthquake were assigned Ms values of only about 8.3 and 8.4 -- nearly indistinguishable -- yet their seismic moments differ by roughly a factor of three, putting them at Mw 9.5 and Mw 9.2. Twenty seconds simply is not long enough to sample ruptures lasting several minutes, and that gap is exactly what moment magnitude was built to close.

lessons.workedExample: Two earthquakes rupture for very different durations: one for 15 seconds, one for 150 seconds, and both are measured with a 20-second-period Rayleigh wave. For the 15-second rupture, one cycle of the wave is longer than the entire rupture -- only about three-quarters of a cycle (15/20 = 0.75) elapses while the fault is still slipping -- so a single swing of that wave is driven by essentially the whole source, and its amplitude scales sensibly with the earthquake's size. For the 150-second rupture the ratio flips: the wave runs through roughly seven and a half cycles (150/20 = 7.5) before the fault stops moving, and any one 20-second cycle spans only about an eighth of the rupture's duration. Each measured cycle therefore carries only the slice of moment released during those 20 seconds, not the total, so the peak 20-second amplitude stops growing once ruptures get much longer than 20 seconds and Ms underestimates the second earthquake even though its true moment release may be vastly larger.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe saturation because it exposes whether a student understands magnitude scales as measurements with a physical bandwidth, not abstract numbers. The strong answer explains saturation as a mismatch between the period of the wave being measured and the duration of the rupture -- a short-period measurement registers only a slice of a slow, drawn-out process, the way a fast shutter speed captures only an instant of a long, slow movement. A student who instead says 'the scale just maxes out' without explaining why has memorized the fact but not the mechanism, which is the actual content being tested here.

questions.prompt: Body-wave magnitude mb is calculated from P waves at approximately what period, and Ms from Rayleigh waves at approximately what period?

options.text: mb from 1-second P waves; Ms from 20-second Rayleigh waves
mb from 20-second P waves; Ms from 1-second Rayleigh waves
Both are measured at the same 10-second period
mb from 100-second P waves; Ms from 5-second Rayleigh waves

explanations.a: Correct -- mb uses roughly 1-second P-wave amplitude/period; Ms uses roughly 20-second Rayleigh-wave amplitude.
explanations.b: This reverses the actual period assignments of the two scales.
explanations.c: The two scales are deliberately built on different periods, which is exactly why they saturate at different magnitudes.
explanations.d: These periods are far outside either scale's actual definition.

questions.prompt: Which best explains why mb saturates at a lower magnitude (around 6.5) than Ms (around 8.3-8.5)?

options.text: mb uses a much shorter-period wave, which cannot sense the long durations of very large ruptures
mb is measured at more seismic stations than Ms
mb saturates later because P waves travel faster than surface waves
The two scales use different logarithm bases

explanations.a: Correct -- the shorter ~1 s period of mb runs out of headroom sooner because large ruptures radiate much of their energy at periods far longer than 1 s.
explanations.b: Station count does not determine saturation; the period of the measured wave does.
explanations.c: P-wave travel speed is unrelated to why the amplitude reading saturates.
explanations.d: Both scales use base-10 logarithms; the difference lies in the wave period sampled, not the math.

questions.prompt: A rupture lasts 150 seconds and is measured with a 20-second-period Rayleigh wave. What happens during that rupture, and why does it cause Ms to saturate?

options.text: The wave completes about 7.5 cycles, so any single 20-second cycle reflects only about an eighth of the moment released -- the peak amplitude never registers the total
The wave completes only a fraction of one cycle, so it never finishes a full swing and the amplitude reads near zero
The wave's period stretches to match the 150-second rupture, so the amplitude grows without limit
The wave is absorbed by the crust before the rupture ends, so no amplitude is recorded at all

explanations.a: Correct -- 150/20 = 7.5 cycles fit inside the rupture, and each one samples only the slip occurring in its own 20 seconds, so the largest single-cycle amplitude stops tracking total moment.
explanations.b: Backwards: a rupture far longer than the wave period contains many cycles, not less than one. A rupture shorter than 20 seconds is the case where less than a full cycle elapses.
explanations.c: A 20-second measurement band is fixed by the instrument and procedure; it does not stretch to match the source.
explanations.d: Attenuation is handled by the distance term in the Ms formula and is not what causes saturation.

questions.prompt: Order these events from shortest to longest characteristic period/duration being discussed in this lesson.

items.text: The ~1 second period used for mb
The ~20 second period used for Ms
A rupture duration of roughly 150 seconds, as in a great subduction earthquake

questions.explanation: mb's ~1 s period is shortest, Ms's ~20 s period is longer but still short compared to the multi-minute rupture duration of the largest earthquakes, which is exactly why both magnitude scales run out of headroom before moment magnitude does.

lessons.label: Moment Magnitude and the Biggest Earthquakes

sections.heading: Anchoring magnitude to the physics of the fault
sections.body: Hiroo Kanamori, in 1977, proposed replacing amplitude-based magnitudes with one derived directly from seismic moment M0 -- a physical quantity defined as M0 = mu * A * D, the product of the shear modulus of the rock, the ruptured fault area, and the average slip across it. Moment is computed from the low-frequency, long-period part of the seismic spectrum or from geodetic and geologic measurements of the fault itself, so it does not depend on a single fixed-period wave amplitude the way mb or Ms do. Thomas Hanks and Kanamori formalized the conversion in 1979 with the now-standard formula Mw = (2/3) log10(M0) - 10.7, with M0 expressed in dyne-centimeters, chosen so that Mw values line up closely with Ms and ML in the moderate-magnitude range where those older scales still behave well.

sections.heading: Why it does not saturate
sections.body: Because moment is built from fault area and slip rather than a wave's amplitude at one fixed period, Mw keeps climbing correctly no matter how large or how slowly a rupture unfolds -- there is no bandwidth ceiling analogous to the mb or Ms saturation problem. The mechanism behind this is spectral: every earthquake's displacement spectrum is flat at low frequencies, below a source-dependent corner frequency, and only rolls off above it. M0 is read from the height of that flat, low-frequency plateau, not from any single fixed-period amplitude -- so as a rupture grows larger and slower, its corner frequency simply shifts to lower frequencies, and the plateau (and the M0 estimate drawn from it) keeps growing right along with it, with no fixed 'tick mark' on the spectrum for the source to run out of room against. This is precisely why Mw is now the standard scale reported for any earthquake large enough for the difference to matter, and why the historical record for the world's largest earthquakes had to be revised once moment magnitude became available.

sections.heading: The record holders, and how fast Mw can now be known
sections.body: By Mw, the four largest instrumentally recorded earthquakes are the 1960 Valdivia, Chile earthquake at Mw 9.5 (the largest ever recorded), the 1964 Prince William Sound, Alaska earthquake (the Good Friday earthquake) at Mw 9.2, the 2004 Sumatra-Andaman earthquake at Mw 9.1, and the 2011 Tohoku, Japan earthquake at Mw 9.0. All four are subduction-zone megathrust ruptures, the only tectonic setting capable of generating fault areas large enough to produce moments in this range. Today, agencies such as the USGS routinely issue a preliminary Mw estimate within minutes of a large earthquake using W-phase or centroid moment tensor inversion of long-period waveforms, refining it as more distant stations report in over the following tens of minutes to hours.

lessons.workedExample: The 2011 Tohoku earthquake had an estimated seismic moment M0 of roughly 5 x 10^22 newton-meters, which converts to about 5 x 10^29 dyne-cm (1 N*m = 10^7 dyne-cm). Plugging into Mw = (2/3) log10(M0) - 10.7 with M0 = 5 x 10^29: log10(5 x 10^29) is about 29.7, two-thirds of that is about 19.8, minus 10.7 gives Mw about 9.1 -- consistent with the reported value of about Mw 9.0 to 9.1 for Tohoku, illustrating how directly the fault-area-and-slip quantity M0 converts into the reported magnitude.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking 'what does moment magnitude actually measure, and why did it replace Ms for big earthquakes' is checking whether a student can connect a formula to physical mechanism rather than reciting Mw as just 'the modern Richter scale.' The strong answer names seismic moment as fault area times slip times rigidity, explains that this quantity has no fixed-period bandwidth limit, and can place real numbers on the largest recorded earthquakes. It signals real understanding to note that Mw is now estimated within minutes for a fast tsunami warning, not just calculated after the fact from a slow post-processed dataset.

questions.prompt: Seismic moment M0 is defined as the product of which three quantities?

options.text: Rock shear modulus, ruptured fault area, and average slip
P-wave amplitude, dominant period, and distance
Earthquake depth, magnitude, and duration
Peak ground acceleration, station count, and epicentral distance

explanations.a: Correct -- M0 = mu * A * D: shear modulus (rigidity) times fault area times average slip.
explanations.b: That combination describes inputs to amplitude-based scales like mb, not the physical definition of moment.
explanations.c: Depth, magnitude, and duration are not the three quantities that define seismic moment.
explanations.d: Peak ground acceleration and distance describe shaking intensity measurement, not the moment tensor's physical definition.

questions.prompt: Why does Mw not suffer the saturation problem that affects mb and Ms?

options.text: Because it is derived from fault area and slip rather than a fixed-period wave amplitude
Because Mw uses a higher-frequency wave than mb
Because Mw was calibrated using more seismometers worldwide
Because Mw is only reported for earthquakes below magnitude 6.5

explanations.a: Correct -- since Mw is built from the physical quantity M0 rather than one fixed wave period's amplitude, there is no bandwidth ceiling for it to run into.
explanations.b: Mw uses long-period spectral information or geodetic/geologic slip, not a higher-frequency wave.
explanations.c: Station count affects precision, not whether the underlying scale has a saturation ceiling.
explanations.d: Mw is precisely the scale used for the largest earthquakes, well above 6.5, which is the opposite of this claim.
