questions.prompt: Order these four earthquakes from largest to smallest moment magnitude.

items.text: 1960 Valdivia, Chile
1964 Prince William Sound, Alaska
2004 Sumatra-Andaman
2011 Tohoku, Japan

questions.explanation: By Mw, 1960 Chile (9.5) is the largest instrumentally recorded earthquake, followed by 1964 Alaska (9.2), 2004 Sumatra (9.1), and 2011 Tohoku (9.0) -- all four are subduction megathrust ruptures.

questions.prompt: In the Hanks and Kanamori (1979) formula Mw = (2/3) log10(M0) - 10.7, in what unit must M0 be expressed?

options.text: Dyne-centimeters
Newton-meters
Joules
Kilograms

explanations.a: Correct -- the standard Hanks-Kanamori (1979) formula is calibrated for M0 in dyne-cm; using newton-meters directly would shift the result by a constant offset.
explanations.b: Newton-meters is the SI unit for moment, but the -10.7 constant in this specific formula is calibrated for dyne-cm, not newton-meters.
explanations.c: Joules measure energy, a related but distinct quantity from seismic moment.
explanations.d: Kilograms measure mass, not the fault-area-times-slip-times-rigidity quantity that is seismic moment.

lessons.label: Energy, Apparent Stress, and What Magnitude Hides

sections.heading: Moment is not energy
sections.body: Seismic moment M0 measures how much fault slipped and over what area -- it says nothing directly about how violently that slip radiated seismic waves versus how much energy was lost to heat and fracturing at the fault. Radiated seismic energy Es is a separate quantity, and Kanamori's widely used approximation relates them as Es is roughly M0 / (2 x 10^4), an empirical ratio built on the assumption of a roughly constant stress drop across earthquakes. Because moment magnitude is built from log10(M0) with a 2/3 exponent, and energy scales close to linearly with M0 in this approximation, radiated energy grows roughly as 10^(1.5 x Mw) -- about 31.6-fold more energy per whole magnitude unit, and about 1000-fold (10^3) more energy per two magnitude units.

sections.heading: Apparent stress: a diagnostic for how an earthquake actually broke
sections.body: Because Es/M0 is not truly constant across all earthquakes, seismologists use the deviation as a diagnostic. Apparent stress, defined as roughly mu times the ratio Es/M0 (rigidity times the energy-to-moment ratio), estimates how efficiently the available stress on the fault converted into radiated seismic energy versus heat, fracturing, and slow afterslip. A rupture with unusually low apparent stress radiated its energy inefficiently for its size -- it moved a lot of rock a long way (high moment) without shaking nearly as hard as that moment would normally predict. Typical earthquakes cluster in the range of roughly 0.1 to 10 MPa of apparent stress, so that range is the yardstick against which 'unusually low' is judged; the tsunami earthquakes discussed below fall well under 1 MPa, an order of magnitude or more below an ordinary rupture of the same moment.

sections.heading: Tsunami earthquakes: the case where magnitude actively misleads
sections.body: The 1992 Nicaragua earthquake is the textbook case. Its surface-wave magnitude Ms was only about 7.0 to 7.2 -- and shaking onshore was so mild it barely reached modified Mercalli intensity III, hardly felt by residents -- yet its moment magnitude Mw was 7.6 to 7.7, and its rupture unfolded over an unusually long 100 to 150 seconds rather than the tens of seconds typical of that size. The mismatch reflected genuinely low apparent stress: a slow, low-rigidity, near-trench rupture radiated weak high-frequency shaking (so people were not warned) while still displacing enormous seafloor area, generating a tsunami with run-up of 3 to 8 m that killed about 170 people. It is the clearest illustration that energy and moment are not interchangeable, and that a slow-source earthquake can be catastrophic exactly because its shaking undersells its true size.

lessons.workedExample: Two hypothetical earthquakes both have Mw 7.0, so both have the same seismic moment M0. If earthquake A has typical apparent stress, its radiated energy Es follows Kanamori's Es = M0/(2x10^4) approximation directly. If earthquake B is a tsunami-earthquake-style slow rupture with apparent stress five times lower than typical, its Es is only about one-fifth of earthquake A's, even though both have identical M0 and identical Mw. A coastal resident feeling earthquake B would sense far weaker shaking than the 'Mw 7.0' label implies -- while the seafloor displacement, and therefore the tsunami hazard, is unchanged.
lessons.judgeFraming: This concept is exactly the kind of thing a science-fair judge probes to see if a student understands the difference between a proxy and the thing it stands for. A magnitude number is a proxy for fault size, not a direct measurement of shaking violence or hazard, and the 1992 Nicaragua case is the sharpest real-world proof: modest Ms, mild shaking, yet a deadly tsunami. A student who can explain apparent stress as an efficiency ratio -- how much of the available energy became shaking versus heat and slow slip -- has grasped that magnitude alone cannot be trusted to predict every hazard.

questions.prompt: Using the approximation that radiated energy scales as roughly 10^(1.5 x Mw), about how many times more energy does a magnitude 7.0 earthquake radiate compared to a magnitude 6.0 earthquake?

options.text: About 10 times more
About 31.6 times more
About 100 times more
About 1000 times more

explanations.a: A factor of 10 would apply if energy scaled linearly with magnitude, not with the 1.5 exponent this scale uses.
explanations.b: Correct -- one whole magnitude unit corresponds to 10^1.5, or about 31.6 times more radiated energy.
explanations.c: 100-fold (10^2) is not what a 1.5 exponent per unit produces for a single magnitude step.
explanations.d: A 1000-fold jump corresponds to two magnitude units, not one.

questions.prompt: What made the 1992 Nicaragua earthquake a classic 'tsunami earthquake'?

options.text: Its Ms was much higher than its Mw, so it shook harder than the tsunami warranted
Its Ms was much lower than its Mw, its shaking was mild, its rupture unusually slow, yet it produced a large deadly tsunami
It had no measurable seismic moment at all
It was a strike-slip rupture with no vertical seafloor displacement

explanations.a: This reverses the actual mismatch -- shaking was weaker, not stronger, than its true size implied.
explanations.b: Correct -- Ms of about 7.0-7.2 versus Mw of about 7.6-7.7, mild onshore shaking (barely Mercalli III), a slow 100-150 s rupture, and a deadly 3-8 m tsunami runup.
explanations.c: The earthquake had a well-estimated, substantial seismic moment; the mismatch was between Ms and Mw, not an absence of moment.
explanations.d: It was a subduction thrust event with vertical seafloor displacement, which is precisely what generated the tsunami.

questions.prompt: Match each quantity to what it represents.

right.text: Rigidity times fault area times average slip
Roughly M0 divided by 2 x 10^4 under Kanamori's approximation
Rigidity times the energy-to-moment ratio Es/M0
A slow, low apparent-stress rupture with mild shaking but a deadly tsunami

questions.explanation: M0 is the fault-geometry quantity (rigidity x area x slip); Es is the radiated-energy approximation tied to M0; apparent stress is the efficiency ratio (rigidity x Es/M0); and 1992 Nicaragua is the real case where low apparent stress produced weak shaking alongside a devastating tsunami.

lessons.label: The Gutenberg-Richter Law and the b-Value Debate

sections.heading: A power law for how many earthquakes happen at each size
sections.body: In 1944, Gutenberg and Richter showed that if you count earthquakes above some magnitude M in a region over a fixed time window, the counts follow log10 N = a - bM, where N is the cumulative number of earthquakes at or above M, a describes overall regional seismic productivity, and b -- almost always close to 1.0 worldwide -- describes how quickly the number of earthquakes drops off as magnitude increases. A b near 1.0 means each whole magnitude step down brings roughly ten times as many earthquakes: for every magnitude-6, expect roughly ten magnitude-5s and a hundred magnitude-4s in that same catalog and time window.

sections.heading: Fitting b in practice: completeness and Aki's estimator
sections.body: Before fitting b, an analyst must find the magnitude of completeness Mc, the smallest magnitude above which the catalog reliably detects every earthquake that occurred (below Mc, small events are missed simply because the network is not sensitive enough, which would artificially bend the count-versus-magnitude curve). Above Mc, Aki (1965) derived a maximum-likelihood estimator for b, based on the fact that magnitudes above a threshold are distributed exponentially: b works out to log10(e) divided by the difference between the mean magnitude of the catalog and Mc (adjusted by half the magnitude bin width for a discretized catalog). Aki's estimator is now the standard for computing b in a seismicity catalog rather than eyeballing a slope on a log-count plot.

sections.heading: The live argument: does b actually forecast anything?
sections.body: Christopher Scholz's 1968 lab experiments found that acoustic-emission b-values from fracturing rock samples fall as differential stress rises, and his 2015 recalibration quantified that relationship directly -- giving b a physical reading as an inverse proxy for stress: low b, high stress. Building on that idea, Laura Gulia and Stefan Wiemer proposed in 2019 a 'traffic-light' forecasting system: because b-values reportedly drop before mainshocks (higher stress, fewer small events relative to large) and rise during aftershock sequences (stress relief), a real-time drop in local b could flag an ongoing sequence as more likely to culminate in a larger event. The idea remains genuinely contested -- laboratory rock-fracture experiments show the stress relationship cleanly, but field catalogs are noisier, Mc shifts during an active sequence in ways that can fake a b-value change, and follow-up studies applying the traffic-light method to new sequences have produced mixed results, so b-value forecasting is an active research question rather than settled science.

lessons.workedExample: A regional catalog above its magnitude of completeness Mc = 2.0 has a mean magnitude of 2.44 (bin width 0.1, so the half-bin correction is 0.05). Aki's estimator gives b = log10(e) / (mean magnitude - Mc + half bin) = 0.4343 / (2.44 - 2.0 + 0.05) = 0.4343 / 0.49, which is about 0.89 -- a slightly below-average b consistent with a moderately high-stress patch of the fault system, the kind of reading a Gulia-Wiemer-style traffic-light analysis would flag as worth watching rather than dismissing as noise.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing the Gutenberg-Richter law and b-value is testing whether a student can distinguish a robust empirical regularity (the log-linear relationship itself, and b clustering near 1.0) from a genuinely unsettled forecasting claim (whether a local b-value drop predicts a coming mainshock). The strong answer states the law, explains why Mc must be estimated before b can be trusted, and then explicitly flags the b-as-stress-proxy and pre-mainshock-drop ideas as debated rather than proven -- naming Scholz's stress relationship and the Gulia-Wiemer traffic-light concept while being honest that field results disagree with the clean lab picture is exactly the kind of calibrated uncertainty a judge wants to see.

questions.prompt: In the Gutenberg-Richter law log10 N = a - bM, what does a b-value close to 1.0 imply about a region's earthquakes?

options.text: Roughly ten times as many earthquakes occur one magnitude unit lower
Exactly the same number of earthquakes occur at every magnitude
Earthquakes only occur above magnitude 1.0
The region has no small earthquakes at all

explanations.a: Correct -- with b near 1.0, the cumulative count grows roughly tenfold for each magnitude unit decrease, per the log-linear relationship.
explanations.b: A flat count across magnitudes would require b = 0, not b near 1.0.
explanations.c: b describes the slope of the count-versus-magnitude relationship, not a minimum magnitude cutoff.
explanations.d: The law describes a steady decline in frequency with increasing magnitude, not an absence of small events -- small events are typically the most numerous.

questions.prompt: Why must the magnitude of completeness Mc be estimated before fitting a b-value with Aki's maximum-likelihood method?

options.text: Below Mc, the seismic network misses many small earthquakes, which would distort the count-versus-magnitude slope if included
Mc has no effect on the b-value calculation
Aki's method requires magnitudes measured only in mb, never Mw
Mc determines the fault's rigidity, which is unrelated to b

explanations.a: Correct -- below Mc, detection is incomplete, so small-magnitude counts are artificially low, which would bias the fitted b if those magnitudes were included.
explanations.b: Mc is a required input to Aki's formula; including data below it directly biases the estimate.
explanations.c: Aki's estimator is agnostic to which magnitude scale is used, as long as it is applied consistently.
explanations.d: Mc is a catalog-detection threshold, unrelated to rock rigidity.

questions.prompt: Match each researcher or study to their contribution discussed in this lesson.

right.text: Formulated log10 N = a - bM from earthquake catalog counts
Derived the maximum-likelihood estimator for b above Mc
Showed b falls as differential stress rises in lab fracture experiments
Proposed a real-time traffic-light system using b-value drops to flag possible foreshock sequences

questions.explanation: Gutenberg and Richter established the log-linear frequency-magnitude law; Aki gave the maximum-likelihood way to fit b; Scholz linked b to differential stress in lab experiments; and Gulia and Wiemer proposed using real-time b-value drops as a foreshock-forecasting signal, a still-debated method.

lessons.label: Aftershocks, Foreshocks, and Clustering

sections.heading: A decay law more than a century old
sections.body: Fusakichi Omori, in 1894, found that aftershock rates following a mainshock decay predictably over time, fitting n(t) = K / (t + c), where n(t) is the rate of aftershocks at time t after the mainshock, K sets the overall productivity, and c is a small early-time offset. Utsu, in 1957, showed that many real sequences decay somewhat faster than Omori's original law predicts and generalized it to n(t) = K / (t + c)^p, with the exponent p typically between about 0.9 and 1.5 -- this modified Omori-Utsu law is still the standard curve fit to real aftershock sequences today, over a century after Omori's original paper.

sections.heading: Bath's law: a strangely consistent gap
sections.body: Markus Bath, in the 1960s, noticed an empirical regularity independent of a mainshock's absolute size: the largest aftershock in a sequence is, on average, about 1.2 magnitude units smaller than its mainshock, whether the mainshock is magnitude 5 or magnitude 9. Because magnitude is logarithmic, a 1.2-unit gap corresponds to the largest aftershock releasing roughly one-sixty-third the energy of the mainshock. Bath's law is a statistical regularity rather than a strict rule -- sequences occasionally produce an aftershock that violates it, and when the 'aftershock' turns out comparable to or larger than the initial event, seismologists reclassify the sequence as two separate mainshocks rather than a mainshock-aftershock pair.

sections.heading: ETAS: modeling every earthquake as a possible trigger
sections.body: Yosihiko Ogata's 1988 Epidemic-Type Aftershock Sequence (ETAS) model generalizes Omori-Utsu into a full statistical engine for seismicity: every earthquake, not just a designated mainshock, can trigger its own cascade of aftershocks following the same Omori-Utsu decay and Gutenberg-Richter magnitude distribution, so a sequence's full rate is the sum of contributions from every prior event. ETAS underlies today's operational aftershock forecasts, the short-term probability statements agencies issue after a damaging earthquake -- but it also reframed a harder question: if any earthquake can trigger any other, are foreshocks a physically distinct precursory process, or just ordinary triggered seismicity that only earns the label 'foreshock' in hindsight, once a bigger event follows? Agnes Helmstetter and Didier Sornette argued in 2003 that ordinary cascade triggering alone reproduces the statistical properties of real foreshock sequences without invoking any special precursory physics, a view still actively tested against cases like the two-day, Mw 7.3-led foreshock sequence before the 2011 Tohoku earthquake and the roughly year-long, migrating foreshock sequence before the 2014 Iquique, Chile earthquake.

lessons.workedExample: A magnitude 7.0 mainshock is followed, by Bath's law, by a largest aftershock expected around magnitude 5.8 (7.0 minus 1.2). Using the Omori-Utsu law with p = 1.0, if the aftershock rate one day after the mainshock is 50 events per day above the catalog's completeness threshold, the modified law predicts the rate ten days later falls to roughly K/(10+c)^1 -- for c small compared to 10, that is close to one-tenth of the day-1 rate, or about 5 events per day, illustrating how quickly, and how predictably, an aftershock sequence quiets down even though it never fully stops.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking about aftershock statistics is testing whether a student can tell a genuinely predictive empirical law (Omori-Utsu decay, Bath's law, ETAS forecasting) from an open scientific argument dressed up as settled fact. The strong answer states the decay law and Bath's regularity with real numbers, explains that ETAS treats every earthquake as a potential trigger, and then explicitly frames the foreshock question as unresolved -- citing that ordinary cascade-triggering models can reproduce foreshock statistics without new physics, while pointing at cases like Tohoku 2011 and Iquique 2014 as the real data the debate is fought over, rather than asserting foreshocks are either a known warning sign or pure hindsight bias.

questions.prompt: What change did Utsu (1957) make to Omori's original 1894 aftershock decay law?

options.text: He added an exponent p, since many real sequences decay faster than the original 1/(t+c) form
He removed the time dependence entirely
He replaced aftershock rate with magnitude of completeness
He proved Omori's original law never fit any real sequence

explanations.a: Correct -- Utsu generalized n(t)=K/(t+c) to n(t)=K/(t+c)^p, since real decay is often faster than p=1 predicts.
explanations.b: The modified law is still explicitly a function of time; it was generalized, not stripped of time dependence.
explanations.c: Magnitude of completeness is a separate concept from Utsu's aftershock-rate modification.
explanations.d: Omori's original law fits many sequences reasonably; Utsu's point was that an added exponent improves the fit further, not that the original was useless.

questions.prompt: According to Bath's law, roughly how does the largest aftershock's magnitude compare to its mainshock's, and does this gap depend on the mainshock's size?

options.text: About 1.2 magnitude units smaller, and roughly independent of mainshock size
About 1.2 magnitude units smaller, but only for mainshocks below magnitude 6
About equal to the mainshock, regardless of size
About 1.2 magnitude units larger than the mainshock

explanations.a: Correct -- Bath's law states the gap is about 1.2 magnitude units on average, holding roughly regardless of whether the mainshock is small or great.
explanations.b: The regularity is reported across mainshock sizes generally, not restricted to smaller mainshocks.
explanations.c: An aftershock comparable to the mainshock would violate Bath's law and typically gets reclassified as a second mainshock.
explanations.d: The largest aftershock is smaller than the mainshock, not larger -- this reverses the direction of the gap.

questions.prompt: Order these developments in aftershock/foreshock science chronologically.

items.text: Omori's original aftershock decay law
Utsu's modified decay law with exponent p
Bath's empirical mainshock-to-largest-aftershock gap
Ogata's ETAS model

questions.explanation: Omori published the original 1894 decay law, Utsu generalized it with an exponent in 1957, Bath's regularity followed in the 1960s, and Ogata's ETAS model, unifying triggering across all earthquakes, came in 1988.

questions.prompt: What is the core unresolved question about foreshocks that this lesson raises, using the 2011 Tohoku and 2014 Iquique sequences as examples?

options.text: Whether foreshocks reflect a distinct precursory physical process or are ordinary triggered seismicity only labeled 'foreshocks' in hindsight
Whether earthquakes can be predicted to the exact day using foreshocks
Whether foreshocks always occur before every large earthquake
Whether Omori's law applies only to foreshocks and never to aftershocks

explanations.a: Correct -- Helmstetter and Sornette's cascade-triggering argument versus the idea of special precursory physics is the live debate, tested against real sequences like Tohoku 2011 and Iquique 2014.
explanations.b: This lesson does not claim exact-day prediction is possible; the debate is about mechanism and hindsight labeling, not day-level forecasting.
explanations.c: Not every large earthquake has an identified foreshock sequence, so universality is not the claim being debated here.
explanations.d: Omori's law was formulated for aftershock decay, and the ETAS framework applies triggering broadly, not as an inversion restricted to foreshocks only.

units.label: Landmark Work and Open Debates

lessons.label: 1906 San Francisco and the Birth of Earthquake Science

sections.heading: A disaster becomes a research program
sections.body: The April 18, 1906 San Francisco earthquake killed roughly 3,000 people and burned much of the city, but it also produced the first systematic scientific investigation of an earthquake. California's governor appointed a State Earthquake Investigation Commission chaired by geologist Andrew Lawson; more than twenty scientists mapped the rupture along roughly 480 km (about 300 miles) of the San Andreas Fault, surveyed offset fences and roads, and compiled felt reports. Their findings appeared as the two-volume Lawson Report in 1908 — the template for how earthquakes would be studied ever since: go to the field, measure the fault, don't just describe the shaking.

sections.heading: Reid's elastic rebound theory
sections.body: The Lawson Report's most consequential contribution came from geologist Henry Fielding Reid, who compared triangulation surveys of the region from the 1850s–1880s against post-earthquake resurveys. He found that points on opposite sides of the fault, tens of kilometers apart, had crept about 3.2 meters relative to each other over the preceding half-century — while the fault itself stayed locked. Reid's 1910 synthesis proposed elastic rebound: rock on either side of a locked fault bends and stores elastic strain energy for decades, then snaps back past its unstrained shape when the fault finally slips, releasing that energy as an earthquake. This became — and remains — the standard model of the earthquake cycle.

sections.heading: Milne's global instruments make it recordable
sections.body: None of this geodetic detective work would have meant much without instruments to record shaking precisely, and that piece came from Japan, not California. British geologist John Milne, teaching in Tokyo, was jolted by the 1880 Yokohama earthquake into co-founding the Seismological Society of Japan and building a horizontal-pendulum seismograph sensitive enough to capture ground motion as a readable trace. By the early 1900s, Milne was coordinating roughly 40 stations worldwide, each reporting back to his home observatory at Shide on the Isle of Wight via standardized 'Milne circulars' that tabulated arrival times and amplitudes from every corner of the globe. That habit of routine, comparable, worldwide reporting is what gave 1906's California rupture — and every earthquake after it — a network capable of recording it precisely and comparing it against quakes elsewhere, and it laid the groundwork for the International Seismological Summary founded in 1918 — the direct ancestor of today's global earthquake catalogs.

lessons.workedExample: A surveyor in 1855 places a benchmark 20 km east of the San Andreas Fault and another 20 km west. Resurveying in 1906, Reid found the western benchmark had crept about 3.2 meters northwest relative to the eastern one over that half-century, while a fence crossing the fault trace itself was found offset by roughly 6 meters in the earthquake — evidence that decades of slow, silent strain had accumulated elastically in the crust and then released in seconds, exactly as the rebound model predicted.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks this because 1906 is the case study that shows how a single well-instrumented disaster becomes a durable scientific model rather than just a casualty count. A strong answer traces the actual inference chain: Lawson's commission collected the fault and geodetic data, Reid used repeat surveys (not the shaking itself) to infer decades of stored strain, and Milne's independent instrument network is what let quakes be measured and compared at all. A weak answer just says 'earthquakes are caused by faults slipping' without naming who showed that, how, or with what data.

questions.prompt: What kind of data did Reid actually use to formulate elastic rebound theory?

options.text: Seismograph traces of the 1906 shaking itself
Repeated geodetic surveys showing decades of slow crustal creep before the earthquake
Laboratory experiments bending small rock samples
Felt-intensity reports collected door-to-door after the quake

explanations.a: Reid's key evidence was pre- and post-earthquake land surveys, not the seismograph record of the shaking.
explanations.b: Correct — comparing triangulation surveys from decades before 1906 to post-earthquake resurveys showed roughly 3.2 m of accumulated relative motion, the evidence that strain had built up slowly and released suddenly.
explanations.c: No laboratory rock-bending experiments were involved in Reid's 1910 synthesis; it was field geodesy.
explanations.d: Felt reports helped map shaking intensity for the Lawson Report generally, but they are not what led Reid to elastic rebound.

questions.prompt: Order these events from earliest to latest.

items.text: Milne co-founds the Seismological Society of Japan after the Yokohama earthquake
The San Francisco earthquake ruptures the San Andreas Fault
The Lawson Report is published
Reid publishes the elastic rebound synthesis

questions.explanation: Milne's instrument-building followed the 1880 Yokohama earthquake; the San Francisco earthquake struck in 1906; the Lawson Report appeared in 1908; Reid's elastic rebound synthesis followed in 1910, built on the report's geodetic data.

questions.prompt: Match each person to their specific contribution.

right.text: Chaired the commission that mapped the fault rupture and compiled the 1908 report
Proposed elastic rebound from repeat geodetic surveys
Built the horizontal-pendulum seismograph and a global recording network

questions.explanation: Lawson led the investigation commission, Reid derived elastic rebound from geodetic data within that report, and Milne independently supplied the instruments that made global earthquake recording possible.

lessons.label: Reading Earth's Interior Off a Seismogram

sections.heading: Oldham finds the core in a shadow
sections.body: Nobody has ever drilled to Earth's core; every layer inside the planet was inferred from how seismic waves bend and vanish. Richard Dixon Oldham started the chain in his 1906 paper, comparing earthquake records at many distances and noticing that P waves arrived late, and S waves arrived weakened or missing entirely, at stations roughly 120° or more around the globe from an earthquake. Since S waves cannot travel through a fluid, Oldham argued this pattern meant the deep interior — a core he estimated at roughly 0.4 Earth's diameter — must be in a physically distinct state from the mantle, most plausibly fluid, unlike anything solid rock above it.

sections.heading: Mohorovičić finds the crust's floor
sections.body: Three years later, a much shallower discontinuity turned up close to home. Croatian seismologist Andrija Mohorovičić studied the October 8, 1909 Kupa Valley earthquake and noticed that stations beyond about 200 km recorded two separate sets of P arrivals — one direct, one faster. The only explanation was a sharp velocity jump, from roughly 6 km/s above to about 8 km/s below, at a boundary near 38 km depth beneath Croatia. That boundary — the crust-mantle discontinuity, now called the Moho — turned out to exist everywhere, just at different depths under oceans versus continents.

sections.heading: Gutenberg pins the core boundary; Lehmann finds a core within the core
sections.body: In 1913, Beno Gutenberg used the global shadow zone Oldham had identified to calculate exactly where the core began, placing the core-mantle boundary near 2,900 km depth — a figure still essentially accepted today. The boundary shows up so sharply because P-wave velocity drops abruptly there, from roughly 13.7 km/s in the lowermost mantle to about 8 km/s in the outer core, a contrast large enough to bend and partly reflect the wave energy that produces the shadow zone in the first place. That seemed to close the question until 1936, when Danish seismologist Inge Lehmann, studying a 1929 New Zealand earthquake, noticed faint P' arrivals inside the shadow zone where theory said no P energy should reach at all. In her famously terse paper titled simply 'P',' Lehmann deduced these anomalous arrivals were reflecting off a second, deeper boundary — evidence for a solid inner core nested inside the fluid outer core, confirmed by later researchers and now measured at a radius of roughly 1,220 km.

lessons.workedExample: Picture four seismometers at increasing distance from one quake. The nearest two, within about 100°, record clean P and S arrivals on schedule. A station near 120° records P but the S wave is missing or badly weakened — Oldham's shadow-zone signature of a fluid core. A station at roughly 130° should, by simple ray theory, receive no P energy at all, yet still records a faint, delayed P' pulse — Lehmann's signature. Two anomalies, same setup, two different boundaries: the outer one blocks S entirely; the inner one bends a sliver of P back out.
lessons.judgeFraming: This lesson matters to a judge because it is a clean example of inference from indirect evidence — nobody has seen the core, so the whole model rests on chains of reasoning from arrival times and missing waves at specific distances. A strong presenter can say which observation (delayed/missing S, a velocity-jump P pair, a shadow-zone P') supports which boundary, and in what order the boundaries were found. A weak one just recites 'crust, mantle, core' as a memorized diagram with no sense of how any of it was actually discovered.

questions.prompt: Why did the absence of S waves at large distances from an earthquake matter to Oldham's argument?

options.text: S waves cannot travel through fluid, so their disappearance implied a fluid deep interior
S waves are always weaker than P waves regardless of the material they cross
The seismometers of that era simply could not detect S waves at any distance
S waves disappear only near active volcanoes, unrelated to Earth's core

explanations.a: Correct — S waves require shear strength to propagate, so their absence at large angular distances pointed to a core in a physically different, fluid-like state.
explanations.b: S-wave amplitude relative to P depends on material properties, not a fixed universal ratio; the disappearance was localized to specific distances, which is the key clue.
explanations.c: Instrument limitations are not the explanation Oldham gave; the pattern was distance-dependent, matching a real physical boundary rather than instrument failure.
explanations.d: The effect is global and depth-related, not tied to volcanic activity.

questions.prompt: Order these seismological discoveries from earliest to latest.

items.text: Oldham identifies the shadow-zone evidence for Earth's core
Mohorovičić finds the crust-mantle velocity jump near 38 km depth
Gutenberg places the core-mantle boundary near 2,900 km
Lehmann deduces a solid inner core from faint P' arrivals

questions.explanation: Oldham's core evidence came in 1906, Mohorovičić's crust-mantle boundary in 1909, Gutenberg's core-mantle depth in 1913, and Lehmann's inner-core deduction in 1936.

questions.prompt: Match each researcher to the specific boundary or feature their data revealed.

right.text: Existence of a physically distinct, likely fluid core
Crust-mantle discontinuity near 38 km depth
Core-mantle boundary depth near 2,900 km
Solid inner core within the outer core

questions.explanation: Each researcher's data pinned down a distinct layer boundary: Oldham the core's existence, Mohorovičić the crust-mantle contact, Gutenberg its precise depth, and Lehmann the solid inner core nested within it.

lessons.label: Wadati, Benioff Zones, and the Deep-Earthquake Puzzle

sections.heading: Wadati finds a plane of deep hypocenters
sections.body: Earthquakes were long assumed to be a shallow, crustal phenomenon, confined to the outer few kilometers where rock is cold and brittle enough to fracture. That assumption broke in 1927, when Japanese seismologist Kiyoo Wadati published travel-time evidence for earthquakes occurring far deeper than 300 km beneath central Honshu — far below where ordinary brittle faulting should be possible. By his 1935 follow-up paper, Wadati had plotted lines of equal focal depth and shown these deep hypocenters were not scattered randomly but lined up along an inclined plane, dipping away from the Japan Trench down toward the Asian continent.

sections.heading: Benioff globalizes it, and plate tectonics explains it
sections.body: In the 1940s and 1950s, American seismologist Hugo Benioff compiled similar dipping planes of hypocenters beneath island arcs and trenches worldwide, showing this was not a Japan-specific quirk but a global pattern reaching depths near 700 km. Two events illustrate how much energy that deep zone can release. The 1994 Bolivia earthquake, magnitude 8.2 at roughly 631 km depth, was felt across much of South America despite its extreme depth, and held the record for the largest instrumentally recorded deep-focus earthquake until the 2013 Sea of Okhotsk earthquake, magnitude 8.3 at roughly 609 km depth, surpassed it. When plate tectonics coalesced as a unified theory in the 1960s, these dipping seismic zones — now called Wadati-Benioff zones — became some of the clearest direct evidence for subduction: they trace the outline of a cold, rigid oceanic plate sinking beneath another plate, lighting up with earthquakes as it bends and sinks.

sections.heading: But what actually breaks rock at 700 km?
sections.body: Locating the zones did not explain them. At depths beyond roughly 300 km, pressure and temperature should make rock ductile, flowing rather than fracturing suddenly — ordinary brittle faulting shouldn't work. Both the Bolivia and Sea of Okhotsk events sit well within this puzzling depth range, and the mechanism question remains genuinely open. One leading hypothesis, transformational faulting, proposed by Harry Green and Pamela Burnley in a 1989 Nature paper, argues that olivine in the cold core of a subducting slab can remain metastable, failing to convert to its denser high-pressure phase at the expected depth; when it finally transforms, tiny anticracks nucleate and cascade into a fault-like rupture. The competing idea, dehydration embrittlement, argues that water released from hydrous minerals as the slab heats up raises fluid pressure enough to trigger brittle failure — a mechanism generally favored for shallower, intermediate-depth events rather than the very deepest ones.

lessons.workedExample: A subducting slab carries cold oceanic mantle to 600 km depth in only a few million years — fast enough that its interior stays far colder than the surrounding mantle at that depth. Ordinary mantle at 600 km has long since converted its olivine to denser spinel-structured minerals, but inside this cold slab core, olivine can persist metastably, unconverted, well past the depth where it 'should' have transformed. Under transformational faulting, it is exactly this trapped, metastable olivine wedge that suddenly transforms and ruptures, producing a deep earthquake at a depth where classic brittle fracture is not physically expected.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes this because it separates 'earthquakes happen at subduction zones' from actually understanding why deep earthquakes are a scientific puzzle at all — ordinary rock at 300-700 km should flow, not fracture, so something else has to be going on. A strong answer names Wadati's dipping-plane discovery, explains why depth makes brittle failure implausible, and can state that transformational faulting and dehydration embrittlement are competing, not settled, explanations. Judges specifically listen for 'this is still debated,' since presenting an open mechanism as settled science is a common overreach.

questions.prompt: Why is the mechanism of deep-focus earthquakes (300-700 km) considered puzzling?

options.text: At those depths, pressure and temperature should make rock ductile rather than able to fracture brittlely
Seismometers cannot detect earthquakes below 300 km
No deep earthquakes had ever actually been recorded before 1989
Deep earthquakes only occur beneath continents, never beneath oceans

explanations.a: Correct — the physical conditions at those depths should suppress ordinary brittle faulting, which is why alternative mechanisms like transformational faulting and dehydration embrittlement were proposed.
explanations.b: Deep earthquakes were detected via travel-time data by Wadati as early as 1927; detection was never the barrier.
explanations.c: Wadati documented deep earthquakes beneath Japan in 1927, decades before Green and Burnley's 1989 mechanism paper.
explanations.d: Wadati-Benioff zones occur along subduction zones globally, wherever an oceanic plate sinks beneath another plate.

questions.prompt: Match each contribution to the person or people responsible for it.

left.text: Found the first dipping plane of deep hypocenters beneath Japan
Compiled similar dipping zones globally, tying them to subduction
Proposed transformational faulting in metastable olivine

right.text: Kiyoo Wadati
Hugo Benioff
Green and Burnley

questions.explanation: Wadati found the original Japan-specific dipping plane, Benioff globalized the pattern, and Green and Burnley proposed the transformational-faulting mechanism decades later in 1989.

questions.prompt: Which earthquake is the largest deep-focus event ever recorded instrumentally?

options.text: The 2013 Sea of Okhotsk earthquake, magnitude 8.3 at roughly 609 km depth
The 1994 Bolivia earthquake, magnitude 8.2 at roughly 631 km depth
The 2011 Tohoku earthquake, magnitude 9.1 at roughly 29 km depth
The 1960 Chile earthquake, magnitude 9.5 at roughly 25 km depth

explanations.a: Correct — the May 2013 Sea of Okhotsk event surpassed Bolivia 1994 and is the largest deep-focus earthquake in the instrumental record.
explanations.b: Bolivia 1994 held that record for nearly two decades, but it was surpassed by the 2013 Sea of Okhotsk earthquake.
explanations.c: Tohoku was far larger overall, but it was a shallow megathrust rupture, not a deep-focus earthquake.
explanations.d: Chile 1960 is the largest earthquake ever recorded at any depth, but it too was shallow, not deep-focus.

questions.prompt: Which two mechanisms currently compete to explain deep and intermediate-depth earthquakes?

options.text: Transformational faulting in metastable olivine and dehydration embrittlement
Elastic rebound and thermal expansion
Tidal loading and volcanic degassing
Aftershock triggering and foreshock swarms

explanations.a: Correct — these are the two leading, still-competing hypotheses for how rock ruptures at depths where ordinary brittle faulting should not work.
explanations.b: Elastic rebound explains shallow tectonic earthquakes generally, not the specific deep-focus puzzle, and thermal expansion is not a proposed mechanism here.
explanations.c: Neither tidal loading nor volcanic degassing is a proposed mechanism for deep-focus earthquake rupture.
explanations.d: Aftershock triggering and foreshock swarms describe earthquake sequences in time, not the physical mechanism that lets deep rock fracture at all.

lessons.label: The Prediction Wars

sections.heading: Haicheng's success, Tangshan's failure
sections.body: On February 4, 1975, Chinese officials evacuated Haicheng, Liaoning province, roughly five and a half hours before a magnitude 7.3 earthquake struck, based on a rising swarm of foreshocks plus reported groundwater and animal-behavior anomalies. The evacuation is credited with limiting deaths to about 2,000 in a quake that could otherwise have killed well over 100,000 — the only confirmed case in history of a successful evacuation ahead of a major earthquake. Just eighteen months later, on July 28, 1976, the magnitude 7.5 Tangshan earthquake struck with no foreshocks, no anomalies, and no warning; roughly 250,000 people died, officially, with some estimates far higher. The contrast crushed the assumption that precursors were a reliable, general-purpose tool.

sections.heading: Parkfield: a forecast that arrived eleven years late
sections.body: The Parkfield segment of the San Andreas Fault had produced a string of roughly magnitude-6 earthquakes in 1857, 1881, 1901, 1922, 1934, and 1966, averaging about 22 years apart — an unusually regular pattern that led William Bakun and Allan Lindh in 1985 to forecast, with 95% confidence, that another such quake would strike before 1993. The U.S. earthquake-prediction evaluation council formally endorsed it, and Parkfield became the most densely instrumented fault segment on Earth, bristling with seismometers, creepmeters, and strainmeters awaiting the expected event. The forecast earthquake did not arrive until September 28, 2004 — eleven years after the window closed. Parkfield taught the field that recurrence intervals, however regular they look in a short record, are not reliable enough for deterministic forecasting.

sections.heading: VAN, Geller, and the field's retreat to probability
sections.body: A parallel, more contentious claim came from Greek physicists Panayiotis Varotsos, K. Alexopoulos, and Kostas Nomicos, who argued in the 1980s that transient seismic electric signals (SES) preceded earthquakes and could be used to predict them — the VAN method. Statisticians and seismologists disputed nearly every part of the claim, from signal reality to the odds of matching a vague forecast to any earthquake by chance, and the method never gained acceptance. That skepticism crystallized in a blunt 1997 Science paper by Robert Geller, David Jackson, Yan Kagan, and Francesco Mulargia, titled 'Earthquakes Cannot Be Predicted,' arguing no short-term precursor had ever been validated. The field's consensus since has shifted from deterministic prediction to probabilistic hazard forecasting — stating the odds of an earthquake in a region over decades, not naming a date.

lessons.workedExample: Compare two claims: 'There is a 30% chance of a magnitude 8+ earthquake on this fault segment in the next 30 years' versus 'A magnitude 6 earthquake will strike this town in 2019.' The first is probabilistic hazard forecasting — the modern standard, built from recurrence statistics and fault slip rates, and it is falsifiable only over decades. The second is deterministic prediction — exactly the kind of specific claim Bakun and Lindh made for Parkfield in 1985 and that failed to arrive on schedule, and exactly what Geller and coauthors argued in 1997 has never been reliably achieved for any precursor-based method.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge presses on this because 'can earthquakes be predicted' is a question students love to answer with false confidence in either direction. A strong answer separates prediction (a specific time, place, magnitude) from forecasting (a probability over a long window), cites at least one specific case on each side of the ledger — Haicheng's evacuation success and Tangshan's silence, or Parkfield's eleven-year miss — and lands on the field's actual current position: probabilistic hazard assessment, not deterministic prediction. A weak answer either claims prediction is solved or claims nothing useful can ever be said about future earthquakes.

questions.prompt: What is the key scientific lesson usually drawn from the Parkfield experiment's outcome?

options.text: Seismographs are too inaccurate to record magnitude-6 earthquakes reliably
A short historical record of regular-looking recurrence is not a reliable basis for a specific deterministic forecast window
The San Andreas Fault stopped producing earthquakes after 1993
Animal behavior is the most reliable earthquake precursor

explanations.a: Instrument accuracy was not the issue; the forecast quake was eventually recorded fine in 2004, just eleven years later than expected.
explanations.b: Correct — the 1985 forecast of an M6 quake before 1993 relied on a seemingly regular recurrence pattern that turned out not to hold precisely, and the quake did not arrive until 2004.
explanations.c: The fault remained active; the forecast earthquake did eventually occur, in 2004.
explanations.d: Animal-behavior anomalies were reported before Haicheng but are not established as a reliable general precursor; Parkfield's lesson is specifically about recurrence-interval forecasting.

questions.prompt: Order these events chronologically.

items.text: Haicheng evacuation ahead of a magnitude 7.3 earthquake
Tangshan earthquake strikes with no warning
Bakun and Lindh publish the Parkfield forecast
Geller and coauthors publish 'Earthquakes Cannot Be Predicted'
The forecast Parkfield earthquake finally occurs

questions.explanation: Haicheng (1975) preceded Tangshan (1976); Bakun and Lindh's Parkfield forecast came in 1985; Geller and coauthors' critique was published in 1997; the Parkfield earthquake itself did not arrive until 2004.

questions.prompt: Match each case or claim to its outcome.

right.text: Successful evacuation credited with saving tens of thousands of lives
No warning; roughly 250,000 deaths
Disputed by statisticians and seismologists, never widely accepted
Argued no validated method exists for short-term prediction

questions.explanation: Haicheng's evacuation is the field's one clear success story; Tangshan is the counterexample with no warning; VAN remained scientifically contested; and Geller's 1997 paper argued against short-term prediction altogether.

lessons.label: Tohoku 2011 and the Maximum-Magnitude Problem

sections.heading: A model that capped the fault too low
sections.body: Before March 11, 2011, Japan's official national hazard models treated the Japan Trench off Tohoku as a series of segments capable of roughly magnitude-7.5 to 8 earthquakes, based on the historical instrumental record of repeating ruptures in that size range over roughly the preceding century. The actual earthquake that day was magnitude 9.0 — releasing something like thirty times more energy than an M8 event, and nearly 180 times more than the M7.5 lower bound — because the entire margin ruptured as one, rather than in the smaller independent segments the models assumed. Making it worse, slip near the shallow, offshore part of the fault reached roughly 50 meters or more — a figure established by post-quake seafloor GPS-acoustic and seismic-inversion surveys reported in Fujiwara et al. (2011) and Ide et al. (2011) — an extraordinarily large displacement concentrated exactly where it does the most damage: generating tsunami.

sections.heading: The warning that was in the sediment, not the model
sections.body: The unsettling part is that evidence for a Tohoku-scale event already existed. Geologist Koji Minoura and colleagues published research in 2001 documenting sand deposits on the Sendai coastal plain from the Jogan tsunami of 869 CE, showing that tsunami of comparable scale had struck the same coast roughly every thousand years and had reached kilometers further inland than any tsunami in the modern instrumental record. That paleotsunami evidence existed in the scientific literature for a decade before 2011, but it had not been fully incorporated into official seawall design and hazard planning, which anchored more heavily on the shorter instrumental earthquake catalog.

sections.heading: L'Aquila: when uncertainty communication became a criminal case
sections.body: Two years before Tohoku, a different kind of failure to communicate risk played out in Italy. Ahead of the April 6, 2009 L'Aquila earthquake (magnitude 6.3, about 309 deaths), a scientific commission met during an ongoing foreshock swarm and gave what residents took as reassurance that a major quake was unlikely. In 2012, six scientists and one government official were convicted of manslaughter for that communication. An appeals court overturned the scientists' convictions in 2014, and Italy's supreme court confirmed the acquittal in 2015, while upholding a reduced sentence for the official who made the public statement. The case became the reference point for how scientists should — and should not — communicate uncertainty about hazards they cannot rule out.

lessons.workedExample: Imagine a hazard model built entirely from a roughly century-long instrumental catalog showing repeating M7.5-8 quakes on adjacent fault segments off Tohoku. Now add the Jogan deposits: sand layers on the Sendai plain, radiocarbon-dated to 869 CE, extending kilometers further inland than any tsunami since. Those deposits are physical evidence that the whole margin can rupture together at far larger magnitude than the short instrumental record suggests — exactly what happened at magnitude 9.0 in 2011. The gap between the two records is the maximum-magnitude problem: an instrumental catalog too short to have ever recorded the fault's true maximum event.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about Tohoku because it is the clearest real-world case where a hazard estimate was wrong by an order of magnitude, and the warning signs existed but weren't acted on. A strong answer names the actual mismatch — models capped near M7.5-8, the real event at M9.0 with roughly 50 m of shallow slip — and cites the 869 Jogan deposits as evidence available beforehand. It should also distinguish the L'Aquila case as a separate lesson: not about magnitude estimation, but about criminal and ethical consequences for how uncertainty gets communicated to the public.

questions.prompt: What made the 2011 Tohoku earthquake's tsunami especially destructive, beyond its overall magnitude?

options.text: Slip was concentrated at depth far from the trench, away from the seafloor
Slip reached roughly 50 meters or more in the shallow part of the fault near the trench
The earthquake occurred on land rather than offshore
The rupture was too small to be classified as a megathrust event

explanations.a: Deep slip far from the seafloor does not efficiently displace the water column the way shallow slip does; that is not what drove the tsunami's severity.
explanations.b: Correct — extreme slip concentrated in the shallow, near-trench portion of the megathrust efficiently displaces the overlying seafloor and water column, driving an unusually large tsunami.
explanations.c: The earthquake was offshore, on the subduction megathrust beneath the Pacific, which is exactly why it generated a major tsunami.
explanations.d: At magnitude 9.0, Tohoku was one of the largest recorded megathrust earthquakes, not a small event.

questions.prompt: Match each element of the Tohoku/L'Aquila story to its description.

left.text: Pre-2011 Japanese hazard model for the Japan Trench

right.text: Treated the trench as capable of roughly M7.5-8 events based on the instrumental record
Documented by Minoura and colleagues in 2001, evidence of a similarly large ancient tsunami
Scientists' convictions overturned on appeal; official's reduced sentence upheld

questions.explanation: The pre-2011 model underestimated the trench's maximum magnitude, the Jogan deposits were published evidence of a larger prior event that wasn't fully incorporated, and the L'Aquila case ended with the scientists acquitted on appeal while the official's conviction stood, reduced.

questions.prompt: What was the final legal outcome for the six scientists convicted in the initial L'Aquila manslaughter trial?

options.text: Their convictions were overturned on appeal and the acquittal was confirmed by Italy's supreme court
Their original convictions and prison sentences were fully upheld
The case was dismissed before any trial began
Only one of the six scientists was acquitted; the rest remained convicted

explanations.a: Correct — an appeals court overturned the scientists' convictions in 2014, and Italy's supreme court confirmed that acquittal in 2015.
explanations.b: The initial 2012 convictions were not upheld for the scientists; they were overturned on appeal.
explanations.c: The case went through a full first-instance trial and conviction in 2012 before the later appeal and acquittal.
explanations.d: All six scientists were acquitted on appeal, not just one; the official who made the public statement was the one whose conviction stood, reduced.

lessons.label: Slow Earthquakes: A Whole New Class

sections.heading: Obara finds tremor with no volcano nearby
sections.body: Ordinary earthquakes radiate sharp, high-frequency, impulsive waves lasting seconds. In 2002, Japanese seismologist Kazushige Obara was analyzing continuous data from Hi-net, a dense borehole seismometer network built across Japan after the 1995 Kobe earthquake, when he found something unfamiliar: hours-long episodes of weak, low-frequency, rumbling ground vibration deep beneath southwest Japan's subduction zone, with no volcano nearby to explain it. He called it non-volcanic tremor. It didn't look like an earthquake and didn't look like ordinary volcanic tremor either — a genuinely new seismic signal, hiding in plain sight in continuous records that had simply never been examined this closely before.

sections.heading: Rogers and Dragert connect it to silent slip in Cascadia
sections.body: The following year, Canadian geophysicists Garry Rogers and Herb Dragert tied a version of this phenomenon to something GPS stations in the Pacific Northwest had already been tracking: episodes of 'silent' fault slip on the Cascadia subduction zone, too slow to generate normal earthquake shaking, detectable only as slow reversals in surface GPS motion. Rogers and Dragert's 2003 paper showed that tremor and slip occurred together — episodic tremor and slip, or ETS — recurring with remarkable regularity, roughly every 14 months beneath southern Vancouver Island. Suddenly tremor had a mechanical partner: it was the seismic signature of a fault slipping, just enormously more slowly than in a normal earthquake.

sections.heading: A new place on the moment-duration diagram, and an open question
sections.body: Ordinary earthquakes and slow-slip events turn out to occupy different territory on a plot of seismic moment against rupture duration: regular earthquakes scale as moment proportional to duration cubed, while slow-slip events scale linearly, moment proportional to duration — meaning slow events can release large moment over months without ever producing strong shaking. What remains genuinely unresolved is what these slow events mean for the earthquake hazard next door: do they relieve accumulated stress on the adjacent locked, seismogenic part of the megathrust — a kind of pressure valve — or do they instead load additional stress onto that locked patch, nudging it closer to failure? Both mechanisms have supporting evidence, and the field has not settled which dominates. Non-volcanic tremor and episodic tremor-and-slip are not just a Japan-Cascadia curiosity, either: they have since been documented at subduction zones worldwide, including the Nankai Trough, Mexico, and New Zealand's Hikurangi margin, showing this is a global class of fault behavior rather than a feature of two specific coastlines.

lessons.workedExample: A GPS station above the Cascadia subduction zone normally creeps steadily landward as the Juan de Fuca plate is dragged beneath North America. Every roughly 14 months, that motion briefly reverses for one to several weeks — a small seaward jog of a few millimeters — while nearby Hi-net-style borehole seismometers simultaneously record days of faint, low-frequency tremor with no associated large shaking felt at the surface. Rogers and Dragert's 2003 insight was recognizing that these two independently observed signals, GPS reversal and tremor, are two views of the exact same slow-slip event.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes slow earthquakes because they are a genuinely recent, still-unsettled discovery, and a strong presenter should be able to say what makes them a distinct class rather than just 'small earthquakes' — the linear rather than cubic moment-duration scaling is the specific evidence. Equally important is naming the two competing, unresolved hypotheses about their hazard relationship to the locked megathrust (relieving stress versus loading it) as an open question, not settled fact — overclaiming a definitive answer here is the easiest way to lose credibility on this topic.

questions.prompt: What was distinctive about the signal Obara identified in 2002 using Hi-net data?

options.text: Sharp, high-frequency shaking lasting only a few seconds near a volcano
Hours-long episodes of weak, low-frequency tremor deep in the subduction zone with no nearby volcano
A sudden magnitude 7 earthquake with a clear foreshock sequence
A single well-recorded aftershock following the 1995 Kobe earthquake

explanations.a: Sharp, brief, high-frequency signals describe ordinary earthquakes or volcanic tremor, not the non-volcanic tremor Obara found.
explanations.b: Correct — Obara's non-volcanic tremor was a novel, extended, low-frequency signal unrelated to volcanic activity, discovered in continuous Hi-net records.
explanations.c: The signal was not a discrete large earthquake with a foreshock sequence; it was a diffuse, extended tremor signal.
explanations.d: Hi-net was built after the 1995 Kobe earthquake, but Obara's discovery was a new class of continuous signal, not an aftershock of that quake.

questions.prompt: Match each discovery to the researcher(s) credited with it.

left.text: Non-volcanic deep tremor in southwest Japan
Episodic tremor and slip recurring roughly every 14 months in Cascadia

right.text: Obara (2002)
Rogers and Dragert (2003)

questions.explanation: Obara identified non-volcanic tremor in Japan using Hi-net in 2002; Rogers and Dragert linked tremor to slow slip in Cascadia, finding the roughly 14-month recurrence, in 2003.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes slow-slip events from ordinary earthquakes on the moment-duration scaling diagram?

options.text: Slow-slip events scale linearly (moment proportional to duration), while ordinary earthquakes scale as moment proportional to duration cubed
Slow-slip events release far more total seismic moment than any earthquake ever recorded
Ordinary earthquakes and slow-slip events follow an identical scaling relationship
Slow-slip events have no measurable duration at all

explanations.a: Correct — this different scaling relationship is the specific evidence that slow-slip events are a mechanically distinct class of fault motion, not just smaller or quieter earthquakes.
explanations.b: The scaling difference is about the relationship between moment and duration, not a claim that slow events release more total moment than all earthquakes.
explanations.c: The two follow different scaling laws — linear for slow-slip events, cubic for ordinary earthquakes — which is precisely the point of distinguishing them.
explanations.d: Slow-slip events are defined partly by their unusually long duration, from days to months, which is central to their distinct scaling behavior.

lessons.label: Test-Ban Seismology and Explosion Discrimination

sections.heading: A nuclear-monitoring program built modern seismology
sections.body: Much of the seismic instrumentation modern earthquake science relies on was not built to study earthquakes at all. Starting in 1961, the U.S. defense-funded VELA Uniform program financed the World-Wide Standardized Seismograph Network (WWSSN), eventually around 120 identically calibrated stations across some 60 countries. Its purpose was Cold War verification: detect and characterize underground nuclear tests well enough to police a test-ban treaty. The side effect was enormous for basic science — uniform, globally distributed, high-quality data that let researchers compare earthquakes anywhere on Earth on the same scale, underpinning much of the plate-tectonics-era seismology that followed.

sections.heading: Telling a bomb from a quake
sections.body: Verification required more than detecting a seismic signal — it required distinguishing an explosion from a natural earthquake recorded at similar size. Two discriminants proved most useful. The mb:Ms discriminant compares short-period body-wave magnitude (mb) against long-period surface-wave magnitude (Ms): an explosion is an efficient, compact, isotropic source that generates strong body waves but relatively weak surface waves, so explosions plot with unusually high mb relative to Ms compared to earthquakes of the same mb, which have an extended shear-slip source that radiates surface waves efficiently. The second is a P/S spectral ratio: because an explosion has no shear component, it radiates proportionally more P energy than S energy, especially at high frequency, while an earthquake's double-couple shear source radiates strong S waves. Depth and location matter too — explosions occur at shallow, engineering-limited depths, often at known test sites, unlike many natural earthquakes.

sections.heading: From WWSSN to the CTBTO, and a contested modern test
sections.body: That Cold War-era approach evolved into the modern International Monitoring System run by the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty Organization (CTBTO), combining seismic, hydroacoustic, infrasound, and radionuclide sensors worldwide, even though the underlying treaty has not yet entered into force. The discriminants get tested in the real world: North Korea's sixth and largest nuclear test, on September 3, 2017, registered around magnitude 6.3 — an order of magnitude more energy than its prior tests — yet yield estimates from different monitoring groups ranged enormously, from roughly 50-60 kilotons to over 250 kilotons, reflecting real uncertainty in converting seismic magnitude to explosive yield. About eight minutes after the main shock, a smaller seismic signal was recorded at the site, widely interpreted as a partial tunnel collapse.

lessons.workedExample: Two seismic events both register mb 4.5. Event A plots with Ms around 3.0, and its spectrum at high frequency shows P energy far exceeding S energy — the mb:Ms and P/S signatures of an explosion, and it is located precisely at a known test facility at shallow depth. Event B plots with Ms around 4.3, closer to the mb:Ms line typical of earthquakes, with comparable P and S energy, and it is located along a mapped fault at 10 km depth. Analysts flag Event A for further review as a probable explosion and treat Event B as an ordinary tectonic earthquake, using exactly the discriminants built for nuclear-test verification.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge raises this because it is a rare case where geophysics numbers carry direct policy and legal weight — a wrongly classified seismic signal is a treaty-compliance dispute, not just a data point. A strong answer explains the actual discriminants (mb:Ms, P/S spectral ratio, depth and location) rather than vaguely saying 'seismologists can tell the difference,' and can cite the 2017 DPRK test's wide yield-estimate range as evidence that even confirmed explosions carry real quantitative uncertainty. Naming the WWSSN's origin in test-ban verification, not pure science, shows the funding history is understood too.

questions.prompt: Why do explosions typically show a higher mb relative to Ms than earthquakes of the same mb?

options.text: Explosions are compact, isotropic sources that generate body waves efficiently but surface waves weakly, unlike an earthquake's extended shear-slip source
Explosions always occur at greater depth than earthquakes
Seismometers are less sensitive to explosions than to earthquakes
Ms cannot be measured at all for explosion sources

explanations.a: Correct — the source geometry difference (compact and isotropic versus extended and shear-based) is exactly why the mb:Ms ratio separates the two populations.
explanations.b: Explosions are typically shallower than many earthquakes, not deeper, which is itself a separate discriminant.
explanations.c: Sensitivity is not the issue; the discriminant relies on a genuine physical difference in how the two source types radiate energy.
explanations.d: Ms can be measured for explosions; it is simply smaller relative to mb than for an earthquake of the same size, which is the basis of the discriminant.

questions.prompt: Order these developments in test-ban seismology from earliest to most recent.

items.text: The WWSSN is established, funded by VELA Uniform
The CTBTO's International Monitoring System is built out
North Korea's sixth nuclear test registers around magnitude 6.3

questions.explanation: The WWSSN began in 1961; the CTBTO's monitoring system developed later under the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty; the 2017 North Korean test is the most recent event.

questions.prompt: What did the wide range of yield estimates for the 2017 DPRK test illustrate?

options.text: That seismic magnitude alone leaves real, substantial uncertainty when converted to explosive yield
That the event was definitively not a nuclear test at all
That mb:Ms discrimination failed to identify the event as an explosion
That no seismic stations detected the event

explanations.a: Correct — different monitoring groups derived yield estimates spanning roughly 50 to over 250 kilotons from the same magnitude, showing that magnitude-to-yield conversion carries substantial uncertainty even for a confirmed test.
explanations.b: The event was recorded and analyzed as North Korea's sixth nuclear test, with location and depth consistent with the known Punggye-ri test site.
explanations.c: The discriminants correctly identified the event's explosive character; the uncertainty was in yield estimation, not in explosion-versus-earthquake classification.
explanations.d: The event was well recorded globally at magnitude around 6.3, an order of magnitude larger than North Korea's prior tests.

units.label: Ground Motion, Site Effects, and Shaking Intensity

lessons.label: Measuring Shaking: PGA, PGV, and Response Spectra

sections.heading: From accelerogram to PGA, PGV, PGD
sections.body: A strong-motion accelerograph records ground acceleration directly, but the raw trace needs baseline correction and filtering (removing instrument response and long-period drift) before it is usable. Peak ground acceleration (PGA) is simply the largest absolute value in the corrected acceleration time series, in g or cm/s^2. Integrating once gives velocity, whose peak is peak ground velocity (PGV, cm/s); integrating twice gives displacement, whose peak is peak ground displacement (PGD, cm). Each captures a different slice of the shaking: PGA is dominated by high-frequency energy, PGV tracks intermediate-period motion and correlates better with damage to mid-rise structures, and PGD reflects long-period, near-source permanent offset.

sections.heading: The response spectrum: a family of oscillators
sections.body: A response spectrum asks a different question than "how big was the ground motion" - it asks "how would a building respond to it." Imagine a suite of idealized single-degree-of-freedom (SDOF) oscillators, each a mass on a spring with a different natural period T and a fixed damping ratio (conventionally 5% of critical, matching typical building damping), all shaken by the same recorded ground motion. For each oscillator, compute its peak response acceleration; plotting that peak against period T produces the 5%-damped acceleration response spectrum Sa(T). Building codes specify design forces directly from Sa(T), because it tells you how hard a structure of a given period will actually shake, not just how hard the ground shook.

sections.heading: Arias intensity and significant duration
sections.body: Peak values miss how long shaking lasts and how much cumulative energy a record carries. Arias intensity, defined by Arias (1970), integrates the square of acceleration over the full record (scaled by pi/2g), giving one number in m/s reflecting cumulative shaking energy rather than any single peak. From the resulting build-up curve, significant duration - commonly the interval between 5% and 95% of total Arias intensity - measures how long strong shaking actually persists. A long, moderate-amplitude record can do more cumulative damage than a short sharp spike sharing the same PGA.

sections.heading: Why PGA alone is a poor damage predictor
sections.body: PGA is easy to record and report, but it is dominated by brief, high-frequency spikes a flexible structure barely feels - a building's mass cannot respond fast enough to a millisecond-scale acceleration peak. Spectral acceleration at the structure's own fundamental period, Sa(T1), is a far better damage predictor because it captures the resonant amplification a real building experiences. This is why post-Northridge (1994) and post-Kobe (1995) engineering practice moved decisively toward spectral-acceleration-based design criteria and away from PGA-only thresholds.

lessons.workedExample: An M6 event at 10 km produces an accelerogram with PGA = 0.4g from a brief high-frequency spike, but PGV only 15 cm/s. A 12-story building with fundamental period T1 = 1.2 s reads Sa(1.2s) = 0.35g off the response spectrum; engineers use that 0.35g, not the 0.4g spike, to estimate the force the building actually feels, since the building cannot resonate with a millisecond-scale transient. Meanwhile Arias intensity integrated over the full 25 s record is high despite the modest PGA, and the 5-95% significant duration spans 18 s - signaling a long, energetic episode capable of triggering liquefaction or cumulative fatigue even without an extreme single peak.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks "your project used PGA to predict damage - why?" is testing whether the student understands PGA as a high-frequency, source-side artifact rather than what a structure experiences. A strong answer names spectral acceleration at the structure's own period as the more damage-relevant quantity, explains that a 5%-damped SDOF oscillator sweep produces that curve, and can cite Arias intensity or significant duration as a second, independent axis - cumulative energy and duration - that PGA also misses entirely. Conflating "biggest number on the trace" with "how much damage occurred" signals the student never got past the first rung of ground-motion characterization.

questions.prompt: Which processing step produces peak ground velocity (PGV) from a corrected accelerogram?

options.text: Differentiating the acceleration record twice
Integrating the acceleration record once and taking the peak
Reading the peak directly off the raw, uncorrected trace
Squaring and integrating acceleration over the whole record

explanations.a: Differentiating acceleration would produce jerk, not velocity; velocity requires integration, not differentiation.
explanations.b: Correct - integrating corrected acceleration once yields velocity, and PGV is the peak absolute value of that integrated trace.
explanations.c: The raw trace must be baseline-corrected and filtered first; peaks off an uncorrected record are unreliable.
explanations.d: Squaring and integrating over the record is how Arias intensity is computed, not PGV.

questions.prompt: Match each ground-motion measure to what it primarily reflects.

right.text: High-frequency peak instantaneous shaking
Intermediate-period motion correlating with mid-rise damage
Cumulative shaking energy over the full record
Resonant response amplification of a specific structure

questions.explanation: PGA is dominated by brief high-frequency spikes, PGV tracks intermediate-period motion tied to mid-rise damage, Arias intensity integrates squared acceleration into a cumulative-energy measure, and Sa(T) captures how a structure resonates at its own period.

questions.prompt: Order the steps used to build a 5%-damped acceleration response spectrum Sa(T).

items.text: Obtain a corrected ground-acceleration record
Select a range of SDOF oscillator periods T, each damped at 5% of critical
Subject each oscillator to the recorded ground motion and record its peak response acceleration
Plot each oscillator's peak response acceleration against its period T

questions.explanation: The response spectrum starts from a real corrected accelerogram, defines a family of 5%-damped SDOF oscillators across periods, drives each with that same record to get its peak response, then plots peak response versus period to produce Sa(T).

questions.prompt: Why does spectral acceleration at a structure's own period, Sa(T1), predict damage better than PGA?

options.text: Sa(T1) is always a larger number than PGA
Sa(T1) captures the resonant amplification the structure actually experiences
Sa(T1) ignores damping, making it a purer measure
Sa(T1) is easier and cheaper to measure than PGA

explanations.a: Sa(T1) is not systematically larger than PGA - it depends on the record and the structure's period relative to the shaking's frequency content.
explanations.b: Correct - Sa(T1) reflects how an oscillator with the building's own natural period actually responds, capturing resonance that a raw peak-value statistic like PGA cannot.
explanations.c: Sa(T) is defined at a fixed damping ratio (typically 5%), not by ignoring damping.
explanations.d: Sa(T1) requires computing a response spectrum from the full record, which is more work than reading a single peak value like PGA.

lessons.label: Ground-Motion Models and Their Scatter

sections.heading: Which distance do you mean?
sections.body: Ground-motion models (GMMs, also called attenuation relations) predict a shaking parameter - say PGA or Sa(T) - as a function of magnitude, distance, and site condition, plus an uncertainty term. "Distance" is not one number: Rjb (the Joyner-Boore distance) is the closest horizontal distance to the surface projection of the fault rupture, while Rrup is the closest distance to the rupture plane itself, including depth. For a large earthquake whose rupture reaches the surface, Rjb can be zero for a site sitting directly above the fault even though the rupture nucleated 15 km down; Rrup is generally the more physically meaningful term for near-source shaking because it honors the fault's actual three-dimensional geometry.

sections.heading: Geometric spreading and anelastic attenuation
sections.body: Amplitude falls off with distance for two separate physical reasons. Geometric spreading is purely geometric: radiated energy spreads over an expanding wavefront, so amplitude decays as some power of distance even in a perfectly elastic medium. Anelastic attenuation is a separate, physical loss of energy to heat as rock deforms inelastically, captured in a quality factor Q describing how many wavelengths a wave travels before losing a fixed fraction of its energy. Low-Q regions (fractured, warm crust) attenuate high frequencies quickly, while high-Q cratonic rock, such as much of the central and eastern US, carries shaking efficiently for hundreds of kilometers.

sections.heading: Magnitude scaling and the NGA-West2 family
sections.body: GMMs scale ground motion with magnitude, but not linearly forever: near-source, motion saturates - above roughly M6.5-7, further magnitude increase adds much less to near-fault PGA than it would at smaller magnitudes, because rupture area grows and the fault plane occupies more of the near field rather than acting like a point source. The NGA-West2 project, published in 2014 by the Pacific Earthquake Engineering Research Center, packaged this magnitude-distance-site behavior into five community-vetted models - Abrahamson-Silva-Kamai, Boore-Stewart-Seyhan-Atkinson, Campbell-Bozorgnia, Chiou-Youngs, and Idriss - each fit to an expanded global strong-motion database including near-source recordings.

sections.heading: The sigma that dominates hazard
sections.body: Every GMM reports not just a median but an aleatory (irreducible) standard deviation, sigma, typically 0.5-0.7 in natural-log units for a given magnitude-distance-site combination. Because ground motion is modeled as lognormal, a sigma near 0.6 means one standard deviation above the median is roughly a factor of e^0.6, about 1.8 times larger - a factor of roughly 2 either way. In probabilistic seismic hazard analysis, this scatter, not the median curve, often controls the shaking level at low annual-exceedance-probability targets, because rare, large exceedances are exactly what a long return period samples from the tail.

lessons.workedExample: For an M7.0 strike-slip earthquake and a dipping fault, a site 20 km from the surface trace but 25 km from the nearest point on the rupture plane at depth has Rjb = 20 km and Rrup = 25 km. Two NGA-West2 models, say Boore-Stewart-Seyhan-Atkinson (2014) and Chiou-Youngs (2014), each given the same M, Rrup, and Vs30 = 300 m/s, both return a median PGA near 0.25g but each also reports sigma around 0.6 ln units. At the 84th percentile (median times roughly 1.8), predicted PGA jumps to about 0.45g - nearly double the median - showing why a hazard curve built from many such simulations extends much further into strong shaking than the median prediction alone would suggest.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing a project that cites "the model predicts 0.2g of shaking" is testing whether the student knows that number is a median, not a certainty, and that competing models disagree by design about which distance metric and attenuation shape to use. A strong answer distinguishes Rjb from Rrup for a dipping fault and states that the reported aleatory sigma - 0.5-0.7 ln units, roughly a factor of 2 in either direction - is often the single biggest driver of a hazard estimate at the tail, larger than the differences between competing median models.
