questions.prompt: For a fault whose rupture reaches the surface, which distance metric can be zero for a site directly above the surface trace, even if the site is far from the deepest part of the rupture?

options.text: Rrup
Rjb
Hypocentral distance
Epicentral distance

explanations.a: Rrup measures distance to the closest point on the full rupture plane, including depth, so it is not zero just because the site sits above the surface trace.
explanations.b: Correct - Rjb is the horizontal distance to the surface projection of the rupture, so a site directly above the trace has Rjb = 0 regardless of how deep the rupture extends.
explanations.c: Hypocentral distance is measured to the point of nucleation specifically, not the surface projection of the whole rupture.
explanations.d: Epicentral distance is measured to the epicenter alone, a single point, not the rupture's surface projection.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

right.text: Amplitude loss from the wavefront simply expanding with distance
Energy lost to heat during inelastic deformation, quantified by a quality factor
Near-source ground motion growing much more slowly with magnitude above roughly M6.5-7
Irreducible scatter around a GMM's median prediction

questions.explanation: Geometric spreading is purely geometric wavefront expansion; anelastic attenuation is physical energy loss to heat, described by Q; magnitude saturation is the near-source flattening of ground-motion growth above about M6.5-7; aleatory sigma is the irreducible scatter every GMM reports around its median.

questions.prompt: Order the stages a rupture's energy passes through, from source to a recording site.

items.text: Magnitude-scaled energy is released at the fault source
Amplitude decays through geometric spreading along the travel path
Amplitude is further reduced by anelastic attenuation (Q) along the path
The wave is modified by local site response at the recording station

questions.explanation: Energy release scaled by magnitude comes first, then geometric spreading and anelastic attenuation act along the travel path in sequence, and finally local site conditions modify the motion at the recording station.

questions.prompt: What did the 2014 NGA-West2 project produce?

options.text: A single universal ground-motion equation replacing all prior models
Five community-vetted ground-motion models fit to an expanded global strong-motion database
A new seismometer network for the western United States
A revised moment-magnitude formula for large earthquakes

explanations.a: NGA-West2 produced multiple models, not one universal equation - the community deliberately retained several vetted alternatives.
explanations.b: Correct - NGA-West2, published in 2014, packaged five models (Abrahamson-Silva-Kamai, Boore-Stewart-Seyhan-Atkinson, Campbell-Bozorgnia, Chiou-Youngs, and Idriss) fit to an expanded database including near-source recordings.
explanations.c: NGA-West2 was a ground-motion modeling project, not a hardware deployment.
explanations.d: NGA-West2 concerns ground-motion prediction as a function of magnitude and distance, not the definition of moment magnitude itself.

questions.prompt: Why does the aleatory sigma of a ground-motion model often dominate a probabilistic hazard result at long return periods?

options.text: Because rare, large exceedances live in the tail of the lognormal scatter distribution
Because median predictions from GMMs are always incorrect
Because the quality factor Q cannot be estimated for any region
Because Rjb cannot be computed for dipping faults

explanations.a: Correct - a long return period samples rare, high-exceedance events, which live in the tail of the lognormal ground-motion distribution set by sigma, so the scatter term - not the median - drives the result.
explanations.b: Median predictions are approximations, not universally wrong; sigma quantifies scatter around them, it does not mean the median is invalid.
explanations.c: Q can be estimated regionally from attenuation studies; its uncertainty is not the main driver described here.
explanations.d: Rjb is computable for any fault geometry, including dipping faults; this is unrelated to why sigma dominates the hazard tail.

lessons.label: Site Response and Vs30

sections.heading: Impedance contrast: why soft soil shakes harder
sections.body: Seismic wave amplitude scales inversely with the square root of seismic impedance (density times shear-wave velocity, rho times Vs), roughly conserving energy flux as a wave crosses from stiff rock into soft sediment. Because sediment has much lower Vs, and often lower density, than the bedrock beneath it, a wave slowing down as it enters soft soil must grow in amplitude to conserve that energy flux. This impedance-contrast amplification is the single biggest reason soft-soil sites shake harder than nearby rock sites for the same earthquake, sometimes by a factor of 2-5 for moderate shaking.

sections.heading: Vs30 and NEHRP site classes
sections.body: Because measuring a full soil profile is expensive, engineers use a single proxy: Vs30, the time-averaged shear-wave velocity in the top 30 meters, chosen because that depth captures most of the near-surface impedance contrast affecting building-period shaking. The NEHRP (National Earthquake Hazards Reduction Program) site classification bins Vs30 into classes from A (hard rock, Vs30 greater than 1500 m/s) down to E (soft soil, Vs30 less than 180 m/s), with class D (stiff soil, 180-360 m/s) covering much ordinary urban ground. US building codes assign larger design amplification factors to softer classes.

sections.heading: Quarter-wavelength resonance
sections.body: A soil layer of thickness H sitting on stiffer bedrock has a natural resonant frequency where the layer amplifies incoming waves through constructive interference: f = Vs/(4H), the quarter-wavelength relation, because a wave making a round trip down and back up the layer picks up a phase shift that reinforces surface motion for wavelengths four times the layer thickness. A 30 m soil column with Vs = 200 m/s therefore resonates near 1.7 Hz (200 divided by 4 times 30); thinner, softer basins resonate at higher frequencies, and deep sedimentary basins resonate at very low frequencies, well under 1 Hz.

sections.heading: Measuring resonance in the field, and the strong-motion cap
sections.body: The horizontal-to-vertical spectral ratio (HVSR) method, developed by Nakamura (1989) from ambient microtremor noise, estimates a site's resonant frequency cheaply: the horizontal component of ambient vibration is amplified near the site's resonance while the vertical component is not, so the ratio of horizontal to vertical spectra peaks near the true resonant frequency without needing an earthquake at all. But amplification is not unlimited: at strong shaking, soil behaves nonlinearly - it softens (Vs drops) and its internal damping rises, both lowering the resonant frequency and capping the amplification factor, so a soft-soil site that amplifies a small earthquake by a factor of 4 may amplify a very strong one by only 1.5-2.

lessons.workedExample: A site sits on 30 m of soft clay (Vs = 200 m/s) over stiff rock. The quarter-wavelength formula predicts resonance near f = 200/(4x30) = 1.7 Hz, in the range that damages 3-6 story buildings. An ambient-noise HVSR survey run before any earthquake confirms a clear peak near 1.6 Hz, matching the prediction closely. During a moderate M5 event the site amplifies rock-site motion by about 4x near that frequency, but during a much larger M7 event soil nonlinearity kicks in - the clay softens and damps more, and observed amplification drops to only about 1.8x despite the far larger input motion, illustrating the strong-shaking cap directly.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking "why does the same site amplify small earthquakes proportionally more than big ones?" is testing whether the student understands soil nonlinearity, not just linear resonance theory. A strong answer names the quarter-wavelength relation for the linear regime, cites Nakamura's HVSR method as a way to measure resonant frequency without an earthquake, and then explains that strong shaking softens soil and raises its damping, which caps amplification - a student who treats amplification as a fixed multiplier regardless of shaking level has missed the nonlinearity that governs real strong-motion site response.

questions.prompt: Why does a seismic wave amplify as it enters soft sediment from underlying bedrock?

options.text: Conservation of energy flux as impedance (density times Vs) drops means amplitude must rise
Soft sediment has a higher density than the bedrock beneath it
Soft sediment does not attenuate seismic energy at all
Waves travel faster through soft sediment than through bedrock

explanations.a: Correct - impedance is density times shear-wave velocity; as impedance drops in soft sediment, amplitude must grow to conserve the energy flux carried by the wave.
explanations.b: Soft sediment typically has lower density than bedrock, not higher, and density alone is not what drives the amplification.
explanations.c: Soft sediment can attenuate high frequencies through nonlinear damping; it is not immune to energy loss.
explanations.d: Waves slow down, not speed up, entering soft sediment - the slowing is exactly what forces the amplitude to rise.

questions.prompt: What does Vs30 measure?

options.text: The time-averaged shear-wave velocity in the top 30 meters of a site
The P-wave velocity at 30 kilometers depth
The peak ground velocity recorded within 30 seconds of an earthquake
The average shear-wave velocity over an entire sedimentary basin

explanations.a: Correct - Vs30 is the time-averaged shear-wave velocity in the top 30 meters, chosen because that depth captures most of the near-surface impedance contrast affecting building-period shaking.
explanations.b: Vs30 is a near-surface measure, over the top 30 meters, not a deep crustal P-wave velocity.
explanations.c: Vs30 is a site property based on shear-wave velocity, unrelated to peak ground velocity or a 30-second time window.
explanations.d: Vs30 is defined for the near-surface 30 m column at a specific site, not averaged over an entire basin.

questions.prompt: Match each NEHRP site class to its Vs30 description.

right.text: Hard rock, Vs30 greater than 1500 m/s
Stiff soil, Vs30 180-360 m/s
Soft soil, Vs30 less than 180 m/s

questions.explanation: NEHRP Class A is hard rock above 1500 m/s, Class D is stiff soil in the 180-360 m/s range covering much ordinary urban ground, and Class E is soft soil below 180 m/s.

questions.prompt: Order the stages of site response, from bedrock shaking to the amplification actually observed at the surface.

items.text: Bedrock ground motion is generated by the earthquake source
Impedance-contrast amplification occurs as the wave slows entering soft sediment
Quarter-wavelength resonance amplifies specific frequencies within the soil column
Nonlinear soil damping caps amplification once shaking becomes strong

questions.explanation: Bedrock motion arrives first, impedance contrast amplifies it entering soft soil, the soil column's quarter-wavelength resonance further amplifies specific frequencies, and at strong shaking levels nonlinear damping caps how much amplification actually occurs.

questions.prompt: What does the Nakamura (1989) horizontal-to-vertical spectral ratio (HVSR) method use to estimate a site's resonant frequency?

options.text: The ratio of horizontal to vertical spectra from ambient microtremor noise
A borehole log of soil layers drilled at the site
GPS displacement recorded during a large earthquake
An explosive charge detonated near the site

explanations.a: Correct - HVSR uses ambient microtremor noise, comparing horizontal and vertical spectra, whose ratio peaks near the site's true resonant frequency without needing an earthquake.
explanations.b: Borehole logging can measure Vs directly but is not what defines the HVSR method itself.
explanations.c: HVSR does not require an earthquake or GPS displacement; it works from passive ambient noise.
explanations.d: HVSR is a passive method using existing ambient vibration, not an active-source method requiring an explosive.

lessons.label: Basins, Directivity, and Near-Fault Pulses

sections.heading: Mexico City, 400 km from the source
sections.body: On September 19, 1985, the Mw 8.0 Michoacan earthquake ruptured the subduction interface off Mexico's Pacific coast, roughly 400 km from Mexico City. Rock sites in the city recorded modest shaking, consistent with normal attenuation over that distance. But downtown Mexico City sits atop the drained bed of ancient Lake Texcoco - tens of meters of soft, saturated lacustrine clay - whose quarter-wavelength resonant period lands near 2 seconds, and the subduction-zone rupture happened to radiate unusually strong energy near that same period. The lakebed clay amplified incoming motion by roughly an order of magnitude relative to surrounding rock, and mid-rise buildings of 6-15 stories, whose own fundamental periods cluster near 1-2 seconds, resonated with the amplified ground motion; several hundred buildings collapsed, an unusually deadly outcome for a site so far from the epicenter.

sections.heading: Basin edges generate their own waves
sections.body: Sedimentary basins do more than resonate vertically - their edges, where soft fill abuts stiffer rock, can convert incoming body waves into locally generated surface waves that then reverberate within the basin, extending shaking duration well beyond what the source alone would produce. This basin-edge-generated surface wave effect, documented for basins including the Los Angeles and Mexico City basins, means deep sedimentary basins are dangerous for two separable reasons: resonant amplification at the basin's characteristic period, and prolonged duration from trapped, internally reflecting waves.

sections.heading: Forward directivity: outrunning your own wavefront
sections.body: Near-fault ground motion has a second hazard mechanism unrelated to site geology: rupture directivity. When a rupture propagates toward a site at a speed close to the shear-wave speed, most of the fault's radiated energy arrives almost simultaneously, packed into one large, long-period velocity pulse rather than spread over many cycles - forward directivity. This mechanism produced the damaging near-fault pulses recorded in the 1994 Northridge earthquake (Mw 6.7) and the 1999 Chi-Chi earthquake in Taiwan (Mw 7.6), both of which caused disproportionate damage to structures directly in the rupture's forward path.

sections.heading: Fling step and why long-period structures suffer
sections.body: A related, separate near-fault effect is fling step: a permanent, one-sided ground displacement left behind by the static slip of the fault itself, distinct from the oscillatory directivity pulse. Both directivity pulses and fling step concentrate energy at long periods, roughly 1-4 seconds and beyond, which is exactly the period range of tall buildings, long-span bridges, and base-isolated structures. Short, stiff buildings are comparatively unaffected, while long-period structures near the fault face motion far more severe than a standard, non-near-fault design spectrum would predict.

lessons.workedExample: Consider two structures near a hypothetical M7 rupture, each 5 km from the fault: one directly updip in the rupture's forward path, one to the side in a backward-directivity position. The forward-path structure records a single large velocity pulse near 3 s period reaching roughly 80 cm/s, while the equidistant side structure records a longer, lower-amplitude, many-cycle record peaking near 25 cm/s - same distance and magnitude, wildly different demand from directivity geometry alone. If the forward-path site also sits in a sedimentary basin whose edge generates locally trapped surface waves, shaking duration stretches further still, layering basin effects on top of the directivity pulse.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing near-fault hazard is testing whether the student separates three distinct mechanisms that get conflated in casual descriptions: basin resonance and edge-generated waves (a site-geology effect that can operate hundreds of kilometers from the source, as at 1985 Michoacan), forward directivity (a rupture-propagation effect independent of site geology, seen at Northridge and Chi-Chi), and fling step (a static, permanent offset distinct from either). A strong answer also connects all three to the same consequence: long-period structures - tall buildings, long-span bridges, base-isolated systems - bear the brunt, while short stiff buildings are comparatively spared.

questions.prompt: Why did the 1985 Michoacan earthquake devastate Mexico City despite the roughly 400 km distance from the rupture?

options.text: The lakebed clay's quarter-wavelength resonant period matched the rupture's radiated energy near 2 seconds
The earthquake's epicenter was actually located beneath Mexico City
Mexico City sits on hard bedrock that fractured under the strain
PGA recorded in Mexico City exceeded PGA recorded at the coast near the rupture

explanations.a: Correct - the lakebed clay's roughly 2-second quarter-wavelength resonance coincided with unusually strong 2-second energy radiated by the rupture, producing roughly an order-of-magnitude amplification.
explanations.b: The rupture was on the Pacific coast subduction interface, roughly 400 km from Mexico City, not beneath the city.
explanations.c: Downtown Mexico City sits on soft lacustrine clay from the former Lake Texcoco, not hard bedrock.
explanations.d: PGA at rock sites in the city was modest and consistent with normal attenuation; the damage came from long-period spectral amplification in the clay, not from a higher PGA than near the source.

questions.prompt: What causes a forward-directivity pulse in near-fault ground motion?

options.text: Rupture propagating toward the site near the shear-wave speed packs radiated energy into one large pulse
Reflection of seismic waves off a sedimentary basin's edges
The permanent offset left by static fault slip
Anelastic attenuation of high frequencies along the travel path

explanations.a: Correct - when the rupture front moves toward a site at close to the shear-wave speed, most of the radiated energy arrives nearly simultaneously, concentrated into a single large, long-period pulse.
explanations.b: Basin-edge reflection produces trapped surface waves that extend duration and amplify shaking, a related but distinct mechanism from rupture-directivity pulses.
explanations.c: That describes fling step, a separate, permanent-displacement effect, not the oscillatory directivity pulse.
explanations.d: Anelastic attenuation reduces amplitude over distance; it does not generate a directivity pulse.

questions.prompt: Match each near-fault or basin phenomenon to its example or defining feature.

right.text: 1985 Michoacan earthquake amplifying Mexico City's lakebed clay by roughly an order of magnitude
1994 Northridge and 1999 Chi-Chi earthquakes damaging structures in the rupture's forward path
A permanent, one-sided displacement offset from static fault slip

questions.explanation: 1985 Michoacan illustrates long-distance basin resonance damage; 1994 Northridge and 1999 Chi-Chi illustrate near-fault forward-directivity pulses; fling step is the permanent, one-sided displacement left by the fault's own static slip.

questions.prompt: Which structures are most vulnerable to near-fault directivity pulses and fling step?

options.text: Short, stiff one- or two-story buildings
Tall buildings, long-span bridges, and base-isolated structures
All structures equally, regardless of period
Only underground pipelines and tunnels

explanations.a: Short, stiff structures have short natural periods and are comparatively unaffected by the long-period energy in directivity pulses and fling step.
explanations.b: Correct - directivity pulses and fling step concentrate energy at long periods (roughly 1-4+ seconds), which matches the natural periods of tall buildings, long-span bridges, and base-isolated structures.
explanations.c: Vulnerability depends strongly on structural period, so the effect is not uniform across all structures.
explanations.d: Underground pipelines and tunnels are affected by permanent ground deformation generally, but the specific long-period vulnerability described here applies to long-period surface structures, not exclusively buried infrastructure.

lessons.label: Macroseismic Intensity: MMI, EMS-98, and ShakeMap

sections.heading: Intensity is about effects, not energy
sections.body: Magnitude is a single number describing the energy released at the source. Intensity is different: it describes the effects of shaking at a particular place, so a single earthquake produces one magnitude but many intensities - one at every location, generally decreasing with distance and modified by local site conditions. The Modified Mercalli Intensity (MMI) scale, based on Mercalli's 1902 scale and revised by Wood and Neumann in 1931, runs from I (not felt) to XII (total destruction) using descriptions of human perception, object movement, and structural damage. The European Macroseismic Scale (EMS-98) refines this with explicit building vulnerability classes and quantified damage grades, giving more consistent results across differing local construction. Japan's JMA scale (0-7) is calibrated instead to instrumentally recorded ground motion combined with damage observation, reflecting Japan's dense strong-motion network.

sections.heading: Crowdsourcing intensity: Did You Feel It?
sections.body: Historically, intensity maps required trained observers touring the damage zone after the event. The USGS "Did You Feel It?" (DYFI) system, described by Wald et al. (1999), instead collects a structured online questionnaire from anyone who felt the earthquake, converting each respondent's answers about shaking and damage into a Community Decimal Intensity (CDI) for their location, then aggregates thousands of individual reports into a near-real-time intensity map within minutes of an event - far denser and faster than door-to-door surveys.

sections.heading: Ground-motion-to-intensity conversion equations
sections.body: Because instrumental peak values, such as PGA and PGV, and intensity are both routinely available for recent earthquakes, empirical ground-motion-to-intensity conversion equations (GMICEs) have been fit relating instrumental PGA or PGV to MMI. These equations let USGS ShakeMap blend two data streams into one consistent shaking map: instrumentally recorded ground motion near seismometers, and DYFI or historical intensity observations extrapolated through the GMICE where no instrument exists, filling gaps in sparsely instrumented regions. ShakeMap does not simply connect these points - it interpolates between them using ground-motion prediction equations and spatial correlation of shaking, then reports an explicit uncertainty at every grid cell that shrinks close to stations and DYFI reports and grows in gaps between them, so the published map carries its own confidence alongside the shaking estimate.

sections.heading: Recovering shaking before seismometers existed
sections.body: The same logic runs backward in time: for earthquakes predating seismographs entirely, historical intensity from newspaper accounts, damage records, and diaries can be assigned MMI or EMS-98 values at each location and mapped, then the GMICE relationship inverted to estimate the equivalent instrumental ground motion, and, combined with attenuation modeling, the likely magnitude and location of the causative fault - the standard method for reconstructing pre-instrumental earthquakes such as the 1811-1812 New Madrid sequence.

lessons.workedExample: For a single M6.5 earthquake: an instrumented station 10 km away records PGA = 0.35g, which a GMICE converts to about MMI VIII; a cluster of DYFI responses 60 km away, reporting shaking felt but only minor damage, self-scores near CDI VI; and a small town 150 km away where nobody felt anything sits at MMI I. All three numbers describe the same single earthquake and its single Mw 6.5 magnitude - one magnitude, three of many possible local intensities, each driven by distance and local site amplification rather than by the source itself.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking "how many magnitudes did this earthquake have?" is checking whether the student conflates a single source-energy measure with the many, location-dependent intensity values an earthquake produces. A strong answer explains that intensity, not magnitude, varies by location, names a specific scale (MMI, EMS-98, or JMA) and how it is assigned, and can describe how modern systems like DYFI crowdsource that variation in near-real time via Wald et al.'s 1999 design, or how GMICEs let engineers move between instrumental and intensity data when reconstructing historical earthquakes.

questions.prompt: Why does a single earthquake have many different intensities but only one magnitude?

options.text: Intensity describes local shaking effects that vary by location, while magnitude is a single source-energy measure
Magnitude is also measured separately at every recording station
Intensity is only ever assigned at the epicenter
Intensity and magnitude are simply two names for the same quantity

explanations.a: Correct - magnitude describes energy released at the source and is a single value, while intensity describes local effects that depend on distance and site conditions, so it differs from place to place.
explanations.b: Magnitude is a single source property; while different stations can be used to estimate it, the reported magnitude is one value for the event, not a per-station intensity.
explanations.c: Intensity is assigned at every location that experienced or reported shaking, not only at the epicenter, which is precisely why one earthquake produces many intensity values.
explanations.d: Magnitude and intensity are distinct concepts - one measures source energy, the other measures local effects - and are not interchangeable.

questions.prompt: Match each intensity scale to its defining feature.

right.text: I-XII scale based on Mercalli's 1902 scale, revised by Wood and Neumann in 1931, using perception and damage descriptions
European scale with explicit building vulnerability classes and quantified damage grades
0-7 scale calibrated to instrumentally recorded ground motion, used in Japan

questions.explanation: MMI (I-XII) descends from Mercalli's 1902 scale as revised by Wood and Neumann in 1931; EMS-98 adds explicit building vulnerability classes and damage grades; the JMA scale (0-7) is calibrated to instrumental ground motion, reflecting Japan's dense strong-motion network.

questions.prompt: What does the USGS "Did You Feel It?" system, described by Wald et al. (1999), produce from its online questionnaire?

options.text: A Community Decimal Intensity aggregated for each respondent's location
A precise map of fault rupture slip
An automatically calculated earthquake magnitude
GPS-measured surface displacement fields

explanations.a: Correct - DYFI converts each respondent's structured answers into a Community Decimal Intensity for their location, then aggregates many reports into a near-real-time intensity map.
explanations.b: DYFI produces intensity estimates from felt reports, not a rupture slip map, which requires seismic, geodetic, or InSAR data.
explanations.c: DYFI is an intensity-reporting system, not a method for calculating magnitude.
explanations.d: DYFI relies on human questionnaire responses, not GPS instrumentation.

questions.prompt: Order the steps used to reconstruct ground motion for a pre-instrumental earthquake.

items.text: Collect historical accounts such as newspapers, damage records, and diaries
Assign MMI or EMS-98 intensity values at each location
Invert the GMICE relationship to estimate equivalent instrumental ground motion
Combine with attenuation modeling to estimate the earthquake's magnitude and location

questions.explanation: Reconstruction starts from historical accounts, converts them into intensity values at each location, inverts the GMICE to recover equivalent instrumental ground motion, then combines that with attenuation modeling to estimate the source magnitude and location.

lessons.label: Imaging the Rupture Itself

sections.heading: Finite-fault inversion: turning waveforms into a slip map
sections.body: A point-source magnitude and location say nothing about how slip was distributed across the fault plane - which patches slipped a lot, which barely moved, and in what direction rupture propagated. Finite-fault inversion divides an assumed fault plane into a grid of subfaults and solves for the slip amplitude, rake, and rupture timing on each one that together best reproduce observed data at every recording station. Modern inversions jointly combine complementary data: teleseismic body waves recorded worldwide (sensitive to overall moment and the general slip pattern), strong-motion accelerograms near the source (sensitive to detailed near-fault slip and timing), static GPS displacements (sensitive to the final, permanent deformation field), and InSAR, satellite radar interferometry sensitive to centimeter-scale surface displacement over a wide area. Combining data types this way reduces the ambiguity any single dataset leaves behind.

sections.heading: Back-projection: watching rupture propagate in real time
sections.body: A different technique, back-projection, uses a large seismic array at teleseismic distance to track high-frequency energy sources as they migrate along the fault during rupture, forming an image of where energy is radiating frame by frame rather than solving for total slip. Back-projection of the December 26, 2004 Sumatra-Andaman earthquake (Mw 9.1) showed the rupture front propagating northward along the Sunda trench for roughly 1300 km over about 8-10 minutes, an extraordinarily long and slow rupture that back-projection captured directly from array data even as the rupture was still unfolding.

sections.heading: Tohoku 2011: where the high frequencies came from
sections.body: Back-projection of the March 11, 2011 Tohoku earthquake (Mw 9.0) revealed that the highest-frequency radiation came from a different part of the fault than the largest slip: the shallow, near-trench patch produced the enormous slip, tens of meters, responsible for the tsunami, while high-frequency radiation concentrated further downdip, closer to the coast. This showed that where slip was largest and where damaging high-frequency shaking originated are not necessarily the same location on the fault.

sections.heading: Non-uniqueness: rival models of the same earthquake disagree
sections.body: Finite-fault inversion is fundamentally non-unique: different research groups, using different fault-plane assumptions, velocity models, and data weighting, routinely produce substantially different slip distributions for the identical earthquake. The SRCMOD database, compiled by Mai and collaborators, archives published finite-fault slip models and makes this visible directly - side-by-side comparisons for well-studied earthquakes like Tohoku or Landers show peak slip location, magnitude, and rupture directivity varying considerably between models, a reminder that a single published slip map is one plausible solution among several, not a unique ground truth.

lessons.workedExample: For the 2011 Tohoku earthquake, teleseismic-only, GPS-only, and InSAR-only inversions each independently suggest peak slip is largest near the trench, roughly tens of meters, but the three data types disagree on exactly how far downdip that peak patch extends and how much slip occurred on deeper subfaults closer to the coast. A joint inversion combining all three, cross-checked against back-projected high-frequency source locations found further downdip than the peak-slip patch, produces a more constrained composite model - yet SRCMOD entries from different published Tohoku studies still show peak-slip estimates differing by tens of percent, illustrating why "the slip model" for a major earthquake is really several competing models.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking "is that the slip map, or a slip map?" is testing whether the student understands finite-fault inversion as an underdetermined inverse problem rather than a direct measurement. A strong answer names the specific data types combined (teleseismic, strong-motion, GPS, InSAR) and what each constrains, cites the SRCMOD database as documented evidence that independent groups disagree on the same earthquake, and can distinguish back-projection's real-time energy tracking, as used for 2004 Sumatra and 2011 Tohoku, from finite-fault inversion's static slip-distribution result.

questions.prompt: What does finite-fault inversion solve for that a single point-source magnitude cannot provide?

options.text: The distribution of slip amplitude and timing across subfaults on the fault plane
The exact hypocenter depth only
The total seismic moment only
The crustal P-wave velocity structure

explanations.a: Correct - finite-fault inversion grids the fault plane into subfaults and solves for slip amplitude, rake, and timing on each, giving a spatial slip distribution a point source cannot.
explanations.b: Hypocenter depth is a single-point-source parameter; finite-fault inversion instead resolves an entire spatial slip pattern.
explanations.c: Total seismic moment is also obtainable from a point-source solution; the added value of finite-fault inversion is the spatial and temporal slip distribution.
explanations.d: Crustal velocity structure is typically an input assumption to the inversion, not its output.

questions.prompt: Match each data type used in finite-fault inversion to what it primarily constrains.

right.text: Overall moment and general slip pattern from global stations
Detailed near-fault slip and timing
Final permanent surface displacement at point stations
Wide-area centimeter-scale surface displacement from satellite radar

questions.explanation: Teleseismic body waves constrain overall moment and the general slip pattern; strong-motion records near the source constrain detailed near-fault slip and timing; GPS constrains final permanent displacement at discrete points; InSAR constrains wide-area, centimeter-scale surface displacement from satellite radar.

questions.prompt: Back-projection of the 2004 Sumatra-Andaman earthquake showed the rupture propagating northward over approximately what distance and duration?

options.text: 1300 km over about 8-10 minutes
100 km over about 30 seconds
3000 km over about 1 hour
500 km over about 2 minutes

explanations.a: Correct - back-projection tracked the rupture front propagating northward along the Sunda trench for roughly 1300 km over about 8-10 minutes.
explanations.b: This distance and duration are far too small for the Mw 9.1 Sumatra-Andaman rupture, which propagated over an unusually long fault length.
explanations.c: This overstates both the distance and duration well beyond what back-projection recorded for this event.
explanations.d: This underestimates both the rupture length and duration observed for the 2004 event.

questions.prompt: What did back-projection of the 2011 Tohoku earthquake reveal about the relationship between high-frequency radiation and the largest fault slip?

options.text: They came from the same shallow, near-trench patch
High-frequency radiation concentrated downdip, closer to the coast, while the largest slip was shallow and near-trench
There was no high-frequency radiation detected in this earthquake
The largest slip occurred downdip, not near the trench

explanations.a: Back-projection showed these two features were spatially separated, not co-located.
explanations.b: Correct - the shallow near-trench patch produced the largest slip (responsible for the tsunami), while high-frequency radiation concentrated further downdip, closer to the coast.
explanations.c: High-frequency radiation was detected and mapped by back-projection; the finding was about its location relative to peak slip, not its absence.
explanations.d: The largest slip was shallow and near-trench, not downdip; it was the high-frequency radiation that was located downdip.

questions.prompt: What do SRCMOD comparisons of finite-fault models from different research groups demonstrate about the same earthquake?

options.text: All models agree closely because the data uniquely constrains slip
Finite-fault inversion is non-unique - different groups can produce substantially different slip distributions for the same event
InSAR data is generally unreliable for earthquake studies
Magnitude estimates vary by an order of magnitude between research groups

explanations.a: SRCMOD comparisons show the opposite - models diverge considerably rather than agreeing closely, because the inversion problem is underdetermined.
explanations.b: Correct - side-by-side SRCMOD comparisons for earthquakes like Tohoku or Landers show peak slip location, magnitude, and directivity varying considerably between independently produced models.
explanations.c: The lesson does not conclude InSAR is unreliable; it is one of several valuable but individually incomplete constraints combined in joint inversion.
explanations.d: Magnitude estimates across groups are generally much closer than slip-distribution details; the large disagreement described is in spatial slip pattern, not magnitude.

units.label: Seismic Hazard, Forecasting, and Early Warning

lessons.label: Probabilistic Seismic Hazard Analysis

sections.heading: Cornell's four steps
sections.body: Before 1968, seismic design leaned on the largest earthquake anyone could recall for a region — a deterministic worst case with no sense of how often it might recur. In 1968, Allin Cornell published "Engineering Seismic Risk Analysis," the paper that turned hazard into a probability calculation, now called probabilistic seismic hazard analysis (PSHA). It has four steps. First, identify seismic source zones — faults or areal zones capable of generating earthquakes — and estimate each one's rate of activity. Second, describe the magnitude distribution within each source, typically a Gutenberg-Richter recurrence relation truncated at a maximum magnitude. Third, apply a ground-motion model (a ground-motion prediction equation, or GMPE) that converts magnitude and source-to-site distance into an expected shaking level, such as peak ground acceleration, with its own scatter. Fourth, integrate over every source, every magnitude, and every distance to get the total annual rate that shaking at a site exceeds any given level.

sections.heading: The hazard curve and the uniform-hazard spectrum
sections.body: That integration produces a hazard curve: annual exceedance probability plotted against ground-motion level, computed separately at each period of vibration (0.2 s, 1.0 s, and so on). Reading off the ground motion at a chosen exceedance probability across all periods yields a uniform-hazard spectrum — a design spectrum where every point carries the same probability of exceedance, even though the earthquakes generating it differ by period. A hazard curve can also be deaggregated: for a chosen exceedance probability, the contributing sources are broken back out by magnitude and distance to show which magnitude-distance combinations actually dominate the hazard at that level. Deaggregation often produces a bimodal result — for example, a nearby moderate-magnitude earthquake and a more distant large earthquake both contributing substantially to the same peak ground acceleration — which tells engineers which controlling scenario(s) to design against, rather than leaving them with only the aggregate rate.

sections.heading: From annual rate to a design number
sections.body: Design codes then pick a target rate and invert the curve for a ground-motion value. The commonly quoted "2% probability of exceedance in 50 years" converts to an average return period via T = -50/ln(1-0.02), giving roughly 2,475 years — not a claim that such a quake strikes every 2,475 years, but that its annual rate is about 1/2475. The USGS National Seismic Hazard Model runs Cornell's integral over the whole US using mapped faults plus background seismicity, and the resulting maps of shaking-at-2%-in-50-years become the seismic design maps adopted into building codes such as ASCE 7.

lessons.workedExample: A site sits 15 km from a fault with a Gutenberg-Richter rate of 0.02 M≥6 earthquakes per year and a background zone contributing smaller, more frequent shocks. A PSHA run combines both sources through a GMPE, producing a hazard curve showing 0.001 annual probability (a 1-in-1,000-year rate) corresponds to 0.3g peak ground acceleration. Reading the same 0.001 annual-rate point off curves computed at 0.2 s and 1.0 s period, instead of just PGA, and connecting those points across periods is exactly how a uniform-hazard spectrum is built for a building code. Deaggregating that same 0.001 annual-rate, 0.3g point might show it is dominated by both a nearby M6.2 event on the fault and a rarer, more distant M7.5 background event — two very different earthquakes that happen to produce comparable shaking at this site and probability level.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks "what does your 2%-in-50-years number actually mean?" is testing whether a student can convert probability into a return period and knows that a hazard curve is built by integrating over every source, magnitude, and distance rather than reading off one worst-case fault. Students who reach for a single deterministic scenario when the question is about code-level hazard have missed that PSHA's whole point is aggregating many uncertain contributors into one rate, and confusing "2,475-year earthquake" with "an earthquake every 2,475 years" is the single most common and most revealing error.

questions.prompt: A design ground motion is specified at 2% probability of exceedance in 50 years. What average return period does this correspond to?

options.text: About 50 years
About 475 years
About 2,475 years
About 10,000 years

explanations.a: 50 years is the exposure window used in the probability statement, not the return period itself.
explanations.b: 475 years corresponds to a 10%-in-50-years probability, a different and more frequent design level used for lower-consequence structures.
explanations.c: Correct — T = -50/ln(1-0.02) ≈ 2,475 years, the standard return period behind the 2%-in-50-years design level.
explanations.d: 10,000-year return periods appear in some critical-facility criteria, but not for the 2%-in-50-years figure itself.

questions.prompt: Put Cornell's four PSHA steps in the order they are carried out.

items.text: Identify seismic source zones and their activity rates
Assign a magnitude-recurrence distribution to each source
Apply a ground-motion model to convert magnitude and distance to shaking
Integrate over all sources, magnitudes, and distances to build the hazard curve

questions.explanation: Cornell's framework first defines where earthquakes come from, then how often each size occurs there, then how that shaking reaches the site, and only then combines everything into the site's total hazard curve.

questions.prompt: What does a uniform-hazard spectrum represent?

options.text: The shaking recorded from a single historical earthquake at every period
A spectrum where every period's ground motion shares the same annual exceedance probability
The average of all recorded ground motions at a site
The maximum possible ground motion a fault could ever produce

explanations.a: A single earthquake's spectrum reflects one event's specific source and path, not a probability level held constant across periods.
explanations.b: Correct — a uniform-hazard spectrum is built by reading the ground motion at the same chosen exceedance probability (e.g., 2% in 50 years) off separately computed hazard curves at each period.
explanations.c: It is not a simple average of recordings; it comes from integrating probabilistically over all contributing sources.
explanations.d: That describes a deterministic maximum scenario, the opposite of the probabilistic construction behind a uniform-hazard spectrum.

lessons.label: Probabilistic vs Deterministic, and the Critics

sections.heading: Logic trees and two kinds of uncertainty
sections.body: Real PSHA studies do not commit to one fault geometry, one recurrence model, or one ground-motion equation — they run a logic tree, branching at each modeling choice (is the fault segmented or does it rupture as one unit? which GMPE? what maximum magnitude, Mmax?) with each branch assigned a weight reflecting expert judgment, then combining branches into a weighted hazard curve with explicit percentiles. This structure separates two kinds of uncertainty that are easy to conflate. Aleatory uncertainty is the natural, irreducible randomness of the physical process itself — the scatter in ground motion between two earthquakes of identical magnitude and distance. Epistemic uncertainty is uncertainty about the model — which we don't yet know well enough to pick a single right answer, like whether a fault's true Mmax is 7.5 or 8.2. Logic trees exist specifically to carry epistemic uncertainty forward instead of pretending a single best-guess model is the truth.

sections.heading: The Klügel-Bommer exchange
sections.body: Mmax is the sharpest fight in the field because it is unobservable — you cannot measure the largest earthquake a fault will ever produce, only bound it from geology and analogy. J.U. Klügel argued in a 2005 Engineering Geology paper, "Problems in the application of the SSHAC probability method for assessing earthquake hazards at Swiss nuclear power plants," that SSHAC-style PSHA — SSHAC being the Senior Seismic Hazard Analysis Committee, the formal expert-elicitation procedure developed for U.S. nuclear-facility hazard assessment — when applied to nuclear facilities requiring ground motions at annual frequencies of 10⁻⁴ to 10⁻⁶, was being extrapolated far beyond anything a short instrumental or historical catalog could constrain, and that expert-elicitation weighting amounted to manufactured consensus rather than physical justification. Julian Bommer and coauthors countered that logic-tree epistemic uncertainty is precisely the tool for expressing that ignorance honestly, and that abandoning PSHA for a single deterministic scenario hides uncertainty rather than resolving it — a deterministic number looks more certain only because it stops asking the question.

sections.heading: Testing forecasts against the future
sections.body: The response from the seismology community was to make forecasts falsifiable. The Collaboratory for the Study of Earthquake Predictability (CSEP) and its predecessor, the Regional Earthquake Likelihood Models (RELM) experiment, register time-stamped forecasts before the fact and score them against subsequent seismicity, so competing recurrence models can be graded rather than argued. California's Uniform California Earthquake Rupture Forecast (UCERF, now UCERF3) is built and retested this way, folding in multi-fault ruptures and updated recurrence statistics as new data arrive.

lessons.workedExample: A logic tree for a coastal nuclear-site hazard study might branch three ways on Mmax (7.5, 8.0, 8.5, weighted 0.3/0.5/0.2) and two ways on GMPE choice, yielding six weighted hazard curves. Klügel's critique would target the Mmax weights themselves as expert opinion dressed as data at a facility needing 10⁻⁵ annual-frequency ground motion; Bommer's reply is that showing the full spread of six curves, rather than collapsing to one "best" number, is what lets a regulator see how much the answer actually depends on an unresolved geological question.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing this concept wants to see that a student can name what kind of uncertainty a logic tree branch represents — aleatory scatter versus epistemic model choice — because conflating the two is the most common shortcut in student risk write-ups. The stronger tell is recognizing that the Klügel-Bommer disagreement is not about whether PSHA's math is correct but about whether any catalog is long enough to justify claims at 10⁻⁴-10⁻⁶ frequencies, and that CSEP-style prospective testing is the field's answer to "how would we know if this model is wrong?"

questions.prompt: Match each term to its correct description.

right.text: Irreducible natural randomness in ground motion for a fixed magnitude and distance
Uncertainty about which model is correct, carried forward via logic-tree branches
The unobservable largest earthquake a source can produce
A framework for registering forecasts in advance and scoring them against later seismicity

questions.explanation: Aleatory uncertainty is physical randomness; epistemic uncertainty is model ignorance handled with weighted logic-tree branches; Mmax is the unmeasurable ceiling magnitude at the center of PSHA disputes; CSEP and RELM make forecasts testable by scoring them prospectively.

questions.prompt: What was the core of Klügel's critique of PSHA as applied to critical facilities?

options.text: That ground-motion prediction equations use the wrong units
That extrapolating short catalogs to 10⁻⁴-10⁻⁶ annual frequencies relies on expert-weighted judgment rather than data long enough to support it
That earthquakes cannot be modeled probabilistically at all
That deterministic hazard assessment had already been abandoned by regulators

explanations.a: Klügel's argument was about the epistemic basis of the estimates, not a unit or arithmetic error in GMPEs.
explanations.b: Correct — Klügel argued that at the very low annual frequencies required for nuclear-facility design, PSHA leans on expert-elicited weights (like Mmax branches) rather than a catalog long enough to constrain them empirically.
explanations.c: Klügel did not reject probabilistic modeling outright; the dispute was about extrapolation limits and expert-weighting methodology.
explanations.d: Deterministic assessment remains in use alongside PSHA; it was not the subject of this exchange.

questions.prompt: What is the primary purpose of the logic-tree structure in modern PSHA?

options.text: To average away all uncertainty into a single deterministic number
To carry forward and weight competing modeling choices as explicit epistemic uncertainty
To replace ground-motion models with historical intensity reports
To eliminate the need for source-zone identification

explanations.a: The point of a logic tree is the opposite — preserving the spread across branches rather than collapsing it away.
explanations.b: Correct — each branch represents a distinct, weighted modeling choice (fault geometry, Mmax, GMPE), so the tree carries epistemic uncertainty through to the final hazard curve.
explanations.c: Ground-motion models remain a required PSHA step; logic trees branch on choices within that step, not a replacement for it.
explanations.d: Source-zone identification is Cornell's first PSHA step and logic trees still branch on how sources are defined; they don't remove the step.

lessons.label: Paleoseismology and Recurrence Intervals

sections.heading: Reading past ruptures out of the ground
sections.body: Paleoseismology reconstructs earthquakes that happened before any instrument or written record by digging trenches across a fault and reading the stratigraphy: a rupture that reaches the surface offsets and buries soil layers, and radiocarbon-dated organic material above and below each offset brackets when that event occurred. At Wallace Creek, in California's Carrizo Plain, Kerry Sieh mapped a small stream channel that the San Andreas fault has repeatedly sliced and dragged sideways; the present channel sits offset about 128 m from where it used to drain, and trenching plus dating of individual past ruptures (each jumping the channel roughly 8-9 m) let Sieh reconstruct a sequence of large earthquakes stretching back thousands of years, yielding an average recurrence interval on the order of 250 years for that fault segment.

sections.heading: Cascadia's silent giant, pinned by a tsunami on the other side of the Pacific
sections.body: The Cascadia subduction zone off the Pacific Northwest produces no historical earthquake record at all — no written account of a great quake exists in the region. Brian Atwater found the physical scars anyway: coastal marshes buried abruptly under tidal mud, and stands of cedar killed instantly by sudden saltwater incursion, the drowned "ghost forests" still standing near Willapa Bay and elsewhere, plus offshore turbidites (sediment layers dumped by underwater slope failures during shaking). None of that alone gives a precise date. The date came from Japan: Kenji Satake and coauthors (1996) matched a tsunami that struck Japan's coast on 27 January 1700 with no accompanying local earthquake — an "orphan tsunami" in Japanese record-keeping — to a Cascadia rupture the night before, back-calculating a moment magnitude near 9.0 from tsunami travel time and wave heights. Stacking that single dated event against the longer turbidite and marsh record gives Cascadia an average recurrence interval of roughly 500 years, though individual intervals in the turbidite record vary widely.

sections.heading: Characteristic quakes versus Gutenberg-Richter
sections.body: Wallace Creek's repeating, similarly sized offsets are the classic evidence for the characteristic-earthquake model: a given fault segment tends to rupture in similarly sized events at roughly regular intervals, rather than following the smooth power-law size distribution (Gutenberg-Richter) that describes a whole region's seismicity. Critics counter that trenching only samples large surface-rupturing events and cannot see the smaller earthquakes a pure Gutenberg-Richter model predicts in between, so apparent "characteristic" clustering may partly reflect what paleoseismology is capable of detecting rather than what the fault is actually doing.

lessons.workedExample: A trench across a fault reveals four buried soil horizons, each abruptly displaced by the same amount and each capped by a layer with distinct radiocarbon ages: 1200, 950, 680, and 310 years before present. That gives three inter-event intervals of roughly 250, 270, and 370 years, averaging near 300 years — the same style of calculation Sieh applied at Wallace Creek, and the same logic Atwater and Satake used for Cascadia when turbidite counts were combined with the single precisely dated 1700 event to estimate a recurrence interval near 500 years.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking about recurrence intervals wants to see the difference between a single average number and the actual scatter behind it — Cascadia's ~500-year average recurrence, for instance, is built from a record with much shorter and much longer individual gaps, not evenly spaced clockwork. The strongest answers also engage the characteristic-earthquake versus Gutenberg-Richter tension directly: acknowledging that trenching is biased toward detecting only the largest, surface-rupturing events is what separates a student who understands the method's limits from one who treats a trench count as a complete earthquake history.

questions.prompt: How was the date of the Cascadia earthquake pinned to 26 January 1700 despite no local written record?

options.text: Radiocarbon dating of a single buried soil layer at one Oregon trench site
Matching an unexplained ('orphan') tsunami recorded in Japan on 27 January 1700 to a Cascadia rupture the prior night
A Spanish colonial mission log describing the shaking
Counting annual growth rings in the drowned ghost forests alone

explanations.a: Radiocarbon dating brackets events to a range of years, not a specific calendar day; the precise date came from a different source.
explanations.b: Correct — Satake and coauthors (1996) matched Japanese records of a tsunami with no local earthquake to a Cascadia rupture the night before, using travel time to fix the date and modeled wave heights to estimate a magnitude near 9.0.
explanations.c: No Cascadia-region historical account of the earthquake exists; the region had no written record of the event at the time.
explanations.d: Ghost-forest tree-ring dating narrows a range of possible years but does not by itself provide a specific calendar date; the precision came from the Japanese tsunami record.

questions.prompt: Match each paleoseismic evidence type to the location where it was used.

left.text: Offset stream channel, dated by trenching
Drowned ghost forests and buried marsh soils
An orphan tsunami recorded on the opposite side of an ocean

right.text: Wallace Creek, San Andreas fault
Cascadia subduction zone coastline
Japan's 1700 written tsunami records

questions.explanation: Sieh used the repeatedly offset Wallace Creek channel to reconstruct San Andreas recurrence; Atwater used drowned ghost forests and buried marsh soils along the Cascadia coast; Satake used Japan's 1700 tsunami records, which had no accompanying local earthquake, to date and size the Cascadia rupture.

questions.prompt: What is the main criticism of the characteristic-earthquake model as inferred from trenching studies like Wallace Creek?

options.text: Trenching cannot detect any earthquakes at all
Trenching mainly detects large surface-rupturing events, so apparent regular 'characteristic' sizing may partly reflect a detection limit rather than the fault's true full size distribution
Radiocarbon dating is always inaccurate by centuries
The Gutenberg-Richter relation has been fully disproven by trenching data

explanations.a: Trenching does detect earthquakes — that is its core method — the criticism is about which sizes it can detect, not whether it works at all.
explanations.b: Correct — because trenches mainly preserve evidence of large, surface-breaking ruptures, the similarly sized 'characteristic' events they reveal may be a sampling artifact rather than proof the fault only produces one size of earthquake.
explanations.c: Radiocarbon dating has known, well-characterized uncertainty ranges but is not simply 'always inaccurate'; that is not the criticism at issue here.
explanations.d: Gutenberg-Richter still describes regional seismicity well overall; the debate is about whether individual fault segments follow it or behave more characteristically, not a wholesale disproof.

lessons.label: Earthquake Early Warning

sections.heading: A race between wave types
sections.body: Earthquake early warning (EEW) works because seismic waves radiate at different speeds while a warning can travel at the speed of light over a network and phone signal. The fast, low-damage P wave arrives first; the slower S wave and surface waves that do most of the shaking damage arrive seconds to tens of seconds later depending on distance. A network of sensors near the source detects the P wave, estimates location and magnitude within seconds, and fires an alert to more distant users before the damaging waves reach them. That gap shrinks toward zero close to the epicenter, creating a blind zone — a radius within which the damaging waves arrive before any useful warning can be issued, no matter how fast the algorithm runs.

sections.heading: Point-source versus finite-fault estimation
sections.body: Early EEW algorithms treated the earthquake as a point source, estimating magnitude from the first few seconds of P-wave amplitude and frequency content at one or a few stations. That works well for small-to-moderate events but saturates for very large ruptures, because a fault that keeps growing for tens of seconds or minutes cannot have its final size known from an instant of P-wave data. Finite-fault algorithms instead track how the rupture is propagating across an extended fault plane in real time, updating the magnitude and expected shaking as more stations report in, which better captures a slowly unzipping mega-rupture.

sections.heading: Real systems, a real failure, and a real tradeoff
sections.body: Japan's Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) system began operating nationally in 2007 as the first EEW system to issue public alerts. During the 2011 Tohoku earthquake, JMA's point-source algorithm initially estimated the magnitude near 7.9 within its first few minutes (an initial estimate released about 3 minutes after the quake), well below the eventual moment magnitude of about 9.0, because the point-source method could not yet see how far the rupture would continue to grow; JMA has since added finite-fault-style methods to correct this. On the US West Coast, ShakeAlert (run by USGS with state partners) issues alerts through apps and the Wireless Emergency Alert system, while the phone-based MyShake network out of UC Berkeley uses ordinary smartphone accelerometers as a crowdsourced sensor array. Every EEW system runs on a latency budget of just a few seconds between detection and alert, and must trade off false alerts (alerting when shaking will not actually be damaging) against missed alerts (failing to warn before real damage), since tightening the trigger threshold to avoid one type of error worsens the other.

lessons.workedExample: A magnitude 7 earthquake ruptures a fault, and a city sits 100 km from the epicenter. P waves (~6 km/s) reach the city in about 17 seconds; damaging S waves (~3.5 km/s) arrive around 29 seconds after origin time. If the network detects the P wave and issues an alert within 5 seconds of the origin time, the city gets roughly 24 seconds of warning — enough to stop trains and open elevator doors. A town only 10 km from the epicenter sits inside the blind zone: P waves arrive in under 2 seconds, well before a 5-second-latency alert can even be issued, so no meaningful warning is possible there regardless of network speed.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing EEW wants a student to explain the physical reason a blind zone exists — it is not a software limitation but the unavoidable consequence of P and S waves both radiating from the same point and converging in travel time as distance shrinks. The Tohoku underestimate is the sharpest test case: a student who can explain why a point-source algorithm undersized a still-growing rupture, and why finite-fault tracking addresses that, has grasped the real engineering tradeoff, versus a student who only says the system 'malfunctioned.'

questions.prompt: Why does a 'blind zone' exist close to an earthquake's epicenter for early warning systems?

options.text: Sensors are never installed near epicenters
The gap between P-wave detection and the arrival of damaging S/surface waves shrinks toward zero as distance to the source decreases
Phone networks lose signal near fault lines
Point-source algorithms refuse to process nearby stations

explanations.a: Sensor placement is a practical, addressable choice, not the physical reason a blind zone exists at all.
explanations.b: Correct — because both P and damaging S/surface waves originate at the same point, the time between them at a given site shrinks as that site gets closer to the source, eventually leaving no usable gap for a warning to arrive before the damage does.
explanations.c: Signal loss is not the mechanism; the blind zone is a travel-time physics problem, not a communications problem.
explanations.d: Algorithms do process nearby stations; the limitation is the physical travel-time gap, not a deliberate exclusion.

questions.prompt: Why did JMA's system initially underestimate the magnitude of the 2011 Tohoku earthquake?

options.text: Its point-source method estimated magnitude from early P-wave data before the still-growing rupture had fully unzipped
All of its seismic sensors failed simultaneously
It had never issued a public alert before and was untested
The earthquake was too far offshore to detect at all

explanations.a: Correct — a point-source algorithm reads an early, brief window of P-wave data, which cannot capture a rupture that continues extending across the fault for tens of seconds, so it undersized Tohoku's eventual scale.
explanations.b: Sensor failure was not the issue; the algorithm processed real data but with a method unsuited to a very large, slowly propagating rupture.
explanations.c: JMA's system had been operating publicly since 2007, well before 2011; it was an established system, not an untested one.
explanations.d: The earthquake was detected and did trigger alerts; the problem was underestimating its magnitude, not failing to detect it.

questions.prompt: Match each earthquake early warning system or method to its description.

right.text: Japan's national system, public since 2007, first to issue nationwide public EEW alerts
USGS-run system with state partners issuing alerts on the US West Coast
Crowdsourced network using ordinary smartphone accelerometers as sensors
Tracks a rupture's real-time growth across an extended fault rather than assuming a single point

questions.explanation: JMA launched the first public national EEW system in 2007; ShakeAlert covers the US West Coast under USGS; MyShake crowdsources phone sensors; finite-fault algorithms track ongoing rupture growth rather than treating the source as a single point, addressing the weakness point-source methods showed at Tohoku.

lessons.label: Induced and Triggered Seismicity

sections.heading: Pore pressure and Coulomb stress
sections.body: A fault sits in balance between the friction holding it locked and the shear stress trying to slide it. Injecting fluid into the surrounding rock raises pore-fluid pressure, which reduces the effective normal stress clamping the fault shut — the same shear stress can now overcome a weaker effective friction, and the fault slips. This is elevated pore pressure triggering, and it can act at a distance from the injection point as pressure diffuses through connected rock over months to years. A related but distinct mechanism is Coulomb stress transfer: slip on one fault mechanically nudges the stress field on nearby faults, bringing some closer to failure and pushing others further from it, which is how one earthquake (natural or induced) can trigger another nearby.

sections.heading: The founding case and Oklahoma's ramp-up
sections.body: The Rocky Mountain Arsenal near Denver, Colorado, deep-injected chemical waste from 1962 to 1966, and a swarm of earthquakes beneath the site tracked the injection schedule closely enough that a 1968 study identified fluid injection as the cause — the case that established the mechanism scientists still use today. Decades later, Oklahoma experienced a far larger version of the same physics: shale-gas-related wastewater disposal wells injected enormous volumes of saltwater brought up alongside oil and gas, and the state's rate of magnitude-3-or-greater earthquakes rose from a historical background of roughly one or two per year to a peak of about 900 in 2015, before regulatory limits on injection volumes brought the rate back down. William Ellsworth's 2013 review in Science laid out the pore-pressure mechanism behind this US mid-continent rise and argued that only a small fraction of the tens of thousands of disposal wells nationally were responsible, typically the highest-volume ones communicating directly with basement faults.

sections.heading: Traffic-light protocols and liability
sections.body: Two European cases show the regulatory response. The Netherlands' Groningen gas field, one of the largest in Europe, saw induced earthquakes tied to reservoir compaction from decades of extraction, ultimately forcing the government to order production cuts and, eventually, full closure to limit seismic risk to residents. In Basel, Switzerland, a 2006 enhanced-geothermal-system project injected water at depth to fracture hot rock for power generation; within days it produced a felt magnitude 3.4 earthquake, and the project was halted and later permanently cancelled after a risk study found the ongoing hazard unacceptable. Traffic-light protocols now govern many injection projects: green allows normal operation, yellow requires reduced injection rates or increased monitoring once seismicity crosses a threshold, and red halts injection outright — with disputes over who bears liability for damage sitting at the center of debates over how conservatively those thresholds should be set.

lessons.workedExample: A wastewater disposal well injects at a steady rate for two years with no seismicity, then a fault 3 km away that was unmapped begins slipping as the pressure front from injection finally diffuses that far — the same delayed, at-a-distance pattern documented in Oklahoma, where individual induced sequences sometimes lagged the start of nearby injection by months. A traffic-light protocol would have required operators to log a 'yellow' response (cutting injection volume) as soon as felt seismicity above a set magnitude threshold appeared, rather than waiting for a larger event, mirroring how Basel's operators halted injection within days of the felt magnitude 3.4 shock in 2006.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking about induced seismicity wants the mechanism named precisely — pore-pressure reduction of effective normal stress, not a vague 'fracking causes earthquakes' — plus recognition that the fault triggered is often not the injection well itself but a nearby, sometimes previously unmapped fault reached by pressure diffusion. Citing a specific case (Rocky Mountain Arsenal's 1962-66 timeline, Oklahoma's rise to about 900 M3+ events in 2015, or Basel's 2006 M3.4 shutdown) and connecting it to a traffic-light threshold is what distinguishes an evidence-based hazard argument from a general environmental claim.

questions.prompt: What is the primary physical mechanism by which fluid injection induces earthquakes on a nearby fault?

options.text: Injected fluid directly lubricates the fault surface like an oil
Elevated pore-fluid pressure reduces the effective normal stress clamping the fault, allowing existing shear stress to overcome friction
The added weight of injected fluid physically pushes the fault sideways
Injection changes the fault's rock composition, weakening it chemically

explanations.a: It is not simple lubrication; the mechanism operates through effective stress, not surface friction reduction from a lubricant film.
explanations.b: Correct — raising pore pressure lowers the effective normal stress holding the fault locked, so the same ambient shear stress can now exceed the fault's reduced frictional resistance and cause slip.
explanations.c: The mass of injected fluid at these volumes is not the driver; the effect is a stress-balance change, not a mechanical push.
explanations.d: Chemical alteration of rock is not the established mechanism; the accepted explanation is the pore-pressure and effective-stress pathway.

questions.prompt: Order these induced-seismicity cases by when their key event occurred.

items.text: Rocky Mountain Arsenal injection and seismicity identified as linked
Basel geothermal project produces a magnitude 3.4 earthquake and is halted
Ellsworth's Science review lays out the injection-induced-earthquake mechanism
Oklahoma's M3+ earthquake rate peaks at about 900 in a single year

questions.explanation: Rocky Mountain Arsenal (1962-66) is the founding case; Basel's induced M3.4 and shutdown occurred in 2006; Ellsworth published the mechanism review in Science in 2013; Oklahoma's M3+ rate peaked at about 900 in 2015.

questions.prompt: Under a traffic-light protocol for an injection project, what does a 'yellow' status require?

options.text: Immediate and permanent shutdown of the project
No change, since yellow indicates normal safe operation
Reduced injection rates and increased seismic monitoring once seismicity crosses a defined threshold
A public referendum on whether to continue the project

explanations.a: Permanent shutdown corresponds to the 'red' stage, reached only if seismicity continues to escalate beyond the yellow response.
explanations.b: Normal, unrestricted operation is the 'green' stage; yellow specifically signals that a threshold has been crossed and a response is required.
explanations.c: Correct — yellow is the intermediate warning stage, calling for operators to cut injection volumes and step up monitoring in response to detected seismicity.
explanations.d: Traffic-light protocols are technical/regulatory monitoring thresholds set by operators and regulators, not public votes.

lessons.label: Tsunami Warning and Megathrust Case Studies

sections.heading: How a megathrust makes a tsunami
sections.body: A subduction-zone megathrust earthquake ruptures the shallow, gently dipping interface where an oceanic plate slides beneath a continental or another oceanic plate. When that shallow patch of the interface slips, the overriding plate above it springs upward or downward over an area that can span hundreds of kilometers, displacing the entire water column above it. That vertical seafloor displacement is the tsunami source: unlike wind-driven waves, a tsunami's wavelength is set by the rupture's dimensions, letting it travel at hundreds of kilometers per hour in deep water while carrying enormous energy that only piles up into a destructive wave as it shoals near shore.

sections.heading: Detecting it fast: DART buoys and W-phase inversion
sections.body: Two tools shortened the response time between rupture and warning. DART (Deep-ocean Assessment and Reporting of Tsunamis) buoys sit on the open-ocean floor with pressure sensors that detect the passing tsunami directly, relaying data via a surface buoy to satellite — a direct physical measurement rather than an inference from seismic waves. On the seismic side, Hiroo Kanamori and Luis Rivera (2008) developed W-phase inversion, which uses a long-period seismic phase arriving before the S wave to estimate a reliable moment magnitude within tens of minutes, correcting the historic problem that traditional magnitude scales saturate and underestimate the very largest earthquakes — the ones that matter most for tsunami hazard.

sections.heading: Two megathrusts, two failures of a different kind
sections.body: The 26 December 2004 Sumatra-Andaman earthquake (moment magnitude about 9.1) struck a region with no tsunami warning system at all; the resulting waves killed roughly 230,000 people across the Indian Ocean rim, largely because no detection-to-alert infrastructure existed to give coastal communities any lead time. That total absence of warning infrastructure directly prompted the establishment of the Indian Ocean Tsunami Warning and Mitigation System (IOTWMS) in 2006, under UNESCO's Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission, to close exactly that gap before the next major Indian Ocean event. The 11 March 2011 Tohoku earthquake struck a nation with an established warning system and extensive coastal defenses, and still killed roughly 18,000 people, because the initial warning underestimated the earthquake's true size and the tsunami that followed exceeded the height that existing seawalls were engineered to hold back. The two disasters point to different failure modes: Sumatra lacked any warning system, while Tohoku had one whose accuracy and whose downstream engineering assumptions were both outmatched by the earthquake's actual scale.

lessons.workedExample: A subduction-zone rupture displaces the seafloor by several meters over a 300-km-long patch. A DART buoy 200 km offshore detects the resulting pressure pulse and confirms wave generation within roughly 15-20 minutes, while a W-phase inversion run on the seismic data in parallel converges on a moment magnitude near 8.9 within about 20-30 minutes of the origin time — together giving forecasters an independent seismic estimate and a direct physical confirmation before the wave reaches a distant coastline hours later. A defensible student hazard project would claim exactly this kind of bounded statement (an estimated tsunami arrival window and wave-height range at a named coastline, sourced to a specific rupture scenario) rather than an unqualified 'this fault could cause a tsunami.'
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking about tsunami hazard is testing whether a student can name the actual source mechanism — vertical seafloor displacement from shallow megathrust slip, not just 'a big underwater earthquake' — and can distinguish a detection tool (DART, which measures the wave itself) from a magnitude tool (W-phase inversion, which measures the earthquake). The contrast between 2004 and 2011 is the key test: a strong answer explains that Sumatra failed from having no system at all while Tohoku's system existed but underestimated the earthquake and its defenses were built to an insufficient design wave, showing that 'a warning system exists' and 'the warning and defenses were adequate' are two different claims.

questions.prompt: What physically generates a megathrust tsunami?

options.text: Strong shaking alone stirring up the ocean surface
Vertical displacement of the seafloor and the water column above it when the shallow subduction interface slips
Underwater landslides are always the direct cause of megathrust tsunamis
Wind generated by the earthquake's energy release

explanations.a: Shaking of the water surface itself does not produce a tsunami's characteristic long wavelength and energy; the source is deeper.
explanations.b: Correct — when the shallow megathrust interface slips, the seafloor and overlying water column are displaced vertically over a large area, and that displacement is the tsunami's source.
explanations.c: Landslides can generate tsunamis, but the defining mechanism for a megathrust tsunami specifically is direct co-seismic seafloor displacement, not landslides.
explanations.d: Tsunamis are not wind-driven waves; their generation and wavelength come from seafloor displacement, not atmospheric effects.

questions.prompt: Match each tool or concept to what it measures or provides.

right.text: Direct open-ocean pressure measurement of a passing tsunami wave
Rapid, saturation-resistant moment magnitude estimate from a long-period seismic phase

questions.explanation: DART buoys physically detect the tsunami wave itself via seafloor pressure sensors; W-phase inversion, developed by Kanamori and Rivera (2008), estimates a reliable moment magnitude from seismic data within tens of minutes, avoiding the saturation that affects some traditional magnitude scales for very large earthquakes.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes the failure at Tohoku (2011) from the failure at Sumatra (2004)?

options.text: Tohoku had no tsunami warning system at all, exactly like Sumatra
Sumatra's warning system worked correctly but coastal defenses failed

Tohoku had an established warning system and seawalls, but the initial warning underestimated the earthquake and the tsunami exceeded the defenses' design height, while Sumatra had no warning infrastructure at all
Both disasters were caused by warning systems issuing false alarms that were ignored

explanations.a: Japan had an established seismic and tsunami warning infrastructure in 2011; the failure was in the accuracy and engineering assumptions of that existing system, not its absence.
explanations.b: The Indian Ocean in 2004 had no tsunami warning system in place at all; there was no functioning system to have 'worked' incorrectly or correctly.
