explanations.c: Correct — Tohoku's warning underestimated the earthquake's true size and the tsunami exceeded existing seawalls' design height, while Sumatra's disaster stemmed from the complete absence of any warning system in the Indian Ocean at the time.
explanations.d: Neither disaster's core failure was a false alarm being ignored; Sumatra had no alert to ignore, and Tohoku's alert underestimated rather than falsely triggered.

units.label: Sediment in Motion: Entrainment, Transport, and Deposition

lessons.label: Settling: Stokes' Law and Its Limits

sections.heading: Balancing gravity against drag
sections.body: A grain falling through still water accelerates until gravity (minus buoyancy) exactly balances viscous drag, at which point it falls at a constant terminal settling velocity. For a smooth sphere in slow, laminar (viscous) flow, George Gabriel Stokes worked out the drag force in 1851, and rearranging the force balance gives ws = (g(rhoS - rhoF)d^2) / (18*mu), where d is grain diameter, rhoS and rhoF are grain and fluid density, and mu is dynamic viscosity. The d-squared dependence is the headline result: doubling grain size quadruples settling velocity, which is why even modest sorting by current speed produces strongly size-segregated deposits.

sections.heading: Where the balance breaks down
sections.body: Stokes' Law assumes laminar flow around the grain, which only holds when the particle Reynolds number Rep = ws*d/nu stays below about 0.5 — in practice this restricts pure Stokes settling to quartz-density spheres finer than roughly 0.1 mm (fine sand and silt). Above that, flow does not jump straight to fully turbulent drag: between roughly Rep 1 and Rep 1000 lies an intermediate, or transitional, settling regime, where flow separates behind the grain and sheds an unsteady wake, but has not yet reached the fully turbulent state. In this transitional band the drag coefficient Cd falls steeply as Rep rises, rather than staying fixed the way it does at either end of the spectrum, so settling velocity grows more slowly with grain size than either the pure-Stokes or pure-turbulent formulas alone would predict. Only once Rep climbs past roughly 1000 does drag enter the Newtonian, or fully turbulent, regime, where Cd flattens out to a roughly constant value near 0.4-1 and settling velocity scales close to the square root of grain diameter instead of the diameter-squared scaling of Stokes' Law. Two widely used fixes patch the full size range: Rubey's 1933 impact-law formula added an empirical drag term for the turbulent regime, and Ferguson and Church (2004) proposed a single continuous equation blending viscous and turbulent drag with two calibrated constants, matched against published settling-tube data from silt through gravel.

sections.heading: Shape, density, and hindered settling
sections.body: Real grains are not spheres. Platy mica flakes and irregular lithic fragments have more surface area per unit volume than a sphere, so drag is higher and true settling velocity is lower than a sphere of the same volume — this is why any settling-based method (settling tube, pipette analysis) reports an equivalent spherical diameter, the diameter of a quartz sphere that would settle at the same rate, not a literal caliper measurement. Density also matters: heavy minerals like magnetite (rhoS around 5.2 g/cm3) settle faster than quartz (2.65 g/cm3) of the same size, which is the physical basis of placer concentration. Finally, at high sediment concentrations grains interfere with each other's return flow and settle slower than they would alone, a phenomenon called hindered settling.

lessons.workedExample: A 0.05 mm quartz silt grain (rhoS = 2650 kg/m3) settling in 20C water (mu = 0.001 Pa*s, rhoF = 1000 kg/m3) gives ws = (9.8 * 1650 * (5e-5)^2) / (18 * 0.001) = about 2.2 mm/s by Stokes' Law. Checking Rep = (0.0022 * 5e-5)/1e-6 = 0.11, far below 0.5, so Stokes applies cleanly. Repeat for a 1 mm quartz sand grain and the naive Stokes formula predicts ws around 900 mm/s — but Rep for that answer would be near 900, wildly turbulent, so the true settling velocity (from Ferguson and Church, or a settling-tube calibration) is only about 100-140 mm/s, roughly six to nine times slower than uncorrected Stokes predicts.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who sees a settling-velocity claim will ask which formula was used and why, because Stokes' Law silently overpredicts settling speed for anything coarser than fine sand — a student who runs Stokes on 1 mm sand without checking the particle Reynolds number has computed a number that is off by several-fold and doesn't know it. The strong answer states the Rep < 0.5 boundary, names Ferguson and Church (2004) or Rubey as the coarse-grain correction, and flags that any settling-tube result is an equivalent spherical diameter shaped by both grain shape and mineral density, not a direct size measurement.

questions.prompt: In Stokes' Law, ws = g(rhoS-rhoF)d^2/(18*mu), doubling the grain diameter d while holding everything else constant changes the settling velocity by what factor?

options.text: 2x
4x
8x
No change

explanations.a: That would be true if velocity scaled linearly with diameter, but the formula has d squared.
explanations.b: Correct — d appears squared in Stokes' Law, so doubling diameter quadruples the predicted terminal settling velocity.
explanations.c: 8x would be the cube relationship, which describes grain volume/mass, not settling velocity under Stokes' Law.
explanations.d: Settling velocity depends strongly on grain size in the Stokes regime; it does not cancel out.

questions.prompt: Why does pure Stokes' Law fail to predict the settling velocity of a 1 mm quartz sand grain?

options.text: The grain is too small for gravity to act on it
The particle Reynolds number is well above the ~0.5 laminar-flow limit, so drag is no longer purely viscous
Quartz is not dense enough to settle at 1 mm
Stokes' Law only applies to fluids other than water

explanations.a: Gravity acts on all grains regardless of size; that is not the limiting assumption.
explanations.b: Correct — at 1 mm the flow around the grain becomes turbulent (Rep well above 0.5), and Stokes' viscous-drag assumption breaks down, so measured settling is much slower than the naive Stokes prediction.
explanations.c: Quartz density is fixed and irrelevant to why the formula's underlying flow assumption fails.
explanations.d: Stokes' Law's fluid-independence is not the issue; its restriction is to laminar (low Reynolds number) flow around the grain.

questions.prompt: Match each concept to its correct description.

right.text: A single equation blending viscous and turbulent drag across the full grain-size range
The diameter of a quartz sphere settling at the same rate as the real, often non-spherical grain
Grains settle more slowly than expected because of interference at high sediment concentration

questions.explanation: Equivalent spherical diameter is the size a settling method actually reports; hindered settling is the concentration-dependent slowdown from grain interference; Ferguson and Church (2004) supplied the practical formula spanning both the Stokes and turbulent drag regimes.

lessons.label: Boundary Shear Stress and the Shields Curve

sections.heading: The force a flow actually applies to the bed
sections.body: It is not the water's average speed that moves a grain — it is the shear stress the flow exerts right at the bed, tau0. For steady, uniform open-channel flow this is given simply by tau0 = rhoF*g*H*S, where H is flow depth and S is the water-surface (energy) slope. Dividing tau0 by fluid density and taking the square root gives the shear velocity, u* = sqrt(tau0/rhoF), a velocity-scaled stand-in for bed stress that is far more useful for sediment-transport problems than depth-averaged flow velocity. Near the bed, velocity does not simply decay linearly; it follows the logarithmic law-of-the-wall profile, u(z) = (u*/kappa)*ln(z/z0), where kappa is the von Karman constant (about 0.4) and z0 is a roughness length tied to grain size. Fitting a measured velocity profile to this log form is the standard way to back out u* in a flume or river without a direct stress sensor.

sections.heading: Reading the Shields diagram
sections.body: Albert Shields' 1936 flume experiments produced the classic threshold-of-motion diagram: the dimensionless Shields parameter theta = tau0/(g(rhoS-rhoF)d) on the vertical axis, plotted against the particle (or boundary) Reynolds number Re* = u*d/nu on the horizontal axis. For coarse, well-sorted, cohesionless grains in the fully turbulent, high-Re* range (roughly gravel and coarse sand), the curve flattens to a critical Shields parameter theta_c of about 0.03 to 0.06 — motion begins once bed stress reaches a few percent of the grain's submerged weight per unit bed area. At lower Re* (fine sand and silt), the curve turns upward sharply, meaning finer grains need disproportionately more stress relative to their weight to move, because they sit within the thin viscous sublayer that shelters them from the full turbulent stress.

sections.heading: Why cohesive mud departs from the curve entirely
sections.body: The Shields curve describes cohesionless, granular beds where the only resisting force is submerged particle weight and friction. Below roughly 0.05-0.1 mm, clay and fine silt develop electrochemical cohesion between grains (and often organic or mineral cementation), so resistance to erosion no longer scales with grain weight at all — a consolidated mud can require far higher stress to erode than the Shields curve for its grain size would predict, while a freshly deposited, unconsolidated mud can erode more easily. This is why sedimentologists treat the rising left limb of Shields' curve as a rough guide for silt but abandon the granular framework altogether for consolidated clay, relying instead on empirically measured critical erosion stresses.

lessons.workedExample: A river reach has depth H = 2 m and water-surface slope S = 0.0005. Boundary shear stress is tau0 = rhoF*g*H*S = 1000 * 9.8 * 2 * 0.0005 = 9.8 Pa, giving shear velocity u* = sqrt(9.8/1000) = 0.099 m/s. For a 2 mm gravel grain (rhoS = 2650 kg/m3), the critical Shields stress at theta_c = 0.045 requires tau0,crit = 0.045 * 9.8 * 1650 * 0.002 = 1.45 Pa. Since the reach's actual tau0 of 9.8 Pa exceeds 1.45 Pa several-fold, this gravel should be well within the transport regime, not sitting at incipient motion.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe boundary shear stress because it is the variable that actually predicts erosion, and many student projects report flow velocity when they mean bed stress. A student who can compute tau0 = rhoF*g*H*S, convert it to a Shields number, and compare it to theta_c for their grain size has shown they understand what a flow does to a bed rather than just how fast the water moves; a student who cannot say why fine sand needs more relative stress than gravel, or why mud breaks the whole framework, has not gotten past the surface reading of the diagram.

questions.prompt: Boundary shear stress in steady, uniform open-channel flow is calculated as:

options.text: tau0 = rhoF * g * H * S
tau0 = rhoF * v^2, where v is mean velocity
tau0 = g * d, where d is grain diameter
tau0 = kappa * ln(z/z0)

explanations.a: Correct — boundary shear stress equals fluid density times gravity times flow depth times energy slope.
explanations.b: This resembles a dynamic-pressure term, not the depth-slope product that defines bed shear stress.
explanations.c: This mixes grain size into a stress formula with no fluid or flow terms; it isn't the shear-stress relation.
explanations.d: That expression is the log law-of-the-wall velocity profile, used to back out u* from measurements, not the direct formula for tau0.

questions.prompt: On the Shields diagram, why does the critical Shields parameter rise sharply at low particle Reynolds number (fine sand and silt) instead of staying flat at ~0.03-0.06?

options.text: Fine grains are denser than coarse grains
Fine grains sit within the viscous sublayer, sheltered from the full turbulent bed stress, so relatively more stress is needed to move them
The Shields diagram is only valid for grains coarser than 1 mm
Cohesion between fine grains is captured directly by the theta axis

explanations.a: Grain density does not systematically change with size in the diagram; density is already built into the theta calculation.
explanations.b: Correct — at low Re*, grains are small relative to the viscous sublayer thickness and are sheltered from full turbulent shear, so the critical stress relative to grain weight rises.
explanations.c: The diagram covers a wide grain-size range including fine sand and silt, which is exactly where the upturn appears.
explanations.d: The Shields framework is built for cohesionless grains; true cohesion (in mud) is not represented on the curve at all and requires abandoning the granular approach.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its role in the shear-stress framework.

right.text: Departs from the Shields curve because resistance is not set by grain weight alone
sqrt(tau0/rhoF); can be recovered from fitting the log velocity profile
The flat critical Shields parameter for coarse, cohesionless grains at high Reynolds number

questions.explanation: Shear velocity is derived from bed stress or the log-law profile; theta_c around 0.03-0.06 is the flat, coarse-grain plateau of the Shields curve; cohesive mud breaks the granular Shields framework because electrochemical bonding, not particle weight, controls erosion resistance.

lessons.label: Hjulstrom-Sundborg: Erosion, Transport, Deposition

sections.heading: The 1935 Hjulstrom curve
sections.body: Filip Hjulstrom's 1935 diagram plots mean flow velocity (not shear stress) against grain size on log-log axes, and draws a single curve marking the velocity at which grains of a given size begin to erode from a bed. The curve has a distinctive U-shape with its minimum at medium-to-fine sand, roughly 0.2 to 0.5 mm: grains in this range are the easiest of all to entrain, needing velocities of only about 20-30 cm/s. Coarser grains (gravel, cobbles) need higher velocities because they are heavier, which is intuitive. But the curve also climbs steeply for grains finer than fine sand — silt and especially clay need surprisingly high velocities to erode, several tens of cm/s or more for consolidated clay, because cohesive electrochemical bonding between fine particles resists entrainment even though the grains themselves are tiny and light.

sections.heading: Sundborg's 1956 refinement
sections.body: Ake Sundborg revised the diagram in 1956, separating it into distinct fields for erosion, transport, and deposition, and adding a second, lower curve for the velocity at which a moving grain settles back out (the fall/deposition velocity). This second curve is critical for fine sediment: once clay and silt are entrained and put into suspension, they can remain suspended and continue traveling at velocities far below the ones that were needed to erode them in the first place — the deposition velocity for clay-sized material can be a small fraction of a cm/s, meaning that once picked up, fine mud may travel enormous distances (or stay suspended almost indefinitely in turbulent flow) before ever settling out.

sections.heading: Where the diagram gets misused
sections.body: Two misreadings recur constantly. First, both curves plot depth-averaged velocity, not the boundary shear stress that actually mobilizes a grain (see the Shields framework) — the same mean velocity produces very different near-bed stress in a shallow, rough channel versus a deep, smooth one, so the Hjulstrom-Sundborg velocity thresholds are only rough field guides, not a substitute for a proper shear-stress calculation, and they were calibrated mainly from flume and river data rather than covering every flow type. Second, students often reduce the diagram to one curve when the entire point of Sundborg's 1956 revision was that erosion and deposition are separate processes with separate threshold velocities for fine sediment — treating them as the same curve erases the very asymmetry (easy to erode, hard to deposit once fine mud is suspended) that explains why muds get transported so far from their source.

lessons.workedExample: A river flowing at 40 cm/s encounters a mixed bed of gravel, medium sand, and consolidated clay. By the Hjulstrom curve, the medium sand (around 0.3 mm) needs only about 20-25 cm/s to erode, so it mobilizes easily at 40 cm/s. The consolidated clay may need well over 100 cm/s to erode from Hjulstrom's curve, so it stays put as a resistant bed even though the flow is easily fast enough to keep any already-suspended clay from settling (its Sundborg deposition velocity is a tiny fraction of a cm/s). This is exactly why river channels can be lined with intact clay banks even while sand on the bed is actively moving: the same flow is above sand's erosion threshold but far below clay's.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge hearing '20-30 cm/s moves sand' will ask what curve that number comes from and whether it is erosion or deposition velocity, because conflating the two curves is the most common Hjulstrom-Sundborg error. The strong answer names Hjulstrom (1935) for the original erosion threshold and Sundborg (1956) for splitting erosion from deposition, explains why clay needs a high velocity to erode but a very low one to finally settle, and flags that these are depth-averaged velocity thresholds, not shear stress, so they're approximate compared to a Shields-based calculation.

questions.prompt: According to the Hjulstrom curve, which grain size requires the LOWEST velocity to begin eroding from a bed?

options.text: Clay (< 0.004 mm)
Medium-to-fine sand (~0.2-0.5 mm)
Coarse gravel
Boulders

explanations.a: Clay sits at the high-velocity end of the erosion curve because cohesive bonding resists entrainment despite its small grain size.
explanations.b: Correct — the Hjulstrom curve's minimum sits at medium-to-fine sand, around 0.2-0.5 mm, needing only about 20-30 cm/s to erode.
explanations.c: Coarse gravel needs higher velocity than sand because it is heavier and less easily lifted.
explanations.d: Boulders sit at the highest-velocity end of the curve; they are the hardest cohesionless material to move.

questions.prompt: What was the key change Sundborg's 1956 revision made to Hjulstrom's original 1935 diagram?

options.text: It replaced velocity with shear stress on the horizontal axis
It added a separate deposition (fall) velocity curve, distinct from the erosion threshold curve
It removed the fine-grain (clay and silt) portion of the diagram entirely
It showed that erosion and deposition velocities are identical for all grain sizes

explanations.a: Both Hjulstrom's and Sundborg's diagrams plot mean flow velocity, not shear stress; that substitution is a separate, later framework (Shields).
explanations.b: Correct — Sundborg (1956) split the diagram into erosion, transport, and deposition fields, adding a distinct deposition-velocity curve well below the erosion curve for fine sediment.
explanations.c: Sundborg's revision kept and clarified the fine-grain fields; it did not remove them.
explanations.d: The entire point of the revision was that erosion and deposition velocities diverge sharply for fine sediment, not that they match.

questions.prompt: Order the life of a clay particle in a river from lowest to highest velocity requirement, based on the Hjulstrom-Sundborg framework.

items.text: Clay particle settles out of suspension (deposition)
Clay particle travels in suspension at reduced flow
Consolidated clay bed is eroded and entrained

questions.explanation: Deposition velocity for clay is extremely low, transport in suspension can persist across a range of moderate velocities once entrained, and erosion of a consolidated clay bed requires the highest velocity of the three because cohesion resists initial entrainment.

lessons.label: Bedload, Suspended Load, and Washload

sections.heading: The Rouse number sorts transport mode
sections.body: Whether a grain rolls along the bed or rides in the water column depends on the competition between its settling velocity ws (pulling it down) and the turbulence that keeps it stirred up, scaled by shear velocity u*. The ratio, the Rouse number P = ws/(kappa*u*) with von Karman's constant kappa around 0.4, sets the transport mode. Grains with P greater than about 2.5 are too heavy for turbulence to lift meaningfully; they move as bedload, rolling, sliding, or hopping (saltating) in a thin layer at the bed. Grains with P between about 0.8 and 2.5 are light enough to be regularly lofted into the flow and carried as suspended load, moving with the water but still exchanging with the bed. Grains with P below about 0.8 are so fine that turbulence keeps them essentially always in suspension.

sections.heading: The Rouse profile and vertical sorting
sections.body: For suspended load, the Rouse equation predicts how sediment concentration varies with height above the bed: c(z)/c(a) = [(H-z)/z * a/(H-a)]^P, where a is a reference height near the bed and H is flow depth. Because the exponent is the Rouse number itself, coarser grains (higher P) have concentration profiles that fall off sharply with height, staying concentrated near the bed, while fine grains (low P) are distributed almost uniformly through the water column. This is the mechanistic reason a single flow can simultaneously carry coarse sand low in the flow and fine silt evenly mixed throughout it, and why a single suspended-sediment sample taken near the surface underestimates the coarse fraction actually being moved.

sections.heading: Washload: sediment the bed never sees
sections.body: The finest fraction, with Rouse numbers well under 0.8, is called washload. Washload is defined not just by grain size but by supply: it is sediment fine enough, and turbulent enough to be kept in the water column, that it is present in the flow at concentrations set by upstream supply (soil erosion, tributary input) rather than by the capacity of the local flow to pick it up from the bed. Because washload essentially never exchanges with, or equilibrates with, the local bed material, it cannot be predicted from local hydraulics or bed grain size at all, and it is the reason deposits record only bedload and suspended load reliably — washload passes through a reach and is deposited far downstream or offshore, so a river's bed and bar deposits are systematically missing the finest fraction that was actually being carried.

lessons.workedExample: A river has shear velocity u* = 0.05 m/s (kappa = 0.4). A coarse sand grain with ws = 0.10 m/s gives P = 0.10/(0.4*0.05) = 5.0, well above 2.5, so it travels as bedload. A fine sand grain with ws = 0.02 m/s gives P = 0.02/(0.4*0.05) = 1.0, inside the 0.8-2.5 suspended-load window, so it is regularly lofted and carried in suspension but still exchanges with the bed. A clay grain with ws = 0.001 m/s gives P = 0.001/(0.4*0.05) = 0.05, far below 0.8, so it is washload: it rides through the reach at a concentration set by upstream supply, not by anything happening on this reach's bed.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask about washload specifically because it is the piece students most often get backwards: they assume more sediment supply always means more deposition locally, when washload by definition passes through without equilibrating with the bed. A strong answer computes or at least estimates a Rouse number to justify calling something bedload, suspended load, or washload, and explains that a deposit's grain-size record is therefore biased toward bedload and suspended load, silently missing the finest, most abundant fraction the river was actually transporting.

questions.prompt: A grain has a Rouse number P = 4.0. How does it move?

options.text: As bedload, rolling and hopping along the bed
As suspended load, regularly lofted into the water column
As washload, uniformly mixed and never touching the bed
It does not move under any flow condition

explanations.a: Correct — P = 4.0 is above the ~2.5 bedload threshold, meaning the grain's settling velocity is too high relative to turbulence for it to be lofted into suspension; it travels as bedload.
explanations.b: Suspended load corresponds to P roughly between 0.8 and 2.5; P = 4.0 is above that range.
explanations.c: Washload corresponds to P well below 0.8; P = 4.0 is at the opposite end of the scale.
explanations.d: A high Rouse number changes transport mode, not whether the grain can move at all under sufficient shear stress.

questions.prompt: Why can't washload concentration be predicted from the local river bed's grain size or local hydraulics?

options.text: Washload does not actually exist in real rivers
Washload is fine enough to stay in suspension regardless of local bed conditions, so its concentration is set by upstream supply, not local capacity to erode the bed
Washload always has a Rouse number above 2.5
Washload settles out immediately upon entering any river reach

explanations.a: Washload is a well-documented, standard category of fine suspended sediment in fluvial transport.
explanations.b: Correct — because washload never equilibrates with the bed, its concentration reflects upstream supply (soil erosion, tributaries) rather than the capacity of the local flow to entrain it.
explanations.c: A Rouse number above 2.5 describes bedload, the opposite transport mode from washload.
explanations.d: Washload is defined by staying in suspension, not by settling out quickly; that is the opposite of its behavior.

questions.prompt: Match each Rouse number range to its transport category.

right.text: Bedload
Suspended load
Washload

questions.explanation: P > 2.5 marks bedload (too heavy to loft), 0.8-2.5 marks suspended load (regularly lofted, still exchanges with the bed), and P < 0.8 marks washload (fine enough to stay suspended, set by upstream supply rather than local bed exchange).

lessons.label: Bedform Stability: Ripples, Dunes, Antidunes

sections.heading: A phase diagram for the bed itself
sections.body: Given a grain size and a flow strength, a sandy bed does not stay flat — it self-organizes into a predictable sequence of bedforms, and Southard and Boguchwal compiled the definitive version of this relationship in 1990 from decades of flume data, plotting flow velocity (or stream power) against grain size. At low flow strength the bed is a flat lower-plane bed (no bedforms, grains barely moving). As velocity increases, small ripples appear, then grow into larger dunes, then at high velocity the bed flattens again into an upper-plane bed with intense sheet-like bedload transport, and at the highest velocities, standing antidunes develop. The same sequence, run in reverse as flow wanes, is why a single flood can leave a vertically stacked record of several bedform types in one bed.

sections.heading: The grain-size cutoff for ripples
sections.body: One of the most useful, testable results from the Southard and Boguchwal compilation is that ripples do not form in grains coarser than about 0.7 mm (roughly the medium-to-coarse sand boundary), regardless of flow velocity — coarser sand and gravel skip ripples entirely and go straight from plane bed to dunes as velocity increases. This matters because ripple cross-lamination in ancient rock is sometimes read as a low-energy indicator, but it is equally a grain-size indicator: fine sand can show ripples across a wide range of flow strengths, so ripple lamination alone constrains grain size more reliably than it constrains flow speed. Antidunes, at the opposite extreme, form when the Froude number (flow speed divided by the speed of a surface gravity wave, sqrt(g*H)) approaches 1, meaning the bedform is in resonance with in-phase standing waves on the water surface above it.

sections.heading: From migrating bedform to preserved cross-strata
sections.body: A dune or ripple does not simply sit still; it migrates downstream as sediment avalanches down its lee slope, and each avalanche deposits an inclined foreset lamina. If the bed is also aggrading (net sediment accumulation, not just bypass), successive foresets get preserved as a set of cross-strata, and erosion by the next bedform typically truncates the top of the set. Critically, the thickness of a preserved cross-bed set is controlled by the amount of erosion during migration and net aggradation rate, not simply by the height of the bedform that made it — Leclair and Bridge (2001) found that mean preserved set thickness runs about 0.3 times mean dune height (dune height about 3.3 times set thickness), so preserved cross-sets record only roughly a third of the original bedform height, and reconstructing paleo-dune size directly from cross-bed set thickness without that correction systematically underestimates the bedform, and by extension the flow, that produced it.

lessons.workedExample: A flume runs 0.3 mm sand at increasing velocity. At low velocity it stays a flat lower-plane bed; raising velocity produces small ripples (allowed, since 0.3 mm is below the ~0.7 mm ripple cutoff); raising velocity further grows dunes; pushing velocity higher still flattens the bed into upper-plane bed with intense sheet flow; and at the highest velocity, with Froude number approaching 1, antidunes appear with in-phase standing surface waves. Now repeat with 1.5 mm coarse sand: ripples never appear at any velocity (above the 0.7 mm cutoff), so the sequence skips directly from lower-plane bed to dunes as velocity rises.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge examining a ripple-marked sample will ask whether the student is reading it as a flow-speed indicator or a grain-size indicator, because the ~0.7 mm cutoff means fine sand ripples across a wide velocity range while coarse sand never ripples at all. A judge examining cross-bedding will also ask whether set thickness was equated with dune height, because preserved set thickness is systematically thinner than the original bedform due to erosional truncation during migration — conflating the two overestimates how small the original flow features actually were.

questions.prompt: According to the Southard and Boguchwal (1990) bedform phase diagram, what happens to ripples in grains coarser than about 0.7 mm?

options.text: They form at even higher velocities than in fine sand
They do not form at all, regardless of flow velocity
They form only underwater, never in wind
They form identically to fine-sand ripples

explanations.a: The relationship is not a shift to higher velocity — ripples are absent entirely above the ~0.7 mm threshold in the Southard and Boguchwal data.
explanations.b: Correct — above about 0.7 mm, the bed skips ripples entirely and transitions directly from plane bed to dunes as velocity increases.
explanations.c: The 0.7 mm cutoff is about the subaqueous bedform diagram; it is not a statement distinguishing water from wind environments.
explanations.d: Ripples in coarser grains are absent, not identical, distinguishing them sharply from the fine-sand case.

questions.prompt: Antidunes form when:

options.text: Grain size exceeds 0.7 mm
The Froude number approaches 1, putting the bedform in resonance with in-phase standing surface waves
Flow velocity is at its lowest, near the threshold of motion
The bed is not aggrading at all

explanations.a: Grain size alone does not produce antidunes; the 0.7 mm figure describes the ripple-formation cutoff, a separate part of the diagram.
explanations.b: Correct — antidunes form at the high-velocity end of the phase diagram, where Froude number nears 1 and standing surface waves develop in phase with the bedform.
explanations.c: Low velocity near the threshold of motion produces a flat lower-plane bed, not antidunes, which require the highest velocities in the sequence.
explanations.d: Aggradation rate controls whether bedforms get preserved as cross-strata, not whether antidunes form in the first place.

questions.prompt: Order the bedform sequence for fine sand as flow velocity increases from very low to very high.

items.text: Lower-plane bed
Ripples
Dunes
Upper-plane bed
Antidunes

questions.explanation: As flow velocity rises for fine sand, the bed progresses from a flat lower-plane bed, through ripples and then dunes, to a flattened upper-plane bed at high transport intensity, and finally to antidunes as Froude number approaches 1.

lessons.label: Sediment Gravity Flows

sections.heading: Four ways to keep a grain off the bed
sections.body: Ordinary river or wind transport keeps grains moving because a fluid flow drives them; a sediment gravity flow is different — the sediment-water (or sediment-air) mixture itself is denser than the surrounding fluid and flows downslope under its own weight, carrying the fluid along with it. Middleton and Hampton's classification, developed in the early 1970s, sorts these flows by which mechanism supports the grains against settling: turbulence (turbidity currents, where upward eddies keep grains suspended, the same principle as the Rouse framework applied to a dense underflow), dispersive pressure (grain flows, where grain-to-grain collisions push grains apart, the mechanism Ralph Bagnold described experimentally in 1954), matrix strength (debris flows, where a cohesive mud-and-water matrix has enough yield strength to hold coarser clasts in suspension without any flow at all), and escaping pore fluid (fluidized/liquefied flows, where fluid squeezed upward through the grain pack temporarily supports the grains, a mechanism that dies out over minutes as the excess pore pressure drains).

sections.heading: Turbidity currents that feed themselves
sections.body: A turbidity current can be self-sustaining, or ignitive: if the flow is fast and turbulent enough to keep entraining sediment from the bed faster than sediment settles out, the added excess density accelerates the flow further, entraining still more sediment — a positive feedback sometimes called autosuspension, a concept traced to Bagnold and formalized by Gary Parker in the 1980s. This is why a single submarine slope failure can trigger a turbidity current that travels hundreds of kilometers across a flat abyssal plain, growing rather than dying, until the slope shallows or sediment supply runs out and the flow finally decelerates and deposits its load, typically fining upward as coarser grains settle first (a Bouma sequence).

sections.heading: Downflow transformation and hybrid beds
sections.body: A single flow event rarely stays in one category along its whole path. A submarine landslide often begins as a cohesive debris flow, but turbulent mixing at its margins can strip water into the flow, lower its effective strength, and transform its front into a turbidity current while the body remains debris-flow-like — a downflow transformation documented in outcrop and flume studies since the 1980s. The result, increasingly documented in deep-marine successions, is the hybrid event bed: a single depositional unit that grades from a turbulent, well-sorted turbidite base or top into a muddy, poorly sorted, clast-supported debrite in the middle, recording one flow that crossed the debris-flow-to-turbidity-current continuum rather than two separate events.

lessons.workedExample: A submarine canyon fails and sends a dense slurry of mud and sand downslope. Near the source it behaves as a debris flow: mud matrix strength holds pebble-sized clasts in suspension with no turbulence needed. Farther down-canyon, turbulent shear at the flow's upper surface entrains ambient seawater, dilutes the mixture, and the flow front becomes turbulent enough to qualify as a turbidity current, self-accelerating via autosuspension as it entrains more sediment from the canyon floor. When it reaches the flat basin plain, the flow finally decelerates, and the resulting bed records this whole history: a chaotic, poorly sorted debrite in the lower/middle part directly overlain by a graded, well-sorted turbidite cap, deposited by the transformed, more dilute turbulent tail — a single hybrid event bed.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking about a graded, muddy sandstone bed wants to hear a specific grain-support mechanism named, not just 'it was a turbidity current' by default — Middleton and Hampton's four mechanisms (turbulence, dispersive pressure, matrix strength, escaping pore fluid) let a student justify why a bed looks the way it does. The strongest answers also recognize that many real beds are hybrid, recording downflow transformation from a cohesive debris flow into a turbulent turbidity current within a single event, rather than assuming every gravity-flow deposit fits one clean category.

questions.prompt: Match each sediment gravity flow type to its grain-support mechanism in the Middleton and Hampton classification.

right.text: Turbulence
Dispersive pressure from grain-to-grain collisions
Matrix strength of a cohesive mud-water mixture
Escaping pore fluid, supporting grains temporarily as it drains upward

questions.explanation: Middleton and Hampton sorted sediment gravity flows by what physically keeps grains from settling: turbulent eddies for turbidity currents, grain collisions (Bagnold's dispersive pressure) for grain flows, cohesive matrix yield strength for debris flows, and escaping pore fluid for fluidized flows.

questions.prompt: What is autosuspension in a turbidity current?

options.text: A positive feedback where entraining more sediment increases flow density and speed, which entrains still more sediment
The moment a flow completely stops moving
A mechanism unique to debris flows, not turbidity currents
The process by which pore fluid drains out of a fluidized flow

explanations.a: Correct — autosuspension is the self-reinforcing feedback where a sufficiently fast, turbulent flow entrains bed sediment faster than it settles, gaining density and speed, allowing it to travel great distances before finally decelerating.
explanations.b: Autosuspension describes a flow sustaining or accelerating itself, the opposite of stopping.
explanations.c: Autosuspension is specifically a turbidity-current concept, tied to turbulence as the support mechanism, not to cohesive debris flows.
explanations.d: Pore-fluid drainage describes fluidized flow decay, a different mechanism from the turbulence-driven feedback of autosuspension.

questions.prompt: A hybrid event bed, as documented through downflow transformation studies, typically records:

options.text: Two completely unrelated flow events deposited on top of each other
A single flow that transformed along its path, grading from a muddy, poorly sorted debrite into a well-sorted turbidite (or vice versa) within one bed
A bed made entirely of wind-blown sediment
A bed that shows no vertical grain-size variation at all

explanations.a: A hybrid bed specifically records one continuous flow event that changed character downflow, not two separate depositional events.
explanations.b: Correct — downflow transformation lets a single event cross the debris-flow-to-turbidity-current continuum, producing one bed with both debrite and turbidite character.
explanations.c: Hybrid event beds are a deep-marine, subaqueous sediment-gravity-flow phenomenon, unrelated to aeolian transport.
explanations.d: The defining feature of a hybrid bed is exactly the opposite: a marked vertical change in sorting and grain-support character within one unit.

lessons.label: Wind, Waves, and Sticky Mud

sections.heading: Two wind thresholds and the saltation-reptation cycle
sections.body: Ralph Bagnold's 1941 book on blown sand established that wind entrainment has two distinct thresholds, not one. The fluid threshold is the wind speed needed to lift a grain directly off a static bed by aerodynamic drag and lift alone. But once any grains are already saltating (bouncing in low, ballistic arcs), their impacts on landing can kick up additional grains at a much lower wind speed than the fluid threshold — this lower impact threshold is why aeolian sand transport, once started, can continue at wind speeds well below what was needed to start it. Most of the grains dislodged by saltation impacts do not launch into full saltation arcs themselves; instead they undergo reptation, short, low, disorganized hops of only a few grain diameters. Reptating grains are the primary mechanism that builds and migrates wind ripples, since their short hop length matches the ripple wavelength far better than the long saltation trajectories do.

sections.heading: Wave orbital motion, wave base, and combined flow
sections.body: Water waves move sediment differently from unidirectional river or wind flow: an oscillatory wave induces a roughly circular (or, near the bed, flattened elliptical) orbital motion of water particles, whose orbital diameter and near-bed velocity decay exponentially with depth below the surface. Wave base — conventionally about half the wavelength for deep-water waves — is the depth below which orbital velocities become negligible for sediment stirring; below it, waves cannot rework the seabed. Above wave base, oscillatory wave motion often combines with a superimposed steady current (tidal, wind-driven, or fluvial) to produce combined flow, which generates distinctive bedforms — combined-flow ripples with asymmetric crests and characteristic internal lamination — that differ from both pure current ripples and pure symmetric wave ripples.

sections.heading: When biology beats physics: microbial mats and cohesion
sections.body: The Hjulstrom-Sundborg and Shields frameworks assume a purely physical, cohesionless (or simply cohesive) bed, but many muddy tidal flats and lakebeds are colonized by microbial mats and biofilms of diatoms and cyanobacteria that secrete extracellular polymeric substances (EPS) — sticky mucilage that binds sediment grains together. Flume and in-situ erosion-meter studies, including work associated with Paterson's research on microphytobenthic biofilms, have shown that a well-developed biofilm can raise the critical erosion shear stress of a mud bed several-fold compared to an otherwise identical, biologically inert mud. This biological stabilization means a purely physical entrainment prediction from grain size and cohesion alone can substantially underestimate the actual erosion threshold of a real-world tidal flat, and it is one reason mudflats and salt marshes persist as stable, low-energy depositional environments even where physical models would predict more erosion.

lessons.workedExample: A dune field starts calm. Wind speed rises past the fluid threshold, and the first grains lift directly off the static surface into saltation. As saltating grains land, their impacts kick up far more grains than aerodynamic lift alone would at that same wind speed — transport continues even if wind speed then drops to just above the lower impact threshold. Most of the impact-ejected grains only reptate a few grain-diameters, and it is this swarm of short reptating hops, not the long saltation arcs, that piles sand into the characteristic wind-ripple wavelength seen migrating across the dune's windward face.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who hears 'the wind speed needed to move sand' will ask whether that is the fluid threshold or the lower impact threshold, since conflating them misses why aeolian transport is self-sustaining once started. For a muddy tidal-flat project, a judge will specifically ask whether biofilms or EPS were considered, because a purely physical erosion-threshold prediction from grain size can be several-fold too low for a real, microbially colonized bed — citing this biological correction is what separates a textbook physical answer from one that engages with the actual field system.

questions.prompt: Why can aeolian sand transport continue at wind speeds below the fluid threshold, once it has started?

options.text: Because the lower impact threshold lets saltating grains' bed impacts dislodge more grains at a lower wind speed than aerodynamic lift alone requires
Because wind speed always increases once sand starts moving
Because the fluid threshold and impact threshold are identical
Because saltating grains lose all their momentum instantly on landing

explanations.a: Correct — Bagnold (1941) showed the impact threshold, driven by saltating grains striking the bed, is lower than the fluid threshold needed to lift grains from rest, so transport self-sustains at reduced wind speed.
explanations.b: Wind speed is an independent external condition; sand transport does not cause wind to increase.
explanations.c: The two thresholds are distinct by definition, with the impact threshold lower than the fluid threshold — that gap is the entire point.
explanations.d: Saltating grains retain enough momentum on impact to eject other grains; that transferred energy is exactly what powers the lower impact threshold.

questions.prompt: Wind ripple wavelength is best explained by which grain motion?

options.text: Long ballistic saltation arcs
Short, low reptation hops of a few grain diameters
Grains permanently fixed at the fluid threshold
Suspended load carried far above the bed

explanations.a: Saltation trajectories are much longer than a ripple wavelength, so they do not match the spacing of wind ripples.
explanations.b: Correct — reptating grains, ejected by saltation impacts but hopping only a few grain diameters, build up in a pattern whose spacing matches the wind-ripple wavelength.
explanations.c: Grains at the fluid threshold are on the verge of motion, not actively building a migrating bedform.
explanations.d: Suspended load in wind transport moves too far above the bed to control the short-wavelength spacing of ripples.

questions.prompt: What effect do EPS-secreting microbial mats and biofilms have on the erosion threshold of a muddy bed?

options.text: They have no measurable effect on erosion resistance
They lower erosion resistance by lubricating the grains
They can raise the critical erosion shear stress several-fold compared to an otherwise identical, biologically inert mud
They only affect wave orbital velocity, not erosion thresholds

explanations.a: Flume experiments on EPS-bound muds have documented a clear, substantial effect on erosion resistance, not a negligible one.
explanations.b: EPS mucilage binds grains together, increasing cohesion and resistance rather than lubricating and weakening the bed.
explanations.c: Correct — biofilm-secreted EPS binds sediment and has been shown to raise critical erosion shear stress several-fold relative to inert mud of the same composition.
explanations.d: Wave orbital velocity is a purely physical, depth-dependent phenomenon unrelated to biological stabilization of the bed.

units.label: Grain Size, Sorting, and the Texture Lab

lessons.label: The Phi Scale and Why Sedimentologists Log Their Data

sections.heading: Wentworth's ladder of doubling sizes
sections.body: In 1922 Chester Wentworth published a grain-size scale built entirely on doubling: boulder is anything coarser than 256 mm, cobble runs 64-256 mm, pebble 4-64 mm, granule 2-4 mm, sand 0.0625-2 mm, silt 0.0039-0.0625 mm, and clay is finer than 0.0039 mm. Each class boundary is exactly half (or double) its neighbor. That geometric spacing exists because grain populations in nature are themselves generated by processes that act multiplicatively — repeated fracturing, abrasion, and selective transport — so a scale built on ratios, not equal steps, matches how sediment actually varies.

sections.heading: Krumbein's logarithmic transform
sections.body: A doubling scale is awkward arithmetic: you cannot average 2 mm and 8 mm and get a meaningful 'typical' grain size the way you can average two masses. In 1934, Krumbein converted Wentworth's boundaries into a logarithmic phi (φ) unit: φ = -log2(d), with d in millimeters. Each whole-phi step is one halving of grain diameter, so 1 mm is 0 φ, 0.5 mm is 1 φ, 0.25 mm is 2 φ, and so on — the medium/fine sand boundary at 0.25 mm sits at exactly 2 φ. The negative sign is the classic trap: because coarser grains have diameters greater than 1 mm, and log2 of a number greater than 1 is positive, the minus sign flips it, so boulders and cobbles carry negative phi values (a 256 mm boulder is -8 φ) while silts and clays carry increasingly positive phi (a 0.001 mm clay particle is roughly 10 φ). Students who forget the sign consistently rank their coarsest sediment as 'largest phi' when it is actually the most negative.

sections.heading: Why the log transform earns its keep statistically
sections.body: The real payoff of working in phi is not just tidier arithmetic. Grain-size distributions produced by natural sorting processes — repeated selective transport, winnowing, mixing of source populations — tend to be approximately log-normal: normal on a logarithmic size axis, strongly skewed on a linear millimeter axis. By plotting and computing on phi units, a sedimentologist can legitimately apply ordinary Gaussian statistics (mean, standard deviation, percentiles) to a distribution that would otherwise be badly skewed and resistant to simple averaging. This is the entire justification for every graphic and moment statistic covered later in this unit: they only behave well because phi linearizes what is fundamentally a multiplicative, not additive, natural process.

lessons.workedExample: A student measures three grains: 0.125 mm, 4 mm, and 32 mm. Converting with phi = -log2(d): the 0.125 mm grain is -log2(0.125) = -(-3) = 3 φ (fine sand); the 4 mm grain is -log2(4) = -2 φ (granule); the 32 mm grain is -log2(32) = -5 φ (pebble). Notice the ordering flips relative to millimeters: the coarsest grain (32 mm) has the most negative phi (-5), and the finest (0.125 mm) has the most positive phi (+3). Averaging in mm would be dominated by the 32 mm outlier; averaging in phi ((3 + -2 + -5)/3 = -1.33 φ, about 2.5 mm) treats the three measurements on a scale where equal phi differences represent equal ratios of size, not equal absolute differences.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'what's a phi unit and why not just report millimeters?' is testing whether a student understands that they transformed their data, not just relabeled it. The tell of real understanding is naming the sign convention correctly (coarse = negative phi) without hesitation, and explaining that the log transform is what lets them legitimately compute a mean and standard deviation at all — because raw millimeter distributions from natural sediment are skewed, not because phi is simply the 'standard' unit geologists happen to use.

questions.prompt: A pebble measures 16 mm across its intermediate axis. What is its size in phi units?

options.text: 4 φ

explanations.a: Correct: phi = -log2(16) = -(4) = -4 φ. Since log2(16) = 4, the negative sign makes this coarse grain's phi value negative.
explanations.b: This drops the required negative sign; -log2(16) is -4, not +4, and forgetting the sign is the classic phi mistake for coarse grains.
explanations.c: This would be the phi value for a 4 mm grain (-log2(4) = -2), not a 16 mm grain.
explanations.d: Phi is a logarithm of the diameter, not the diameter itself; 16 φ would correspond to an impossibly small size (2^-16 mm).

questions.prompt: Why do sedimentologists compute mean and standard deviation on phi values rather than on millimeter values?

options.text: Millimeters are illegal units in sedimentology
Natural grain-size distributions are typically closer to log-normal, so phi (a log transform) makes ordinary Gaussian statistics valid
Phi values are always smaller numbers and easier to write down
Sieves can only be labeled in phi units

explanations.a: Millimeters remain the fundamental physical unit; phi is simply the analytical unit used for statistics.
explanations.b: Correct — because sediment is produced by multiplicative processes, its size distribution is approximately log-normal, and phi linearizes it so mean and standard deviation are meaningful.
explanations.c: Convenience of digit size is not the reason; the statistical justification is the log-normal shape of natural distributions.
explanations.d: Sieves are physically manufactured and labeled with mm/mesh sizes; phi is a computed conversion applied afterward.

questions.prompt: Order these Wentworth-scale classes from coarsest to finest.

items.text: Cobble (64-256 mm)
Pebble (4-64 mm)
Clay (<0.0039 mm)

questions.explanation: Wentworth's scale runs from cobble down through pebble, sand, and finally clay, each boundary halving the diameter of the coarser class above it — cobble is coarsest, clay is finest.

lessons.label: Sieving Done Right - and Its Error Budget

sections.heading: Shake time, loading, and the mass-balance check
sections.body: A stack of sieves nested by mesh size (each roughly half or a fixed root-2 step apart, matching whole and half-phi intervals) is shaken mechanically, often on a Ro-Tap-style shaker, until an added minute of shaking moves less than about 1% of a size fraction's mass across a mesh — the accepted definition of a stable endpoint, typically reached within 10-15 minutes. Overloading defeats this: a stack loaded much beyond roughly 100 g total sample blinds the mesh openings with grains that never get a fair chance to fall through, biasing the whole run coarse. After sieving, every fraction is weighed and summed; a good run recovers close to 100% of the starting mass, and sedimentologists typically flag anything losing more than a percent or two (dust loss, static cling to plastic sieve frames, or spillage) as suspect rather than silently normalizing the percentages to force them to add up.

sections.heading: Splitting a sample without introducing bias
sections.body: Before sieving, a bulk sample must be reduced to a workable subsample without biasing the size distribution — a step many student projects skip entirely. The two standard techniques are the riffle (chute) splitter, which pours the sample through a set of alternating chutes that divide it into two equal, statistically representative halves in one pass, and cone-and-quarter, where the sample is poured into a cone, flattened, cut into quarters, and two opposite quarters discarded. Riffle splitting is preferred in careful work because cone-and-quarter is operator-dependent: an inconsistent pour or an uneven cone systematically over- or under-represents certain size fractions, especially at the coarse end where a handful of large grains can dominate one quarter.

sections.heading: The sieve's hidden axis bias
sections.body: A sieve does not measure a grain's true diameter — it measures whether the grain can tumble through a square or round mesh opening, which depends almost entirely on the particle's intermediate (second-longest) axis, not its longest or shortest axis. A flat, platy grain (a mica flake or a tabular limestone chip) can have a long axis far larger than the mesh opening yet still slip through edge-on, because its intermediate axis is small. This means sieve data systematically under-represents platy, low-sphericity particles relative to what a shape-blind method like laser diffraction or a settling method would report, and it is why sieved 'grain size' is really closer to 'intermediate-axis size.'

lessons.workedExample: A student sieves a 150 g beach sample loaded into one stack — 50% over the ~100 g guideline. After 8 minutes of shaking they weigh the fractions and get a 146 g total, a 4 g (2.7%) loss they attribute to dust. Suspicious of the overloading, they re-split a fresh 90 g subsample with a riffle splitter, shake 12 minutes, and recover 89.1 g (99%). The re-run shows noticeably less material retained on the coarsest sieve than the first run — evidence the overloaded stack had blinded its top mesh and let coarse grains get reported in finer fractions than they belonged.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe sieving because it looks trivially mechanical but hides real methodological choices. A student who can state their shake time, their sample mass relative to the ~100 g loading guideline, and their mass-balance recovery percentage has shown they treated sieving as a measurement with an error budget, not a black box. Naming the intermediate-axis bias — that a sieve is blind to platy grains passing edge-on — signals they understand what the instrument actually measures, not just what number it outputs.

questions.prompt: Which particle axis primarily determines whether a grain passes through a given sieve mesh?

options.text: The longest axis
The intermediate (second-longest) axis
The shortest axis
The particle's volume, regardless of shape

explanations.a: A long, thin grain can pass through a mesh smaller than its longest axis by tumbling through end-on or edge-on, so the longest axis is not the controlling dimension.
explanations.b: Correct — a grain must present its intermediate axis to the mesh opening to pass through, which is why sieving under-samples flat, platy grains relative to their true long-axis size.
explanations.c: The shortest axis matters less than the intermediate axis for whether the grain can orient itself to slip through the opening.
explanations.d: Two grains of equal volume but very different shapes (a sphere versus a flat disc) behave very differently on a sieve, so volume alone does not determine passage.

questions.prompt: A sieve stack is loaded with 300 g of sample, roughly three times the ~100 g guideline. What is the most likely consequence?

options.text: The result is unaffected because sieving is purely mechanical
Mesh openings become blinded by excess grains, biasing the reported distribution toward coarser fractions
The sample will show artificially higher recovery mass
Shake time can be shortened to compensate

explanations.a: Loading matters a great deal; overloaded sieves do not give the same result as properly loaded ones.
explanations.b: Correct — excess mass clogs mesh openings so grains that should pass through are retained instead, shifting the apparent distribution coarse.
explanations.c: Recovery mass (total weighed out versus weighed in) is a separate check from loading bias and is not systematically inflated by overloading.
explanations.d: Overloading requires longer shaking to reach a stable endpoint, not shorter, since grains take longer to work down through a clogged stack.

questions.prompt: Order the correct workflow for preparing and sieving a bulk sediment sample.

items.text: Riffle-split the bulk sample into a representative subsample
Load the subsample onto the sieve stack (within loading limits)
Shake until an added minute moves less than about 1% of mass
Weigh each fraction and check total recovery against starting mass

questions.explanation: A representative subsample must be split first, then loaded within safe limits, shaken to a stable endpoint, and finally checked for mass-balance recovery — skipping or reordering any step undermines the ones that follow it.

lessons.label: Settling Methods: Hydrometer, Pipette, and Settling Tubes

sections.heading: Stokes' law and why fines cannot be sieved
sections.body: Below about 0.0625 mm (4 φ, the silt/sand boundary) mesh sieving stops working — openings that fine clog instantly and static forces dominate over gravity. Instead, fines are sized by settling velocity through Stokes' law, v = (2/9)(ρs - ρf)gr²/μ, which says a sphere's terminal velocity scales with the square of its radius and inversely with the fluid's viscosity μ. Because μ changes noticeably with temperature (water's viscosity nearly doubles between 25°C and 0°C), every settling method requires a temperature correction or a controlled water bath, and every calculation implicitly assumes spherical grains — an assumption that gets worse for clay minerals, which are platy, not spherical, and so settle slower than a sphere of equal mass and volume.

sections.heading: Dispersant and the flocculation trap
sections.body: Clay particles carry surface charges that make them stick together (flocculate) in ordinary water, forming aggregates that settle far faster than the individual clay platelets that compose them. Left untreated, flocculated clay settles at silt-like velocities and gets misreported as coarser material than it is. The standard fix is a dispersant, most commonly sodium hexametaphosphate (the compound behind the old trade name Calgon), which coats particle surfaces and neutralizes the charges holding aggregates together, along with mechanical agitation to break flocs apart before the settling test begins. A poorly dispersed sample systematically under-reports its true clay content and over-reports silt.

sections.heading: Three settling techniques, three different readouts
sections.body: The hydrometer method (the Bouyoucos-style approach used widely in soil science) reads bulk suspension density at fixed times, back-calculating the size that has just finished settling past the hydrometer's bulb depth at each reading — cheap and fast, but low-resolution, typically yielding only a handful of size cut points. The pipette method withdraws a small, precisely measured volume from a fixed depth at a time computed from Stokes' law for a target diameter, then ovendries and weighs the residue — slower and more labor-intensive, but able to build a full cumulative curve at many size cuts. A settling tube (used for coarser sand-silt mixes) drops the whole sample at once and continuously records mass or optical density accumulating at the tube base, converting arrival time to size for the whole population in a single run. Because each method makes different simplifying assumptions — the hydrometer assumes a uniform initial concentration profile, the pipette assumes negligible disturbance during withdrawal, the tube assumes minimal grain-grain hindered settling — the same sample analyzed by all three routinely yields noticeably different silt/clay splits, and the discrepancy is not a mistake to eliminate but an artifact of method to disclose.

lessons.workedExample: A lake-mud sample is split three ways. Run without dispersant on a hydrometer, it reads 25% clay. The student adds sodium hexametaphosphate, breaks up the sample with a mechanical stirrer for several minutes, and reruns: clay jumps to 41%, because the deflocculated platelets now settle at their true (slow) individual velocity rather than as fast-settling aggregate clumps. A pipette analysis on the same dispersed sample gives 38% clay — close to, but not identical to, the corrected hydrometer figure, illustrating that even two properly dispersed methods still disagree somewhat because of their different depth, timing, and volume assumptions.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking 'did you use a dispersant, and how do you know it worked?' is checking whether a student understands that an undispersed fines analysis silently reports flocs, not grains — a systematic error, not noise. The strongest answers name sodium hexametaphosphate specifically, describe the before/after clay percentage shift as evidence dispersion worked, and can explain in one sentence why hydrometer, pipette, and settling-tube numbers on the same sample are expected to differ rather than treating any disagreement as a mistake.

questions.prompt: A lake-mud sample analyzed without dispersant reads 25% clay on a hydrometer. After adding sodium hexametaphosphate and mechanical stirring, the reading rises to 41% clay. What best explains the increase?

options.text: The dispersant chemically dissolved some of the silt into clay-sized particles
Without dispersant, clay platelets were flocculated into aggregates that settled at silt-like speeds and were undercounted as clay
The hydrometer was miscalibrated in the first run
Adding dispersant increases the total mass of clay minerals present in the sample

explanations.a: Sodium hexametaphosphate disperses particles by neutralizing surface charge; it does not chemically convert silt into clay minerals.
explanations.b: Correct — flocculated clay settles as fast aggregates and reads as coarser (silt-like) material; dispersing the flocs lets individual clay platelets settle at their true slow velocity, revealing the true higher clay fraction.
explanations.c: There is no indication of an instrument fault; the physical difference is flocculation state, not calibration.
explanations.d: The total mass of clay minerals in the sample is fixed; dispersant only changes how that mass reports out, not how much clay exists.

questions.prompt: Why does Stokes' law require a temperature correction (or a controlled water bath) in settling analyses?

options.text: Temperature changes the density of the mineral grains themselves
Water's viscosity changes substantially with temperature, and Stokes' terminal velocity depends inversely on viscosity
Warmer water causes grains to dissolve
Temperature has no real effect; the correction is a historical formality

explanations.a: Mineral grain density is essentially fixed by composition and does not shift meaningfully with the temperature ranges used in settling tests.
explanations.b: Correct — Stokes' law includes viscosity μ in the denominator, and water's viscosity changes markedly between cold and warm conditions, directly changing settling velocity for a given grain size.
explanations.c: Ordinary settling-test temperature ranges do not dissolve silicate or clay mineral grains.
explanations.d: The correction is physically necessary, not a formality, because uncorrected viscosity differences shift the size calculated from a given settling time.

questions.prompt: Match each settling method to how it actually produces its size data.

right.text: Reads bulk suspension density at fixed times to infer which sizes have settled past the instrument's depth
Withdraws small fixed volumes from a fixed depth at Stokes-computed times, then ovendries and weighs the residue
Drops the whole sample at once and continuously records mass or optical density arriving at the base

questions.explanation: The hydrometer infers size from bulk suspension density readings, the pipette method physically withdraws and weighs timed aliquots, and the settling tube continuously records the whole population arriving at its base in one run.

lessons.label: Laser Diffraction vs Sieve and Pipette

sections.heading: How laser diffraction actually infers a size
sections.body: A laser diffraction analyzer passes a beam through a flowing suspension and measures the angular pattern of scattered light on a detector array, then inverts that scattering pattern into a size distribution using an optical model. Coarser particles scatter light at small forward angles, finer particles scatter more widely, and the instrument reports whatever equivalent spherical diameter would produce the observed scattering pattern — it never sees particle shape or settling behavior directly, only optics. Two inversion models are in use: the older Fraunhofer approximation, which ignores the particle's refractive index and assumes opaque spheres large relative to the light's wavelength, and the fuller Mie theory, which accounts for refractive index and works down to much finer sizes but requires the operator to input the correct refractive index and absorption values for the mineral being measured — values that are rarely known precisely for a mixed natural sediment.

sections.heading: Why laser diffraction reports more silt and less clay
sections.body: Konert and Vandenberghe (1997), published in Sedimentology, ran laser diffraction alongside pipette and sieve analysis on the same samples and found a consistent, systematic pattern: laser diffraction underestimates the clay fraction and correspondingly overestimates the silt fraction compared with pipette results. The mechanism is shape, not error: clay minerals are platy, and a flat platelet lying broadside to the laser scatters light the way a much larger, more equant particle would, so the optical model reports it as a coarser equivalent sphere than its true settling-equivalent size. Pipette and hydrometer methods, by contrast, measure settling velocity directly, and a platy particle's slow fall (due to high drag relative to its volume) correctly registers it as fine. The two methods are measuring genuinely different physical properties — optical scattering cross-section versus hydrodynamic settling — so they are not expected to agree, and the size of the mismatch scales with how platy (clay-mineral-rich) a given sample is.

sections.heading: The operating rule: never mix methods, always state one
sections.body: Because the laser-versus-pipette offset is sample-specific — driven by each sample's particular mix of clay mineralogy, particle shape, and refractive index — published regression equations that convert one method's numbers to the other's are only reliable for sediments similar to the ones used to derive them, and do not transfer cleanly to a new depositional setting. The safe practice a science-fair project should follow is simple: pick one grain-size method for an entire study and never merge sieve, pipette, and laser-diffraction numbers into a single dataset as if they were interchangeable, and always report which method produced a stated grain-size percentage, since '34% clay' means something different depending on which instrument generated it.

lessons.workedExample: A student measures the same estuarine mud sample by pipette and by laser diffraction. The pipette reports 35% clay, 55% silt, 10% sand. The laser diffraction analyzer, run with a Fraunhofer inversion, reports 18% clay, 72% silt, 10% sand — the sand fraction (least platy, most sphere-like) roughly agrees, but the clay/silt split is very different. Rather than average the two, the student reports both figures side by side, explicitly labeled by method, and notes that the platy clay minerals in the sample scatter light as if they were larger particles, which is the documented direction of the laser-diffraction bias relative to pipette settling data.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this because mixing grain-size methods inside one dataset is a common, invisible error — the numbers look compatible (both are percentages of clay, silt, sand) even though they measure different physical properties. A student who can explain that laser diffraction reports an optical equivalent sphere while pipette reports a settling equivalent, and that platy clay is the reason the two disagree, has understood the instrument rather than just operated it. Simply averaging two disagreeing methods, or not stating which method produced a number, are the tells of a student who has not.

questions.prompt: Konert and Vandenberghe (1997) compared laser diffraction to pipette analysis on the same samples. What was the consistent pattern they documented?

options.text: Laser diffraction underestimated the clay fraction and overestimated silt, relative to pipette
Laser diffraction overestimated clay and underestimated silt, relative to pipette
The two methods agreed closely across all fractions
Laser diffraction only disagreed with pipette on the sand fraction

explanations.a: Correct — Konert and Vandenberghe (1997) found laser diffraction systematically reports less clay and more silt than pipette analysis of the same sediment.
explanations.b: This reverses the documented direction; laser diffraction under-, not over-, reports clay compared with pipette.
explanations.c: The 1997 study's key finding was a systematic disagreement, not close agreement, particularly in the fine fractions.
explanations.d: The disagreement is concentrated in the clay/silt fractions, driven by particle shape; the sand fraction (more equant grains) tends to show closer agreement.

questions.prompt: Why do platy clay minerals cause laser diffraction to report a coarser size than pipette settling analysis gives for the same particles?

options.text: Laser diffraction measures optical scattering, and a flat platelet scatters light like a larger equivalent sphere, while pipette measures settling velocity, where the platelet's high drag makes it fall (and register) as fine
Laser diffraction machines are simply miscalibrated for clay minerals
Pipette analysis cannot detect particles finer than sand, so it misses clay entirely
Clay minerals dissolve during laser diffraction analysis, artificially reducing the clay signal

explanations.a: Correct — the two methods measure different physical properties (optical scattering cross-section versus hydrodynamic settling), and a platy particle's shape affects each property differently.
explanations.b: The offset is a documented, mechanistic shape effect, not a calibration failure of the instrument.
explanations.c: Pipette analysis is specifically designed via Stokes' law settling to resolve silt and clay sizes; it is the sieve method that cannot handle fines.
explanations.d: Clay minerals are stable in the aqueous suspensions used for laser diffraction and do not dissolve during the measurement.

questions.prompt: Order the correct practice for a study reporting grain-size data from multiple instruments.

items.text: Choose one grain-size method for the entire study
Run all samples with that single method
Report each percentage together with the method that produced it
Avoid merging numbers from a different method into the same dataset without a documented, sample-specific conversion

questions.explanation: Sound practice starts with committing to a single method, applying it consistently across all samples, labeling every reported figure with its method, and never silently combining a different method's numbers without accounting for the fact that inter-method conversions are sample-specific.

lessons.label: Folk & Ward vs Method of Moments

sections.heading: Graphic statistics: read five points off the curve
sections.body: Folk and Ward (1957) built a set of formulas that need only five points read from a cumulative grain-size curve: the phi values at the 5th, 16th, 50th, 84th, and 95th percentiles. The graphic mean is Mz = (φ16 + φ50 + φ84)/3, averaging the median with two symmetric percentiles to resist distortion from a long tail. The inclusive graphic standard deviation, σI = (φ84-φ16)/4 + (φ95-φ5)/6.6, combines a narrow spread (16-84) with a wide spread (5-95) so both the bulk of the distribution and its tails contribute to the sorting value. Skewness, SkI = [(φ16+φ84-2φ50)/(2(φ84-φ16))] + [(φ5+φ95-2φ50)/(2(φ95-φ5))], compares how far the tails sit from the median relative to how far the shoulders sit — a distribution with a disproportionately long fine tail (excess silt/clay in an otherwise sandy sample) reads as positively skewed.

sections.heading: Moment statistics: use every gram of data
sections.body: The method of moments instead computes the true statistical mean, variance, skewness, and kurtosis using the weight retained in every size class across the whole distribution, the same formulas used for any statistical dataset. In principle this is more information-rich than five percentile points. In practice, moment statistics are much more sensitive to what happens at the open tails of a sieved or settled distribution — the finest pan fraction and the coarsest retained fraction are often lumped catch-all classes rather than precisely resolved size intervals, and because moments weight extreme values heavily, an imprecisely characterized tail can swing the moment mean, skewness, or kurtosis substantially, even when it represents only a few percent of the sample's total mass.

sections.heading: Folk's verbal sorting scale and reporting disagreement
sections.body: Folk attached descriptive words to ranges of σI (in phi units) so sorting could be communicated without forcing every reader to interpret a raw number: below 0.35 is very well sorted, 0.35-0.50 well sorted, 0.50-0.71 moderately well sorted, 0.71-1.00 moderately sorted, 1.00-2.00 poorly sorted, 2.00-4.00 very poorly sorted, and above 4.00 extremely poorly sorted. When graphic and moment statistics for the same sample disagree — commonly on skewness, since it is most tail-sensitive — the correct response is not to average them or silently pick the more flattering one, but to report both values, note which method's percentile boundaries or open tail is driving the difference, and let the disagreement itself be informative about how much fine or coarse material sits outside the well-resolved part of the curve.

lessons.workedExample: A dune sand yields φ5=-0.5, φ16=0.3, φ50=1.5, φ84=2.4, φ95=3.9. Graphic mean: Mz=(0.3+1.5+2.4)/3=1.4φ. Inclusive graphic standard deviation: σI=(2.4-0.3)/4 + (3.9-(-0.5))/6.6 = 0.525+0.667=1.19φ, which Folk's verbal scale labels poorly sorted. Skewness: SkI=[(0.3+2.4-3.0)/(2×2.1)] + [(-0.5+3.9-3.0)/(2×4.4)] = (-0.3/4.2)+(0.4/8.8)=-0.071+0.045=-0.026φ, essentially symmetric (near-zero). Computing the method-of-moments skewness on the full weight distribution instead gives a noticeably positive value, because a thin but imprecisely resolved fine tail below the 95th percentile pulls the moment calculation toward positive skew in a way the percentile-based graphic method, which stops at φ95, does not capture.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking 'why report two different sorting or skewness numbers for the same sample?' is testing whether the student understands these are two legitimately different calculations, not a mistake needing correction. The strong answer names the mechanism: graphic (Folk & Ward) statistics use five fixed percentiles and are insensitive to what happens beyond φ5-φ95, while moment statistics use the whole distribution and are correspondingly vulnerable to imprecision in open-ended tail classes — so a disagreement between the two is itself a clue about how much material sits in poorly resolved tails.

questions.prompt: Using the Folk and Ward formula σI = (φ84-φ16)/4 + (φ95-φ5)/6.6, a sample has φ16=0.3, φ84=2.4, φ5=-0.5, φ95=3.9. What is the inclusive graphic standard deviation?

options.text: About 1.19 φ
About 0.53 φ
About 2.10 φ
About 4.40 φ

explanations.b: This is only the first term, (φ84-φ16)/4; the formula requires adding the second (5-95) term as well.
explanations.c: 2.10 is the raw (φ84-φ16) difference before dividing by 4, not the final sorting value.
explanations.d: 4.40 is the raw (φ95-φ5) difference before dividing by 6.6, not the final sorting value.

questions.prompt: A sample's Folk & Ward graphic skewness comes out near zero (symmetric), but its method-of-moments skewness is noticeably positive. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: One of the two calculations must contain an arithmetic error
The moment calculation is pulled by a thin, imprecisely resolved fine tail beyond φ95 that the percentile-based graphic method does not include
Graphic and moment skewness always agree exactly for well-sorted sediment
Skewness cannot be computed by two different methods on the same dataset

explanations.a: Both calculations can be arithmetically correct and still disagree, because they are different statistics computed from different parts of the distribution.
explanations.b: Correct — moment statistics use every gram of the sample including open-ended tail classes, so a poorly resolved fine tail can swing the moment skewness even when it is a small fraction of total mass, while the graphic method (bounded at φ5-φ95) is insensitive to it.
explanations.c: Sorting quality (well- versus poorly-sorted) does not guarantee agreement between the two skewness methods; tail sensitivity is the driving factor, independent of overall sorting.
