sections.body: A real error budget adds up the known sources of uncertainty rather than reporting a single unexplained plus-or-minus. For sieve analysis, mass loss is the standard check: sum the mass retained on every sieve plus the pan, compare it to the sample's starting mass, and a loss beyond roughly 1-2% signals a compromised run (spilled material, incomplete shaking) that should be flagged or redone. Operator variance is a second named source: two people reading the same sieve fraction or measuring the same pebble can disagree by a measurable amount, which is exactly what blind duplicates are designed to quantify. Judges at a science fair reliably probe three specific weaknesses: an n=1 transect (one line of samples generalized to a whole formation or region), a cherry-picked outcrop (the cleanest, most photogenic exposure standing in for a unit that is mostly covered or messy), and a facies model read further than the data support (calling a single fining-upward bed a "point bar" without the lateral accretion surfaces or cross-bedding orientation that claim actually requires).

lessons.workedExample: A student drops individual 0.5 mm quartz sand grains down a 1-meter settling column and times the fall over the middle 60 cm, repeating each grain size 5 times. Measured settling velocity averages 6.5 cm/s. Stokes' law (valid strictly for very fine, slowly settling grains, roughly under 0.1 mm) predicts a much higher value for 0.5 mm quartz because it ignores turbulent drag, which dominates at this size. The student reports the measured 6.5 cm/s, states that Stokes' law over-predicts outside its valid grain-size range, and cites a turbulent-settling formulation as the better comparison — turning a "my number doesn't match the textbook" problem into a correctly explained result.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about sampling design and error budgets because sedimentology projects are unusually easy to fake convincingly with a single nice-looking outcrop or one lucky transect. The strong defense is procedural: naming the replicate count, the spacing rule, whether blind duplicates were run, and the specific error sources (sieve mass loss, operator variance) that were tracked — and being upfront about where a facies interpretation stops being supported by the data actually collected. A student who says "I only sampled one section, so I can't claim this for the whole formation" has passed the test that a student claiming a sweeping conclusion from that same section has failed.

questions.prompt: A settling-column trial measures a settling velocity for 0.5 mm quartz sand that is much lower than Stokes' law predicts. What is the best explanation?

options.text: The sand grains must be a different mineral than quartz
Stokes' law is only strictly valid for very fine, slowly settling grains, and turbulent drag (not accounted for in Stokes' law) dominates at 0.5 mm
The settling column must have been too short to give any valid reading
Settling velocity cannot be measured experimentally at all

explanations.a: Mineral identity affects density and thus settling velocity somewhat, but the size-dependent breakdown of Stokes' law is the specific, well-known reason for this mismatch, not mineralogy.
explanations.b: Correct — Stokes' law assumes laminar flow around the settling grain, which holds only for very fine grains; at 0.5 mm, turbulent drag dominates and Stokes' law over-predicts, so a turbulent-settling formulation fits better.
explanations.c: A column length is a design choice that affects precision, but the described mismatch is a known limitation of Stokes' law's assumptions, not necessarily a column-length problem.
explanations.d: Settling velocity is routinely and directly measured this way; the issue is which theoretical formula to compare it against, not measurability.

questions.prompt: In a sieve analysis, the sum of mass retained on all sieves plus the pan comes to 3% less than the sample's starting mass. What should this trigger?

options.text: Nothing — a few percent mass loss is expected and can be ignored
Flagging or redoing the run, since mass loss beyond roughly 1-2% signals a compromised sieving process
Concluding that the grain-size distribution is invalid and cannot be reported at all
Recalculating the sample's original starting mass to match the sieved total

explanations.a: A 3% loss exceeds the roughly 1-2% threshold typically used as an acceptable-loss check; it should not simply be waved off.
explanations.b: Correct — mass-balance checking against the starting mass is the standard sieve-analysis quality check, and a loss beyond about 1-2% signals spilled material or an incomplete run that should be flagged or redone.
explanations.c: A failed mass-balance check means the run needs scrutiny or repeating, not that grain-size data is permanently unreportable.
explanations.d: The starting mass is the fixed reference measured before sieving; adjusting it to match a flawed sieved total would hide the error rather than fix it.

questions.prompt: Order these steps in setting up a defensible sampling design, from the design decision made first to the check applied last.

items.text: Decide replicate count and transect spacing in advance, before collecting data
Collect samples, including blind duplicates the operator does not know are repeats
Process samples (e.g., sieve) and check mass balance against starting mass
Compare blind-duplicate results to quantify operator variance

questions.explanation: A defensible design fixes replicate count and spacing before any data exists, then collects samples including unlabeled blind duplicates, then processes and mass-balance-checks each sample, and finally compares duplicate pairs to quantify how much of the variance comes from the operator rather than the sediment itself.

questions.prompt: Match each judge attack to the specific weakness it targets.

left.text: "Your facies model claims more than your data show"

right.text: A single line of samples generalized to an entire formation or region
The most complete, photogenic exposure standing in for a unit that is mostly covered or messy
A depositional-environment interpretation (e.g., point bar) asserted without the specific structures that claim requires

questions.explanation: These are the three standard science-fair attacks on a sedimentology study: an n=1 transect overgeneralizes from one sampled line, a cherry-picked outcrop substitutes the best-looking exposure for the whole unit, and an over-read facies model claims a specific depositional environment beyond what the observed structures actually support.

units.label: Crystal Chemistry: What a Mineral Is and Why Structure Rules Everything

lessons.label: The Mineral Definition and the Crystalline State

sections.heading: The five-part test
sections.body: A mineral, by the working definition maintained by the International Mineralogical Association's Commission on New Minerals, Nomenclature and Classification (IMA-CNMNC), must be: naturally occurring, formed without human intervention; solid at the temperature it forms and is classified at; essentially inorganic, though the modern rule admits some biologically mediated crystalline solids (like certain shell aragonite) case by case rather than banning biology outright; of definite but generally variable chemical composition, meaning a formula with room for substitution, not a single fixed molecule; and possessing an ordered internal atomic structure, a crystal lattice. All five must hold at once. A synthetic diamond grown in a lab press fails 'naturally occurring' and is not a mineral no matter how perfect its lattice; ordinary window glass fails the ordered-structure test even though it is solid and inorganic.

sections.heading: Why opal, obsidian, and amber are not minerals
sections.body: Opal (hydrated amorphous silica), obsidian (volcanic glass), and amber (fossilized tree resin) are all familiar, solid, naturally occurring earth materials, yet none is a true mineral, because none has long-range atomic order. Obsidian cools too fast for silicate tetrahedra to link into a repeating lattice, freezing in a disordered, glassy arrangement; opal's silica spheres pack without a crystal lattice; amber is an organic polymer with no periodic atomic arrangement at all. Mineralogists call these mineraloids. The test is never appearance, hardness, or luster - it is whether X-ray diffraction shows the sharp, repeating spacing of a lattice or the diffuse smear of an amorphous solid.

sections.heading: Order can be damaged, not just absent
sections.body: Some minerals start with a perfect lattice and lose it. Zircon (ZrSiO4) incorporates trace uranium and thorium substituting for zirconium; their radioactive decay releases alpha particles that blast the surrounding lattice apart, atom by atom, over hundreds of millions of years. A zircon crystal that has accumulated enough of this self-damage becomes metamict: still the same chemical formula and often still an intact crystal face, but internally amorphous, having lost its long-range order to radiation rather than never having had it. Metamict zircon is a mineral in name and history but structurally has converged toward the same disordered state as a glass, which is why the structural test, not the chemical formula, is the one that actually decides the question.

sections.heading: A short list runs the crust
sections.body: The IMA-CNMNC has approved roughly 6,000 distinct mineral species, yet only about 20 rock-forming minerals - feldspars, quartz, micas, pyroxenes, amphiboles, olivine, calcite, and a handful of others - make up the overwhelming majority of the volume of Earth's crust. The other thousands are mostly rare accessory or ore minerals, often known from a single locality, that matter for chemistry and economic geology but contribute almost nothing to bulk rock volume.

lessons.workedExample: A student is handed three unlabeled samples: a chunk of milky quartz, a piece of black obsidian, and a fire opal. All are hard, solid, glossy, and naturally occurring - by casual inspection they seem like a matched set of 'rocks.' Applying the five-part test changes the answer: quartz gives a sharp hexagonal diffraction pattern (true mineral); obsidian and opal both give diffuse, broad diffraction humps with no repeating spacing (both mineraloids, despite one being called an opal 'gem'). The lesson is that 'looks crystalline' (faceted, glassy, colorful) and 'is crystalline' (has a periodic lattice provable by diffraction) are entirely different claims, and only the second one matters for classification.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'is your sample actually a mineral, or a mineraloid?' is testing whether a student can apply a formal definition instead of eyeballing hardness and shine. The strong answer names the specific failing criterion - obsidian fails ordered structure because rapid quenching prevents lattice formation, not because it isn't naturally occurring or solid - and can say what evidence (X-ray diffraction pattern) would settle it. A student who answers 'it's shiny and hard so it must be a mineral' has not engaged with the definition at all.

questions.prompt: Why does obsidian fail the mineral definition even though it is a naturally occurring, inorganic solid?

options.text: It lacks a definite chemical composition entirely
It cools too quickly for a repeating atomic lattice to form, so it has no long-range order
It is not hard enough to count as a mineral
It was formed by biological processes

explanations.a: Obsidian does have a broadly consistent silicate composition; composition is not the failing test here.
explanations.b: Correct - rapid volcanic quenching freezes silicate tetrahedra into a disordered, glassy arrangement before they can link into a repeating lattice, so obsidian fails the ordered-internal-structure criterion.
explanations.c: Hardness plays no role in the IMA definition at all; many true minerals (talc, gypsum) are very soft.
explanations.d: Obsidian is igneous, not biological in origin; biological formation is not why it is excluded.

questions.prompt: What does it mean for zircon to become 'metamict'?

options.text: It has recrystallized into a new, more ordered mineral
Radiation damage from decaying U and Th has destroyed its original crystal lattice over time
It has been reclassified by the IMA as a mineraloid from the start
It has lost all zirconium from its formula through weathering

explanations.a: Metamictization is a loss of order, the opposite of recrystallizing into a more ordered state.
explanations.b: Correct - trace U and Th substituting for Zr undergo radioactive decay, and the resulting alpha-particle damage progressively destroys the lattice's long-range order, converging it toward an amorphous state.
explanations.c: Zircon starts as a true crystalline mineral; metamictization is a process it undergoes over geologic time, not its initial classification.
explanations.d: The chemical formula is largely retained; it is the atomic order, not the composition, that is destroyed.

questions.prompt: Match each material to the reason it fails the strict mineral definition (or, for zircon, the process that can remove its order).

right.text: Organic polymer with no periodic atomic arrangement
Silica spheres packed without a crystal lattice
Radiation damage from decaying U/Th destroyed original order
Quenched too fast to form a repeating lattice

questions.explanation: Opal's silica spheres pack without long-range order, amber is an organic resin polymer, obsidian quenches too fast for a lattice to form, and metamict zircon started ordered but was disordered by self-irradiation from its own trace uranium and thorium.

questions.prompt: Roughly how many rock-forming mineral species make up the large majority of the volume of Earth's crust, out of the roughly 6,000 IMA-approved species overall?

options.text: About 20
About 500
About 3,000
All roughly 6,000 contribute nearly equally

explanations.a: Correct - roughly 20 rock-forming minerals (feldspars, quartz, micas, pyroxenes, amphiboles, olivine, calcite, and a few others) account for the overwhelming majority of crustal rock volume, while the rest of the ~6,000 approved species are rare accessory or ore minerals.
explanations.b: This overstates how many species actually dominate crustal volume; the true rock-forming set is much narrower.
explanations.c: This is far too many; most of the ~6,000 approved species are rare, not volumetrically significant.
explanations.d: Mineral abundance in the crust is extremely skewed, not remotely even across species.

lessons.label: Lattices, Symmetry, and Miller Indices

sections.heading: From a broken calcite rhomb to the unit cell
sections.body: The lattice concept did not start as abstract math - it started with observation. In 1669 Nicolas Steno, dissecting quartz crystals of wildly different sizes and habits, noticed that the angles between equivalent faces were always the same, regardless of how distorted or stubby a given crystal looked. This law of constant interfacial angles said that something invisible and regular was constraining crystal growth even when the visible shape varied. Over a century later, in 1784, René Just Haüy dropped a calcite crystal and it shattered into small rhombohedra with identical angles to the original. Haüy proposed that the whole crystal was built from a stack of these tiny identical building blocks - the first physical model of a repeating unit cell, the smallest 3D box (defined by edge lengths a, b, c and angles alpha, beta, gamma) that tiles space to build the entire lattice by translation alone.

sections.heading: Seven systems, fourteen lattices, thirty-two classes
sections.body: Unit cells sort into 7 crystal systems (cubic, tetragonal, orthorhombic, hexagonal, trigonal, monoclinic, triclinic) based on the relative lengths of a, b, c and the angles between them. When you also ask where lattice points can sit inside that cell (only at corners, or also body-centered, face-centered, or base-centered), you get exactly 14 distinct arrangements, the Bravais lattices, proved complete by Auguste Bravais in 1848. Layering point symmetry (mirrors, rotations, inversion) onto each lattice yields 32 crystal classes, also called point groups - every possible combination of symmetry operations consistent with translational periodicity. Symmetry operations themselves come in a few types: mirror reflection, rotation (2-, 3-, 4-, or 6-fold, never 5-fold in a periodic lattice), inversion through a center, and the compound operations screw axes (rotation plus translation) and glide planes (reflection plus translation). Hermann-Mauguin notation compactly names a class's symmetry - for example 4/m 2/m 2/m for a common tetragonal class - by listing the rotation and mirror elements along each symmetry direction.

sections.heading: Miller indices name a face
sections.body: To describe any crystal face or internal plane without redrawing the whole crystal, mineralogists use Miller indices (h k l): take the reciprocals of the face's intercepts on the a, b, c axes (in units of the cell edge), then clear fractions to the smallest integers. A face parallel to the b and c axes but cutting a at one cell length is (100); one cutting all three axes at one cell length each is (111). Because Miller indices are reciprocals, a face indexed (100) and one indexed (200) describe the same orientation, just at different spacing within a family - this reciprocal convention is what makes the notation additive and easy to combine with X-ray diffraction geometry later in the field.

lessons.workedExample: A cubic mineral face intercepts the a-axis at 2 unit-cell lengths, the b-axis at 1 unit-cell length, and never crosses c (it runs parallel to c, so its intercept is at infinity). Taking reciprocals gives 1/2, 1/1, 1/infinity = 1/2, 1, 0. Clearing to the smallest integers (multiply by 2) gives (1 2 0) - wait, multiplying 1/2, 1, 0 by 2 gives 1, 2, 0, so the Miller index is (120). This is exactly the kind of arithmetic Steno's constant-angle observation predicts will recur crystal to crystal: any face parallel to c with this same intercept ratio, on any sample of the same mineral, gets the identical index and the identical interfacial angle, however large or small the crystal.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing symmetry and indexing wants to see that a student understands crystallography as a predictive, historical science, not a memorized vocabulary list. The strong signal is connecting Steno's constant-angle observation and Haüy's broken-rhombohedra insight to the modern unit cell - explaining why a lattice model, not surface appearance, is what predicts a mineral's angles and faces. A student who can index a face with Miller notation and explain what the numbers physically mean (reciprocal axial intercepts) shows real command; one who recites '7 systems, 14 lattices, 32 classes' without connecting them to symmetry operations has memorized labels only.

questions.prompt: What did Steno's 1669 law of constant interfacial angles establish?

options.text: That all quartz crystals are exactly the same size
That equivalent faces on crystals of the same mineral always meet at the same angle, regardless of overall crystal size or shape
That crystals have no internal structure at all
That mineral hardness determines interfacial angle

explanations.a: Steno explicitly studied crystals of very different sizes and shapes; his point was that size and habit vary while angles do not.
explanations.b: Correct - regardless of how distorted or differently sized a crystal was, equivalent faces met at the same angle, implying a hidden regular internal cause.
explanations.c: The observation is the reason mineralogists later inferred internal structure exists; it does not claim structure is absent.
explanations.d: Hardness is unrelated to interfacial angle in Steno's observation.

questions.prompt: A crystal face intercepts the a-axis at 1 cell length, the b-axis at 1 cell length, and the c-axis at 1 cell length. What is its Miller index?

explanations.a: (100) describes a face parallel to b and c, intercepting only a - not this face.
explanations.b: Correct - reciprocals of 1, 1, 1 are 1, 1, 1, already the smallest integers, giving Miller index (111).
explanations.c: (010) describes a face parallel to a and c, intercepting only b - not this face.
explanations.d: (000) is not a valid Miller index; it would require infinite reciprocals of zero intercepts.

questions.prompt: Match each historical figure to their contribution to crystallography.

right.text: Law of constant interfacial angles across differently shaped crystals
Proposed crystals are built from stacked identical rhombohedral building blocks after observing calcite cleavage
Proved there are exactly 14 distinct lattice-point arrangements

questions.explanation: Steno established constant interfacial angles, Haüy's broken calcite led to the stacked-unit-cell model of crystal structure, and Bravais proved there are exactly 14 distinct lattices consistent with 3D periodicity.

questions.prompt: Order these levels of crystallographic classification from broadest (fewest categories) to most specific (finest distinctions).

items.text: 7 crystal systems
14 Bravais lattices
32 crystal classes (point groups)

questions.explanation: The 7 crystal systems are the broadest grouping by cell shape; splitting those by lattice-point centering gives the 14 Bravais lattices; layering point symmetry operations onto those gives the still-finer 32 crystal classes.

lessons.label: Bonding, Pauling's Rules, and Predicting Properties

sections.heading: Four bond types, one crystal
sections.body: Minerals rarely use just one bond type. Ionic bonding (electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, as in halite's Na-Cl) and covalent bonding (shared electron pairs, as in diamond's C-C framework) dominate most silicates and oxides, usually in some mixture - the Si-O bond itself is roughly half covalent, half ionic. Metallic bonding, with delocalized electrons, appears in native metals like gold and copper, explaining their malleability and conductivity. Van der Waals bonding, a weak residual attraction between electrically neutral layers, holds sheets together in graphite and in some clay minerals, and is almost always the weakest link in an otherwise strongly bonded structure.

sections.heading: Radius ratio sets coordination number - usually
sections.body: Treat ions as hard spheres and one number predicts how many anions pack around a cation - the coordination number. Divide the cation radius by the anion radius (for oxygen, about 1.40 angstroms) and read off the classic windows: 0.155 to 0.225 gives 3-fold (triangular), 0.225 to 0.414 gives 4-fold (tetrahedral), 0.414 to 0.732 gives 6-fold (octahedral), and 0.732 to 1.0 gives 8-fold. Magnesium (0.72 A) gives 0.72/1.40 = 0.51, squarely 6-fold, which is what the Mg site in olivine and in periclase actually is; ferrous iron (0.78 A) gives 0.56, also 6-fold. Calcium in an 8-fold site (1.12 A) gives 1.12/1.40 = 0.80, an 8-fold prediction that matches pyroxene's M2 site and plagioclase's largest cation site. Aluminum straddles a boundary: 0.39 A in 4-fold coordination gives 0.28, while 0.535 A in 6-fold gives 0.38, both inside the tetrahedral window but climbing toward the 0.414 tetrahedral-octahedral crossover - which is exactly why Al substitutes for Si in 4-fold sites and for Mg or Fe in 6-fold sites, the basis of feldspar and mica chemistry.

sections.heading: Silicon is the exception that shows the rule's limit
sections.body: Run the same arithmetic on silicon and it fails. Si4+ has an effective ionic radius near 0.26 A, so 0.26/1.40 = 0.19 - below the 0.225 threshold, landing in the 3-fold triangular window. Yet silicon is essentially always 4-fold in minerals, and the SiO4 tetrahedron underlies every silicate. The rule under-predicts here because it assumes purely ionic, non-directional bonding, and the Si-O bond is about half covalent. Covalent bonding is directional: silicon's sp3 hybrid orbitals point at the corners of a tetrahedron and hold four oxygens in place regardless of what hard-sphere packing would allow. (Some sources dodge this by quoting crystal radii instead of effective ionic radii, which shifts Si4+/O2- to roughly 0.32 and inside the tetrahedral window - but the honest lesson is that the ratio you get depends on which radius set you use, and covalency, not geometry, is what actually fixes silicon at 4-fold.)

sections.heading: Pauling's rules turn geometry into prediction
sections.body: Linus Pauling's 1929 paper laid out five rules that let a chemist predict silicate structures before solving them by diffraction. The most quoted are the radius-ratio/coordination rule above, the electrostatic valence rule (the sum of electrostatic bond strengths reaching an anion from all surrounding cations should equal the anion's charge, which is why isolated SiO4 tetrahedra need extra cations to balance oxygen's charge), and the rule that shared edges and especially shared faces between coordination polyhedra are destabilizing, because sharing them forces like-charged cations too close together - explaining why SiO4 tetrahedra in silicates almost always share corners, never edges or faces.

sections.heading: Bonding predicts hardness, cleavage, density, and melting point
sections.body: Diamond and graphite are both pure carbon, yet diamond is Mohs hardness 10 with no cleavage because every carbon is covalently bonded in a rigid 3D sp3 tetrahedral network, while graphite is hardness 1 to 2 and slips apart in one direction because strong covalent bonds within its sheets are held together only by weak van der Waals forces between sheets. The same logic predicts density (compact, high-coordination structures pack denser) and melting point (strong, uniform bonding in all three directions raises melting point far above a structure with a weak-bond direction).

lessons.workedExample: Given only radius ratios, predict whether Mg2+ (radius about 0.72 A) in an oxide will take 4-fold or 6-fold coordination against O2- (radius 1.40 A). The ratio is 0.72/1.40 = 0.51, which falls in the 0.414 to 0.732 window favoring octahedral (6-fold) rather than tetrahedral coordination. This correctly predicts that MgO (periclase) and the Mg site in olivine (Mg2SiO4) are both octahedrally coordinated, matching what X-ray structure solutions show - hard-sphere arithmetic alone gets the right answer without running a diffraction experiment, because Mg-O bonding is largely ionic. Now try the same method on Si4+ (about 0.26 A): 0.26/1.40 = 0.19, which sits below 0.225 and predicts 3-fold coordination. That prediction is wrong - silicon is 4-fold in every rock-forming silicate. The lesson is diagnostic, not discouraging: when a radius-ratio prediction misses, suspect covalent, directional bonding, and for Si-O that is exactly the cause. Use the ratio as a first guess for largely ionic cations, and check it against known structures before building an argument on it.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking 'why does diamond scratch glass but graphite doesn't, even though both are pure carbon?' is testing whether a student understands that composition alone never determines a mineral's physical properties - bonding architecture does. The strong answer names the mechanism (3D covalent network with no weak-bond direction versus strongly bonded sheets held by weak van der Waals forces) rather than reciting 'diamond is harder than graphite' as a memorized fact. A judge will be even more impressed by a student who knows where their own rules break: saying 'radius ratio predicts Mg2+ octahedral and that checks out, but it predicts 3-fold for Si4+ and reality is 4-fold because the Si-O bond is half covalent' shows you are testing your model rather than trusting it.

questions.prompt: Diamond and graphite are both pure carbon but differ hugely in hardness. What explains this?

options.text: Graphite contains hidden impurities that diamond lacks
Diamond is a rigid 3D covalent network, while graphite's strongly bonded sheets are held together only by weak van der Waals forces
Diamond has more carbon atoms per unit volume by chemical formula
Graphite is ionic while diamond is covalent

explanations.a: Both are essentially pure carbon; impurities are not what drives the hardness difference.
explanations.b: Correct - diamond's sp3 carbons form a continuous 3D covalent framework with no weak direction, while graphite's strong in-sheet covalent bonds are stacked via weak van der Waals attraction, giving it a slip direction and low hardness.
explanations.c: Both are the same element (carbon); the formula gives no information about coordination or bond type, which is what actually differs.
explanations.d: Graphite, like diamond, is bonded covalently within its sheets; the difference is the weak van der Waals bonding between sheets, not an ionic/covalent split.

questions.prompt: Si4+ has an effective ionic radius near 0.26 A and O2- near 1.40 A, giving a radius ratio of about 0.19 - below the 0.225 boundary, so hard-sphere geometry predicts 3-fold coordination. Silicon is nevertheless 4-fold in every rock-forming silicate. What does this tell you?

options.text: The radius-ratio rule assumes purely ionic, non-directional bonding, and the Si-O bond's substantial covalent character - directional sp3 orbitals - holds four oxygens around silicon regardless of hard-sphere packing
Silicon carries a +4 charge, and charge alone fixes the coordination number at 4
Tetrahedral coordination is simply the most common coordination for any cation, so no explanation is needed
The measured radii must be wrong, since a correct radius ratio would always land in the right window

explanations.a: Correct - radius ratio is a hard-sphere, purely ionic approximation. It works for largely ionic cations (Mg2+ at 0.51 gives 6-fold, Ca2+ at 0.80 gives 8-fold, both confirmed by structure solutions) but under-predicts for small, highly charged cations whose bonds are strongly covalent and directional, which is why Si4+ is 4-fold rather than the 3-fold the ratio implies.
explanations.b: Charge and coordination number are separate things. Charge feeds Pauling's electrostatic valence rule, which is about how bond strength is shared with the anion. Al3+ carries the same charge in both 4-fold and 6-fold sites, so charge cannot be what sets the count of neighbors.
explanations.c: Coordination number varies by cation - Mg2+ and Fe2+ favor 6-fold, Ca2+ favors 8-fold - so 4-fold is not a default, and silicon's 4-fold coordination is a fact that needs explaining rather than assuming.
explanations.d: The radii are fine; the model is the approximation. Effective ionic radii reproduce real interatomic distances well, and it is the hard-sphere assumption behind the ratio windows - not the measurements - that fails when bonding is directional and covalent.

questions.prompt: Match each cation to the coordination number it typically adopts with oxygen in minerals.

left.text: Silicon (Si4+) - 4-fold despite a radius ratio of 0.19

right.text: 4-fold (tetrahedral)
6-fold (octahedral)
8-fold

questions.explanation: Mg2+/Fe2+ (0.51 to 0.56) and Ca2+ (0.80) land in the 0.414-0.732 and 0.732-1.0 windows respectively, so radius ratio predicts their 6-fold and 8-fold sites correctly - as in olivine, pyroxene's M2 site, and plagioclase. Silicon is the case where the hard-sphere rule misses: its 0.19 ratio would imply 3-fold, and it is the Si-O bond's directional covalent character that fixes it at 4-fold instead.

questions.prompt: According to Pauling's rules, why do SiO4 tetrahedra in silicate minerals almost always share only corners with each other, never edges or faces?

options.text: Corner-sharing is required to keep the mineral electrically neutral
Shared edges or faces would force the positively charged silicon cations too close together, which is electrostatically destabilizing
Edge- and face-sharing tetrahedra cannot exist geometrically
Corner-sharing was simply the first arrangement discovered and other silicates copy it

explanations.a: Electrical neutrality is handled by balancing cations elsewhere in the structure (electrostatic valence rule), not specifically by the sharing mode of the tetrahedra.
explanations.b: Correct - Pauling's rule on shared polyhedral elements says edge- and especially face-sharing bring like-charged cations too close together, which is destabilizing, so corner-sharing is strongly preferred.
explanations.c: Edge- and face-sharing tetrahedra are geometrically possible and occur in some structures; they are simply energetically disfavored, not impossible.
explanations.d: The preference is explained by electrostatic energetics (Pauling's rule), not by historical precedent or convention.

lessons.label: Silicate Architecture: Polymerization from Olivine to Quartz

sections.heading: The building block and the polymerization ladder
sections.body: Every silicate mineral is built from the SiO4 tetrahedron - one silicon at the center, four oxygens at the corners - and the entire silicate class is organized by how many corners each tetrahedron shares with its neighbors, which fixes the Si:O ratio. Nesosilicates (from Greek nesos, island) share zero corners: isolated tetrahedra linked only by other cations, giving Si:O of 1:4, as in olivine (Mg,Fe)2SiO4. Sorosilicates share one corner, pairing two tetrahedra (Si2O7) as in epidote, giving Si:O of 2:7. Cyclosilicates share two corners each around a closed ring, as in beryl's six-membered rings and tourmaline's rings, giving Si:O of 1:3. Inosilicates form chains: single chains (each tetrahedron sharing two corners, Si:O of 1:3) as in pyroxene, or double chains (alternating tetrahedra sharing two or three corners, Si:O of 4:11) as in amphibole. Phyllosilicates share three corners each, building continuous sheets with Si:O of 2:5, as in mica and clay. Tectosilicates share all four corners, building a fully 3D framework with Si:O of 1:2, as in quartz and feldspar.

sections.heading: Cleavage is a direct readout of chain geometry
sections.body: Cleavage breaks along planes of weakest bonding, and in chain and sheet silicates that weakest bonding is between structural units, not within them - so cleavage angles are a direct geometric fingerprint of the polymerization type. Pauling's electrostatic valence rule explains why: the Si-O bonds inside a tetrahedron are strong, short, and highly covalent, while the bonds linking one tetrahedron's unshared oxygens to the interlayer or interchain cations (Mg2+, Fe2+, K+) that hold neighboring units together are longer, weaker, and more ionic, so the structure fails along that inter-unit path first. Single-chain pyroxenes cleave in two directions at roughly 87 and 93 degrees, reflecting the angle at which single Si-O chains pack against each other. Double-chain amphiboles cleave in two directions at roughly 56 and 124 degrees, a distinctly different angle set because the wider double chains pack differently. This 87/93 versus 56/124 contrast is the single most reliable field test for telling pyroxene from amphibole in hand sample when color and habit are ambiguous. Mica (a phyllosilicate) has one perfect cleavage direction, parallel to its sheets, because bonding within a sheet (strong Si-O-Al covalent-ionic bonds) is far stronger than bonding between sheets (weaker interlayer cations like K+). Quartz, a tectosilicate with every tetrahedron corner shared in a fully 3D framework, has no direction of weak bonding at all, so it lacks cleavage entirely and instead fractures conchoidally - smooth, shell-shaped fracture surfaces typical of breaking a fully bonded, isotropic-ish framework rather than splitting along a plane.

lessons.workedExample: A hand sample shows a dark, prismatic mineral with two cleavage directions visible under a hand lens. Measuring the angle between the two cleavage traces with a protractor gives approximately 56 degrees on one side. Comparing to the reference angles - pyroxene's near-right-angle 87/93 versus amphibole's 56/124 - the 56-degree measurement identifies this as an amphibole (likely hornblende), not a pyroxene, without needing any chemical test. This works because the double-chain geometry that defines amphibole structurally forces its cleavage planes into that specific oblique angle, a direct, testable consequence of Si:O = 4:11 chain packing rather than a coincidence of two similar-looking dark minerals.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'how do you tell pyroxene from amphibole without a lab' is testing whether a student understands that cleavage is not an arbitrary property to memorize but a direct geometric consequence of how SiO4 tetrahedra link together. The strong answer explains that single chains and double chains pack at different angles, producing the 87/93 versus 56/124 cleavage contrast, and can derive quartz's total lack of cleavage from its fully-shared tectosilicate framework rather than just quoting Mohs hardness or color. That derivation - structure explains property - is the whole point of the polymerization series.

questions.prompt: Why does quartz lack cleavage entirely and instead fracture conchoidally?

options.text: Quartz tetrahedra share all four corners in a fully 3D framework, leaving no plane of distinctly weaker bonding
Quartz has no silicon-oxygen bonds at all
Quartz is amorphous like obsidian
Quartz's tetrahedra are isolated from one another

explanations.a: Correct - as a tectosilicate, every corner of every tetrahedron is shared, so bonding strength is nearly uniform in all directions, leaving no distinct weak plane for cleavage to follow, so quartz breaks conchoidally instead.
explanations.b: Quartz is built entirely from Si-O bonds in SiO4 tetrahedra; it simply shares all four corners rather than lacking such bonds.
explanations.c: Quartz is a true crystalline mineral with long-range order, unlike amorphous obsidian; that is not why it lacks cleavage.
explanations.d: Isolated tetrahedra describes nesosilicates like olivine, the opposite of quartz's fully connected framework.

questions.prompt: A dark prismatic mineral shows two cleavage directions at approximately 56 and 124 degrees. Based on cleavage-angle diagnostics, is it more likely pyroxene or amphibole?

options.text: Pyroxene, because 56/124 matches its near-right-angle chain packing
Amphibole, because its double-chain structure produces this oblique 56/124 cleavage angle set
Neither, because both minerals have identical cleavage angles
Mica, because 56/124 is the sheet-cleavage angle

explanations.a: Pyroxene's single-chain structure produces cleavage near 87/93 degrees, close to a right angle, not 56/124.
explanations.b: Correct - amphibole's double-chain (Si:O = 4:11) geometry packs at a distinctly oblique angle, producing the characteristic 56/124-degree cleavage set used to distinguish it from pyroxene in hand sample.
explanations.c: The two minerals have measurably different cleavage angle sets (87/93 vs 56/124), which is exactly what makes this a useful field diagnostic.
explanations.d: Mica has only one perfect cleavage direction (parallel to its sheets), not two directions at an oblique angle.

questions.prompt: Match each silicate structural class to its Si:O ratio and a representative mineral.

right.text: Si:O = 1:4, olivine
Si:O = 1:3, pyroxene
Si:O = 2:5, mica
Si:O = 1:2, quartz

questions.explanation: Nesosilicates like olivine have isolated tetrahedra (1:4); single-chain inosilicates like pyroxene share two corners per tetrahedron (1:3); phyllosilicates like mica share three corners in sheets (2:5); tectosilicates like quartz share all four corners in a 3D framework (1:2).

questions.prompt: Order these silicate structures from fewest shared tetrahedral corners to most shared corners.

items.text: Nesosilicate (olivine) - zero corners shared
Inosilicate single chain (pyroxene) - two corners shared
Phyllosilicate (mica) - three corners shared
Tectosilicate (quartz) - four corners shared

questions.explanation: Polymerization increases from isolated tetrahedra (nesosilicate, zero shared corners) through single chains (two shared corners) and sheets (three shared corners) to fully connected 3D frameworks (four shared corners), which is also the order of increasing Si:O ratio denominator relative to Si.

lessons.label: Solid Solution, Exsolution, and Ordering

sections.heading: Three ways one lattice tolerates chemical change
sections.body: A mineral's formula is often a range, not a point, because a lattice can substitute one ion for another without breaking. Simple substitution swaps ions of the same charge and similar size at one site: olivine's Fo-Fa series runs continuously from forsterite (Mg2SiO4) to fayalite (Fe2SiO4) because Mg2+ and Fe2+ are close enough in radius (about 0.72 and 0.78 A) to swap freely in the octahedral M sites at any ratio. Coupled substitution swaps two ions at once across two sites to keep the overall charge balanced: plagioclase feldspar's An0-An100 series exchanges NaSi for CaAl (Na+ + Si4+ replaced by Ca2+ + Al3+), because a lone Na-to-Ca swap would leave the structure with unbalanced charge unless a paired Si-to-Al swap compensates it. Vacancy or omission substitution leaves a lattice site partly empty, with the missing charge made up elsewhere in the structure, as seen in some feldspathoid and zeolite chemistries.

sections.heading: Vegard's law links composition to measurable properties
sections.body: Lars Vegard's 1921 observation, now called Vegard's law, states that for many solid solutions, unit cell parameters vary roughly linearly with composition between the two end members. This gives mineralogists a practical tool: measure a plagioclase grain's refractive index or cell dimension by X-ray diffraction, and read off its An (anorthite) content from a calibration curve without a full chemical analysis. The linearity is an approximation, not an exact law, and real solid solutions can deviate from it, but it is reliable enough that refractive-index-versus-composition curves are still used to estimate plagioclase composition in thin section.

sections.heading: Exsolution: solid solutions that fall apart on cooling
sections.body: A single-phase solid solution stable at high temperature can become unstable as it cools, because the entropy that favored mixing at high temperature no longer outweighs the energy cost of forcing dissimilar ions to coexist in one lattice. The mixture then unmixes into two coexisting phases while still solid - exsolution. Perthite is the classic textbook case: alkali feldspar crystallizing at high temperature as a single K-Na solid solution exsolves on slow cooling into visible or microscopic intergrown lamellae of K-rich (orthoclase/microcline) and Na-rich (albite) feldspar, because the K+ and Na+ ions are too size-mismatched to share one lattice comfortably at low temperature. Pigeonite similarly exsolves fine augite lamellae in slowly cooled pyroxene. Because exsolution requires atomic diffusion, which needs time and heat, the coarseness of the resulting lamellae is itself a cooling-rate thermometer: coarse, visible lamellae mean slow cooling (deep intrusive rock), while fine or absent lamellae mean fast cooling (a quenched volcanic rock preserves the high-temperature single phase, sanidine, rather than exsolving).

sections.heading: Order-disorder: where Al and Si sit is a clock, too
sections.body: Beyond composition, the arrangement of Al and Si among otherwise-equivalent tetrahedral sites can itself vary. High-temperature, fast-cooled alkali feldspar (sanidine) has Al and Si distributed nearly randomly among its tetrahedral sites (disordered), while slowly cooled, low-temperature alkali feldspar (microcline) has Al and Si sorted into distinct, ordered sites, because slow cooling gives ions enough time to migrate into their lowest-energy configuration. Sanidine versus microcline is therefore read as a cooling-rate indicator independent of exsolution, and the two effects (composition-driven exsolution and Al/Si ordering) often occur together in the same alkali feldspar.

lessons.workedExample: Two alkali feldspar samples of nearly identical bulk composition (about Or60Ab40) are collected: one from a rapidly chilled volcanic flow, one from a slowly cooled granite pluton. The volcanic sample is a single, optically homogeneous sanidine crystal with Al/Si disordered among its tetrahedral sites. The plutonic sample shows visible perthitic lamellae under the microscope - alternating K-rich and Na-rich feldspar bands - and its K-rich host has ordered into microcline. Both started as the same high-temperature solid solution; only cooling rate differed, and that single variable produced both the exsolution texture and the ordering state, which together let a geologist read the plutonic sample's slow cooling history directly off a thin section.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'what does perthite texture tell you, beyond just the mineral's composition?' is testing whether a student understands that a mineral's structure records its history, not only its chemistry. The strong answer explains that exsolution requires time and heat for ions to diffuse apart, so lamellae coarseness is a cooling-rate proxy, and can distinguish that idea from Al/Si ordering (sanidine vs microcline), a related but separate cooling clock. A student who says 'perthite just means it has some sodium in it' has missed that the texture itself, not the bulk formula, is the informative part.

questions.prompt: Why does plagioclase substitution require a coupled exchange of NaSi for CaAl rather than a simple Na-for-Ca swap?

options.text: Because Na and Ca are identical in size so no substitution is actually needed
Because swapping Na+ for Ca2+ alone would unbalance the structure's charge, so Si4+ must simultaneously swap for Al3+ to compensate
Because plagioclase has no tetrahedral sites available for Al or Si
Because Ca2+ cannot fit anywhere in the feldspar structure

explanations.a: Na and Ca differ in both charge and size; substitution is real and is exactly why the coupled mechanism is needed.
explanations.b: Correct - replacing Na+ (1+) with Ca2+ (2+) adds positive charge, so an accompanying Si4+-to-Al3+ swap removes matching positive charge elsewhere, keeping the overall structure electrically neutral.
explanations.c: Feldspar's tectosilicate framework is exactly where Al substitutes for Si in this coupled exchange; tetrahedral sites are central to the mechanism.
explanations.d: Ca2+ is the defining large cation of the anorthite end member; it fits readily in the same large cation site Na+ occupies in albite.

questions.prompt: What does Vegard's law state, and how is it used in plagioclase mineralogy?

options.text: Unit cell parameters vary roughly linearly with composition, allowing composition to be estimated from measured refractive index or cell dimensions
All solid solutions are unstable and must eventually exsolve
Cell parameters are unrelated to chemical composition
Refractive index is constant regardless of An content

explanations.a: Correct - Vegard's law (1921) describes an approximately linear relationship between composition and unit cell parameters in many solid solutions, letting mineralogists estimate composition from a measured physical property like refractive index instead of a full chemical analysis.
explanations.b: Vegard's law is about a property-composition relationship within a single, currently stable solid solution; it says nothing about whether exsolution must eventually occur.
explanations.c: Vegard's law specifically asserts a relationship between the two, not their independence.
explanations.d: Refractive index changing measurably with An content, via Vegard's law, is exactly what makes optical estimation of plagioclase composition possible.

questions.prompt: Match each substitution mechanism to its example.

right.text: Mg2+ and Fe2+ swap freely across the entire olivine Fo-Fa series
NaSi replaced by CaAl across the plagioclase An0-An100 series
A lattice site is left partly empty, with charge balance made up elsewhere, as in some zeolites

questions.explanation: Simple substitution swaps same-charge, similar-size ions at one site (Mg/Fe in olivine); coupled substitution swaps two ions across two sites to preserve charge balance (NaSi for CaAl in plagioclase); vacancy substitution leaves a site partly unoccupied, as in some zeolite and feldspathoid structures.

questions.prompt: Why does coarse, visible perthitic lamellae texture indicate slow cooling, while a single homogeneous sanidine crystal indicates fast cooling?

options.text: Exsolution requires atomic diffusion, which needs time and sustained heat to unmix K-rich and Na-rich feldspar into visible bands
Fast cooling always produces coarser exsolution lamellae than slow cooling
Perthite and sanidine have completely different bulk chemical compositions
Lamellae coarseness is unrelated to cooling rate and instead reflects original magma pressure

explanations.a: Correct - unmixing a single high-temperature solid solution into two distinct feldspar phases requires K+ and Na+ ions to diffuse apart, a slow process; ample time at elevated temperature (slow cooling) produces coarse, visible lamellae, while quenching preserves the single disordered high-temperature phase.
explanations.b: This reverses the relationship: slow cooling, not fast cooling, gives ions time to diffuse and produce coarse lamellae.
explanations.c: Perthite's host and lamellae, and homogeneous sanidine, can share essentially the same bulk composition; the difference is texture and cooling history, not overall chemistry.
explanations.d: The described relationship is specifically to cooling rate via diffusion time, not to pressure.

lessons.label: Polymorphism as a Pressure and Temperature Gauge

sections.heading: Same formula, different lattice, different stability field
sections.body: Polymorphs are different crystal structures built from the identical chemical formula, and because each structure has a different density and internal energy, each is thermodynamically stable only over a specific range of pressure and temperature - which makes finding a polymorph in a rock a direct readout of the conditions the rock once experienced. The Al2SiO5 system is the classic teaching case: kyanite, andalusite, and sillimanite are all exactly Al2SiO5, differing only in how Al is coordinated and how the structure packs. Kyanite is the dense, high-pressure form; andalusite is stable at low pressure; sillimanite is stable at higher temperature. Michael Holdaway's 1971 experimental recalibration of this system placed the triple point - the single pressure-temperature condition where all three coexist - at approximately 500 degrees Celsius and about 0.4 GPa (roughly 4 kilobars), a substantial revision from earlier estimates, and that recalibration is itself still debated because different experimental methods (piston-cylinder versus other techniques) and different mineral standards give measurably different triple-point locations, so metamorphic petrologists still argue over exactly which calibration to trust for a given rock.

sections.heading: SiO2 and carbon systems record even more extreme conditions
sections.body: The SiO2 system runs from ordinary quartz through coesite, a denser polymorph stable above roughly 2.7 GPa, up to stishovite, stable only above about 8 to 9 GPa, pressures reached in Earth's mantle or during meteorite impact. Coesite was first synthesized in the lab by Loring Coes in 1953, then found in nature by Eugene Shoemaker and Edward Chao in 1960 at Meteor Crater, Arizona - the first mineralogical proof that a natural impact, not volcanism, created that crater, because only a shock event could momentarily generate the multi-gigapascal pressures coesite requires. The carbon system (graphite versus diamond) and the CaCO3 system (calcite versus aragonite) work the same way: diamond is the dense, high-pressure carbon polymorph, and aragonite is the denser, higher-pressure calcium carbonate polymorph favored in subduction-related blueschist metamorphism, while calcite is stable at Earth's surface.

sections.heading: Fast versus sluggish transitions - why metastable polymorphs survive
sections.body: Not all polymorphic transitions happen at the same rate. Displacive transitions involve only small bond-angle adjustments without breaking bonds, and happen essentially instantly - the alpha-to-beta quartz transition at 573 degrees Celsius (at 1 atmosphere) is a textbook displacive transition, occurring on cooling or heating with no activation barrier worth mentioning. Reconstructive transitions, by contrast, require breaking and rebuilding the entire bond network - converting coesite to quartz, or diamond to graphite, needs atoms to break old bonds and form new ones throughout the structure, which needs enough thermal energy to overcome a large activation barrier. At Earth's surface temperature, that barrier is high enough that these reconstructive transitions proceed too slowly to matter on human timescales, which is precisely why diamonds and Meteor Crater's coesite survive intact at the surface for millions of years despite technically being metastable (thermodynamically unstable at surface conditions, but kinetically frozen in).

lessons.workedExample: A metamorphic rock contains sillimanite needles growing directly on top of relict andalusite crystals, with no kyanite present anywhere in the sample. Using the Al2SiO5 phase diagram, this succession says the rock crossed from the andalusite stability field into the sillimanite field without ever entering kyanite's field - meaning the rock experienced a temperature increase at relatively low, near-surface-crustal pressure (below roughly 0.4 GPa, staying under the Holdaway triple point) rather than a pressure increase at depth. If kyanite had appeared instead of sillimanite, the same mineral formula (Al2SiO5) would instead indicate the rock was buried to much higher pressure - the polymorph identity alone, with no other data, distinguishes a low-pressure contact-metamorphic history from a high-pressure regional one.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'why does it matter which Al2SiO5 polymorph you found?' is testing whether a student understands that polymorphism converts a mineral identification into a pressure-temperature measurement. The strong answer names the specific stability relationships (kyanite = high pressure, andalusite = low pressure, sillimanite = high temperature) and can explain why some polymorphs like diamond or coesite survive at the surface at all - because reconstructive transitions are kinetically sluggish, not because they are thermodynamically stable there. A student who just says 'they're all made of the same atoms' has missed that the whole point is what each structure reveals about the rock's history.

questions.prompt: Approximately where did Holdaway's 1971 experimental work place the Al2SiO5 triple point?

options.text: About 500 C and 0.4 GPa
About 1200 C and 5 GPa
About 100 C and 0.01 GPa
About 573 C and 1 atmosphere

explanations.a: Correct - Holdaway's 1971 recalibration placed the kyanite-andalusite-sillimanite triple point at roughly 500 C and about 0.4 GPa (around 4 kilobars).
explanations.b: This is far too hot and high-pressure for the Al2SiO5 triple point; those conditions are closer to mantle territory, not typical crustal metamorphism.
explanations.c: This is far too low a pressure and temperature for any of the three Al2SiO5 polymorphs to coexist.
explanations.d: 573 C at 1 atmosphere is the alpha-beta quartz transition, an entirely different (SiO2) system, not the Al2SiO5 triple point.

questions.prompt: Why did the discovery of coesite at Meteor Crater in 1960 prove the crater was formed by impact rather than volcanism?

options.text: Coesite requires pressures above roughly 2.7 GPa, which only a shock event, not ordinary volcanic processes, can momentarily generate
Coesite only forms from meteorite material itself, not from terrestrial rock
Coesite is a lower-density form of SiO2 than quartz
Volcanic eruptions cannot produce quartz at all

explanations.a: Correct - coesite's stability field starts around 2.7 GPa, pressures ordinary volcanic processes do not reach; only the near-instantaneous shock of a hypervelocity impact generates that pressure at Earth's surface, so finding coesite is direct mineralogical proof of impact.
explanations.b: Coesite at Meteor Crater formed from shocked terrestrial sandstone, not from the meteorite's own material.
explanations.c: Coesite is denser than quartz, consistent with being the higher-pressure SiO2 polymorph, not lower-density.
explanations.d: Volcanic processes readily produce ordinary quartz; the issue is specifically that they cannot reach the multi-gigapascal pressures coesite requires.

questions.prompt: Why can diamond and coesite persist at Earth's surface for millions of years despite being thermodynamically unstable there?

options.text: Converting them to their surface-stable polymorphs (graphite, quartz) is a reconstructive transition requiring bond-breaking, which faces a large activation barrier at surface temperature
They are actually stable at surface conditions after all
Surface pressure is still high enough to keep them in their high-pressure stability field
They spontaneously convert back within days, so surviving samples are always freshly exposed

explanations.a: Correct - reconstructive transitions require breaking and rebuilding the entire bond network, which needs enough thermal energy to overcome a large activation barrier; at surface temperature that barrier is rarely crossed, so the metastable, high-pressure polymorph survives kinetically frozen in.
explanations.b: By definition graphite and quartz, not diamond and coesite, are the thermodynamically stable surface polymorphs of carbon and SiO2 respectively; diamond and coesite are metastable at the surface.
explanations.c: Surface pressure (about 1 atmosphere) is nowhere near diamond's or coesite's multi-gigapascal stability fields; they persist despite the pressure mismatch, not because of it.
explanations.d: Diamonds and Meteor Crater's coesite have persisted for geologically long timescales (diamonds for over a billion years in some cases), the opposite of rapid reconversion.

questions.prompt: Match each transition to whether it is displacive (fast, no bond-breaking) or reconstructive (slow, requires bond-breaking).

right.text: Displacive - small bond-angle adjustment, essentially instantaneous
Reconstructive - full bond network must break and rebuild
Reconstructive - full bond network must break and rebuild

questions.explanation: The alpha-beta quartz transition only shifts bond angles slightly and happens essentially instantly at 573 C, while converting coesite to quartz or diamond to graphite requires breaking and reforming the entire bond network, a slow reconstructive process with a large activation barrier that keeps the high-pressure forms metastably preserved at the surface.

lessons.label: Trace Elements: The Mineral as a Chemical Recorder

sections.heading: Goldschmidt's rules decide who gets in
sections.body: Victor Goldschmidt's substitution rules, formalized in the 1930s, predict which trace elements a growing crystal will accept into a major element's lattice site. Substitution is favored when the trace ion's radius is within about 15 percent of the host ion's radius, when the charges either match or can be locally compensated, and when the two ions have similar electronegativity so the bond character (ionic versus covalent) is compatible. When two candidate ions both fit a site reasonably well but differ in charge, Goldschmidt's rules also predict the higher-charged ion is preferentially incorporated at a given temperature (the 'capture' behavior), which is why some trace elements enrich in early-crystallizing minerals disproportionately to their abundance in the melt.

sections.heading: Compatible, incompatible, and the partition coefficient
sections.body: An element is compatible if it partitions preferentially into a crystallizing solid rather than staying in the melt, and incompatible if it does the opposite. This is quantified by the partition coefficient D, the ratio of an element's concentration in the mineral to its concentration in the coexisting melt at equilibrium. Nickel is strongly compatible in olivine, with D values well above 1 (commonly cited in the range of 5 to 30 depending on temperature and composition), because Ni2+ substitutes easily for Mg2+ in olivine's octahedral site - this is why olivine-rich cumulates are enriched in Ni relative to the parent magma. Large ions like rubidium and barium are strongly incompatible in most common rock-forming silicates (D much less than 1), because their large radii do not fit comfortably into major mineral lattice sites (Rb+ is far larger than the K+ sites it substitutes into; Ba2+ is likewise oversized for common Ca2+/K+ sites), so they stay concentrated in the residual melt and end up enriched in late-crystallizing, evolved rocks like granite and pegmatite.

sections.heading: Rare earth element patterns and the europium anomaly
sections.body: The rare earth elements (REEs), from lanthanum to lutetium, all share a 3+ charge and a smoothly decreasing ionic radius across the series, which lets minerals like zircon, apatite, and garnet incorporate them selectively based on radius fit and record a diagnostic pattern of relative enrichment or depletion across the series. Europium is the outlier: under reducing conditions it can exist as Eu2+ instead of the usual Eu3+, and Eu2+ is close in size and charge to Ca2+, so it substitutes readily into plagioclase feldspar (a Ca-bearing mineral) while the other REEs, staying 3+, do not partition into plagioclase nearly as well. This produces the europium anomaly: a rock or mineral that crystallized alongside (or without) significant plagioclase shows a distinctive dip (or spike) in Eu relative to its REE neighbors on a normalized plot, making the anomaly a diagnostic tracer of both plagioclase fractionation history and the oxygen fugacity (how reducing or oxidizing) of the system during crystallization.

sections.heading: Zoning: a growth diary
sections.body: Because trace and major element uptake depends on the melt or fluid composition at the moment a crystal layer grows, a single crystal can preserve a chemical diary in its zoning. Normal zoning (core to rim following one steady direction, like Mg-rich cores grading to Fe-rich rims in olivine or plagioclase becoming more Na-rich outward) records simple fractional crystallization. Reverse zoning (the opposite direction) signals a change like magma mixing or reheating. Oscillatory zoning (repeating fine bands back and forth) records cyclic changes in growth conditions, often tied to fluctuating pressure, temperature, or fluid input during crystal growth.

lessons.workedExample: A crystallizing basaltic magma begins forming olivine early. Because Ni2+ substitutes easily for Mg2+ in olivine (D commonly 5 to 30), the first olivine crystals strip a disproportionate share of nickel out of the melt, so each successive batch of magma left behind is progressively more nickel-poor even before much of the melt has solidified. Meanwhile Rb and Ba, both strongly incompatible in olivine, stay almost entirely in the melt and become progressively enriched in it as crystallization proceeds. A geochemist sampling both the residual melt and the olivine crystals at the same stage would see the olivine reporting a high Ni concentration and low Rb/Ba, and the coexisting melt showing the mirror-image pattern - a direct, testable consequence of each element's partition coefficient rather than a coincidence of the specific rock.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'why does one trace element end up in the crystal and another stays in the liquid?' is testing whether a student can connect ionic radius, charge, and partition coefficient into a predictive framework rather than treating trace element data as a black box. The strong answer names Goldschmidt's radius-and-charge criteria, defines D concretely (mineral concentration over melt concentration), and can explain a specific anomaly like europium's plagioclase-driven behavior rather than reciting 'REE patterns are useful' without mechanism. This is exactly the kind of chemistry-to-geology reasoning that separates a described observation from an explained one.

questions.prompt: Why is nickel strongly compatible in olivine, with a partition coefficient D well above 1?

options.text: Ni2+ is similar enough in radius and charge to Mg2+ that it readily substitutes into olivine's octahedral site
Nickel is more abundant in basaltic melt than magnesium
Olivine has no octahedral sites, so nickel is forced into the structure
D values below 1 always indicate strong compatibility

explanations.a: Correct - Ni2+'s radius and charge closely match Mg2+, which occupies olivine's octahedral M sites, so Ni2+ substitutes easily and partitions strongly into the crystallizing solid, giving D values well above 1.
explanations.b: Magnesium is far more abundant than nickel in basaltic melt; compatibility is about how selectively an element partitions into the crystal, not raw abundance.
explanations.c: Olivine's Mg/Fe sites are octahedral (6-fold coordinated); that is precisely the site Ni2+ substitutes into.
explanations.d: D values well above 1, not below 1, indicate strong compatibility (concentration higher in the mineral than in the melt).

questions.prompt: What causes the europium anomaly in REE patterns?

options.text: Eu can exist as Eu2+ under reducing conditions, allowing it to substitute for Ca2+ in plagioclase while other REEs (staying 3+) do not partition into plagioclase as well
Europium is not actually a rare earth element
All REEs partition equally into every mineral, so no anomaly is possible
Europium's ionic radius is far larger than every other REE regardless of redox state

explanations.a: Correct - under reducing conditions Eu2+ (rather than the usual REE 3+ state) closely matches Ca2+ in size and charge, letting it substitute into plagioclase far more readily than the other, still-3+ REEs, producing a distinctive enrichment or depletion in Eu relative to its neighbors.
explanations.b: Europium is a standard member of the lanthanide/REE series; its anomalous behavior comes from its unusual redox chemistry, not from exclusion from the REE group.
explanations.c: REE partitioning varies systematically with ionic radius and mineral site geometry across the series, which is exactly what produces distinct patterns rather than uniform partitioning.
explanations.d: Eu3+'s radius is comparable to its REE neighbors; it is specifically the reduced Eu2+ state, similar in size to Ca2+, that drives the anomalous plagioclase behavior.

questions.prompt: Match each zoning pattern in a growing crystal to what it records.

right.text: Simple, steady fractional crystallization in one direction (e.g., Mg-rich core to Fe-rich rim)
A change like magma mixing or reheating reversing the compositional trend
Repeating fine bands recording cyclic changes in growth conditions

questions.explanation: Normal zoning records steady fractional crystallization in one direction, reverse zoning signals an interruption like magma mixing or reheating, and oscillatory zoning records repeating cycles of changing growth conditions.

questions.prompt: According to Goldschmidt's substitution rules, which factor is NOT one of the main criteria predicting whether a trace element substitutes into a host mineral site?

options.text: Ionic radius within about 15 percent of the host ion
Charge that matches or can be locally compensated
Similar electronegativity, giving compatible bond character
The trace element's total abundance in Earth's crust

explanations.a: Radius within about 15 percent of the host ion is one of Goldschmidt's core substitution criteria.
explanations.b: Matching or locally compensated charge is one of Goldschmidt's core substitution criteria.
explanations.c: Similar electronegativity (compatible bond character) is one of Goldschmidt's core substitution criteria.
explanations.d: Correct - crustal abundance is not one of Goldschmidt's site-fit criteria; substitution is governed by radius, charge, and electronegativity match, not by how common the element is overall.

units.label: Identifying Minerals: Hand Lens, Polarizing Scope, and Beam

lessons.label: A Determinative Key from Physical Properties

sections.heading: Mohs' scale is ordinal, not a ruler
sections.body: Friedrich Mohs published his ten-mineral hardness scale in 1812, ranking talc (1) through diamond (10) purely by which mineral scratches which. It is ordinal, not linear: diamond's absolute hardness is roughly four times corundum's even though the two sit only one step apart at the very top of the ten-step scale, since diamond is disproportionately hard. In the field you rarely carry the reference minerals, so you substitute proxies: a fingernail is about 2.5, a copper penny about 3.5, a knife blade or window glass about 5.5-6, and a steel file about 6.5. A mineral that scratches glass but not a file sits in the 5.5-6.5 range, narrowing feldspar (6) from calcite (3) instantly without any kit.

sections.heading: Streak, luster, and habit as fast filters
sections.body: Streak, the color of a mineral's powder on an unglazed porcelain plate, is more diagnostic than surface color because it strips away thin-film and impurity effects. Hematite streaks red-brown even when the specimen looks black and metallic; pyrite streaks greenish-black despite its brassy, gold-mimicking surface. Luster (metallic vs. vitreous vs. pearly vs. resinous) and crystal habit (cubic pyrite vs. massive chalcopyrite, prismatic hornblende vs. blocky augite) narrow the field further before any destructive test.

sections.heading: Cleavage vs. fracture, and the angle that separates amphibole from pyroxene
sections.body: Cleavage is breakage along planes of weak atomic bonding, repeatable and flat; fracture is irregular breakage with no preferred plane (conchoidal in quartz, which has no cleavage at all). The single most-tested cleavage discrimination in an intro course is amphibole vs. pyroxene: both are chain silicates with two cleavage directions, but hornblende (amphibole) cleaves at roughly 56 and 124 degrees, while augite (pyroxene) cleaves at roughly 87 and 93 degrees, close to a right angle. Specific gravity separates look-alikes by mass: pyrite (SG about 5.0) and chalcopyrite (SG about 4.2) both look brassy-gold, but native gold runs 15-19, hefting far heavier in the hand for the same volume than either sulfide, the classic fool's-gold test.

sections.heading: The acid test: calcite fizzes, dolomite needs help
sections.body: Dilute (about 10%) hydrochloric acid reacts with calcite (CaCO3) to release visible CO2 bubbles on contact with a solid surface. Dolomite, CaMg(CO3)2, is far less reactive on an unbroken face and effervesces only when scratched to powder first, a distinction geologists use constantly to separate limestone from dolostone in the field. Magnetism is a smaller but useful filter: magnetite is strongly attracted to a hand magnet, while otherwise-similar black minerals like ilmenite or hematite are not.

lessons.workedExample: A student finds a brassy, gold-colored mineral in cubic crystals. Step 1: hardness. It scratches glass but not a steel file, giving roughly 5.5-6.5, ruling out gold (2.5-3) and chalcopyrite (softer, about 3.5-4, too soft to scratch glass). Step 2: streak and habit. It leaves a greenish-black to near-black streak, consistent with pyrite but not by itself distinguishing it from chalcopyrite (both streak greenish-black); the cubic habit with striated faces, versus chalcopyrite's more irregularly massive habit, is what confirms pyrite. Step 3: specific gravity by hefting, roughly 5, consistent with pyrite (SG about 5.0) rather than gold (SG 15-19), confirming fool's gold rather than a bonanza.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who hands a student an unlabeled mineral is testing whether they own a repeatable decision procedure or just a memorized label. The strong answer names an ordered sequence, streak before guessing, hardness against a proxy before a guess, cleavage angle when two silicates look alike, and states the actual numbers (56/124 vs. 87/93 degrees, SG 5 vs. 15-19) rather than saying 'it looked different.' That sequence is exactly what separates a determinative key from pattern-matching.

questions.prompt: A mineral scratches a copper penny but does not scratch window glass. What is its approximate Mohs hardness range?

explanations.a: A hardness under 2.5 would not scratch a copper penny (about 3.5) at all.
explanations.b: Correct — scratching the penny (about 3.5) sets a floor, and failing to scratch glass (about 5.5-6) sets a ceiling, bracketing the mineral between roughly 3.5 and 5.5.
explanations.c: That range would scratch both glass and a steel file, contradicting the observation that it does not scratch glass.
explanations.d: That range describes corundum and diamond, far harder than what the penny/glass test shows here.

questions.prompt: Match each mineral or test to its diagnostic property.

left.text: Gold vs. pyrite, same color and habit

right.text: Red-brown streak despite black surface color
Calcite fizzes on a solid face; dolomite only fizzes when powdered
Roughly 56 and 124 degrees between cleavage planes
Specific gravity of 15-19 versus about 5.0

questions.explanation: Streak reveals hematite's true color independent of surface luster; the HCl reactivity gap separates calcite from dolomite; amphibole's 56/124-degree cleavage is diagnostic against pyroxene's near-right-angle cleavage; and specific gravity separates gold from its much lighter sulfide look-alike.

questions.prompt: Order this field workflow for identifying an unknown brassy mineral, from fastest/least destructive to most destructive.

items.text: Observe luster and crystal habit
Streak the mineral on an unglazed plate
Test hardness with fingernail, penny, and glass
Apply dilute HCl to check for effervescence

questions.explanation: Luster and habit require no contact with the specimen; streak abrades only a small powder sample; hardness testing scratches the mineral or the tester; acid testing is the most chemically invasive and is reserved for carbonates once other tests have narrowed the candidates.

lessons.label: Thin Sections and the Polarizing Microscope

sections.heading: Why 30 micrometers, and what gets destroyed to get there
sections.body: A thin section is a rock chip cut, glued to a glass slide, and ground down to a standard thickness of 30 micrometers, then covered with a thin glass slip. That thickness is not arbitrary: at 30 micrometers, quartz consistently shows a specific first-order grey-white interference color under crossed polars, which technicians use as the calibration check while grinding, stopping the moment quartz grains in the slide hit that color. Making a thin section destroys the specimen's three-dimensional structure and any texture at a scale coarser than the section, so a single slide can never recover original grain shape in the missing dimension, or original size/volume for anything larger than the section footprint. For loose grains (heavy-mineral separates, sand) or opaque ore minerals that need surface reflectance, a grain mount or a polished mount (no cover glass, polished flat for reflected-light study) is the better prep, since thin-sectioning an opaque ore mineral wastes the sample without revealing anything transmitted light can measure.

sections.heading: The light path: polarizer, stage, analyzer, Bertrand lens
sections.body: A polarizing (petrographic) microscope forces light through a lower polarizer before it reaches the sample, then, for crossed-polars work, through a second polarizer (the analyzer) rotated 90 degrees to the first above the sample. With only the lower polarizer engaged (plane-polarized light, or PPL), you observe color, pleochroism, and relief; inserting the analyzer (crossed polars, or XPL) reveals birefringence and extinction. A retractable Bertrand lens, engaged only for interference-figure work, adds a lens into the optical path that lets you view the back focal plane rather than the image plane, converting the scope from ordinary to conoscopic viewing.

sections.heading: Relief and the Becke line: refractive index without a refractometer
sections.body: Relief is how strongly a grain stands out from its mounting medium (index around 1.54) or from adjacent grains, driven by the refractive-index mismatch. High relief (quartz next to a very different mineral) reads as a thick, dark rim; low relief nearly vanishes. The Becke line test pins down which side has the higher index: as you rack the stage down (increasing the working distance), a bright line at the grain boundary moves into the medium of higher refractive index. Quartz (index about 1.55) against Canada-balsam-like mounting medium shows subtle relief; olivine (index roughly 1.65-1.69) shows strong relief against the same medium, both readable from the Becke line's direction of travel.

sections.heading: Color and pleochroism in plane-polarized light
sections.body: In PPL, some minerals are colorless (quartz, feldspar, calcite) while others show intrinsic color from transition-metal ions in their structure, and a subset of those are pleochroic, changing color or intensity as the microscope stage is rotated because absorption depends on the crystal's orientation relative to the vibrating light. Biotite is strongly pleochroic, cycling from pale yellow-brown to deep red-brown; hornblende cycles through green-brown shades; tourmaline is famously pleochroic along its long axis, appearing nearly opaque dark in one orientation and pale in the perpendicular one. Pleochroism is diagnostic precisely because isotropic or colorless minerals never show it, immediately separating biotite from muscovite (colorless, non-pleochroic) at a glance.

lessons.workedExample: A petrologist receives a granite sample and needs to distinguish quartz from untwinned orthoclase feldspar in the same thin section, both appearing colorless in PPL. Under PPL alone, quartz shows very low relief and no cleavage; adjacent orthoclase shows faint relief and two cleavage traces at roughly 90 degrees when a grain happens to be cut favorably. The Becke line test confirms it: racking the stage down moves the bright line toward the quartz grain, meaning quartz (index about 1.55) is higher-index than the adjacent orthoclase (index about 1.52), a small but measurable and repeatable difference that a refractometer would confirm on bulk material.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes thin-section method because it is the moment a petrology project either becomes real optical mineralogy or stays a photo essay. Asking why the section is ground to exactly 30 micrometers checks whether the student understands that the whole downstream color-chart system (birefringence charts, interference colors) is calibrated to that specific thickness and breaks if the section is thicker or thinner. Asking what a thin section cannot tell you (3-D shape, opaque-mineral reflectance) checks whether the student picked the right prep for the question instead of defaulting to the only technique they learned.
