The special case k = 1 is plane strain, where Y is unchanged (intermediate axis equals original length) while X lengthens and Z shortens by matching amounts — the geometry assumed in many 2D structural cross-sections. Because raw a and b values compress badly at high strain, Ramsay (1967) proposed a logarithmic version of the same plot (ln a versus ln b), which spreads out high-strain data without changing the k = 1 boundary's meaning; An alternative approach, adapted from Nadai's plasticity theory and applied to natural strain data by Ramsay (1967), plots octahedral shear strain against Lode's ratio to characterize strain shape rather than using logged Flinn axes.

sections.heading: Coaxial versus non-coaxial, and measuring real rocks
sections.body: Two deformation paths can produce the same finite strain ellipsoid by very different histories. Pure shear is coaxial: the principal strain axes stay fixed in orientation throughout deformation (a rock squashed symmetrically). Simple shear is non-coaxial: material lines rotate progressively relative to the principal strain axes even as they stretch, the geometry of slip along a shear zone. Distinguishing the two in the field requires more than the final ellipse; it needs evidence of rotation, such as asymmetric porphyroclasts. To recover strain from real deformed rocks, structural geologists use the Rf/phi method (Ramsay, 1967; Dunnet, 1969), plotting the final axial ratio Rf and long-axis orientation phi of many originally-elliptical markers (ooids, reduction spots) against theoretical curves for different strain ratios, and the Fry (1979) center-to-center method, which plots the relative positions of grain centers across a thin section and reads the strain ellipse off the empty region (exclusion zone) that emerges around each point.

lessons.workedExample: A deformed oolite bed has strain axes X = 1.8, Y = 1.0, Z = 0.55 (relative to the original unit sphere). Flinn's a = X/Y = 1.8, b = Y/Z = 1.0/0.55 = 1.82. Then k = (a-1)/(b-1) = (0.8)/(0.82) = 0.98, essentially plane strain (k near 1) — X has stretched by 80% while Z has shortened by 45%, and Y is almost unchanged, consistent with a 2D cross-section model of the deformation being adequate for this outcrop, rather than requiring a fully 3D constrictional or flattening analysis.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking a student to justify a claimed strain ellipse is testing whether they measured real markers (Rf/phi or Fry center-to-center) rather than eyeballing an ellipse, and whether they can place their result on a Flinn diagram and say what k actually means. A student who reports k without being able to say whether their fabric is constrictional, flattening, or plane strain — or who cannot distinguish coaxial pure shear from non-coaxial simple shear when asked how the strain was accumulated — has measured a shape without understanding the deformation history behind it.

questions.prompt: A rock's Flinn diagram position gives k = 2.3. What kind of strain ellipsoid does this describe?

options.text: Oblate (flattening), pancake-shaped
Prolate (constrictional), cigar-shaped
Plane strain, with Y unchanged
A perfect sphere, undeformed

explanations.a: Oblate/flattening ellipsoids correspond to k < 1, not k = 2.3.
explanations.b: Correct — k > 1 defines the constrictional (prolate) field on the Flinn diagram, where the ellipsoid is elongated strongly along X relative to Y and Z.
explanations.c: Plane strain is the special boundary case k = 1, not a value as large as 2.3.
explanations.d: An undeformed sphere has X = Y = Z = 1, which is not a meaningful point on the Flinn diagram at all since it represents zero strain, not a k value of 2.3.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between pure shear and simple shear as strain paths?

options.text: Pure shear produces no finite strain ellipsoid at all
Pure shear is coaxial (principal strain axes stay fixed in orientation); simple shear is non-coaxial (material rotates relative to the strain axes)
Simple shear only occurs at k = 1
Pure shear always produces a larger k value than simple shear
There is no meaningful difference; both terms describe the same process

explanations.a: Pure shear does produce a finite strain ellipsoid, just one whose axes remain fixed in orientation throughout the deformation (coaxial).
explanations.b: Correct — coaxiality (or its absence) is exactly the distinguishing feature: pure shear keeps principal strain axes fixed, simple shear rotates material relative to them.
explanations.c: Simple shear is not restricted to plane strain (k = 1); it can occur alongside a range of finite strain geometries.
explanations.d: Neither shear path is systematically tied to a higher or lower k value; k describes ellipsoid shape, which depends on strain magnitude and boundary conditions, not solely on coaxiality.
explanations.e: The two are mechanically distinct deformation paths that can produce the same finite ellipsoid; conflating them ignores the coaxial/non-coaxial distinction entirely.

questions.prompt: Match each strain-measurement method to what it uses.

right.text: Axial ratio and orientation of deformed elliptical markers compared to theoretical curves
Relative positions of grain centers, reading strain from the resulting exclusion zone
Plots X/Y against Y/Z to classify ellipsoid shape via k

questions.explanation: Rf/phi (Ramsay, 1967; Dunnet, 1969) uses deformed marker shape and orientation; the Fry method uses grain-center spacing to reveal an exclusion zone shaped like the strain ellipse; the Flinn diagram classifies the resulting ellipsoid's shape using the k parameter.

lessons.label: Rheology and the Brittle-Ductile Transition

sections.heading: Three idealized behaviors
sections.body: Rheology describes how a material responds to stress over time. Elastic behavior is instantaneous and fully recoverable: strain is proportional to stress and vanishes when stress is removed (Hooke's law), the regime of seismic wave propagation and short-term crustal loading. Plastic behavior has a yield threshold: below it the material does not deform permanently, above it strain accumulates without needing more stress, and the deformation does not reverse when stress is removed. Viscous behavior is rate-dependent: strain rate, not strain, is proportional to stress, so a viscous material keeps deforming as long as stress is applied, however small, over long enough time — the regime relevant to slow ductile flow of hot rock deep in the crust and mantle.

sections.heading: Creep laws and their temperature sensitivity
sections.body: Hot crystalline rock flows by thermally-activated creep mechanisms whose strain rate follows an Arrhenius-type law, strain rate = A * sigma^n * exp(-Q/RT), where Q is an activation energy, R the gas constant, and T absolute temperature. Power-law dislocation creep, with stress exponent n around 3 to 5 for both quartz and olivine, dominates at higher differential stress and is strongly non-linear — small increases in stress produce disproportionately larger strain rate increases. Diffusion creep is linear (n = 1) and depends strongly on grain size (strain rate scaling as roughly 1/d^2 to 1/d^3), dominating at lower stress and fine grain size. Both mechanisms are exponentially sensitive to temperature through the exp(-Q/RT) term, which is why rock strength collapses over just tens of degrees near the brittle-ductile transition rather than declining gradually with depth.

sections.heading: The strength envelope and its two rival shapes
sections.body: Overlaying Byerlee frictional strength (increasing linearly with depth, independent of rock type or temperature) with a ductile flow law (decreasing steeply with depth as temperature rises) produces a crustal strength envelope: strength rises with depth in the brittle regime, peaks, then collapses in the ductile regime as the flow law takes over. For quartz-rich continental crust the intersection occurs near 300-450 degrees Celsius, corresponding to roughly 10-15 km depth — closely matching the observed base of the seismogenic zone, since rock below this transition flows aseismically rather than storing elastic strain to failure. Two rival envelope shapes have long been debated: the "jelly sandwich" model (Brace and Kohlstedt, 1980; Chen and Molnar, 1983) stacks a strong brittle upper crust and a strong upper mantle (olivine) around a weak ductile lower crust (quartz/feldspar), while the "creme brulee" model (argued notably by Jackson, 2002) holds that most lithospheric strength sits in a thin, strong upper crust, with the mantle far weaker than the jelly-sandwich model assumes, based on the observation that earthquakes rarely nucleate below the crust-mantle boundary.

lessons.workedExample: A geotherm of 25 degrees Celsius per kilometer predicts 350 degrees Celsius at 14 km depth. If quartz dislocation creep becomes rate-limiting somewhere between 300 and 450 degrees Celsius, this places the brittle-ductile transition for quartz-dominated crust near 12-18 km at this geotherm — consistent with the observed shutoff of crustal earthquakes below about 10-15 km in many continental settings. A hotter geotherm (35 degrees Celsius per kilometer) would reach 350 degrees Celsius at only 10 km, predicting a shallower seismogenic base — which is exactly why active volcanic or rifting regions with elevated heat flow show shallower maximum earthquake depths than old, cold cratonic crust.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing rheology wants to see the mechanism, not the label: can a student explain why strength collapses over a narrow temperature window (the exp(-Q/RT) term) rather than saying "rock gets weaker when hot"? Naming the specific stress exponents (n around 3-5 for dislocation creep versus n = 1 for diffusion creep), and being able to describe the jelly-sandwich versus creme-brulee debate as a live, evidence-contested question rather than settled fact, distinguishes a student who has read primary structural geology from one repeating a textbook diagram.

questions.prompt: Why does the crustal strength envelope predict a sharp brittle-ductile transition rather than a gradual strength decline with depth?

options.text: Because Byerlee friction stops applying below 10 km
Because ductile flow strength is exponentially sensitive to temperature through the exp(-Q/RT) term, so strength collapses over a narrow depth/temperature window
Because rock density decreases sharply at the transition
Because pore pressure always reaches lithostatic values exactly at the transition depth

explanations.a: Byerlee's law is a frictional law that in principle extends to any depth; it is the ductile flow law overtaking it, not Byerlee's law switching off, that creates the transition.
explanations.b: Correct — the Arrhenius exp(-Q/RT) term makes strain rate (and thus flow strength) extremely sensitive to small temperature increases, so ductile strength drops steeply over a narrow window rather than gradually.
explanations.c: Density changes at the brittle-ductile transition are minor and not the mechanism driving the sharp strength drop; temperature-dependent creep is.
explanations.d: Pore pressure reaching lithostatic values is a separate phenomenon (relevant to overthrust faulting) and is not a general requirement for the brittle-ductile transition.

questions.prompt: How does dislocation creep differ from diffusion creep in its dependence on stress?

options.text: Dislocation creep is linear (n = 1); diffusion creep has n around 3-5
Dislocation creep follows a power law with n around 3-5; diffusion creep is linear (n = 1) and grain-size dependent
Both mechanisms have identical stress dependence but differ only in activation energy
Diffusion creep dominates only at very high stress

explanations.a: This reverses the actual relationship — dislocation creep is the power-law (n around 3-5) mechanism, not diffusion creep.
explanations.b: Correct — dislocation creep is strongly non-linear in stress (n ~ 3-5), while diffusion creep is linear (n = 1) and additionally depends on grain size, unlike dislocation creep.
explanations.c: The two mechanisms differ in both their stress exponent and their dependence on grain size, not just activation energy.
explanations.d: Diffusion creep dominates at lower stress and fine grain size, the opposite of "very high stress."

questions.prompt: Match each lithospheric strength model to its claim about where strength resides.

left.text: "Jelly sandwich" model (Brace and Kohlstedt, 1980; Chen and Molnar, 1983)

right.text: Strong brittle upper crust and strong olivine mantle sandwich a weak ductile lower crust
Most strength sits in a thin, strong upper crust; the mantle is weaker than the jelly-sandwich model assumes

questions.explanation: The jelly-sandwich model layers strong crust and strong mantle around a weak lower crust; the creme-brulee model, motivated by the rarity of earthquakes below the crust-mantle boundary, argues strength is concentrated in a thin upper-crustal shell rather than extending into a strong mantle.

lessons.label: Deformation Mechanisms and Microstructures

sections.heading: From cracking to dissolving to gliding
sections.body: At shallow depth and low temperature, rock deforms by cataclasis: grains fracture and slide frictionally past one another, grinding down into fault gouge and breccia (cataclasite) without any change in crystal structure — the dominant mechanism above the brittle-ductile transition. Where fluid is present even at fairly low temperature, pressure solution (dissolution-precipitation creep) can operate: stress concentrated at grain contacts drives dissolution there, the dissolved material diffuses through a thin fluid film, and it reprecipitates in adjacent low-stress sites, producing the stylolites common in limestones and quartz-rich sandstones. At higher temperature, crystal-plastic mechanisms take over: dislocation glide, where line defects move along specific crystallographic slip planes, and dislocation climb, where a dislocation can bypass an obstacle by diffusing atoms in or out of its own line — climb requires enough thermal energy for that diffusion, so combined glide-plus-climb (dislocation creep) only becomes efficient at higher temperature than glide alone.

sections.heading: Dynamic recrystallization: three mechanisms, three temperature windows
sections.body: As crystal-plastic strain accumulates, grains recrystallize dynamically to relieve stored dislocation strain energy, and the dominant recrystallization mechanism shifts with temperature. At the lowest temperatures, bulging recrystallization (BLG) nucleates new, strain-free grains where an existing grain boundary bulges into a neighboring, more strained grain. At intermediate temperature, subgrain rotation (SGR) progressively increases the misorientation of subgrains (low-angle domains within a crystal) until they rotate into fully independent new grains. At the highest temperatures, grain-boundary migration (GBM) lets boundaries sweep rapidly through strained crystal, consuming dislocations and producing larger, interlocking, lobate grains. For quartz, Stipp and coauthors' study of the Tonale fault zone (2002) calibrated these transitions at roughly 280-400 degrees Celsius for BLG, 400-500 degrees Celsius for SGR, and above about 500 degrees Celsius for GBM, giving field geologists a rough thermometer from microstructure alone.

sections.heading: Reading the record and backing out stress
sections.body: In thin section, undulose extinction — a crystal that darkens unevenly rather than all at once under crossed polars as the stage rotates — reveals heterogeneous dislocation density bending the lattice, an early sign of crystal-plastic strain. Subgrains show up as domains separated by low-angle boundaries with only slight misorientation, a precursor to full recrystallization. Mylonitic fabric — a strong foliation and lineation with markedly reduced grain size relative to the host rock, produced by dynamic recrystallization in ductile shear zones — is the field-scale signature of the same processes. Because recrystallized grain size scales inversely with differential stress (finer grains recording higher stress), empirical grain-size piezometers (calibrated experimentally, notably by Twiss, 1977, and refined for quartz by Stipp and Tullis, 2003) let a geologist measure a mylonite's average recrystallized grain size and back-calculate the differential stress during deformation. Ashby-style deformation-mechanism maps (Frost and Ashby, ~1982), plotting stress against homologous temperature with fields labeled by dominant mechanism, provide the complementary check: knowing temperature and grain size lets you read off which mechanism should dominate and cross-validate the piezometer's stress estimate.

lessons.workedExample: A mylonite sample shows quartz ribbons with lobate, interlocking grain boundaries and little internal substructure, alongside abundant undulose extinction in relict porphyroclasts. The interlocking lobate boundaries indicate grain-boundary migration, placing deformation temperature above roughly 500 degrees Celsius by the Stipp et al. (2002) calibration. Measuring average recrystallized grain size at 45 micrometers and applying the Stipp and Tullis (2003) quartz piezometer yields a differential stress estimate on the order of tens of MPa — a plausible value for deep ductile shear zone deformation, and one a deformation-mechanism map would confirm sits well within the GBM field at that temperature and grain size.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge examining a thin section or a claimed shear-zone temperature wants to see the logic chain: which microstructure (bulging grains, subgrain rotation domains, or lobate GBM boundaries) was actually observed, what temperature window that implies, and whether a grain-size piezometer was used to get an actual stress number rather than a qualitative "it was deformed a lot." A student who names the Stipp et al. (2002) temperature calibrations or a specific piezometer relationship shows they can extract quantitative deformation conditions from a rock, not just describe that deformation occurred.

questions.prompt: Order these dynamic recrystallization mechanisms in quartz from lowest to highest characteristic temperature, per Stipp et al. (2002).

items.text: Bulging recrystallization (BLG)
Subgrain rotation (SGR)
Grain-boundary migration (GBM)

questions.explanation: Stipp et al. (2002) calibrated BLG at roughly 280-400 degrees Celsius, SGR at roughly 400-500 degrees Celsius, and GBM above about 500 degrees Celsius, so temperature increases in the order BLG, SGR, GBM.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes pressure solution (dissolution-precipitation creep) from dislocation creep as a deformation mechanism?

options.text: Pressure solution requires fluid and transports material by dissolution and diffusion through a fluid film, while dislocation creep moves crystal defects through the solid lattice without dissolving material
Pressure solution only occurs above 500 degrees Celsius
Dislocation creep requires the presence of a fluid film at grain boundaries
Both mechanisms are identical, differing only in name

explanations.a: Correct — pressure solution dissolves material at high-stress grain contacts and reprecipitates it elsewhere via a fluid film, a fundamentally different, fluid-mediated mass-transfer process from the lattice-defect motion of dislocation creep.
explanations.b: Pressure solution characteristically operates at relatively low temperature in the presence of fluid, not above 500 degrees Celsius, which is instead in the range of grain-boundary migration.
explanations.c: Dislocation creep operates within the solid crystal lattice via glide and climb of dislocations; it does not require a fluid film, unlike pressure solution.
explanations.d: The two are mechanistically distinct: one is fluid-mediated mass transfer, the other is solid-state defect motion; they are not interchangeable names for the same process.

questions.prompt: A geologist measures fine recrystallized quartz grain size in a mylonite and applies a grain-size piezometer. What is being estimated, and on what principle?

options.text: Deformation temperature, on the principle that grain size increases with temperature
Differential stress, on the principle that finer recrystallized grain size corresponds to higher differential stress
Strain rate, on the principle that grain size is unrelated to stress
The original, pre-deformation grain size of the rock

explanations.a: Grain-size piezometers estimate differential stress, not temperature directly, and the relevant relationship is with stress, not temperature.
explanations.b: Correct — piezometers such as Stipp and Tullis (2003) for quartz are calibrated so that finer recrystallized grain size indicates higher differential stress during deformation.
explanations.c: Grain size is deliberately used because it does relate to stress; the piezometer method depends on that relationship, not its absence.
explanations.d: Piezometers use the recrystallized (new, post-deformation) grain size to infer deformation conditions, not the rock's original pre-deformation grain size.

units.label: Faults, Folds, Joints, and Shear Fabrics

lessons.label: Fault Anatomy, Classification, and Displacement Scaling

sections.heading: Naming a fault: hanging wall, footwall, and slip sense
sections.body: Every non-vertical fault has a hanging wall (the block above the fault surface) and a footwall (below it) — miners' terms, since a hanging-wall block hangs over your head in a tunnel. Dip-slip faults move blocks up or down the dip: normal faults drop the hanging wall relative to the footwall (extension), reverse and thrust faults raise it (shortening, with 'thrust' conventionally reserved for dips under about 30 degrees). Strike-slip faults move blocks horizontally, parallel to the fault trace, classed as right-lateral (dextral) or left-lateral (sinistral) by which way the far block appears to shift when you stand on either side and look across. Oblique-slip faults combine both components. Crucially, what a map shows after erosion — separation, the apparent offset of a marker unit measured in any convenient direction — is not the same as slip, the true vector of relative motion measured on the fault surface itself. Separation can even show the wrong sense of motion if the marker layer dips steeply. The only rigorous way to recover slip is to find piercing points, or read slickenlines and slickenfibers (grooves and fibrous mineral growth, e.g. quartz or calcite, that lineate the fault surface parallel to the transport direction) plus steps or fiber steps that indicate which way the missing block went.

sections.heading: Fault-zone architecture and fault rocks
sections.body: Faults are not knife-edges; Chester and Logan's 1986 study of the Punchbowl Fault and Caine, Evans, and Forster's 1996 synthesis established a two-part architecture: a narrow fault core (millimeters to meters) that hosts most of the displacement and slip-parallel gouge or breccia, surrounded by a damage zone (meters to hundreds of meters) of subsidiary fractures that accommodates strain around the core and controls off-fault permeability. Sibson's 1977 classification sorts fault rocks by cohesion and fabric: incohesive fault breccia and gouge (gouge is more than about 70 percent matrix, i.e. less than 30 percent visible fragments; breccia is the complement) form at shallow, brittle depths, while cohesive cataclasite forms by brittle grain-size reduction and mylonite forms by crystal-plastic deformation deeper in the crust, grading protomylonite to mylonite to ultramylonite as the matrix fraction increases.

sections.heading: Displacement-length scaling and segment linkage
sections.body: Maximum displacement (D) scales with fault length (L) across many orders of magnitude, from centimeter joints to the San Andreas; compilations by Cowie and Scholz (1992) and later Kim and Sanderson (2005) find D/L ratios clustering roughly between 10^-3 and 10^-2, though the exact exponent and whether one power law fits all scales remains debated. Real faults rarely grow as one clean surface — they propagate as segments that link via relay ramps, zones where displacement is transferred between overlapping, underlapping segments through a tilted ramp of intact rock before it eventually breaches into a through-going fault.

lessons.workedExample: A road cut exposes a fault offsetting a coal seam by 4 m of vertical separation, and the fault dips 60 degrees. A student first assumes 4 m of dip-slip. But slickenlines on the fault surface plunge only 20 degrees from horizontal, revealing strong oblique (mostly strike-slip) motion — the 4 m vertical separation is a geometric artifact of cutting an obliquely-slipped, dipping surface with a vertical outcrop face, not the true slip. Using the slickenline plunge and the true offset of a linear marker (a dike edge) crossing the fault, the actual net slip works out to about 4 / sin(20 degrees), roughly 12 m, almost all strike-parallel.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe separation-versus-slip because it is the single most common structural-geology error in student projects: reporting a map or outcrop offset as 'the displacement' without checking the actual slip vector. A student who instead points to slickenlines, states their plunge, and explains why apparent offset can even show a false sense of motion demonstrates they measured a real kinematic indicator rather than eyeballing a cross-section. It also opens into D/L scaling, letting a judge test whether the student can connect a hand-sample observation to a crustal-scale, quantitatively documented relationship.

questions.prompt: A map shows a stream offset across a fault, but the fault plane itself is not exposed. Why can this mapped offset be an unreliable measure of true fault slip?

options.text: Because streams never cross faults in nature
Because the offset is separation, not slip, and can misrepresent the true displacement vector, especially if the marker feature dips
Because maps cannot show any horizontal distances accurately
Because faults erase all markers instantly

explanations.a: Streams commonly cross and are offset by faults; that is a primary tool for measuring strike-slip motion.
explanations.b: Correct — separation is the apparent offset of any marker in a chosen direction, while slip is the true vector of relative motion on the fault surface; they coincide only in special geometric cases, so separation alone can even suggest the wrong sense of slip.
explanations.c: Maps can show horizontal distance accurately; the issue is geometric, not a mapping-accuracy problem.
explanations.d: Faults do not erase markers; offset markers are exactly what lets geologists measure displacement.

questions.prompt: Match each fault-rock or fault-zone term to its defining description.

right.text: Incohesive fault rock with more than 70 percent fine matrix, formed at shallow brittle depths
Cohesive, foliated fault rock formed by crystal-plastic deformation at depth
Narrow zone hosting most of the fault's displacement
Surrounding zone of subsidiary fractures that controls off-fault permeability

questions.explanation: Sibson's 1977 fault-rock classification separates incohesive gouge/breccia (shallow, brittle) from cohesive cataclasite/mylonite (crystal-plastic, deeper); Chester and Logan (1986) and Caine et al. (1996) established the core/damage-zone architecture describing where displacement concentrates versus where subsidiary fracturing spreads out.

questions.prompt: Compilations of fault displacement (D) versus fault length (L) across scales from centimeters to hundreds of kilometers find D/L ratios that typically cluster around what range?

options.text: 1 to 10
Exactly 0.5, a fixed constant for all faults

explanations.a: Correct — studies such as Cowie and Scholz (1992) and Kim and Sanderson (2005) find D/L ratios roughly in the 10^-3 to 10^-2 range across many orders of magnitude of fault size, though scatter and debate over a single universal exponent remain.
explanations.b: A D/L ratio near or above 1 would mean displacement exceeding fault length, which is not observed for tectonic faults.
explanations.c: This range is far too small; it would imply faults hundreds of kilometers long with only millimeters of slip, inconsistent with observed scaling.
explanations.d: D/L is not a fixed constant; it is an empirical range with real scatter, not a single fixed value.

lessons.label: Fold Geometry, Nomenclature, and Classification

sections.heading: The parts of a fold and why age is not geometry
sections.body: A fold's hinge line is the line of maximum curvature on a folded surface; the axial surface is the surface that connects the hinge lines of successive folded layers (it need not be planar, and it need not be vertical or symmetric); the limbs are the flanks on either side. The interlimb angle between limbs sorts folds by tightness: gentle (180-120 degrees), open (120-70), close (70-30), tight (30-10), and isoclinal (under 10, limbs essentially parallel). A cylindrical fold can be generated by moving a straight line (the fold axis) parallel to itself through space, so a single plunge and trend describe the whole structure; non-cylindrical folds (domes, basins, sheath folds) cannot be reduced to one axis and need a fold-axis-per-segment or stereonet best-fit treatment. A critical distinction students often blur: antiform and synform describe pure geometry (an antiform's limbs dip away from the hinge, a synform's dip toward it) with no assumption about which layers are older, whereas anticline and syncline additionally require knowing the younging direction — an anticline has older rocks in its core. An overturned syncline can look exactly like an antiform in cross-section, so without independent way-up evidence (graded bedding, cross-bedding) 'anticline' is an unjustified claim.

sections.heading: Ramsay's dip-isogon classification
sections.body: John Ramsay's 1967 classification sorts folds by dip isogons — lines connecting points of equal dip on successive folded surfaces — into three classes. Class 1 isogons converge toward the fold's core; class 1B, parallel folds, have isogons exactly perpendicular to the layer with constant orthogonal (bed-normal) thickness around the fold, the geometry produced by simple flexural slip/flexure of a competent layer. Class 1A (strongly convergent, thickened hinges relative to parallel geometry) and 1C (weakly convergent, transitional toward class 2) bracket 1B. Class 2, similar folds, have isogons parallel to the axial surface; thickness measured parallel to the axial plane stays constant while orthogonal thickness thins on the limbs and thickens in the hinge, a geometry associated with passive shear parallel to the axial surface. Class 3 has divergent isogons: hinges thinned, limbs thickened, the geometry of buckling in a weak layer or of superposed flattening on a class 1 fold.

sections.heading: Diagnosing mechanism from a thickness plot
sections.body: Ramsay formalized this with dimensionless thickness ratios t' (orthogonal thickness normalized to hinge thickness) and T' (axial-plane-parallel thickness normalized the same way) plotted against dip angle: a parallel (class 1B) fold traces a t' curve that stays flat near 1.0, while a similar (class 2) fold traces a T' curve flat near 1.0 but a t' curve that falls steeply with dip. Plotting real bed-thickness measurements around a fold and comparing the curve shape to these reference trends is a direct, quantitative way to diagnose whether a fold formed by flexure or by shear, without needing to see the mechanism act.

lessons.workedExample: A hand sample shows a folded sandstone bed with interlimb angle 45 degrees (close fold). Measuring orthogonal thickness at 10-degree dip intervals from hinge to limb gives nearly constant values (about 2.1-2.3 cm throughout), while thickness measured parallel to the axial surface increases steadily from 2.1 cm at the hinge to 3.2 cm on the steep limb. Constant orthogonal thickness is the fingerprint of class 1B, a parallel fold, meaning the layer folded largely by flexural slip/flexure rather than ductile shear — consistent with a competent sandstone bounded by weaker shale.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe fold classification because 'it's an anticline' is a claim about age that most students cannot actually justify from geometry alone — pressing for way-up evidence separates students who understand the antiform/anticline distinction from those reciting a label. Asking a student to measure and plot t' or T' around a fold and name the resulting class tests whether they can turn a qualitative sketch into a quantitative, falsifiable diagnosis of folding mechanism, which is exactly the kind of measurable claim a science-fair project needs.

questions.prompt: A cross-section shows a fold whose limbs dip away from the hinge on both sides, but no way-up indicators (like graded bedding) have been checked. What is the most defensible name for this structure?

options.text: Anticline, because the limbs dip away from the hinge
Antiform, since only the geometry — not the relative age of the core rocks — has been established
Syncline, because all folds without way-up data default to synclines
Monocline, because one limb dip was not measured

explanations.a: Anticline requires knowing the core contains the older rocks; that has not been established here, so calling it an anticline is an unjustified age claim.
explanations.b: Correct — antiform/synform are purely geometric terms (limbs dipping away from vs toward the hinge); anticline/syncline additionally require an established younging direction, which is missing here.
explanations.c: There is no default to syncline; without way-up data the only justified description is the geometric term, antiform.
explanations.d: A monocline is a step-like structure with two limbs of similar dip connected by a steeper limb; this is a different geometry issue unrelated to missing one dip measurement.

questions.prompt: Order these interlimb-angle fold categories from loosest (largest interlimb angle) to tightest (smallest interlimb angle).

items.text: Gentle (180-120 degrees)
Open (120-70 degrees)
Close (70-30 degrees)
Tight (30-10 degrees)
Isoclinal (under 10 degrees)

questions.explanation: Interlimb-angle classes run from gentle (broad, shallow folds near 180-120 degrees) through open, close, and tight down to isoclinal, where the interlimb angle is under 10 degrees and the limbs are nearly parallel to each other.

questions.prompt: Match each Ramsay fold class to its dip-isogon and thickness behavior.

right.text: Isogons perpendicular to layering; constant orthogonal thickness around the fold
Isogons parallel to the axial surface; constant axial-plane-parallel thickness, thinned limbs
Divergent isogons; thinned hinge, thickened limbs

questions.explanation: Ramsay's (1967) dip-isogon scheme ties fold class directly to a thickness signature: class 1B parallel folds keep constant orthogonal thickness (flexural mechanism), class 2 similar folds keep constant thickness parallel to the axial surface while orthogonal thickness thins on the limbs (shear-parallel mechanism), and class 3 folds have thinned hinges and thickened limbs from divergent isogons.

lessons.label: Fold Mechanisms: Buckling, Bending, and Fault-Related Folding

sections.heading: Buckling and the dominant wavelength
sections.body: When a layer that is mechanically stiffer (more viscous) than its surroundings is shortened along its length, it does not crumple randomly — it buckles at a preferred, or dominant, wavelength that depends on the layer's thickness and the viscosity contrast with the weaker matrix around it. Maurice Biot's 1961 theory of buckling instability in viscous media, adapted to geology by Hans Ramberg through the 1960s, gives the dominant wavelength as Wd = 2*pi*t*(eta1/(6*eta2))^(1/3), where t is the competent layer's thickness, eta1 its viscosity, and eta2 the matrix viscosity. The cube-root dependence on viscosity contrast means folding wavelength is far more sensitive to layer thickness than to how much stiffer the layer is — a doubled thickness roughly doubles the wavelength, while a doubled viscosity contrast changes it by only about 26 percent. This is why a single sandstone bed folds at a fairly regular spacing while thin interbedded layers develop tighter, shorter-wavelength folds, and it is testable with centrifuge and photoelastic-material experiments, which Ramberg ran extensively at Uppsala.

sections.heading: Flexural slip, flexural flow, and passive folding
sections.body: Layers can accommodate the same fold shape by different internal mechanisms. In flexural slip, bedding planes slide past each other like pages of a bent book, producing bedding-parallel striae (slip lineations) on bedding surfaces and a neutral surface within each bed that separates outer-arc extension from inner-arc compression; this preserves original layer thickness (parallel, class 1B geometry). Flexural flow is the same kinematic idea generalized to continuous ductile shear concentrated along bedding rather than discrete slip. Passive folding, by contrast, involves no mechanical contrast at all — a marker layer with no rheological control simply rotates and thins passively within a more pervasive shear or flattening field, typically producing class 2 similar geometry with no preferred wavelength, since there is no competent layer to select one.

sections.heading: Fault-related folds: three families, three signatures
sections.body: Where a thrust ramps through the crust, folding above it is predictable and diagnostic. John Suppe's 1983 fault-bend fold theory shows that a hanging wall riding up and over a fixed ramp-flat-ramp trajectory must fold to conserve bed length and thickness, producing fixed-geometry kink bands whose limb dips are set entirely by the ramp angle and stay constant through the structure's growth. Fault-propagation folds (formalized by Suppe and Medwedeff in 1990) form ahead of a thrust tip that has not yet broken through; the forelimb progressively tightens and steepens as slip increases and the fault tip propagates forward, so forelimb dip records the fold's growth history rather than staying fixed. Detachment folds (Jamison's 1987 treatment) form above a bedding-parallel detachment with no through-going ramp at all, growing by along-strike shortening of both limbs symmetrically above the flat, without needing a fault to break the surface. The three predict different, testable limb-dip and thickness patterns, letting a cross-section's fold shape diagnose which subsurface fault geometry produced it.

lessons.workedExample: A shortened sandstone-shale sequence shows folds spaced about 40 cm apart in a 10-cm-thick sandstone bed, but folds only 8 cm apart in an adjacent 2-cm-thick sandstone interbed. Applying Wd = 2*pi*t*(eta1/(6*eta2))^(1/3) with the same viscosity contrast for both beds, wavelength should scale linearly with thickness: a 5x thickness ratio (10 cm vs 2 cm) predicts a 5x wavelength ratio, and 40 cm / 8 cm = 5 matches almost exactly, confirming buckling of each competent layer independently rather than one shared mechanism.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe fold mechanism because 'it's a fold' is a shape description, not a mechanical explanation, and the Biot-Ramberg relation gives students a genuine quantitative prediction (wavelength scales with thickness) they can test against their own bed-thickness measurements rather than merely asserting. On the fault-related side, asking a student to predict whether forelimb dip should stay constant (fault-bend) or steepen with growth (fault-propagation) tests whether they understand these as distinct, falsifiable kinematic models rather than synonyms for 'fold near a thrust.'

questions.prompt: According to the Biot-Ramberg dominant wavelength equation Wd = 2*pi*t*(eta1/(6*eta2))^(1/3), if a competent layer's thickness doubles while the viscosity contrast stays the same, what happens to the dominant fold wavelength?

options.text: It roughly doubles, since wavelength is directly proportional to thickness t
It stays exactly the same, since only viscosity contrast controls wavelength
It increases by a factor of 8, since thickness enters as a cube
It decreases, since thicker layers fold at shorter wavelengths

explanations.a: Correct — in Wd = 2*pi*t*(eta1/(6*eta2))^(1/3), thickness t enters linearly (to the first power), so doubling t roughly doubles the dominant wavelength, holding the viscosity ratio fixed.
explanations.b: Thickness t is a direct linear multiplier in the equation, not a fixed term; it strongly affects wavelength.
explanations.c: It is the viscosity ratio term that is raised to the 1/3 power (a cube root), not thickness; thickness itself is linear.
explanations.d: Thicker competent layers produce longer, not shorter, dominant wavelengths under this relation.

questions.prompt: Match each fold mechanism or fault-related fold type to its diagnostic feature.

right.text: Bedding-parallel striae from layer-on-layer slip; preserves original layer thickness
No mechanical layering control; typically produces class 2 similar geometry, no preferred wavelength
Fixed limb dips set by a ramp-flat trajectory, constant through the fold's growth
Forelimb progressively steepens and tightens as the thrust tip propagates forward

questions.explanation: Flexural slip produces bedding-parallel slip striae and preserves thickness; passive folding lacks a competent layer to select a wavelength and yields similar geometry; Suppe's (1983) fault-bend folds have fixed limb dips set by the ramp; Suppe and Medwedeff's (1990) fault-propagation folds have a forelimb that steepens progressively as the fault tip advances.

questions.prompt: Order these events in the growth of a fault-propagation fold as shortening increases.

items.text: Thrust initiates at depth below a still-planar overlying sequence
A gentle fold begins to grow ahead of the propagating fault tip
Continued slip drives the fault tip further forward, tightening and steepening the forelimb
The forelimb reaches its maximum, most tightly folded state for the given amount of slip

questions.explanation: Fault-propagation folding begins with a blind thrust at depth, generates a fold ahead of its tip before the fault breaks the surface, and the forelimb progressively tightens and steepens as slip accumulates and the tip advances (Suppe and Medwedeff, 1990), so dip is a direct record of cumulative growth rather than a fixed value.

lessons.label: Joints, Veins, and Fracture Networks

sections.heading: Three fracture modes and the record they leave
sections.body: Fracture mechanics, following Irwin's 1957 formalization, sorts every crack into three loading modes: mode I (opening, tension perpendicular to the fracture — the mode of essentially all natural joints and extension veins), mode II (sliding, shear displacement parallel to the fracture and perpendicular to its edge), and mode III (tearing, shear parallel to the fracture and parallel to its edge). Because most joints propagate in mode I, a fracture surface records its own growth history as plumose (feather-like) structure: a origin point (often a flaw or inclusion) from which fine ridges called hackle fan outward, coarsening with distance as the crack front accelerates, interrupted by arrest lines — concentric ridges marking pauses where the crack front temporarily stalled, analogous to growth rings. Reading plumose structure lets a geologist reconstruct where a joint nucleated and which direction it propagated, purely from the fracture surface's texture, without any other context.

sections.heading: Joint sets, spacing, and stylolites
sections.body: Joints that share an orientation and formed in one deformation event form a systematic set — cutting across a region with consistent strike, often organized into two roughly orthogonal sets (Hancock, 1985, called cross-cutting orthogonal pairs 'joint systems'). Non-systematic joints are irregular, curved, and typically terminate against systematic ones rather than crossing them, marking a later or subsidiary generation. A well-documented empirical relationship, established through field studies including Ladeira and Price (1981) and later syntheses, is that joint spacing scales roughly proportionally with the thickness of the bed containing the joints: thin, well-bedded layers develop closely spaced joints, thick massive layers develop widely spaced ones, consistent with a stress-transfer model where each layer fractures somewhat independently of its neighbors. Stylolites are the compressional counterpart to joints: irregular, interpenetrating seams marked by insoluble residue (often clay or iron oxide) left behind where pressure solution has dissolved and removed rock along a surface oriented perpendicular to the maximum compressive stress, so the amplitude of stylolite teeth is itself a direct, measurable record of shortening across that surface.

sections.heading: Veins as shear-sense indicators and network connectivity
sections.body: Where fracture opening is filled by mineral precipitation (quartz, calcite) rather than left open, the result is a vein; en-echelon vein arrays — parallel, offset, overlapping veins arranged in a stepped row within a shear zone — form as mode I extension fractures oriented at roughly 45 degrees to a bounding shear surface, and the sense in which the array steps (stepping up to the right versus up to the left along the zone) is a strong kinematic indicator, though continued shear can rotate an originally straight array into a sigmoidal shape that complicates a naive stepping-direction read. At the network scale, the economic and hydrologic significance of joints and veins is connectivity: isolated fractures barely affect bulk permeability, but once a network's fracture density crosses a percolation threshold, connected pathways form and permeability increases by orders of magnitude — the reason fracture-network mapping, not just fracture density, is central to groundwater and reservoir studies.

lessons.workedExample: A sandstone outcrop shows two joint sets: one closely spaced (average 15 cm apart) in a 20-cm-thick bed, and, in an adjacent 80-cm-thick bed of the same sandstone, spacing averages about 60 cm. The spacing-to-thickness ratios are 15/20 = 0.75 and 60/80 = 0.75 — consistent, supporting the empirical proportionality between joint spacing and bed thickness rather than a fixed absolute spacing controlled by some other factor like regional stress alone.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe joints and veins because students often photograph a fracture and stop at 'there's a joint here' without extracting any of the direction-of-formation information the fracture surface itself encodes. Being able to point to plumose hackle and arrest lines and say which way the crack propagated, or to an en-echelon vein step and state the shear sense it implies, shows the student read the rock as a recording instrument rather than treating a fracture as a static, uninformative feature — exactly the kind of specific, falsifiable observation a judge wants to see distinguished from a generic description.

questions.prompt: Which fracture mode describes essentially all natural joints, where the crack opens under tension perpendicular to the fracture surface?

options.text: Mode I (opening)
Mode II (sliding)
Mode III (tearing)
Mode IV (rotation)

explanations.a: Correct — mode I is opening under tension perpendicular to the fracture plane, the mode that governs virtually all natural joint propagation.
explanations.b: Mode II is shear sliding parallel to the fracture and perpendicular to its edge, characteristic of fault surfaces, not typical joints.
explanations.c: Mode III is tearing shear parallel to both the fracture and its edge; it is not the dominant mode for natural joints.
explanations.d: There is no standard 'mode IV' in fracture mechanics; only modes I, II, and III are defined.

questions.prompt: Match each fracture-surface or fracture-network feature to what it records.

right.text: Where a joint nucleated and its direction and pauses in propagation
Shortening across a surface, from pressure-solution removal of rock
The shear sense of the zone containing the array
Whether bulk permeability crosses a percolation threshold

questions.explanation: Plumose structure (hackle fanning from an origin, arrest lines marking pauses) reconstructs joint propagation history; stylolite amplitude records pressure-solution shortening; en-echelon vein stepping direction gives shear sense; and network connectivity, once past a percolation threshold, controls whether permeability is high or negligible.

questions.prompt: Field studies (e.g., Ladeira and Price, 1981) on joint spacing in bedded sequences generally find that joint spacing is best predicted by which factor?

options.text: Bed thickness, with spacing scaling roughly proportionally to thickness
The color of the rock
Distance from the nearest river
The season in which the outcrop is studied

explanations.a: Correct — the well-documented empirical relationship is that joint spacing scales roughly proportionally with the thickness of the jointed bed, consistent with layer-independent stress transfer during fracturing.
explanations.b: Rock color relates to mineralogy or weathering, not to the mechanical stress-transfer process that controls joint spacing.
explanations.c: Distance from a river has no established mechanical connection to joint spacing in bedrock.
explanations.d: Season affects only present-day weathering appearance, not the joint pattern formed during past deformation.

lessons.label: Foliation, Lineation, and Shear-Zone Kinematics

sections.heading: Cleavage, schistosity, and the strain ellipsoid
sections.body: Foliation is any planar fabric produced by preferred mineral alignment or grain flattening. At low metamorphic grade it appears as slaty cleavage, a penetrative, closely spaced parting caused by preferred orientation of clay and mica flakes too fine to see individually; at higher grade, once mica grains are large enough to see, the equivalent fabric is called schistosity. Crenulation cleavage forms when an earlier foliation is itself folded into small, regular microfolds and a new, second cleavage develops parallel to the crenulation's axial surfaces, often concentrating micas into the limbs. Spaced cleavage consists of discrete cleavage domains separated by less-deformed microlithons, rather than being penetrative through the whole rock. In all these cases the foliation plane approximates the XY plane of the finite strain ellipsoid — the plane containing the two longest strain axes (X, the maximum extension direction, and Y, the intermediate) — because platy minerals rotate and grow into the plane of maximum flattening, perpendicular to the shortening (Z) direction.

sections.heading: Lineation and the L-S tectonite spectrum
sections.body: Lineation is any linear fabric element: a stretching lineation (from elongate mineral aggregates or boudinaged grains) parallel to the X axis of the strain ellipsoid, or an intersection lineation, the trace left where two planar fabrics (e.g., bedding and cleavage) intersect. Rocks are classified along a spectrum by which fabric dominates: S-tectonites show only planar foliation with no discernible lineation (flattening-dominated strain), L-tectonites show only linear fabric with no discernible planar foliation (constriction-dominated strain), and L-S tectonites, the most common case, show both a foliation and a lineation within it simultaneously.

sections.heading: Reading shear sense in a mylonite zone
sections.body: Ductile shear zones develop a toolkit of asymmetric fabrics that indicate shear sense unambiguously when viewed on the correct section: perpendicular to foliation and parallel to the stretching lineation, since viewing off this plane can reverse or blur the apparent asymmetry. S-C fabric, described by Berthe, Choukroune, and Jegouzo in 1979, pairs a schistosity (S) at an angle to the shear zone boundary with discrete shear bands (C, from the French 'cisaillement') parallel to the boundary; the acute angle between S and C opens in the direction of shear. S-C' fabric adds a second, extensional shear-band set oblique to C. Passchier and Simpson's 1986 work on porphyroclasts distinguished sigma-type clasts, whose recrystallized tails curve back toward the shear plane without crossing it, from delta-type clasts, whose tails cross the shear plane and connect on the opposite side after wrapping around the clast core, both consistently indicating shear sense from tail asymmetry. Mica fish (elongate mica grains with tapered, asymmetric terminations) and asymmetric boudins (necked competent layers with shear-consistent offset) provide independent confirming indicators. Finally, the mylonite series itself (protomylonite, under 50 percent matrix; mylonite, 50-90 percent; ultramylonite, over 90 percent, per Sibson 1977) tracks progressive grain-size reduction and increasing strain intensity toward the shear zone's core.

lessons.workedExample: A gneiss sample cut perpendicular to its foliation and parallel to its stretching lineation shows sigma-type feldspar porphyroclasts with tails curving down and to the left, plus C-shear bands oriented at a shallow angle to the main foliation, opening toward the same left-down sense. Both independent indicators agree, so the shear sense is read as sinistral (in map view, if the lineation is subhorizontal) with high confidence; had the sample instead been cut at a random, oblique angle to the lineation, the same clasts could have appeared symmetric or even reversed, giving a false reading.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe shear-sense fabrics because determining kinematics (which way did the rock actually move) from a static hand sample is a genuinely hard inference, and the field has a specific, checkable rule for doing it correctly: cut the section perpendicular to foliation and parallel to lineation, then look for at least two independent indicators (S-C angle plus porphyroclast tails, for instance) that agree. A student who cites only one indicator, or who cannot say why the viewing section matters, has not actually earned their shear-sense conclusion — this is a natural place for a judge to test whether 'I determined the shear sense' is backed by a real, reproducible method.

questions.prompt: Why must a shear-sense determination in a mylonite be made on a section cut perpendicular to foliation and parallel to the stretching lineation?

options.text: Because that is simply the traditional convention with no mechanical basis
Because viewing off this plane can blur or even reverse the apparent asymmetry of shear-sense indicators like sigma clasts and S-C fabric
Because minerals are only visible under a microscope on this particular cut
Because this cut is the only one that reveals the rock's mineral composition

explanations.a: The convention has a direct mechanical basis — it is the only section that reliably preserves the true asymmetry of shear-sense indicators.
explanations.b: Correct — sectioning perpendicular to foliation and parallel to lineation captures the true shear plane and transport direction, so asymmetric features like sigma/delta clasts and S-C angles show their genuine, unambiguous asymmetry; other cuts can distort or reverse the apparent sense.
explanations.c: Mineral visibility depends on grain size and thin-section thickness, not specifically on this cutting orientation.
explanations.d: Mineral composition is independent of the cutting plane; this rule is about preserving kinematic asymmetry, not composition.

questions.prompt: Match each fabric or tectonite term to its description.

right.text: Schistosity (S) at an angle to discrete shear bands (C), with the acute angle opening in the shear direction
Recrystallized tails that curve back toward the shear plane without crossing it
Fabric showing only lineation, no discernible planar foliation
New cleavage developing parallel to the axial surfaces of microfolds in an earlier foliation

questions.explanation: S-C fabric (Berthe, Choukroune, and Jegouzo, 1979) pairs schistosity and shear bands at a shear-sense-diagnostic angle; sigma clasts have tails that curve without crossing the shear plane (Passchier and Simpson, 1986); L-tectonites are constriction-dominated with lineation but no foliation; crenulation cleavage is a second-generation cleavage parallel to microfold axial surfaces.

questions.prompt: Order these fault rocks by increasing percentage of fine-grained matrix, from lowest to highest, per Sibson's (1977) mylonite series.

items.text: Protomylonite (under 50 percent matrix)
Mylonite (50-90 percent matrix)
Ultramylonite (over 90 percent matrix)

questions.explanation: Sibson's (1977) mylonite series tracks progressive crystal-plastic grain-size reduction with increasing strain: protomylonite has the least matrix, mylonite an intermediate amount, and ultramylonite the most, typically found closest to the shear zone's high-strain core.

lessons.label: Contractional and Extensional Fault Systems

sections.heading: Thrust systems: ramps, flats, and imbricate architecture
sections.body: Thrusts rarely stay at one dip; they follow a ramp-flat trajectory, climbing at a steeper ramp angle (commonly 20-30 degrees) through more resistant units and flattening into bedding-parallel flats within weaker units. A given bed is offset at hanging-wall and footwall cutoffs — the points where the bed crosses the fault — and comparing the two cutoff positions after restoration is a standard way to measure total slip. Multiple thrusts branching from one basal detachment build an imbricate fan, a stack of subparallel thrust slices. When two thrusts (a lower floor thrust and an upper roof thrust) bound a body of imbricated horses (fault-bounded slivers) between them, the structure is a duplex — first formalized in Boyer and Elliott's influential 1982 synthesis of thrust-belt geometry. Duplexes and imbricate fans can grow in two contrasting sequences: piggyback sequences, where each new thrust breaks forward (toward the foreland) of the last, carrying older thrusts passively along on its back, versus break-back sequences, where new thrusts break backward (toward the hinterland) of the existing stack, a less common but documented order in some belts.

sections.heading: Critical taper: why wedges stop growing at a stable shape
sections.body: Davis, Suppe, and Dahlen's 1983 critical-taper theory treats an actively deforming thrust wedge (like an accretionary prism or fold-thrust belt) as behaving like a bulldozer blade of sand: it maintains a stable, self-similar taper angle (the sum of surface slope and basal dip) set by the internal strength of the wedge material and the friction on its basal detachment. If erosion or a weak basal layer thins the taper below critical, the wedge shortens internally and rethickens; if tectonic accretion overthickens it above critical, the wedge extends and thins, restoring the same critical angle. This self-organizing behavior explains why fold-thrust belts maintain remarkably consistent surface slopes over long distances despite episodic, discrete faulting.

sections.heading: Extensional geometries and metamorphic core complexes
sections.body: Normal faults are often listric — curving from steep near the surface to shallow (sub-horizontal) at depth — and hanging-wall blocks sliding down a listric fault characteristically develop a rollover anticline, a reverse-drag fold that keeps hanging-wall strata in contact with the curving fault surface, commonly cut by smaller antithetic faults dipping the opposite way. Where instead a set of planar normal faults all dip the same direction and rotate together as rigid blocks during extension, the result is domino (bookshelf) faulting, named for its resemblance to a row of tilted books or falling dominoes. A single major normal fault (or fault set) bounding a basin on one side produces a half-graben, asymmetric relative to a full graben's two bounding faults. At the largest extensional scale, metamorphic core complexes (synthesized by Coney in 1980 and explained kinematically by Wernicke's 1981 model of large-magnitude, low-angle detachment faulting, first documented in the Whipple Mountains) expose deep, ductilely deformed and often domed footwall rocks beneath a gently dipping detachment fault, having been unroofed by tens of kilometers of extension on a single low-angle surface.

lessons.workedExample: A cross-section shows a hanging-wall cutoff of a marker limestone bed 3.2 km from the thrust's leading edge, and the corresponding footwall cutoff of the same bed 1.1 km from the leading edge, both measured along the restored, undeformed bed. The difference (3.2 - 1.1 = 2.1 km) is the total slip on that thrust. If a second thrust splay above it shows a piggyback relationship — it clearly cuts and offsets the first thrust's already-formed hanging-wall flat — the sequence is piggyback (younger thrust broke forward, toward the foreland, after the first was already in place).
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe ramp-flat and cutoff geometry because measuring true slip from cutoffs (rather than guessing from bed offset alone) is the concrete, checkable skill underlying real balanced cross-section construction, a standard tool in structural geology. Asking whether a sequence is piggyback or break-back, or why a wedge maintains a stable taper, tests whether a student sees these terms as describing a specific, testable growth history and mechanical balance rather than as decorative jargon for 'there are several thrusts here.'

questions.prompt: Per critical-taper wedge theory (Davis, Suppe, and Dahlen, 1983), what happens if erosion thins a fold-thrust wedge's surface slope below its critical taper angle?

options.text: The wedge shortens internally and rethickens to restore the critical taper angle
The wedge stops deforming entirely and becomes permanently inactive
The basal detachment reverses its dip direction
The wedge extends and thins further with no self-correcting response

explanations.a: Correct — critical-taper theory predicts the wedge behaves self-organizingly: if erosion drops it below critical taper, internal shortening and thickening restore the stable angle, analogous to a bulldozer wedge of sand rebuilding its slope.
explanations.b: The wedge does not become inactive; critical-taper theory specifically predicts continued, self-correcting deformation in response to erosion or accretion.
explanations.c: Basal detachment dip direction is a fixed geometric feature set by the regional setting, not something that reverses in response to erosion.
explanations.d: Further extension and thinning would drive the wedge even further below critical taper; the theory instead predicts a corrective, thickening response.

questions.prompt: Match each extensional structure to its description.

right.text: Reverse-drag fold keeping hanging-wall strata in contact with a curving listric fault
Set of parallel planar normal faults that all rotate together as rigid blocks
Basin bounded by a major normal fault on only one side
Deep footwall rocks unroofed beneath a low-angle detachment after large-magnitude extension

questions.explanation: A rollover anticline forms as hanging-wall strata slide down and stay draped against a listric fault; domino faulting rotates parallel planar fault blocks together; a half-graben is asymmetric, bounded on only one side; and metamorphic core complexes (Coney, 1980; Wernicke, 1981) expose deep rock unroofed by large-scale low-angle detachment faulting, as documented in the Whipple Mountains.

questions.prompt: Order these steps for measuring total slip on a thrust from a balanced cross-section.

items.text: Identify a marker bed cut by the thrust in both the hanging wall and footwall
Locate the hanging-wall cutoff, the point where the bed crosses the fault in the hanging wall
Locate the footwall cutoff, the corresponding point in the footwall
Measure the restored distance between the two cutoffs along the bed; that distance is the total slip

questions.explanation: True fault slip is measured by first identifying a common marker bed, then locating its hanging-wall and footwall cutoffs, and finally measuring the restored (undeformed) distance between those two cutoffs along the bed — that separation is the total slip on the thrust, per standard balanced cross-section practice (Boyer and Elliott, 1982).

lessons.label: Strike-Slip Systems, Transpression, and Riedel Shears

sections.heading: Bends, pull-aparts, and flower structures
sections.body: A strike-slip fault is rarely a single straight line; where its trace bends, the bend's geometry relative to slip direction controls whether it locally shortens or extends the crust. A restraining bend (one that steps toward the compressive side of the slip sense) forces local convergence, uplifting a pop-up or push-up range bounded by reverse faults — the Transverse Ranges bend on the San Andreas is a classic example. A releasing bend (stepping toward the extensional side) forces local divergence, opening a pull-apart basin bounded by normal faults, often deep and rapidly subsiding, as documented at the Dead Sea and Salton Sea basins. In cross-section, these convergent and divergent zones show up as flower structures: a positive flower structure has reverse faults splaying upward and outward from a near-vertical strike-slip root, uplifting a central block, while a negative flower structure has normal faults splaying similarly but downward-dropping a central block, both terms formalized in petroleum-industry structural interpretation through the 1970s-80s. Along strike, a strike-slip fault's displacement does not simply vanish at its tip — it is transferred to other structures (a fold belt, a set of splay faults, or a releasing/restraining bend) that absorb the fault's slip as it dies out, so total displacement is conserved across the transfer zone rather than disappearing.

sections.heading: Riedel shear geometry from clay-cake experiments
sections.body: Riedel (1929) first described this shear-fracture geometry from clay-cake shear-box experiments, and later analog work extended and confirmed it, notably Tchalenko (1970) and the Wilcox, Harding, and Seely (1973) synthesis for wrench tectonics. As a rigid basement block shears beneath a cover of clay or sand, four fracture sets develop in a predictable sequence and geometry relative to the principal displacement zone (PDZ, the through-going master fault direction): R shears (synthetic Riedel shears) form early at a small angle, roughly half the internal friction angle (about 15 degrees for a typical friction angle near 30 degrees), to the PDZ, with the same shear sense as the main zone; R' shears (conjugate, antithetic Riedel shears) form at a much higher angle, roughly 90 degrees minus half the friction angle (around 75 degrees) to the PDZ, with the opposite shear sense; P shears form later, synthetic like R but oriented as a mirror image of R across the zone; and Y shears (also called D shears) form parallel to the PDZ itself, becoming dominant as strain localizes and displacement increases, eventually linking R, R', and P fragments into one through-going fault.

sections.heading: Transpression, transtension, and strain partitioning
sections.body: Real plate boundaries are rarely pure strike-slip; oblique convergence or divergence combines a strike-slip (simple shear) component with a shortening or extensional (pure shear) component across the zone, states formally named transpression and transtension. Sanderson and Marchini's 1984 paper gave transpression its rigorous kinematic treatment, modeling it as simple shear parallel to a vertical zone combined with horizontal pure shear perpendicular to it, and showing that strain partitioning — the separation of oblique motion into a strike-slip-dominated fault (accommodating most of the lateral component) and a separate thrust or fold belt (accommodating most of the shortening component) within the same zone — is the natural outcome rather than a single fault accommodating both components obliquely.

lessons.workedExample: A sandbox shear experiment with basement blocks sheared at a friction angle of about 30 degrees develops early fractures at 14-16 degrees to the imposed shear direction (matching predicted R shears at roughly phi/2 = 15 degrees) and a second, much steeper fracture set at about 74-76 degrees to the same direction (matching predicted R' shears at roughly 90 - phi/2 = 75 degrees). As shear strain increases past about 10-15 percent, a new fracture set parallel to the shear direction itself (Y shears) begins linking the R and R' fragments into one continuous zone, matching the classic Riedel progression documented by Tchalenko (1970).
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe Riedel geometry because the predicted angles (roughly phi/2 for R, roughly 90-phi/2 for R') are a genuine, falsifiable quantitative prediction that a student can test directly against fracture measurements from their own clay or sand shear-box experiment, rather than a vague claim that 'shear produces fractures.' Similarly, asking a student to distinguish a positive from a negative flower structure, or to explain strain partitioning in transpression, tests whether they understand these as specific mechanical outcomes of a stress state rather than as a grab-bag of strike-slip vocabulary.

questions.prompt: In a clay-cake shear experiment with a friction angle of about 30 degrees, at approximately what angle to the principal displacement zone do synthetic Riedel (R) shears form?

options.text: About 15 degrees, roughly half the friction angle
About 75 degrees, roughly 90 minus half the friction angle
About 45 degrees, regardless of friction angle
Exactly 0 degrees, parallel to the principal displacement zone

explanations.a: Correct — R shears form early at roughly phi/2 to the PDZ, about 15 degrees for a friction angle near 30 degrees, with the same shear sense as the main zone.
explanations.b: This angle (roughly 90 - phi/2) describes the conjugate R' shears, which form antithetically at high angle to the PDZ, not the synthetic R shears.
explanations.c: R shear angle depends on the friction angle (phi/2), not a fixed 45 degrees independent of material properties.
explanations.d: 0 degrees (parallel to the PDZ) describes Y shears, which develop later as strain localizes, not the early R shears.

questions.prompt: Match each strike-slip structure or term to its description.

right.text: Local convergence producing a pop-up/push-up range bounded by reverse faults
Local divergence producing a pull-apart basin bounded by normal faults
Reverse faults splaying upward from a near-vertical strike-slip root, uplifting a central block
Oblique convergence combining strike-slip (simple shear) and shortening (pure shear) components

questions.explanation: A restraining bend forces local shortening (pop-up/push-up ranges); a releasing bend forces local extension (pull-apart basins); a positive flower structure shows reverse faults splaying upward from a strike-slip root; and transpression, formalized by Sanderson and Marchini (1984), combines simple shear and pure shear components in oblique convergence.

questions.prompt: Order the classic Riedel shear fracture sets by the sequence in which they typically develop as shear strain increases in a clay-cake experiment.

items.text: R shears (synthetic, at roughly phi/2 to the PDZ)
R' shears (antithetic, at roughly 90-phi/2 to the PDZ)
P shears (synthetic, mirror image of R)
Y shears (parallel to the PDZ, linking the fragments into one through-going fault)

questions.explanation: In the classic Riedel progression documented by Tchalenko (1970) and Wilcox, Harding, and Seely (1973), R shears form earliest at low angle to the PDZ, R' shears form at high angle as a conjugate set, P shears develop later as a mirror-image synthetic set, and Y shears form last, parallel to the PDZ, eventually linking the earlier fragments into one continuous fault.

units.label: Field Measurement, Stereonets, and Directional Statistics

lessons.label: Strike, Dip, Trend, and Plunge in the Field

sections.heading: Reading a Plane: Strike and Dip
sections.body: A structural measurement starts with a compass held against an exposed planar surface — bedding, a fault, a foliation. The standard field tool is the Brunton pocket transit, patented in 1894 by David Brunton, a Colorado mining engineer, or a lighter Silva-style clinometer compass. Strike is the bearing of the horizontal line contained in the plane, read by leveling the compass's bullseye bubble with its edge against the surface. Dip is the plane's maximum inclination below horizontal, measured perpendicular to strike with the clinometer arm and a second bubble. Two notations record this: quadrant notation (N40E, 30SE) gives a bearing under 90 degrees plus a dip-direction quadrant, while azimuth notation under the right-hand-rule (RHR) convention used in orientation software such as Allmendinger's Stereonet records only the strike azimuth, with dip direction fixed 90 degrees clockwise from it, so "220/35" alone is unambiguous. Before any reading, the compass's local magnetic declination must be reset from current declination tables; skipping this rotates every measurement in the dataset by the same systematic error, which can exceed ten degrees in some regions.

sections.heading: Reading a Line: Trend, Plunge, and Rake
sections.body: Linear features — a fold hinge, a slickenline, an intersection lineation — are recorded as trend (the bearing of the vertical plane containing the line) and plunge (the line's angle below horizontal in that same vertical plane). When a lineation lies within a surface already measured, recording its rake (or pitch) — the angle within the plane from the strike line to the lineation — is faster and avoids resetting the compass for a separate trend-and-plunge shot. Rake combined with the plane's strike and dip reconstructs the lineation's true trend and plunge trigonometrically, which is exactly how software back-calculates slickenline orientations from rake measurements on a fault surface.

sections.heading: Apparent Dip and the Sine Relation
sections.body: Any exposure not cut perpendicular to strike shows an apparent dip shallower than the true dip. If beta is the angle between strike and the trend of the section or cliff face, apparent dip (delta_app) relates to true dip (delta) by tan(delta_app) = tan(delta) * sin(beta). The sine, not the cosine, is what belongs here, and the two end members show why. At beta=0 the section trend equals the strike, so the section runs parallel to strike; elevation on the bedding surface is constant along a strike line, so the plane appears horizontal regardless of its true steepness, and sin(0)=0 delivers exactly that. At beta=90 the section is perpendicular to strike — that is, cut parallel to the dip direction — so it exposes the plane's steepest line and apparent dip equals true dip, matching sin(90)=1.

sections.heading: The Real Error Budget
sections.body: Three field errors dominate over instrument precision. Curved or irregular outcrop surfaces bias a single reading toward whatever local bump the compass edge rested on, which is why geologists average several closely spaced readings rather than trusting one. Magnetite-bearing rocks — banded iron formation, some basalts, ore veins — deflect the needle directly, an error invisible to declination correction; the fix is sighting strike from a distance rather than touching the outcrop. And any single station always understates a unit's natural variability, so a formation's reported strike and dip is properly a mean of many stations, not one outcrop.

lessons.workedExample: A geologist measures bedding as strike N30E (030 RHR), dip 40 SE, giving dip direction 120. A road cut exposing the same bed trends N80E (080). The angle beta between strike (030) and the cut's trend (080) is 50 degrees. Applying tan(delta_app) = tan(delta) * sin(beta): tan(40) = 0.8391 and sin(50) = 0.7660, so tan(delta_app) = 0.8391 * 0.7660 = 0.6428 and delta_app = arctan(0.6428) = 32.7 degrees. The bed appears to dip about 33 degrees in the road cut face, roughly seven degrees shallower than its true 40 degrees, purely because the cut is oblique to the dip direction. Note the sanity check the sine relation gives you for free: because the cut is closer to perpendicular to strike (beta=50) than to parallel with it, the apparent dip should land nearer the true 40 degrees than to zero — and 33 degrees does.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask 'is that the true dip or the apparent dip?' because it is the fastest way to expose whether a student measured structure directly or read it off an oblique photo or cliff face. A student who can state beta, apply tan(delta_app)=tan(delta)*sin(beta), and show the arithmetic demonstrates the geometry, not just the compass, produced the number. Being able to name the two end members on demand — parallel to strike shows flat-lying rock, perpendicular to strike shows the full dip — is the quickest proof the student understands the relation rather than having memorized a formula with a coin-flip trig function in it. It also surfaces whether a student can defend error bars with specific, checkable sources — curved-outcrop scatter, magnetite interference, single-station bias — rather than a vague 'measurement error.'

questions.prompt: A plane is recorded as strike 030 using right-hand-rule (RHR) azimuth convention. Which dip direction is necessarily implied?

options.text: Either 120 or 300, depending on the outcrop
030, since dip direction matches strike

explanations.a: Correct — RHR fixes dip direction 90 degrees clockwise from the strike azimuth as written, so 030 always implies dip direction 120; this is the entire point of the single-azimuth convention.
explanations.b: 300 would be 90 degrees counterclockwise from strike, which is the RHR convention read backwards.
explanations.c: RHR removes the ambiguity quadrant notation has; a single RHR strike azimuth always implies one specific dip direction, not two.
explanations.d: Dip direction is always perpendicular to strike, never parallel to it, since dip is measured across the plane's horizontal line.

questions.prompt: A bed truly dips 35 degrees. At what value of beta (the angle between strike and the section trend) will that bed appear horizontal in a vertical exposure?

options.text: beta = 0
beta = 45
beta = 90
No value of beta makes it appear horizontal

explanations.a: Correct — beta=0 means the section trend equals the strike, so the section runs parallel to strike. Elevation on a bedding plane is constant along any strike line, so the bed traces out flat in that face: tan(delta_app) = tan(35)*sin(0) = 0, giving delta_app = 0.
explanations.b: At beta=45, sin(45) is about 0.707, so tan(delta_app) = tan(35)*0.707 = 0.495 and delta_app is about 26 degrees — reduced from the true 35, but clearly not horizontal.
explanations.c: Backwards. beta=90 means the section is perpendicular to strike, which is parallel to the dip direction, so it cuts the plane's steepest line: sin(90)=1 and the apparent dip equals the full true dip of 35 degrees — the maximum, not zero.
explanations.d: The case does exist. Because sin(0)=0 exactly, the apparent dip goes to zero at beta=0 for a bed of any true dip.
