questions.prompt: Order the steps of taking a reliable strike-and-dip measurement in the field.

items.text: Reset the compass to the current local magnetic declination
Locate a clean, representative planar surface
Level the bullseye bubble with the compass edge on the surface to read strike
Rotate the compass 90 degrees and level the clinometer arm on the surface to read dip
Average several closely spaced readings across the outcrop

questions.explanation: Declination is set once before fieldwork begins; then for each station you find a clean surface, read strike, rotate to read dip, and finally average multiple nearby readings to smooth out curved-surface bias.

questions.prompt: Match each structural term to its correct definition.

right.text: Compass bearing of the horizontal line contained in an inclined plane
Maximum angle of inclination of a plane, measured perpendicular to strike
Compass bearing of the vertical plane containing a linear feature
Angle a line makes below horizontal, measured within its trend's vertical plane
Angle measured within an inclined plane, from the strike line to a lineation

questions.explanation: Strike and trend are both bearings (of a plane's horizontal line and a line's vertical plane, respectively); dip and plunge are both inclination angles (of a plane and of a line, respectively); rake uniquely measures an angle within a plane, from strike to a contained lineation.

lessons.label: Stereographic Projection I: Plotting Planes and Lines

sections.heading: Lower Hemisphere, Two Kinds of Net
sections.body: A stereonet projects lines and planes from the lower half of a reference sphere onto a flat circular disk, so every orientation a geologist measures in the field (a dip direction and angle, both pointed into the ground) plots consistently on one diagram. Two projections are in use, and they are not interchangeable. The Wulff net, an equal-angle projection developed by the crystallographer Wulff (1902), preserves true angles between any two features, so it is the correct net for measuring the angle between two planes or the plunge of an intersection line. The Schmidt net, an equal-area projection adapted for structural fabric work by Schmidt (1925), distorts angles slightly but preserves area, so equal numbers of points per unit area on the net represent equal true population density anywhere on the disk. Using a Wulff net to contour point density is a real error: because it stretches area near the rim, real clusters near the primitive circle appear artificially sparse.

sections.heading: Plotting a Plane: Great Circle and Pole
sections.body: A plane plots as a great circle — the full curved trace where it intersects the reference sphere — or, more compactly, as its pole, the single point 90 degrees away in every direction, where a line perpendicular to the plane pierces the sphere. Great-circle curvature reads dip directly: a shallow-dipping plane's great circle bows only slightly from the primitive circle (large radius of curvature), a vertical plane's great circle is a straight diameter through the net's center, and the pole moves in step — the pole of a shallow plane plots near the center, the pole of a vertical plane plots on the primitive circle itself.

sections.heading: The Standard Problems
sections.body: Because every plane has a unique pole, most stereonet problems can be solved either by manipulating great circles directly or by working with poles instead — the pole-to-plane duality. The angle between two planes is the angle between their poles, read along the great circle connecting them. The line of intersection of two planes is the point where their two great circles cross. Apparent dip in a given exposure direction is read where the great circle representing the section's vertical plane crosses the bedding's great circle. Modern practice increasingly replaces hand-plotting with vector algebra: software such as Allmendinger's Stereonet converts each orientation to a unit vector and finds a line of intersection as the cross product of the two poles' normal vectors, reproducing the graphical answer numerically.

lessons.workedExample: Bed 1 strikes 040, dips 30 toward 130 (SE); Bed 2 strikes 120, dips 45 toward 210 (SW). Converting dip direction and dip to poles (pole trend = dip direction, pole plunge = 90 - dip) gives pole 1 at trend 130, plunge 60, and pole 2 at trend 210, plunge 45. Taking the cross product of the two poles' unit vectors and normalizing gives the line where the two beds physically intersect: trend approximately 332, plunge approximately 28 — the same answer a careful hand plot on a Wulff net, drawing both great circles and marking where they cross, would produce.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe stereonet problems because the tool separates students who can only recite 'strike and dip' from those who can extract a genuine 3-D answer, like where two fault surfaces actually meet underground. Asking a student to justify why they used an equal-area net for contouring but would use an equal-angle net for an angle measurement checks whether they understand that the two projections trade off different properties, not just which button their software defaults to. A student who can name the pole-to-plane duality and show it solving the same problem two ways demonstrates real command of the method.

questions.prompt: A student wants to contour hundreds of poles to bedding to find zones of higher point density. Which net should they use, and why?

options.text: The Wulff (equal-angle) net, because it preserves true angles
The Schmidt (equal-area) net, because it preserves area so point density is not distorted
Either net gives identical contours
Neither net; contouring requires a Mercator projection

explanations.a: The Wulff net preserves angles but distorts area, stretching regions near the primitive circle; contouring on it makes real clusters near the rim look artificially sparse.
explanations.b: Correct — the Schmidt net's equal-area property means equal counts per unit area anywhere on the net represent equal true population density, which is exactly the requirement for honest density contouring.
explanations.c: The two nets distort different properties (angle vs. area), so contours drawn on one will systematically differ from contours drawn on the other, especially near the rim.
explanations.d: Mercator projection is used for world maps and is not part of standard stereonet fabric analysis.

questions.prompt: On a stereonet, a plane's great circle plots as a straight diameter passing through the center of the net. What does this indicate?

options.text: The plane is horizontal
The plane is vertical
The plane dips at exactly 45 degrees
The measurement contains an error and cannot be plotted

explanations.a: A horizontal plane plots as the primitive circle itself (its great circle coincides with the net's outer edge), not a diameter.
explanations.b: Correct — as dip increases, a plane's great circle bows further from the primitive circle toward the center; at 90 degrees dip it degenerates into a straight line through the center, the maximum possible curvature.
explanations.c: A 45-degree dip produces a great circle with intermediate curvature, bowed partway between the primitive circle and a straight diameter, not a straight line itself.
explanations.d: A straight diameter is the correct, expected plot for a vertical plane; it is not an error.

questions.prompt: Match each stereonet task to the correct method for solving it.

left.text: Line of intersection of two planes
Apparent dip in a given section direction
Choosing which net measures true angles

right.text: Angle between the two planes' poles, read along the great circle connecting them
The point where the two planes' great circles cross
Where the section's own great circle crosses the bedding's great circle
The Wulff (equal-angle) net

questions.explanation: Angles between planes are read via their poles on an equal-angle net; intersections and apparent dip are both read from where great circles cross, and any task requiring true angular accuracy calls for the Wulff net rather than the area-preserving Schmidt net.

lessons.label: Stereonet Analysis II: Fold Axes, Contouring, and Rotations

sections.heading: Pi-Diagrams versus Beta-Diagrams
sections.body: For a cylindrical fold — one whose hinge line stays parallel to itself along the whole structure — every bedding measurement around the fold shares one property: its pole lies on a single great circle called the pi-circle. The pole to that pi-circle is itself the fold axis, so plotting poles to bedding (a pi-diagram) and fitting a great circle through them recovers the fold axis without ever drawing the bedding planes themselves. The older alternative, the beta-diagram, plots the actual great circles of each bedding measurement; for a cylindrical fold these all cross at one shared point, the beta point, which is the same fold axis found the other way. Beta-diagrams trace to Sander's (1930) foundational work on rock fabric analysis, but with more than a handful of measurements the overlapping great circles become unreadable clutter, which is why pi-diagrams (points, not curves) became the practical default for large field datasets.

sections.heading: Cylindricity and Contouring
sections.body: How tightly the poles hug the best-fit pi-circle measures cylindricity: poles that scatter well off the girdle signal a fold whose axis orientation actually changes along its length — a doubly-plunging or sheath fold — where a single fold-axis number is not a valid summary. To find where poles genuinely concentrate rather than eyeballing scatter, Kamb's (1959) counting-circle method sizes the counting circle so its expected point count under a uniform (random) distribution is known for the given sample size, then expresses every location's actual count in standard deviations (sigma) above that expectation. Contour lines are drawn at fixed sigma intervals, so a 6-sigma maximum is a statistically real concentration regardless of how many total points were plotted, unlike older percent-of-total methods that quietly reward larger datasets with higher apparent percentages at the same true density.

sections.heading: Fabric Shape and Rotating Data
sections.body: Woodcock's (1977) eigenvalue method classifies a pole population's overall shape objectively: one dominant eigenvalue of the orientation tensor signals a cluster (point maximum), two large and one small eigenvalue signal a girdle (planar distribution), and three subequal eigenvalues signal a random fabric — plotted as a shape parameter that ranges from cluster-like to girdle-like. To restore an orientation dataset to its pre-tilt geometry, the whole dataset is rotated about the strike axis of the tilted bedding by an angle equal to the dip, returning bedding to horizontal; this untilting is the structural analog of the paleomagnetic fold test and is exactly how a folded fault population's original, pre-folding slip directions are recovered before kinematic analysis.

lessons.workedExample: Fifteen bedding measurements around a fold are plotted as poles. A best-fit great circle (the pi-circle) fits all fifteen poles within about 5 degrees of scatter, and its own pole plots at trend 210, plunge 15 — the fold axis is a gently plunging, roughly SW-trending hinge. Kamb contouring of the same fifteen poles shows a tight concentration reaching 8 sigma near one end of the girdle and only 2-3 sigma along the rest, meaning the fold's limbs are unevenly sampled rather than the fold itself being asymmetric. If instead the fifteen poles had scattered more than 20 degrees off any single best-fit great circle, that would indicate a non-cylindrical, doubly-plunging fold, for which no single fold-axis value would be meaningful.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges push on fold-axis analysis because it is where students most often confuse 'I plotted a lot of points' with 'I found a real structural axis.' A student who can state that poles falling near one great circle within a few degrees confirms cylindricity, and who knows Kamb contouring expresses density in sigma units so a maximum is statistically defensible rather than an artifact of sample size, is demonstrating quantitative structural literacy rather than pattern-matching a diagram. Naming what a rotation restores (pre-tilt geometry) versus what contouring measures (density) shows the two techniques are not confused with each other.

questions.prompt: In a pi-diagram of a cylindrical fold, what does the pole to the best-fit great circle through the plotted bedding poles represent?

options.text: The average dip of the fold's limbs
The fold axis
The axial-plane orientation
The location of the fold's hinge zone on the map

explanations.a: Average limb dip is not a single meaningful stereonet quantity; the poles instead trace a girdle whose pole is the fold axis.
explanations.b: Correct — for a cylindrical fold, all bedding poles lie on one great circle (the pi-circle), and the pole to that circle is exactly the fold's hinge-line orientation, the fold axis.
explanations.c: The axial plane is a separate surface bisecting the fold's limbs; it is not recovered directly from the pi-circle's pole.
explanations.d: Stereonets record orientation, not map position, so no map location can be read off a pi-diagram.

questions.prompt: Why does Kamb (1959) contouring express pole density in standard-deviation (sigma) units rather than raw percent of points per counting circle?

options.text: Sigma units are easier to draw with a compass and ruler
Sigma units account for sample size, so a contour level is statistically comparable across datasets of different n
Percent-based contouring is illegal to publish in structural geology
Sigma units eliminate the need for a counting circle entirely

explanations.a: The method's advantage is statistical, not about drawing convenience; both approaches require a counting circle stepped across the net.
explanations.b: Correct — by sizing the counting circle to the sample's expected count under a uniform distribution, Kamb contouring reports how many standard deviations above random a density is, making contour levels meaningful regardless of how many total points were measured.
explanations.c: There is no such prohibition; percent-based methods are simply less statistically rigorous for varying sample sizes, not disallowed.
explanations.d: A counting circle is still central to the Kamb method; sigma units are computed from counts within that same circle.

questions.prompt: Match each fabric analysis concept to its correct description.

left.text: Rotating data about the strike axis by the dip angle

right.text: Plots the actual great circles of bedding, which cross at a shared beta point
How tightly poles hug a single best-fit great circle
Classifies a pole population as cluster, girdle, or random
Restores tilted structural data to its pre-tilt, originally horizontal orientation

questions.explanation: Beta-diagrams use great circles rather than poles; cylindricity describes girdle tightness; Woodcock's eigenvalue method classifies overall fabric shape; and untilting rotation restores bedding (and everything measured relative to it) to its original, pre-deformation orientation.

lessons.label: Rose Diagrams and Circular Statistics

sections.heading: Why Ordinary Statistics Break on a Circle
sections.body: Joint orientations, paleocurrent directions, and fold-axis trends are all angles, and angles wrap around: 359 degrees and 1 degree are one degree apart on the ground but the ordinary arithmetic mean of the numbers 359 and 1 is 180, exactly the opposite direction from the true answer. Any dataset straddling the 0/360 boundary breaks a linear mean the same way, so circular data need methods built around vectors on a unit circle rather than numbers on a line. A second complication is axial versus directional data: a directional measurement like a paleocurrent has a true forward sense (it flows one way, not the reverse), while an axial measurement like a joint strike or an ungraded fold axis has no inherent polarity — 040 and 220 describe the identical joint. Curray (1956) solved this by doubling every axial angle (mod 360) before computing circular statistics, which maps 180-degree-periodic data onto a full 360-degree circle, then halving the resulting mean angle to convert back.

sections.heading: Bin Width and the Petal-Area Trap
sections.body: A rose diagram bins measurements into angular sectors, commonly 10 or 20 degrees wide, and draws a petal for each bin. The single most common rose-diagram error is scaling petal radius directly proportional to bin frequency: because a petal's visual area scales with the square of its radius, a bin with twice the count of another gets a petal with four times the apparent area, visually overstating how dominant the leading direction is. Correct practice scales petal area (equivalently, radius proportional to the square root of frequency) so that visual prominence tracks true frequency, a pitfall flagged directly in Fisher's (1993) treatment of circular data.

sections.heading: Mean Vector, Circular SD, and the Rayleigh Test
sections.body: Treating each measurement as a unit vector (cos(theta), sin(theta)) and summing all n vectors gives a resultant of length R; dividing by n gives r (0 to 1), where r near 1 means directions cluster tightly and r near 0 means they scatter broadly. The mean direction is the resultant vector's own angle, and a circular standard deviation follows from r by a standard formula (Fisher, 1993). To test whether an apparent preferred direction is statistically real rather than noise from a small, effectively random sample, the Rayleigh test (Rayleigh, 1919) computes Z = n*r^2 and compares it to a critical value; for large n the critical value at the 0.05 level approximates -ln(0.05), about 3.0, so a computed Z clearly above 3 rejects the null hypothesis of a uniform (random) distribution.

lessons.workedExample: A field team records 20 joint strikes and, after axial doubling and halving, computes a mean resultant length r = 0.6. The Rayleigh statistic is Z = n*r^2 = 20 * 0.36 = 7.2. Comparing this to the large-n approximate critical value of about 3.0 at the 0.05 significance level, 7.2 clearly exceeds it, so the null hypothesis of a uniform (random) joint orientation is rejected: this joint set has a statistically real preferred orientation, not just visual clustering that could plausibly arise from 20 randomly scattered fractures.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe rose diagrams because a bare petal chart looks quantitative while hiding two easy-to-fake choices: bin width, which can be tuned to manufacture a peak, and radius-versus-area scaling, which can visually exaggerate a weak preference. A student who explains why petal area (not radius) must track frequency, and who backs a claimed 'preferred joint set' with an actual Rayleigh Z value rather than 'the biggest petal,' has shown the diagram reflects real structure rather than a plotting artifact.

questions.prompt: Two joint strike measurements are 359 degrees and 1 degree. What is the correct circular mean direction, and why does the ordinary arithmetic mean fail here?

options.text: 180 degrees; the ordinary mean is already correct
0 degrees; the ordinary arithmetic mean of 359 and 1 gives 180, the opposite direction
There is no valid mean for only two measurements
90 degrees, splitting the difference the long way around the circle

explanations.a: 180 is exactly the wrong answer — it is the opposite direction from where the two measurements actually cluster, which is the whole problem this question is illustrating.
explanations.b: Correct — 359 and 1 are one degree apart across the 0/360 wrap, so the true circular mean is 0 (or 360), but naive linear averaging of the numbers 359 and 1 gives 180, exactly reversed.
explanations.c: Circular statistics can compute a resultant vector from as few as two measurements; the issue is method, not sample size.
explanations.d: 90 degrees is not produced by any standard averaging of these two values by either method.

questions.prompt: A rose diagram scales each petal's radius directly proportional to that bin's measurement count. What visual distortion does this produce?

options.text: None; radius-proportional scaling is the statistically correct convention
It understates dominant directions, making the diagram look too uniform
It overstates dominant directions, since petal area grows with the square of radius
It has no effect on appearance, only on printing size

explanations.a: This is the common error the lesson flags, not the correct convention; area, not radius, should scale with frequency.
explanations.b: The distortion runs the opposite way: dominant bins look even more dominant than their true frequency share, not less.
explanations.c: Correct — because a petal's visible area is proportional to the square of its radius, radius-proportional scaling makes a bin with twice the true frequency occupy about four times the visual area, exaggerating apparent dominance.
explanations.d: The distortion changes the diagram's visual proportions, not merely its overall printed size.

questions.prompt: Match each circular-statistics term to its correct role.

right.text: Converts 180-degree-periodic axial data onto a full circle before averaging
Ranges 0 to 1; near 1 means tightly clustered directions
A spread measure derived from r describing scatter about the mean direction
Tests whether an apparent preferred direction differs significantly from a uniform (random) distribution

questions.explanation: Angle doubling handles axial data's 180-degree periodicity; r measures how tightly vectors cluster; circular standard deviation is r's associated spread statistic; and the Rayleigh test uses n and r together to decide whether apparent clustering is statistically significant.

lessons.label: Geologic Maps, Structure Contours, and Cross-Sections

sections.heading: Reading Outcrop Patterns
sections.body: Where a contact crosses a valley, its map trace forms a V, and the shape of that V encodes dip. A horizontal contact's trace exactly parallels the topographic contours, forming a V that points upstream just like the contours themselves. A vertical contact ignores topography entirely, crossing the valley as a straight line. A moderately dipping contact, the most common field case, produces a V that points in the direction of dip whenever the dip is gentler than the valley walls, with the sharpness of the V increasing as dip decreases toward horizontal. Folded units produce their own signature: a plunging anticline's outcrop bands form a nose that points in the down-plunge direction, while a plunging syncline's nose points in the opposite (up-plunge) sense. Faults truncate and offset unit contacts abruptly across the fault trace, while an unconformity truncates only the older, underlying unit's internal contacts and bedding traces, leaving the younger overlying unit's own contacts continuous across the surface — the truncation pattern, not just an abrupt line, is what distinguishes an unconformity from a fault on a map.

sections.heading: The Three-Point Problem and Structure Contours
sections.body: Given three points of known elevation on a single planar contact (drill holes, outcrops, or a shaft), you can recover that surface's strike and dip. Linear interpolation along the line connecting the highest and lowest points locates where the contact reaches the third, intermediate point's elevation; connecting that interpolated point to the third point defines a structure contour, a line of equal elevation on the buried or exposed surface, whose bearing is the true strike. A second structure contour at a different known elevation, combined with the true (map-scale) perpendicular distance between the two contours, gives true dip directly: tan(dip) = elevation difference / perpendicular horizontal distance.

sections.heading: Building an Honest Cross-Section
sections.body: A cross-section translates map and dip data into a vertical slice, and any station not measured exactly on the section line must first be projected into the section plane using the apparent-dip relation. Two classic hand methods preserve bed thickness while interpolating between control points. The Busk (1929) arc method assumes concentric, parallel folding: circular arcs are drawn with radii perpendicular to the local bedding dip, their centers found where perpendiculars from adjacent dip stations intersect, keeping bed thickness constant along each arc. The kink-band (chevron) method instead assumes planar limbs meeting at sharp, angular hinges, appropriate for chevron folds common in thinly bedded turbidite sequences, with thickness preserved by measuring it perpendicular to each planar limb rather than across the hinge.

lessons.workedExample: Three drill holes intersect the same coal seam at elevations of 620 m, 560 m, and 500 m. The holes at 620 m and 500 m lie 240 m apart on the map; linear interpolation along that line locates the point where the seam is also at 560 m, exactly halfway (120 m from each end, since 560 is the midpoint elevation between 620 and 500). Connecting that interpolated point to the 560 m hole defines the 560 m structure contour. A second contour at 500 m lies 240 m away, perpendicular to strike, so tan(dip) = (560 - 500) / 240 = 60/240 = 0.25, giving a true dip of about 14 degrees, with the contours' own bearing giving the strike directly.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask students to justify a cross-section's shape because it is where a project either shows real subsurface reasoning or degenerates into a freehand sketch. A student who can point to the specific bed-thickness assumption behind their chosen method — concentric arcs (Busk) versus planar kink limbs — and explain why they projected an off-line outcrop into the section plane using apparent dip rather than its raw field dip, is demonstrating that the section is a controlled geometric construction, not an artistic guess at what is underground.

questions.prompt: A contact crosses a valley and its map trace forms a straight line, completely unaffected by the valley's topography. What does this indicate about the contact?

options.text: The contact is horizontal
The contact is vertical
The contact is an unconformity
The map has a plotting error

explanations.a: A horizontal contact's trace parallels the topographic contours, forming a V that points upstream, not a straight line indifferent to topography.
explanations.b: Correct — a vertical contact has no dip component for topography to interact with, so its map trace is a straight line regardless of the valley's shape.
explanations.c: Unconformities are identified by truncation of underlying contacts, not by the straightness of a single trace crossing a valley.
explanations.d: A straight-line trace crossing a valley is the expected, correct signature of a vertical contact, not an error.

questions.prompt: Given structure contours 60 m apart in elevation and 240 m apart in true perpendicular map distance, what is the true dip of the contact?

options.text: About 4 degrees
About 14 degrees
About 25 degrees
About 76 degrees

explanations.a: This would require a much larger perpendicular distance for the same 60 m elevation difference; tan(4 degrees) is about 0.07, not 0.25.
explanations.b: Correct — tan(dip) = 60/240 = 0.25, and arctan(0.25) is approximately 14 degrees, matching the lesson's worked example exactly.
explanations.c: This overstates the dip; arctan(0.25) is about 14 degrees, not 25 degrees, which would require a ratio closer to 0.47.
explanations.d: This corresponds to a much steeper ratio (tan(76) is about 4.0), far larger than 60/240 = 0.25.

questions.prompt: Match each cross-section construction method to its defining assumption.

right.text: Concentric, parallel folding with circular arcs of constant bed thickness
Planar limbs meeting at sharp angular hinges, thickness measured perpendicular to each limb
Older unit's internal contacts are truncated; younger unit's contacts remain continuous across the surface
Outcrop bands form a nose pointing in the down-plunge direction

questions.explanation: The Busk method assumes concentric arcs, the kink-band method assumes planar limbs and angular hinges, unconformities are identified by asymmetric truncation of only the older unit, and a plunging anticline's outcrop nose points down-plunge.

lessons.label: Fault-Slip Inversion and Paleostress Analysis

sections.heading: The Wallace-Bott Hypothesis
sections.body: A single fault surface with a striated slickenline records a slip direction, and a population of many differently oriented faults with slip-sense indicators can be treated as an array of tiny strain gauges recording a shared stress field. The link between the two is the Wallace-Bott hypothesis, proposed independently by Wallace (1951) and Bott (1959): slip on a fault occurs parallel to the maximum shear stress resolved onto that specific plane, not necessarily parallel to the regional maximum compressive stress itself. Because a given stress tensor predicts a specific, calculable resolved-shear direction on any plane of known orientation, the hypothesis runs in reverse — observed slip directions on many faults of known orientation can be inverted to solve for the stress tensor that would have produced them.

sections.heading: Right-Dihedra and Numerical Inversion
sections.body: The Angelier-Mechler right-dihedra method (Angelier and Mechler, 1977) gives a fast graphical first pass: each fault plane and its perpendicular movement plane divide the stereonet into compressional and extensional quadrants (dihedra) consistent with the observed slip sense, and overlaying these quadrants across the whole fault population narrows the compatible orientation of sigma1 (maximum compressive stress) to the zone common to most compressional dihedra, and sigma3 similarly from the extensional zones. Formal numerical inversion refines this into a reduced stress tensor: the orientations of sigma1, sigma2, and sigma3, plus the shape ratio Phi = (sigma2 - sigma3) / (sigma1 - sigma3), which describes the stress ellipsoid's shape independent of absolute magnitude — Phi near 0 indicates sigma2 close to sigma3 (uniaxial-compression-like), Phi near 1 indicates sigma2 close to sigma1 (uniaxial-extension-like). Absolute stress magnitudes cannot be recovered from slip directions alone, only these four relative parameters.

sections.heading: Honest Caveats
sections.body: Inversion assumes every fault in the dataset slipped under one shared stress field, so a population mixing faults from two different tectonic events must first be statistically separated (commonly by clustering faults on angular misfit between observed and predicted slip) before either subset is inverted, or the combined result is a physically meaningless average of two real states. Marrett and Allmendinger (1990) raised a deeper, still-live methodological challenge: they argued fault-slip data more directly records finite strain, via a moment-tensor-style summation over the population, rather than stress, since the two quantities need not be coaxial in anisotropic or heterogeneous rock. Finally, reactivated faults — surfaces that slipped again under a stress field different from the one that originally formed them — can violate Wallace-Bott outright, because pre-existing fabric and frictional anisotropy on an old surface can bias the reactivated slip direction away from the resolved-shear-stress direction the new stress field alone would predict.

lessons.workedExample: Numerical inversion of 30 fault-slip measurements from a rift-related fault population yields a reduced stress tensor with sigma1 (most compressive, i.e., least tensile) oriented at trend 000, plunge 70 — steep and roughly vertical — and sigma3 (least compressive, most tensile) oriented at trend 090, plunge 05 — nearly horizontal and east-west. The stress ratio comes out to Phi = 0.3, closer to the uniaxial-compression end of the range. Together, a near-vertical sigma1 and near-horizontal sigma3 with Phi = 0.3 describe a normal-to-oblique-normal faulting regime, consistent with regional extension oriented parallel to sigma3 and perpendicular to the fault strikes measured in the field.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges push on paleostress inversion because it is easy to state a stress tensor's numbers without engaging any of its assumptions. A student who can explain why absolute stress magnitude is unrecoverable but Phi is, why a mixed-age fault dataset must be separated before inversion rather than averaged, and why a reactivated fault is a genuine threat to the Wallace-Bott assumption rather than just noise, is showing they understand the inversion as a model with a domain of validity — not a black box that outputs three arrows and a number.

questions.prompt: According to the Wallace-Bott hypothesis, in what direction does slip occur on a fault plane?

options.text: Parallel to the regional maximum compressive stress (sigma1) direction itself
Parallel to the maximum shear stress resolved onto that specific fault plane
Always perpendicular to the fault's strike
In a direction determined solely by the fault's dip angle, independent of stress

explanations.a: Sigma1's direction is the regional stress axis; the fault's own slip direction is the resolved shear stress on its particular orientation, which generally differs from sigma1's direction unless the plane happens to be oriented just right.
explanations.b: Correct — Wallace (1951) and Bott (1959) independently proposed that slip parallels the maximum shear stress resolved onto the specific plane's orientation, which is what makes fault-slip data invertible for the stress tensor that produced it.
explanations.c: Slip direction depends on the resolved shear stress, which is generally oblique to strike, not fixed perpendicular to it.
explanations.d: Dip angle affects how stress resolves onto the plane, but slip direction is a joint function of the full stress tensor and the plane's full orientation, not dip alone.

questions.prompt: A stress inversion returns Phi = (sigma2 - sigma3)/(sigma1 - sigma3) = 0.05. What does this low value indicate about the stress ellipsoid's shape?

options.text: sigma2 is nearly equal to sigma3, close to a uniaxial-compression-like shape
sigma2 is nearly equal to sigma1, close to a uniaxial-extension-like shape
All three principal stresses are exactly equal (hydrostatic stress)
The stress tensor could not be inverted and the result is invalid

explanations.a: Correct — Phi near 0 means the numerator (sigma2 - sigma3) is small relative to the denominator, so sigma2 sits close to sigma3, giving a stress ellipsoid shape close to uniaxial compression.
explanations.b: That description matches Phi near 1, where sigma2 approaches sigma1 instead, the opposite end of the Phi scale.
explanations.c: A hydrostatic stress state has no differential stress at all and would make Phi undefined (division by zero), not simply a low value.
explanations.d: A low Phi value like 0.05 is a valid, well-defined output describing ellipsoid shape; it does not itself signal a failed inversion.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a fault-slip paleostress analysis from raw field data to a defensible result.

items.text: Measure fault plane orientation and slickenline rake/slip sense at each station
Separate the dataset if faults appear to belong to more than one deformation event
Apply right-dihedra analysis for an initial estimate of sigma1 and sigma3 orientation
Run numerical inversion to solve for the reduced stress tensor and Phi
Check for reactivated faults whose slip may violate the Wallace-Bott assumption

questions.explanation: Field measurement comes first; heterogeneous data must be separated before any inversion is meaningful; right-dihedra gives a fast graphical estimate that numerical inversion then refines into a full reduced stress tensor; and reactivation is checked as a caveat on whether the Wallace-Bott assumption actually held for each fault used.

units.label: Gravity and Magnetic Surveying

lessons.label: The Gravity Field, Anomalies, and Data Reductions

sections.heading: From Newton's Law to the Milligal
sections.body: Newton's law of universal gravitation predicts that any two masses attract with a force proportional to GMm/r^2. At Earth's surface this yields the familiar g ~ 9.8 m/s^2, but exploration geophysics cares about tiny departures from that average, so the field uses its own unit: the Gal (after Galileo), defined as 1 cm/s^2 = 0.01 m/s^2, and its practical subdivision the milligal (mGal), 10^-5 m/s^2. An ore body, cavity, or salt dome typically perturbs gravity by only a few tenths to a few tens of milligals -- a part in roughly 2x10^4 to 5x10^6 of total g (about 5x10^-5 to 2x10^-7) -- which is why gravimeters, not bathroom scales, are built to resolve microgals, millionths of a Gal.

sections.heading: Normal Gravity and the GRS80 Ellipsoid
sections.body: Before any anomaly can be isolated, you must subtract the gravity value expected on a perfectly smooth, rotating reference ellipsoid at that latitude -- normal gravity. The 1980 Geodetic Reference System (GRS80) formula gives this as g0(phi) = 978,032.68 mGal x (1 + 0.0052790414 sin^2(phi) + 0.0000232718 sin^4(phi) + ...), rising from about 978,033 mGal at the equator to roughly 983,220 mGal at the poles, a swing of over 5,000 mGal driven by two effects together: centrifugal acceleration from Earth's spin is greatest at the equator and vanishes at the poles, and the equatorial bulge itself puts the equator farther from the planet's center of mass.

sections.heading: The Reduction Chain
sections.body: Turning a raw meter reading into a usable anomaly means stripping away everything that isn't geology, in order: drift and tide corrections remove instrument creep and the solid-Earth/lunar-solar tidal signal (a few tenths of a mGal, tracked by repeat base readings); the free-air correction, 0.3086 mGal per meter of elevation, adjusts for a station's height above datum without removing any mass -- it just accounts for being farther from Earth's center; the Bouguer slab correction, 0.04193 x rho mGal per meter (rho in g/cm^3), removes the modeled attraction of the rock slab between the station and the datum; a terrain correction accounts for real topography not being an infinite flat slab (nearby hills pulling up and valleys missing mass both pull the reading the same direction); and on a moving ship or aircraft, the Eotvos correction removes the apparent gravity change from the platform's own velocity relative to Earth's rotation, on the order of 7.5 mGal per knot of eastward speed at the equator.

sections.heading: What Each Anomaly Means
sections.body: The free-air anomaly (observed g, corrected for elevation and drift/tide, minus normal gravity) still contains the full attraction of the topographic mass under the station, so it correlates strongly with elevation. The simple Bouguer anomaly subtracts the slab correction too, removing that first-order topographic mass -- what remains reflects real subsurface density contrasts plus terrain irregularities. The complete Bouguer anomaly adds the terrain correction, giving the cleanest local signal. The isostatic residual anomaly goes further, subtracting the gravity effect predicted by an assumed isostatic compensation model (Airy or Pratt roots under mountain belts), isolating shallow, uncompensated density anomalies -- an ore body or basin -- from the deep, wide root that balances the mountain above it.

lessons.workedExample: A station sits at 850 m elevation, latitude 44N. GRS80 gives normal gravity there as g0 ~ 980,529 mGal. The drift-and-tide-corrected reading is 980,362.30 mGal. The free-air correction adds 0.3086 x 850 = 262.31 mGal, giving a free-air anomaly of 980,362.30 + 262.31 - 980,529 ~ +95.2 mGal -- large, because it still carries the pull of 850 m of rock. Assuming an average crustal reduction density of 2.67 g/cm^3, the Bouguer slab correction removes 0.04193 x 2.67 x 850 ~ 95.2 mGal. The simple Bouguer anomaly collapses to roughly 0 mGal: this station sits over ordinary continental crust with no hidden density anomaly.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe the reduction chain because a raw gravimeter number means nothing on its own -- a student who reports 'we measured a gravity anomaly of 20 mGal' without saying which anomaly (free-air, simple Bouguer, complete Bouguer, isostatic residual) has not actually interpreted anything, since free-air anomalies are dominated by elevation and will look anomalous over any hill regardless of subsurface geology. A student who can explain why their Bouguer anomaly flattens the elevation correlation, and why isostatic residual removes the regional root before claiming a local density source, is demonstrating they understand what physically produced their number rather than reporting an instrument readout.

questions.prompt: In the worked example, the free-air anomaly is about +95 mGal but the simple Bouguer anomaly is close to 0 mGal. What removed most of that +95 mGal?

options.text: Subtracting the attraction of the 850 m rock slab beneath the station (Bouguer slab correction)
Subtracting instrument drift measured at the base station
Applying the terrain correction for nearby valleys
Applying the Eotvos correction for platform velocity

explanations.a: Correct -- the Bouguer slab correction (0.04193 x rho mGal/m) removes the modeled attraction of the rock mass between the station and the datum, which is exactly what was inflating the free-air anomaly.
explanations.b: Drift correction was already applied before the free-air anomaly was computed; it is not what separates free-air from Bouguer.
explanations.c: Terrain correction refines the complete Bouguer anomaly beyond the simple Bouguer anomaly; it was not applied here and is not the cause of the ~95 mGal drop.
explanations.d: Eotvos correction only applies to moving-platform surveys (ship or aircraft); this is a static land station.

questions.prompt: Match each reduction to what it does.

right.text: Adds 0.3086 mGal per meter of station elevation without removing any mass
Removes the modeled pull of the rock slab between station and datum (0.04193 x rho mGal/m)
Accounts for hills and valleys that violate the infinite flat-slab assumption
Removes the apparent gravity change from a ship's or aircraft's own velocity

questions.explanation: Free-air corrects for elevation alone, Bouguer slab removes the modeled mass beneath the station, terrain correction fixes the infinite-slab assumption's failure over real topography, and Eotvos removes velocity-driven apparent gravity change on a moving platform.

questions.prompt: Normal gravity (GRS80) rises from about 978,033 mGal at the equator to about 983,220 mGal at the poles. What two effects combine to cause this roughly 5,000 mGal difference?

options.text: Solar tides are stronger at the poles
Centrifugal acceleration from Earth's rotation is largest at the equator, and the equatorial bulge puts the equator farther from Earth's center of mass
The poles have more magnetite in the crust
The free-air correction is only applied at the poles

explanations.a: Solar and lunar tides produce a much smaller, time-varying signal (tenths of a mGal), not the static equator-to-pole difference.
explanations.b: Correct -- rotation reduces effective gravity most at the equator (where centrifugal acceleration is largest), and the equatorial bulge adds extra distance from Earth's center there, both making equatorial gravity smaller.
explanations.c: Magnetite content affects magnetic surveys, not gravity; it is unrelated to normal gravity.
explanations.d: The free-air correction is a per-station elevation adjustment applied everywhere, not a latitude-dependent effect.

questions.prompt: Order the reduction steps applied to a raw shipborne gravimeter reading on the way to a complete Bouguer anomaly.

items.text: Drift and tide correction
Eotvos correction
Free-air correction
Bouguer slab correction
Terrain correction

questions.explanation: Instrument and platform effects (drift/tide, then the platform-velocity Eotvos effect) must be removed first, then elevation (free-air), then the modeled rock-mass slab (Bouguer), then irregular topography (terrain), arriving at the complete Bouguer anomaly.

lessons.label: Gravimeters and Survey Design

sections.heading: Relative Meters: Spring and Quartz
sections.body: Portable field gravimeters are relative instruments -- they measure differences in g, not its absolute value. The classic design, the LaCoste and Romberg meter, grew from Lucien LaCoste's 1930s zero-length-spring principle: a mass suspended on a specially wound spring whose restoring force is proportional to its length from a notional zero point, giving near-constant sensitivity across a wide gravity range so one instrument can survey both continental interiors and mountain passes. Their descendants, the Scintrex CG-5 and newer CG-6, replace the mechanical spring with a fused-quartz elastic system read out digitally, with automated tilt compensation and stacked repeat readings; in careful field use they achieve on the order of 5-10 microgal (0.005-0.01 mGal) repeatability, good enough to see a shallow cavity or a thin ore lens a 1930s meter would miss.

sections.heading: Absolute Meters: The Free-Fall Standard
sections.body: Relative meters drift -- springs creep, electronics age -- so they must periodically tie to an absolute standard. The FG5, built by Micro-g LaCoste, measures g directly: a corner-cube reflector is released in a vacuum chamber and its fall is timed interferometrically against a stabilized laser, with hundreds of drops averaged per set. Achieving roughly 1-2 microgal accuracy, FG5 stations anchor national gravity networks and calibrate every relative meter that ties into them; repeat FG5 occupations over years also track slow mass changes from groundwater depletion or volcanic inflation that a single relative survey could never see.

sections.heading: Superconducting Gravimeters: Precision Without Portability
sections.body: The most precise gravimeters ever built are not field instruments at all. A superconducting gravimeter (built by GWR Instruments) levitates a small superconducting sphere in a persistent magnetic field inside a liquid-helium cryostat; because the field is essentially frictionless and stable, the instrument resolves gravity changes at the nanogal level with drift measured in microgals per year rather than per day. That precision costs portability, so these instruments sit permanently at fixed observatories, continuously recording Earth tides and hydrological loading rather than mapping a survey grid.

sections.heading: Designing the Survey: Loops, Spacing, Elevation
sections.body: Turning any of these meters into a map requires disciplined field design. Instrument drift (a few hundredths of a mGal per day for a spring meter) and solid-Earth tides are removed by base-station looping -- returning to a fixed base every one to two hours so a drift curve can be fit and closed loops reveal blunders. Station spacing is set by target depth, not survey budget: the rule of thumb is spacing at or below the depth of the target, since a body at 50 m depth produces an anomaly a 200 m grid will alias into noise. Finally, because the free-air gradient is 0.3086 mGal per meter, just 3 cm of elevation error injects about 0.01 mGal of spurious signal -- comparable to a CG-6's entire repeatability -- so microgravity surveys need centimeter-level GPS or leveling control, while coarser 1-mGal-scale reconnaissance can tolerate ordinary handheld GPS.

lessons.workedExample: A team surveys a suspected shallow karst cavity at 15 m depth with a Scintrex CG-6 (about 0.005 mGal repeatability). They lay stations on a 10 m grid -- below the 15 m target depth -- and loop back to base every 90 minutes to solve drift. Elevation is tied with RTK GPS good to about 2 cm, which by the free-air gradient (0.3086 mGal/m x 0.02 m ~ 0.006 mGal) injects almost as much error as the meter's own noise floor. Recognizing this, the crew tightens leveling to 1 cm before the final pass, dropping elevation-induced error to about 0.003 mGal -- safely below the instrument's resolution.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges push on instrument choice and survey geometry because these are the decisions a rushed project skips, and skipping them silently caps how small an anomaly can ever be trusted. A student who says 'we used a CG-6 because our target was shallow and small, gridded stations at half the target depth, and controlled elevation with RTK because 3 cm of height error is worth 0.01 mGal' has matched their tools to their target. A student who names an instrument without connecting its precision, spacing, or elevation control to the target size has picked equipment, not designed a survey.

questions.prompt: Why can't a superconducting gravimeter be used to survey a mineral exploration grid despite its unmatched precision?

options.text: It requires an immovable liquid-helium cryostat installation, so it cannot be moved station to station
It cannot measure gravity changes smaller than 1 mGal
It is less precise than a LaCoste and Romberg meter
It only functions at the magnetic poles

explanations.a: Correct -- the levitated sphere and liquid-helium cryostat form a fixed, room-sized installation, so the instrument is used at permanent observatories, not carried station to station.
explanations.b: It is the opposite -- superconducting gravimeters resolve changes far smaller than 1 mGal, down to the nanogal level.
explanations.c: It is far more precise than a spring meter; precision is not the limitation here, portability is.
explanations.d: It has nothing to do with magnetic poles; that describes magnetometers, not gravimeters.

questions.prompt: Match each instrument to its defining feature.

right.text: Zero-length spring, portable mechanical relative meter
Fused-quartz digital relative meter, ~5-10 microgal repeatability
Free-fall absolute meter, ~1-2 microgal accuracy, calibrates relative meters
Levitated superconducting sphere, fixed installation, nanogal-level long-term stability

questions.explanation: Each instrument family trades portability for precision differently: LaCoste and Romberg and CG-6 are portable relative meters, FG5 is a portable-but-slow absolute standard, and superconducting gravimeters give up portability entirely for the best long-term stability.

questions.prompt: Using the free-air gradient of 0.3086 mGal/m, about how much spurious gravity signal does a 3 cm elevation error introduce?

options.text: 0.001 mGal
0.01 mGal
0.1 mGal
1 mGal

explanations.a: Too small by a factor of ten; 0.3086 mGal/m x 0.03 m is about 0.009 mGal, not 0.001.
explanations.b: Correct -- 0.3086 mGal/m x 0.03 m ~ 0.01 mGal, which is why microgravity surveys need centimeter-level elevation control.
explanations.c: Too large by a factor of ten; that would require about 30 cm of elevation error.
explanations.d: Too large by a factor of one hundred; that would require about 3 m of elevation error.

questions.prompt: Order the field workflow for a base-station-looped gravity survey.

items.text: Occupy the base station for an initial reading
Occupy roving grid stations spaced at or below the target depth
Return to the base station within 1-2 hours to close the drift loop
Fit and remove the drift/tide curve from all readings
Compute the corrected anomaly at each station

questions.explanation: A drift loop must start and end at the base station within the 1-2 hour window before drift becomes nonlinear, and the drift curve can only be removed after the loop is closed, ahead of computing final station anomalies.

lessons.label: Interpreting Gravity Anomalies from Density Contrasts

sections.heading: Density Contrast Drives the Anomaly
sections.body: A gravity anomaly is produced by the CONTRAST in density between a body and its surroundings, not either rock's absolute density. Typical values: unconsolidated fill runs about 1.9 g/cm^3, sandstone averages around 2.4 (varying widely with porosity and cementation), granite about 2.67, basalt about 2.9, rock salt about 2.2, and massive sulfide ore bodies (pyrite, pyrrhotite, galena, sphalerite) can exceed 4 g/cm^3. Because salt (2.2) is less dense than the sandstones and shales it typically intrudes (2.4-2.6), a salt dome produces a NEGATIVE anomaly -- an unusual case where the classic exploration target is a gravity low, not a high -- while a massive sulfide body sitting in ~2.7 g/cm^3 country rock produces a sharp POSITIVE anomaly from a contrast that can exceed 1 g/cm^3.

sections.heading: Forward Shapes and the Half-Width Depth Rule
sections.body: Interpreters approximate real bodies with simple forward-model shapes whose gravity response is known analytically: a sphere for an equant ore body or salt plug, a horizontal cylinder for an elongated pipe or dike, an infinite slab for a thick uniform layer, and a fault step for two juxtaposed density blocks. For a buried sphere, the anomaly g(x) = (4/3)*pi*G*Drho*R^3*z / (x^2+z^2)^1.5 peaks directly overhead and falls off with lateral distance x in a shape that depends only on depth z, not radius R or contrast Drho individually -- giving the half-width depth rule: depth to center is about 1.3 times the half-width x-half (the distance from the peak to where amplitude drops to half its maximum). A horizontal cylinder's simpler falloff gives z ~ x-half directly. Because these rules assume a specific shape, a maximum-depth bound (from the anomaly's peak amplitude and steepest gradient) caps how deep the source COULD be regardless of assumed shape, guarding against a shape misjudgment producing a wildly wrong depth.

sections.heading: Nettleton's Profile Method for Reduction Density
sections.body: Choosing the wrong density in the Bouguer slab correction leaves a residual anomaly that mimics topography. Nettleton (1939) proposed a direct fix: compute the Bouguer anomaly across a topographic profile using several trial densities, then pick whichever density produces the flattest curve -- the one with least correlation to elevation -- as the best estimate of true near-surface bulk density, since a real, geology-only Bouguer anomaly should not systematically track hills and valleys.

sections.heading: Reading the Signature: Basin, Dome, Intrusion
sections.body: The three classic gravity targets have distinct signatures. A sedimentary basin gives a broad, long-wavelength negative anomaly, since low-density fill (contrast often -0.3 to -0.4 g/cm^3 against basement) spread over kilometers produces a gentle regional low. A salt dome gives a localized, bullseye negative anomaly from its low density relative to surrounding compacting sediments, often edged with a subtle positive halo where displaced denser sediment banks against the salt's flanks. A buried mafic intrusion gives a sharp, high-amplitude, narrow positive anomaly, since basalt or gabbro's 2.9-3.0 g/cm^3 against 2.6-2.7 g/cm^3 country rock is one of the largest positive contrasts available in ordinary crust.

lessons.workedExample: A circular gravity low over a target thought to be a shallow massive sulfide lens shows a peak amplitude of 3.6 mGal and a half-width x-half of 60 m. Treating the body as a sphere, the half-width rule gives an estimated depth to center of z ~ 1.3 x 60 = 78 m -- a reasonable first drill-depth target. A maximum-depth bound computed independently from the anomaly's peak amplitude and steepest horizontal gradient caps the source at no more than about 120 m regardless of shape, telling the driller the body cannot be hiding twice as deep as the half-width estimate suggests.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe density contrast and depth rules because they expose whether a student actually modeled their anomaly or just eyeballed a bump on a map. Naming the density values behind an assumed contrast, showing the half-width arithmetic that produced a depth estimate, and explaining why a salt dome is a gravity LOW rather than a high (the opposite of intuition, since more rock does not always mean more mass) all signal real quantitative modeling. A student who cannot say why their target should be a low versus a high has not engaged with the physics of density contrast at all.

questions.prompt: A circular gravity anomaly has a half-width x-half of 60 m. Using the sphere half-width rule z ~ 1.3 x x-half, what is the estimated depth to the body's center?

explanations.a: This divides rather than multiplies by 1.3; the rule multiplies the half-width by 1.3.
explanations.b: This applies no factor at all -- the sphere rule requires multiplying by 1.3, not using the half-width unchanged.
explanations.c: Correct -- 1.3 x 60 = 78 m.
explanations.d: This is the maximum-depth bound from the worked example, a separate shape-independent limit, not the sphere half-width estimate.

questions.prompt: Order these rock types from lowest to highest typical density.

items.text: Unconsolidated fill (~1.9 g/cm^3)
Rock salt (~2.2 g/cm^3)
Sandstone (~2.4 g/cm^3)
Granite (~2.67 g/cm^3)
Basalt (~2.9 g/cm^3)
Massive sulfide ore (>4 g/cm^3)

questions.explanation: Density rises from loose fill through salt, sandstone, granite, and basalt to the very dense sulfide minerals (pyrite, galena, sphalerite) that make massive sulfide bodies among the strongest positive gravity targets.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of Nettleton's (1939) profile method?

options.text: To measure absolute gravity at a base station
To select the Bouguer reduction density that minimizes correlation between the Bouguer anomaly and topography
To correct for solid-Earth tides
To estimate the depth of a buried sphere

explanations.a: Absolute gravity measurement is done with an instrument like the FG5, unrelated to Nettleton's density-selection method.
explanations.b: Correct -- Nettleton's method tests several trial densities and picks the one that flattens the Bouguer anomaly against a topographic profile, since a wrong density leaves a residual that mimics elevation.
explanations.c: Tidal correction is part of the drift/tide reduction step, not the Nettleton method, which addresses reduction density.
explanations.d: Depth estimation for a buried sphere uses the half-width rule, a separate technique from choosing a reduction density.

questions.prompt: Match each target type to its characteristic gravity signature.

right.text: Broad, long-wavelength negative anomaly from low-density fill spread over kilometers
Localized bullseye negative anomaly, often edged by a subtle positive halo
Sharp, high-amplitude, narrow positive anomaly from a large positive density contrast

questions.explanation: A basin's low-density fill spread over a wide area gives a broad regional low; a salt dome's localized low density gives a sharper bullseye low with a flank halo; a mafic intrusion's large positive contrast against country rock gives a sharp, strong positive.

lessons.label: Earth's Magnetic Field and Magnetic Surveying

sections.heading: A Dipole Field, Refined by the IGRF
sections.body: Earth's magnetic field is generated mostly by convective currents in the liquid iron outer core -- the geodynamo -- and to first order behaves like a bar magnet (dipole) tilted about 10 degrees from the rotation axis, with smaller non-dipole core contributions and an even smaller crustal component layered on top. Because the field also drifts over years, the International Geomagnetic Reference Field (IGRF), a spherical-harmonic model maintained and updated every five years by the International Association of Geomagnetism and Aeronomy, gives the expected regional field at any location and date so it can be subtracted from survey data, leaving the crustal anomaly of interest. Total field intensity ranges from about 25,000 nT near the magnetic equator up to about 65,000 nT near the magnetic poles. Declination (the angle between true north and magnetic north) and inclination (the dip angle of the field below horizontal) both vary with location -- inclination is near 0 degrees at the magnetic equator and near 90 degrees at the magnetic poles.

sections.heading: What Makes Rock Magnetic
sections.body: Magnetic susceptibility in ordinary crustal rocks is controlled almost entirely by magnetite (Fe3O4) content -- a rock with even a few percent magnetite by volume can produce a signal orders of magnitude stronger than an otherwise identical magnetite-free rock. A rock's total magnetization has two parts: induced magnetization, which aligns with today's ambient field and scales with susceptibility, and remanent magnetization, a direction locked in when the rock cooled through its Curie temperature (or acquired some other permanent magnetization) that stays fixed regardless of the present field. Their ratio, the Koenigsberger ratio Q = remanent/induced, tells you how much to trust an induced-only model: when Q is much greater than 1 (common in basalts and some banded iron formations), the anomaly's shape and even its sign can be dominated by an old, frozen-in direction rather than today's field.

sections.heading: Instruments: From Precession to Optical Pumping
sections.body: A proton-precession magnetometer polarizes protons in a fluid with a coil pulse, then measures the Larmor frequency at which they precess back into alignment with the ambient field -- robust and absolute, with resolution around 0.1-1 nT. The Overhauser magnetometer improves on this using dynamic nuclear polarization to continuously enhance the proton signal, allowing faster sampling and resolution around 0.01-0.1 nT at lower power draw. Cesium-vapor magnetometers use optical pumping of alkali-metal atoms and read continuously rather than in discrete pulses, achieving about 0.01 nT resolution -- the standard for modern aeromagnetic, drone, and gradiometer surveys.

sections.heading: Diurnal Correction and Choosing a Platform
sections.body: Solar-driven ionospheric currents produce diurnal variation of tens of nT over a normal day, growing to hundreds of nT during a geomagnetic storm, so every survey needs a stationary base-station magnetometer logging the same time series to subtract from roving readings -- storm days are typically flagged and discarded outright. Ground surveys (walked, closely spaced) sit nearest the source and give the finest resolution but are slow; drone magnetometry flies a low drape height, roughly 20-50 m, trading some resolution for speed; aeromagnetic surveys cover the most ground with line spacing from a few hundred meters (detailed) to kilometers (regional), but their higher drape altitude smooths and attenuates short-wavelength near-surface signal the way any upward-continued field is smoothed.

lessons.workedExample: A drone survey flies a magnetite-rich dike at 30 m drape height, recording total field readings between 49,850 and 50,120 nT. Its base station, logging simultaneously, drifts from 50,000 to 50,035 nT over the day -- a 35 nT diurnal swing from ionospheric currents. The 49,850 nT low was recorded early, when the base station was still near its 50,000 nT start-of-day value (0 nT of drift so far); the 50,120 nT high was recorded late, when the base had drifted the full 35 nT to 50,035 nT. Subtracting each roving reading's simultaneous base-station value removes that time-varying piece: 50,120 - 35 = 50,085 nT at the high, 49,850 - 0 = 49,850 nT at the low, leaving a corrected dike anomaly of about 235 nT peak-to-peak. Had the crew skipped the base-station correction, the raw 270 nT swing would have overstated the dike anomaly by that same 35 nT of solar-current noise.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe magnetic surveying because the diurnal correction and the induced-versus-remanent distinction are exactly the steps a rushed project skips, and both silently distort the anomaly's amplitude or even its sign. A student who logged a base station and can quote the diurnal swing they subtracted, and who can say whether their target rock likely has Q near 1 or Q much greater than 1, is demonstrating they understand what the instrument actually recorded. A student who reports a raw total-field reading as 'the anomaly' without a base station has not corrected for anything at all.

questions.prompt: Which mineral controls magnetic susceptibility in almost all ordinary crustal rocks?

options.text: Quartz
Magnetite
Calcite
Feldspar

explanations.a: Quartz is essentially non-magnetic and contributes negligibly to a rock's susceptibility.
explanations.b: Correct -- even a few percent magnetite by volume can dominate a rock's magnetic response, overwhelming the contribution of every other common mineral.
explanations.c: Calcite is diamagnetic and essentially non-magnetic, contributing negligibly.
explanations.d: Feldspar, like quartz, is essentially non-magnetic and does not drive susceptibility.

questions.prompt: Match each magnetometer to its defining attribute.

right.text: Measures the Larmor precession frequency of polarized protons; resolution ~0.1-1 nT
Dynamic nuclear polarization enhances the proton signal for faster sampling at ~0.01-0.1 nT
Optically pumped, continuous reading at about 0.01 nT, standard for modern airborne/drone surveys

questions.explanation: Proton-precession is the classic absolute, pulsed method; Overhauser adds dynamic nuclear polarization for faster, more precise sampling; cesium-vapor's optical pumping gives the finest resolution and continuous readout used in most modern airborne and drone surveys.

questions.prompt: A rock has a Koenigsberger ratio Q much greater than 1. What does this mean for interpreting its magnetic anomaly?

options.text: The rock has no magnetite
Remanent magnetization, locked in when the rock cooled, dominates over induced magnetization, so an induced-only model may get the anomaly's shape or sign wrong
The rock's susceptibility cannot be measured
The anomaly must be caused by a fault, not a rock property

explanations.a: A high Q requires magnetite (or another magnetic mineral) to be present and strongly magnetized; it does not mean magnetite is absent.
explanations.b: Correct -- Q = remanent/induced, so Q much greater than 1 means the old, frozen-in remanent direction dominates over today's induced field, which can make the anomaly's shape and sign differ from a simple induced-only model.
explanations.c: Susceptibility is a separate, measurable property; a high Q describes the ratio of remanent to induced magnetization, not whether susceptibility can be measured.
explanations.d: Koenigsberger ratio is a rock-magnetic property of the source material itself, unrelated to whether a fault is present.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of processing a ground or airborne magnetic survey.

items.text: Log base-station diurnal variation throughout the survey
Fly or walk the roving survey
Subtract the diurnal drift from the roving readings
Remove the IGRF regional field
Interpret the remaining crustal anomaly

questions.explanation: The base station must run throughout the roving survey so its diurnal curve can be subtracted from readings first; only after that time-varying noise is removed does subtracting the static IGRF regional field leave the crustal anomaly ready for interpretation.

lessons.label: Enhancing and Depth-Estimating Magnetic Data

sections.heading: Reduction to the Pole -- and Where It Breaks
sections.body: A magnetic anomaly measured at mid-to-high latitude looks skewed and shifted from directly over its source, because the ambient field is inclined rather than vertical. Baranov (1957) introduced reduction to the pole (RTP), a frequency-domain filter that recomputes the anomaly as if both the inducing field and the source's magnetization were vertical -- recentering the anomaly over its source and making shape-based interpretation far more direct. The filter's operator divides by terms involving the sine of the magnetic inclination, and as inclination approaches zero near the magnetic equator, that division blows up, amplifying noise until standard RTP becomes unusable at low magnetic latitudes. Practitioners there instead use reduction to the equator, a related transform avoiding the same near-zero terms, or fall back to amplitude-based products like the analytic signal that don't require RTP at all.

sections.heading: Continuation as a Wavelength Filter
sections.body: Upward continuation mathematically projects the measured field to a higher observation surface; because short-wavelength, near-surface signal decays faster with height than long-wavelength, deep signal, this acts as a low-pass filter emphasizing broad, deep trends while suppressing shallow clutter. Downward continuation reverses this, projecting toward the source to sharpen shallow, high-wavenumber detail -- but it is a high-pass, mathematically ill-posed operation that amplifies noise rapidly, so it is only usable a modest distance before it becomes meaningless.

sections.heading: Derivative Products for Edge Detection
sections.body: The horizontal gradient magnitude peaks over the edges of a tabular or steeply-dipping body, useful for mapping contacts and faults directly. The analytic signal combines the vertical and two horizontal derivatives in quadrature so its amplitude is independent of magnetization direction -- meaning it locates a body's edges correctly even when strong remanence (high Koenigsberger ratio Q) makes the raw anomaly's shape unreliable, without needing RTP first. The tilt derivative, the arctangent of the vertical derivative over the horizontal gradient magnitude, normalizes out amplitude entirely, highlighting both deep, subtle sources and shallow, strong ones on equal footing, with its zero contour tending to sit almost directly over the source edge.

sections.heading: Depth-to-Source Methods
sections.body: Euler deconvolution, developed by Thompson (1982) and extended with a structural index by Reid et al. (1990), solves Euler's homogeneity equation over moving data windows using the field and its derivatives, requiring the interpreter to assume a structural index (SI) matching the source's geometry -- 0.5 for a contact or fault step, 1 for a thin sheet or dike, 2 for a pipe, 3 for a sphere -- and picking the wrong SI both biases the depth and scatters the solutions. Werner deconvolution (Werner, 1953) is a similar linearized, profile-based technique purpose-built for thin sheet-like sources, solving directly for depth, dip, and susceptibility contrast. Spectral depth slicing, from Spector and Grant (1970), instead uses the slope of the radially averaged power spectrum of a magnetic grid to estimate the statistical average depth to an ensemble of sources -- the same logic extended regionally is the basis of Curie-depth mapping, estimating the depth to the base of the magnetized crust (the roughly 580 C Curie temperature of magnetite) as a proxy for regional heat flow.

lessons.workedExample: A 400 nT total-field anomaly over a suspected dike is run through Euler deconvolution with a structural index of 1 (thin sheet/dike), and across many moving windows the depth solutions cluster tightly around 85 m. Rerunning the same data with the wrong structural index, SI = 3 (sphere), shifts the cluster to roughly 50 m and scatters far more widely -- a 40 percent shallower, less reliable answer purely from mismatching the assumed geometry to the real, tabular source.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges push on structural index and RTP stability because both are places where an automated depth-estimation button can quietly return a confident, wrong number. A student who explains why they chose SI = 1 for a tabular dike rather than SI = 3 for a sphere, and who knows why RTP is skipped or replaced near the magnetic equator, shows they understand the assumptions behind the tool rather than trusting default software output. A student who reports an Euler depth without naming the structural index used has not shown the number means anything.

questions.prompt: Why does standard reduction to the pole become unstable at low magnetic latitude, near the magnetic equator?

options.text: The IGRF model has no coverage there
The filter's operator divides by terms involving the sine of inclination, which approaches zero near the equator, amplifying noise
Magnetite does not exist near the equator
Diurnal variation is strongest at the equator

explanations.a: The IGRF covers the whole globe; RTP instability is a property of the filter's math, not a gap in the reference field model.
explanations.b: Correct -- Baranov's RTP operator has sine-of-inclination terms in the denominator, and as inclination approaches zero near the magnetic equator, the division amplifies noise until the transform is unusable.
explanations.c: Magnetite occurs in rocks worldwide; RTP instability is a mathematical property of the transform, not a mineralogical fact.
explanations.d: Diurnal variation depends on ionospheric currents and local time, not on magnetic latitude in the way RTP instability does.

questions.prompt: Match each Euler deconvolution structural index to the source geometry it represents.

right.text: Contact or fault step
Thin sheet or dike
Pipe or cylinder
Sphere

questions.explanation: The structural index scales with how quickly the field falls off with distance for each idealized shape: a broad contact falls off slowest (0.5) and a compact sphere falls off fastest (3), with sheets and pipes in between.

questions.prompt: What makes the analytic signal useful when a source has strong remanent magnetization (high Koenigsberger ratio Q)?

options.text: Its amplitude does not depend on the direction of magnetization, so it still locates edges correctly without RTP
It removes all diurnal variation automatically
It only works for spherical sources
It requires no derivatives of the field

explanations.a: Correct -- the analytic signal's amplitude is independent of magnetization direction, so unlike the raw total field it locates a body's edges correctly even when strong remanence distorts the anomaly's shape, without needing RTP first.
explanations.b: Diurnal variation is removed by base-station correction during processing, before any derivative product like the analytic signal is computed.
explanations.c: The analytic signal is used for tabular bodies, dikes, and contacts as well as spheres -- it is a general edge-detection tool, not sphere-specific.
explanations.d: The analytic signal is built directly from the vertical and horizontal derivatives of the field; it requires derivatives, not the opposite.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of enhancing and depth-estimating a magnetic survey grid.

items.text: Remove the regional (IGRF) field
Apply reduction to the pole or equator, as appropriate to the survey's magnetic latitude
Compute a derivative product (analytic signal or tilt derivative) for edge detection
Run Euler deconvolution with a structural index matched to the expected geometry

questions.explanation: The regional field must be stripped first to leave the crustal anomaly, then the anomaly is recentered over its source (RTP or reduction to the equator) before derivative products sharpen its edges, and finally Euler deconvolution estimates depth using an appropriately chosen structural index.

lessons.label: Non-Uniqueness, Forward Modelling, and Inversion

sections.heading: The Equivalence Problem: Infinite Fits, One Anomaly
sections.body: Potential fields obey Laplace's equation outside their sources, and a direct consequence is the equivalent-source theorem: infinitely many different density (or magnetization) distributions confined within some volume can produce the identical field everywhere outside that volume. In practice this shows up as a depth-density trade-off -- a small, dense, shallow body and a larger, less dense, deeper body can produce the same surface anomaly if their combined mass and distance are matched, so a measured anomaly of a given amplitude never uniquely fixes both the depth and the density contrast of its source. An anomaly alone is consistent with many models; it proves none of them.

sections.heading: Forward Modelling: Talwani's Polygon
sections.body: Talwani, Worzel and Landisman (1959) gave the method still used today for building a gravity model by hand: approximate a 2D (or 2.5D, allowing finite along-strike length) geologic cross-section as an n-sided polygon of constant density, compute its attraction analytically term-by-term around the polygon's vertices, then compare the computed profile to the observed one, adjust vertex positions or densities, and repeat. This forward, geologist-driven approach lets an interpreter fold in independent knowledge -- a known formation top from a well, a mapped fault dip -- directly into the shape being tested, rather than letting an algorithm search blindly.

sections.heading: Inversion and Its Regularizing Choices
sections.body: Regularized inversion turns the problem around: instead of manual trial and error, an algorithm searches for the model that fits the observed data within its noise while minimizing some penalty on the model itself, since the raw least-squares problem is underdetermined and numerically unstable on its own. A smoothness constraint penalizes sharp spatial changes in density or susceptibility, favoring gradually varying models appropriate when no sharp boundary is expected; a compactness constraint instead favors a small, blocky anomalous volume against a uniform background, better suited to an isolated ore body or intrusion. Neither constraint adds real information about the true source -- both merely pick one member of the infinite equivalent family according to a geological bias the interpreter chooses.

sections.heading: Constraining and Reporting the Model
sections.body: The only way to genuinely collapse the ambiguity is independent data: a drillhole's density or susceptibility log anchors the model's physical-property assumptions to real measured rock instead of an assumed constant, and a mapped seismic reflection horizon can be locked into the inversion as a hard boundary, removing the equivalent-source freedom along at least that surface. Because of all this, professional practice reports an interpreted model together with its uncertainty -- a depth range, or a small ensemble of equally-fitting alternatives -- rather than presenting one inverted cross-section as though gravity or magnetic data alone had proven it.

lessons.workedExample: An isolated gravity low is fit equally well by two very different sphere models: Model A, a 50 m-radius body with density contrast -0.5 g/cm^3 centered at 150 m depth, and Model B, an 80 m-radius body with contrast -0.139 g/cm^3 centered at 160 m depth. Using the sphere formula from Lesson 3 (g = (4/3)*pi*G*Drho*R^3/z^2, x-half = z/1.3), both give a peak amplitude of about 0.078 mGal and a half-width of about 115 m and 123 m respectively -- close enough that the survey's noise and station spacing cannot separate them. The two imply completely different drill targets and completely different rock. A drillhole intersecting real material at 160 m either confirms Model A's dense, compact body or rules it out in favor of something closer to Model B -- only that independent log, not the gravity data alone, can decide between them.
