Along the virgin (normally consolidated) compression line the slope is the compression index, Cc; along the much flatter recompression/unload-reload branch, the slope is the smaller recompression index, Cr, typically only about a tenth to a fifth of Cc, because reloading soil that has already experienced a given stress mostly just closes elastic, recoverable structure rather than permanently rearranging grains. The kink between the flat recompression branch and the steep virgin branch marks the preconsolidation pressure, sigma prime_p - the highest effective stress the soil has ever experienced. Arthur Casagrande's 1936 graphical construction locates this point by finding the minimum-radius point on the curve, drawing a line there bisecting the angle between the tangent and the horizontal, and extending the virgin compression line back to intersect that bisector; overconsolidation ratio, OCR = sigma prime_p divided by the current effective overburden stress sigma prime_v0, then tells the engineer whether settlement under a new load will follow the stiff recompression branch (OCR greater than 1) or the much more compressible virgin branch (OCR at or near 1, normally consolidated).

sections.heading: Primary versus secondary compression, and the drainage-path-squared scaling
sections.body: Primary consolidation is the Terzaghi process just described, driven by pore-pressure dissipation; secondary compression continues afterward at essentially constant effective stress, as clay particles creep and rearrange under sustained load with no further water expulsion driving it. Secondary compression is measured by the coefficient of secondary compression, C_alpha, the slope of void ratio against log time past the end of primary consolidation; Mesri's empirical finding (Mesri and Godlewski, 1977) that C_alpha divided by Cc is roughly constant near 0.04 for a wide range of inorganic clays gives a quick way to estimate long-term creep settlement directly from a soil's already-measured compressibility, without a separate long-duration test. Because Tv scales as t proportional to H_dr squared, a doubly drained layer (drainage top and bottom, H_dr = half the thickness) consolidates four times faster than an otherwise identical singly drained layer of the same total thickness (H_dr = full thickness) - a factor that comes directly from the square in the time-factor relationship, not from any difference in cv or Cc, and it is why adding a single drainage blanket beneath a fill can cut waiting time for a construction schedule dramatically.

lessons.workedExample: A 10 m thick clay layer drained on both top and bottom (H_dr = 5 m) has cv = 2 m2/year. Time to reach U = 50 percent: t = Tv H_dr squared / cv = 0.197(5)^2/2 = about 2.5 years. If the same 10 m layer were instead drained on only one side (H_dr = 10 m), the same U = 50 percent would require t = 0.197(10)^2/2 = about 9.85 years - roughly four times longer, exactly the H_dr-squared scaling, even though nothing about the clay's cv or compressibility changed. A geotechnical engineer facing a tight construction schedule would add a drainage blanket at the base specifically to convert this from single to double drainage and cut the wait by that factor of four.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing settlement wants to see the full causal chain, not just 'clay settles slowly': the time factor Tv = cv t / H_dr squared, why doubling drainage paths cuts time by four (the square, not a linear factor), and how Casagrande's construction on an e-log sigma prime_v curve converts a lab test into a real design number, OCR. Naming Mesri's Calpha/Cc ratio to explain why settlement never fully stops even after primary consolidation ends shows the student understands consolidation is a process with two distinct, separately-measured phases, not a single event with a single finish line.

questions.prompt: A 10 m clay layer drained on only one side takes how much longer to reach a given degree of consolidation than an identical 10 m layer drained on both top and bottom?

options.text: About twice as long
About four times as long
The same amount of time
About sixteen times as long

explanations.a: The doubling of H_dr (from 5 m to 10 m) enters the time factor squared, not linearly, so the effect is more than a factor of two.
explanations.b: Correct - since Tv = cv t / H_dr squared, doubling H_dr (single- versus double-drainage of the same total thickness) requires four times the time to reach the same Tv and thus the same degree of consolidation, as shown in the worked example (2.5 years versus about 9.85 years).
explanations.c: Drainage path length directly changes consolidation time through the H_dr squared term; it is not irrelevant.
explanations.d: Sixteen would result from a fourfold change in H_dr, not the twofold change (single versus double drainage of the same layer) described here.

questions.prompt: Order these steps of Casagrande's graphical construction for finding preconsolidation pressure on an e-log(sigma prime_v) curve.

items.text: Locate the point of minimum radius (maximum curvature) on the e-log(sigma prime_v) curve
Draw a line at that point bisecting the angle between the tangent to the curve and the horizontal
Extend the straight virgin compression line back until it intersects the bisector
Read off the effective stress at that intersection as the preconsolidation pressure, sigma prime_p

questions.explanation: Casagrande's method starts by finding the curve's point of maximum curvature, bisects the angle there between the tangent and horizontal, extends the virgin compression line back to meet that bisector, and reads the intersection's effective stress as sigma prime_p, the highest stress the soil has previously experienced.

questions.prompt: Match each consolidation/compressibility term to its description.

right.text: Slope of the steep virgin compression branch on the e-log(sigma prime_v) curve
Slope of the much flatter unload-reload branch, typically a tenth to a fifth of Cc
Ratio of past maximum effective stress to current effective overburden stress
Slope of void ratio versus log time after primary consolidation ends; roughly 0.04 times Cc for inorganic clays per Mesri and Godlewski (1977)

questions.explanation: Cc is the steep virgin-line slope; Cr is the flatter recompression slope; OCR compares past maximum stress to current stress; C_alpha measures ongoing secondary (creep) compression after primary consolidation ends, and Mesri's ratio ties it back to Cc for a quick estimate.

units.label: Site Investigation: Field and Lab Testing

lessons.label: Planning a Ground Investigation

sections.heading: The desk study comes before the drill rig
sections.body: A competent site investigation starts with a desk study, not a borehole. An engineer first pulls published geologic maps and cross-sections, historical air photographs (which can reveal filled quarries, old stream channels, or demolished structures invisible at the surface today), and records of prior site use — old fuel-storage tanks, mine workings, or landfill are common surprises that a desk study catches cheaply and a boring program discovers expensively. Historic Ordnance Survey or USGS topographic sheets going back decades can show a pond or ravine that was later graded flat, which matters enormously if a foundation later settles into buried soft fill. Skipping this step is the single most common cause of an investigation that misses the actual geologic hazard on a site.

sections.heading: How many borings, how deep
sections.body: Boring layout follows the structure's footprint and loading, but depth follows a stress-based rule rather than a fixed number. A widely used guideline is to extend borings to roughly 1.5 to 2 times the footing width (B) below the base, or, for rafts and groups of footings whose stress bulbs overlap, until the induced vertical stress increase (from Boussinesq-type elastic solutions) falls below about 10% of the existing in-situ effective overburden stress — the point beyond which the load has negligible practical effect on settlement or capacity. Hollow-stem augers work efficiently in stable soil above the water table; mud (rotary) drilling stabilizes the borehole with drilling fluid through weak or below-water-table ground; sonic drilling uses high-frequency vibration to advance through mixed fill and boulders with continuous core recovery.

sections.heading: Sampling quality and the pore-pressure regime
sections.body: Undisturbed samples for strength and consolidation testing are usually taken with thin-walled Shelby tubes, whose area ratio — the tube's cross-sectional metal area divided by the sample area it displaces — should be kept under about 10% (ASTM D1587) so the tube displaces as little soil as possible on the way in. Even so, sampling, transport, and extrusion disturb the soil fabric: disturbed clay specimens systematically show a lower measured undrained shear strength su than the true in-situ value, and the sharp break at the preconsolidation pressure on an oedometer curve (the Casagrande construction) becomes rounded and harder to pick, a documented effect studied extensively by Ladd and Lunne. Finally, water levels read directly in an open borehole reflect drilling-fluid level, not the real pore-pressure regime; only a properly sealed piezometer, isolated at a specific depth and allowed to equilibrate, gives the actual static or perched groundwater condition.

lessons.workedExample: A 3-story building will bear on a 2 m wide strip footing. Design guidance calls for borings to 1.5-2B below the base, so at B = 2 m the engineer specifies borings to roughly 3-4 m below footing level at minimum, extended further if fill or soft clay is suspected. The desk study first turns up a 1962 air photo showing a farm pond exactly where the west wing is planned; the pond was filled sometime before 1980. That single finding redirects one boring to sit squarely over the old pond footprint, where a Shelby tube sample later confirms 2.5 m of soft, disturbed fill overlying the natural clay — a hazard the stress-based depth rule alone would never have targeted.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing site investigation design is really testing whether a student understands that geotechnical data collection is hypothesis-driven, not just procedural. The tell is whether a student can justify boring depth with a stress-based rationale (not just "we drilled 10 feet because that's standard") and can name a specific desk-study source — an air photo, a historic map — that changed where they looked. A student who cannot explain why sample disturbance lowers su, or who treats the water level in an open borehole as the real groundwater table, has skipped the step that separates a real investigation from a checklist.

questions.prompt: Why might a water level read directly in an open, uncased borehole be misleading?

options.text: It reflects the level of drilling fluid or slow seepage equilibration, not necessarily the true in-situ pore-pressure regime
Boreholes always read exactly at the ground surface regardless of conditions
Open boreholes cannot hold any water at all
The reading is always identical to a properly installed piezometer

explanations.a: Correct — drilling fluid, disturbed cuttings, and incomplete equilibration time mean an open-hole water level is often not the true static or perched groundwater level; a sealed, depth-isolated piezometer is needed for the real pore-pressure regime.
explanations.b: Borehole water levels vary with the specific ground conditions and drilling method; they are not fixed at the surface.
explanations.c: Open boreholes commonly do hold water; the issue is what that water level actually represents, not whether water is present.
explanations.d: This is backwards — the whole reason piezometers are installed is that the open-hole reading is often unreliable by comparison.

questions.prompt: Order these steps in a properly sequenced ground investigation, from first to last.

items.text: Desk study of geologic maps, air photos, and historic land-use records
Layout of boring locations and target depths based on stress-influence rules
Drilling and thin-walled Shelby tube sampling
Piezometer installation and equilibration to measure true pore pressure

questions.explanation: The desk study informs where hazards might be, which shapes the boring layout and depths; drilling and sampling then physically retrieve the ground data; piezometer installation and equilibration typically follow or accompany drilling since it takes time to yield a reliable reading.

questions.prompt: A common rule of thumb for boring depth beneath an isolated footing of width B is to extend the boring to approximately:

options.text: 0.1-0.2 times B below the footing base
1.5-2 times B below the footing base, or until the induced stress increase falls below about 10% of the in-situ overburden stress
Exactly 10 m regardless of footing size
Only to the top of the first rock layer encountered, however shallow

explanations.a: This depth is far too shallow to capture the zone of significant stress increase beneath a loaded footing.
explanations.b: Correct — this stress-based guideline ensures the boring extends through the soil that will actually experience meaningful load-induced stress increase.
explanations.c: A fixed universal depth ignores footing size and soil stratigraphy, which is exactly what the stress-based rule is designed to account for.
explanations.d: Stopping at the first rock contact regardless of depth would miss deeper stress-influenced zones in the case of a very shallow rock lens over deeper soil, and ignores the general depth guideline.

lessons.label: The Standard Penetration Test and Its Corrections

sections.heading: The test as actually performed
sections.body: The Standard Penetration Test (ASTM D1586) drives a thick-walled split-spoon sampler into the bottom of a borehole using a 63.5 kg (140 lb) hammer free-falling 760 mm (30 in). The sampler is driven three successive 150 mm increments; the blow count N is the sum of blows for the final two increments (the last 300 mm), while the first increment is discarded as seating. What most students miss is that N is not a soil property at all — it is a measure of how much hammer energy actually reached the sampler, and that depends entirely on the rig and operator delivering the blow, not just the soil's resistance.

sections.heading: From raw N to N60: the energy correction
sections.body: In practice, no field rig delivers the full theoretical free-fall energy. A rope-and-cathead rig with a safety hammer typically transfers only about 45-60% of that theoretical energy, while a modern automatic trip hammer, which releases with far less friction loss, commonly delivers 80-90%. Because so much scatter exists between crews and equipment, the profession normalizes every blow count to a reference energy ratio of 60% of theoretical free-fall energy, producing N60 = N x (ERm/60), where ERm is the measured or estimated energy ratio of the hammer actually used. A rig delivering only 45% energy will drive the sampler further per blow than one delivering 90%, so its raw N will be inflated relative to true soil resistance unless this correction is applied.

sections.heading: From N60 to (N1)60, and the honest limits of the test
sections.body: N60 still depends on how deep the test was run, because confining stress increases penetration resistance even in identical soil. The overburden correction factor CN — commonly taken as roughly the square root of a reference stress divided by the effective vertical stress at the test depth, and capped near 1.7 by convention such as Liao and Whitman's widely used relation — normalizes N60 to a common reference stress, giving (N1)60 = N60 x CN. Further corrections adjust for short rod lengths below about 10 m (where the rod-length factor drops as low as 0.75 for very short strings, with essentially no correction needed above 10 m), sampler liner presence, and oversized boreholes. (N1)60 correlates empirically to relative density, effective friction angle phi', and, more loosely, undrained shear strength su in clay. The blunt caveat every practitioner learns: even after all corrections, uncorrected N is documented to repeat only to roughly plus or minus 50% between different crews and rigs testing essentially the same soil — a reminder that SPT is a rugged index test, not a precision instrument.

lessons.workedExample: A borehole at 6 m depth records N = 20 blows using a rope-and-cathead rig with a safety hammer estimated at 55% energy transfer. First, N60 = 20 x (55/60) = 18.3. If the effective overburden stress at 6 m is about twice the reference stress used in the CN formula, CN = sqrt(1/2) is roughly 0.71 (capped at 1.7, so no cap applies here), giving (N1)60 = 18.3 x 0.71 = 13.0. That corrected value, not the raw 20, is what an engineer plugs into relative-density or liquefaction-triggering correlations — using the raw field N directly would have overstated the soil's normalized resistance.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges push on SPT corrections because the raw number is the single most overused-and-misused figure in student geotechnical projects. A student who reports "N = 20" as if it were a soil property has missed the entire point; a student who can walk through why energy ratio, overburden stress, and rig type all distort the raw count — and who volunteers the plus-or-minus 50% repeatability caveat unprompted — demonstrates they understand SPT as an operator-dependent index test rather than a lab-grade measurement.

questions.prompt: Why is the raw SPT blow count N corrected to N60 before use in engineering correlations?

options.text: Because different hammer systems (safety vs. automatic trip) deliver different fractions of the theoretical free-fall energy, and correlations are calibrated to a 60% energy reference
Because the number 60 is simply easier to remember than other reference values
Because N60 removes the need to ever measure soil density
Because the hammer weight changes between tests at the same site

explanations.a: Correct — safety hammers deliver roughly 45-60% of theoretical energy while automatic trip hammers deliver roughly 80-90%, so raw N values from different rigs are not comparable until normalized to a common 60% reference.
explanations.b: The 60% reference was chosen because it approximates typical rope-and-cathead safety hammer performance historically used to build empirical correlations, not for memorability.
explanations.c: N60 is still an index value correlated to density and strength; it does not replace direct density or strength measurement.
explanations.d: The standard hammer weight (63.5 kg) is fixed by the test procedure; what varies is how efficiently that weight's energy is transferred, not the weight itself.

questions.prompt: Order the SPT correction process from the raw field measurement to the fully normalized value used in correlations.

items.text: Record raw blow count N from the last 300 mm of driving
Apply energy ratio correction to obtain N60
Apply overburden stress correction factor CN to obtain (N1)60
Use (N1)60 in correlations for relative density, phi', or su

questions.explanation: The raw count comes first; it is then normalized for hammer energy to N60; that value is further normalized for overburden stress to (N1)60; only then is the fully corrected value used in engineering correlations.

questions.prompt: Match each hammer/rig type to its typical energy transfer efficiency range.

right.text: Roughly 45-60% of theoretical free-fall energy
Roughly 80-90% of theoretical free-fall energy

questions.explanation: Rope-and-cathead safety hammers lose energy to friction and operator variability, typically delivering 45-60% of theoretical energy, while automatic trip hammers release with much less loss, typically delivering 80-90%.

lessons.label: Cone Penetration Testing (CPT and CPTu)

sections.heading: What the cone actually measures, and why it must be corrected
sections.body: A cone penetrometer is pushed hydraulically into the ground at a steady rate (typically 20 mm/s), recording three channels continuously: cone tip resistance qc, sleeve friction fs just above the tip, and, in a piezocone (CPTu), pore pressure u2 measured just behind the tip. Because water pressure acts on the unequal end areas of the cone geometry (the shoulder behind the tip has a different area than the tip face), raw qc must be corrected to total (or "corrected") cone resistance qt = qc + u2(1-a), where a is the net area ratio of the cone, typically 0.70-0.85 and supplied by the manufacturer. Skipping this correction in soft, high-pore-pressure clay can meaningfully understate qt.

sections.heading: Classifying soil behavior from the profile
sections.body: The friction ratio Rf = fs/qt x 100% distinguishes clean sands (low Rf, high qt) from soft clays (higher Rf, low qt) without ever recovering a physical sample. Robertson's soil behavior type (SBT) charts plot qt and Rf (or normalized equivalents) on log axes to assign a zone corresponding to a soil behavior type, and the soil behavior type index Ic condenses that chart position into a single number, with lower Ic indicating cleaner, more sand-like response and higher Ic indicating more clay-like, plastic response. This is a behavior classification, not a grain-size classification — CPT sees how the soil responds mechanically, not what it looks like in a jar.

sections.heading: Strength, consolidation, and shear-wave data from one push
sections.body: Undrained shear strength in clay is estimated from su = (qt - sigma_v0)/Nkt, where sigma_v0 is total overburden stress and Nkt is an empirical cone factor typically in the range of about 10 to 20, calibrated against reference tests such as lab triaxial or field vane at a given site. Pausing the push and monitoring pore-pressure decay over time — a dissipation test — yields the horizontal coefficient of consolidation ch, useful for predicting how fast excess pore pressure will dissipate under a new load. A seismic CPT (SCPTu) adds a geophone to the same probe, so a shear-wave velocity (Vs) profile is captured in the same push that produces qt, fs, and u2 — a major efficiency gain over drilling a separate crosshole or downhole test. The enduring practical trade-off against SPT is this: CPT gives continuous, highly repeatable profiling with far less operator variability, but produces no physical sample an engineer can look at, feel, or classify by eye, so many programs run both, with SPT boreholes calibrating the CPT's Ic-based soil classification.

lessons.workedExample: At 10 m depth in a soft clay, a CPTu records qc = 1.2 MPa, u2 = 300 kPa, and a net area ratio a = 0.75, giving qt = 1.2 + 0.300(1-0.75) = 1.275 MPa. Total overburden stress sigma_v0 at that depth is about 190 kPa. Using a site-calibrated Nkt of 14, su = (1275 - 190)/14 = 77.5 kPa. A dissipation test paused at the same depth shows pore pressure decaying to 50% of its excess value (t50) in 40 minutes, from which ch is back-calculated — informing how quickly a planned embankment's excess pore pressure will dissipate during staged construction.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking about CPT is testing whether a student understands that every derived CPT parameter rests on an assumed or site-calibrated coefficient — Nkt for strength, the area ratio a for the qt correction — rather than being a direct measurement. A student who quotes su from qt without acknowledging that Nkt is empirical and site-dependent, typically ranging from about 10 to 20, is treating a calibrated correlation as a hard fact. The strongest answers also name the core trade-off against SPT: continuous, repeatable profiling versus the total absence of a physical sample to classify by eye.

questions.prompt: Why must raw cone tip resistance qc be corrected to qt using the pore pressure u2?

options.text: Because water pressure acting on the cone's unequal end areas affects the measured resistance, and this correction accounts for that geometric effect
Because qc always overestimates soil strength in every soil type by a fixed percentage
Because qt is simply a unit conversion of qc from kPa to MPa
Because the cone tip wears down during a single push and must be recalibrated

explanations.a: Correct — the unequal end-area effect means pore pressure acting on the cone geometry biases raw qc, especially in soft, high-pore-pressure soils, so qt = qc + u2(1-a) corrects for it using the net area ratio a.
explanations.b: The correction's magnitude depends on pore pressure and the area ratio, not a fixed percentage, and it matters most in soft, high-pore-pressure clay rather than uniformly across all soils.
explanations.c: qt and qc are both typically reported in consistent units (e.g., MPa); the correction is a physical adjustment, not a unit conversion.
explanations.d: The correction addresses the cone's fixed end-area geometry interacting with pore pressure, not mechanical wear during the push.

questions.prompt: Match each CPT-derived quantity to what it is used to estimate.

right.text: Undrained shear strength in clay
Horizontal coefficient of consolidation ch
Shear-wave velocity (Vs) profile
Soil behavior type classification (clay-like vs. sand-like response)

questions.explanation: The su equation uses tip resistance and overburden stress with the empirical cone factor Nkt; dissipation tests monitor pore-pressure decay over time to back out ch; seismic CPT adds a geophone for Vs; and Ic condenses the qt-Rf chart position into a soil behavior classification.

questions.prompt: What is the main practical trade-off between CPT and SPT that engineers weigh when choosing a site investigation method?

options.text: CPT gives continuous, repeatable profiling but no physical sample to classify by eye; SPT gives a physical sample but is less continuous and more operator-dependent
CPT is always cheaper and always preferred with no downside in any soil type
SPT can be run continuously at 20 mm/s while CPT can only test at discrete 1.5 m intervals
CPT and SPT measure identical parameters and are fully interchangeable

explanations.a: Correct — this is the standing practical argument: CPT's continuous, repeatable profile comes at the cost of having no retrievable sample, while SPT retrieves a classifiable sample at discrete intervals with more crew-to-crew variability.
explanations.b: CPT struggles or refuses to advance in gravelly, cobbly, or very dense/cemented ground, where SPT drilling can still penetrate, so it is not a universal replacement.
explanations.c: This reverses the actual capabilities — CPT is the continuous-push method (around 20 mm/s advance rate) while SPT samples at discrete depth intervals.
explanations.d: CPT measures continuous tip resistance, sleeve friction, and pore pressure; SPT measures a discrete blow count and recovers a physical sample — they are complementary, not interchangeable.

lessons.label: Vane, Dilatometer, Pressuremeter, and Plate Load Tests

sections.heading: Field vane shear and Bjerrum's correction
sections.body: The field vane shear test rotates a four-bladed vane, pushed to depth in soft clay, and measures the torque required to shear a cylindrical surface of soil, giving a direct field su without ever cutting a sample. But the raw vane strength systematically overpredicts the strength actually mobilized in a real slow failure, because the vane shears the soil rapidly and along a shape that does not match how an embankment or excavation actually fails. Bjerrum, working through a series of papers in 1972-73, back-analyzed a set of embankments and excavations that had actually failed in the field, comparing their known failure loads to the vane strength measured beforehand, and derived an empirical correction factor mu that is applied as su(design) = mu x su(vane). Mu is close to 1.0 for low-plasticity clay but falls to roughly 0.6 at a plasticity index of 100, reflecting that highly plastic clays show the largest gap between rapid vane strength and the strength actually available during a slow field failure.

sections.heading: Marchetti's flat dilatometer
sections.body: Marchetti introduced the flat plate dilatometer in 1980: a flat steel blade is pushed into the ground, and a membrane on one face is inflated to record two pressures at each depth — the pressure to just lift the membrane off the blade (used to compute the horizontal stress index KD) and the pressure at 1.1 mm of membrane expansion (used with the lift-off pressure to compute the material index ID, distinguishing clay-like from sand-like response) and the dilatometer modulus ED. KD in particular is sensitive to in-situ horizontal stress and stress history, making DMT unusually good at flagging overconsolidated crusts that other tests can miss.

sections.heading: Pressuremeter and plate load tests
sections.body: The Menard pressuremeter inflates a cylindrical probe radially against the borehole wall, directly measuring an in-situ stress-strain curve from which a pressuremeter modulus and a limit pressure (the pressure at which the surrounding soil essentially fails in shear) are read — a genuinely in-situ modulus rather than one back-calculated from an index correlation. Plate load tests, by contrast, load a physical plate at the ground surface and measure settlement, but the zone of influence beneath a small plate is shallow (roughly 1.5-2 plate diameters), so the test easily misses a softer layer just below that depth; naively scaling plate-load settlement up to a full-size footing without correcting for this depth-of-influence and scale effect is a classic and costly interpretation trap.

lessons.workedExample: A vane test in a soft clay with plasticity index 100 records su(vane) = 40 kPa. Using Bjerrum's correction factor of roughly 0.6 at that plasticity index, the design strength becomes su(design) = 0.6 x 40 = 24 kPa — a 40% reduction that, if ignored, would have led an engineer to overestimate the clay's real field strength and under-design a slope or foundation. Separately, a 300 mm diameter plate load test on sand shows only 5 mm of settlement under design load, but because the plate's zone of influence extends only about 450-600 mm deep, a softer lens sitting 1 m down goes entirely undetected — exactly the kind of scale-effect trap that makes plate load results risky to extrapolate directly to a full-size footing.
lessons.judgeFraming: This lesson rewards a student who can explain why a raw in-situ reading is not the same as a design value. The clearest evidence is naming Bjerrum's mu factor and its empirical origin — back-analysis of real embankment failures, not a lab derivation — and being able to say concretely that mu drops toward roughly 0.6 for very plastic clay. A second strong signal is recognizing the plate-load scale-effect trap: a judge will probe whether a student naively assumes a small-plate test result scales linearly to a full-size foundation, when the shallow depth of influence means it may simply never have seen the governing soil layer.

questions.prompt: How did Bjerrum derive the correction factor mu applied to field vane shear strength?

options.text: By back-analyzing real embankments and excavations that had failed in the field and comparing their known failure loads to the vane strength measured beforehand
By running the vane test in a laboratory chamber under perfectly controlled conditions
By assuming a fixed correction of exactly 0.5 for all clays regardless of plasticity
By comparing vane results only to triaxial UU tests on the same samples

explanations.a: Correct — Bjerrum's 1972-73 papers back-analyzed real case histories of embankment and excavation failures, comparing the strength implied by actual failure loads to the vane strength measured before failure.
explanations.b: The correction came from field case histories of actual failures, not controlled laboratory chamber testing.
explanations.c: Mu varies with plasticity index, starting near 1.0 for low-plasticity clay and falling to roughly 0.6 at a plasticity index of 100, rather than being a fixed universal value.
explanations.d: The derivation relied on real field failure case histories, not a laboratory comparison to triaxial UU results.

questions.prompt: Match each in-situ test to the parameter or index it is specifically known for producing.

right.text: Raw undrained shear strength su, corrected by Bjerrum's mu factor
Horizontal stress index KD, material index ID, and modulus ED
Directly measured in-situ modulus and limit pressure
Surface settlement under load, limited by a shallow depth of influence

questions.explanation: The field vane gives raw su needing Bjerrum's correction; the DMT gives KD, ID, and ED from membrane inflation pressures; the pressuremeter directly measures an in-situ modulus and limit pressure; the plate load test measures settlement but only within a shallow zone of influence.

questions.prompt: Why is it risky to naively scale a plate load test's settlement result directly up to a full-size footing?

options.text: The plate's zone of influence is shallow (roughly 1.5-2 plate diameters), so it may miss a softer layer that a larger footing's deeper stress bulb would engage
Plate load tests always overestimate settlement compared to full-size footings by a fixed factor
Plate load tests cannot be performed on sand, only on clay
The plate load test measures shear strength, not settlement, so it has nothing to do with footing settlement at all

explanations.a: Correct — a small plate's shallow depth of influence means it may simply never sense a softer layer at depth that a larger, more heavily loaded footing would engage, making direct scaling unreliable.
explanations.b: There is no single fixed scaling factor; the error direction and magnitude depend on what lies beneath the plate's shallow zone of influence versus the footing's deeper one.
explanations.c: Plate load tests are commonly performed on both sand and clay; the scale-effect concern applies broadly, not just to one soil type.
explanations.d: The plate load test directly measures load-settlement behavior at the surface; the concern is precisely about extrapolating that settlement, not about strength.

lessons.label: Laboratory Strength and Consolidation Testing

sections.heading: Triaxial testing: controlling drainage and stress path
sections.body: A triaxial cell confines a cylindrical soil specimen under an all-around cell pressure and applies additional axial stress until failure, letting the operator independently control drainage and loading rate. In an unconsolidated-undrained (UU) test the specimen is loaded to failure with no drainage allowed at all, giving a quick total-stress su but one that depends on the specimen's initial water content rather than any consolidation stress applied in the cell. A consolidated-undrained (CU) test first lets the specimen consolidate under cell pressure (with pore pressure measured during shear), while a consolidated-drained (CD) test also allows drainage during shear itself, so volume change occurs slowly as the specimen deforms. Before any consolidated test begins, a back-pressure saturation check (Skempton's B parameter, B = change in pore pressure over change in cell pressure) confirms the specimen is fully saturated — B should exceed about 0.95 — because a partially saturated specimen gives unreliable pore-pressure readings throughout the test. Results are commonly plotted as effective stress paths in p'-q space (mean effective stress vs. deviator stress), which reveals not just the failure strength but the entire loading history the specimen followed to get there.

sections.heading: Direct shear and ring shear: forcing the failure plane
sections.body: A direct shear box splits the specimen into upper and lower halves and forces failure along a single predetermined horizontal plane, which is simpler and faster than triaxial testing but cannot control drainage as precisely and imposes a failure geometry that may not match the soil's true weakest surface. Ring shear (commonly the Bromhead apparatus) shears an annular specimen indefinitely in one direction, letting displacement accumulate far beyond what a direct shear box allows, which makes it the standard tool for measuring residual strength — the strength a clay retains after a shear surface has already formed and slid repeatedly, as along an ancient landslide plane.

sections.heading: Consolidation and permeability testing
sections.body: A conventional oedometer applies discrete load increments to a laterally confined specimen and lets settlement stabilize under each one — a process that can take days per specimen. From the resulting e-log(sigma') curve, the preconsolidation pressure is read off graphically via the Casagrande construction, and the compression index Cc is simply the slope of the virgin compression line. The coefficient of consolidation cv comes from a different plot entirely: for each individual load increment, the settlement-vs-log(time) curve is analyzed by Casagrande's log-time method (or, equivalently, Taylor's root-time method), so cv is derived increment-by-increment rather than from the e-log(sigma') curve. Constant-rate-of-strain (CRS) consolidation instead deforms the specimen continuously at a fixed strain rate while measuring the resulting stress, yielding an equivalent consolidation curve far faster, though the result depends on choosing a strain rate slow enough to avoid excess pore-pressure buildup skewing the answer. Permeability itself is measured with falling-head permeameters (tracking a declining water column, suited to low-permeability clay) or constant-head permeameters (holding a steady head across a more permeable sand), each suited to a different order of magnitude of hydraulic conductivity.

lessons.workedExample: A soft clay is tested three ways. A UU triaxial test gives su = 30 kPa, reflecting the specimen's as-sampled water content with no consolidation applied. A CU test on the same clay, first consolidated to the actual in-situ effective stress and then sheared undrained with pore-pressure measurement, gives su = 45 kPa — higher because consolidation under a representative stress stiffened and strengthened the specimen before shearing began. A CD test on a third specimen, sheared slowly enough to fully drain, gives a friction angle phi' = 28 degrees, a fundamentally different kind of result (a drained strength parameter, not an undrained strength in kPa). A student who reports these three results as if they "disagree" without saying which drainage condition and stress path each represents has actually just found three internally consistent answers to three different questions.
lessons.judgeFraming: This is the lesson where a judge tests whether a student can explain apparent contradictions in their own data rather than being alarmed by them. A student who ran both a UU and CU test and got two different su values should be able to say, unprompted, that the UU test never let the specimen consolidate to the real in-situ stress while the CU test did — that is not experimental error, it is two tests answering two different physical questions. Naming the B-check (B greater than about 0.95) as a saturation prerequisite, and knowing that ring shear rather than direct shear is used for residual strength, separates a student who ran a lab protocol from one who understands what each protocol controls.

questions.prompt: A UU triaxial test and a CU triaxial test are run on samples from the same clay layer and give different su values. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: The UU test was sheared without consolidating the specimen to the in-situ stress first, while the CU test consolidated the specimen beforehand, so the two tests measure strength under different stress histories
One of the two tests must have been performed incorrectly, since identical clay should always give identical su
CU tests always give lower su than UU tests, so the CU result should be discarded
The difference only reflects random measurement error with no systematic cause

explanations.a: Correct — UU tests shear the as-sampled specimen with no drainage or consolidation step, while CU tests consolidate the specimen to a chosen effective stress first, so the two are legitimately measuring strength under different, deliberately controlled conditions.
explanations.b: Both tests can be performed correctly and still give different su, because they impose different drainage and stress-path conditions by design, not by error.
explanations.c: There is no universal rule that CU strength is always lower; the relationship depends on the consolidation stress applied and the clay's stress history.
explanations.d: The difference has a clear systematic, mechanistic cause (differing consolidation conditions), not random scatter.

questions.prompt: What does a Skempton's B value of at least about 0.95 confirm before a consolidated triaxial test proceeds?

options.text: That the specimen is essentially fully saturated, which is required for reliable pore-pressure measurement during the test
That the specimen has already failed and the test can be stopped
That the specimen's friction angle has already been determined
That the cell pressure has reached its maximum rated value

explanations.a: Correct — B (the ratio of pore-pressure change to cell-pressure change under undrained loading) approaching 1.0 indicates a fully saturated specimen, without which measured pore pressures during shear cannot be trusted.
explanations.b: The B-check is a saturation check performed before shearing to failure, not an indicator that failure has occurred.
explanations.c: Friction angle is derived from the shearing stage of a CD test, not from the saturation check.
explanations.d: B depends on the specimen's degree of saturation responding to a cell-pressure increment, not on reaching a particular absolute cell pressure.

questions.prompt: Match each lab test to what it is specifically used for.

right.text: Measuring residual strength after large accumulated displacement
Deriving preconsolidation pressure via the Casagrande graphical construction on the e-log(sigma') curve, over multi-day load increments
Obtaining a consolidation curve much faster via continuous strain-controlled loading
Measuring low permeability in fine-grained clay

questions.explanation: Ring shear accumulates large displacement to reach residual strength; the conventional oedometer uses discrete load increments and the Casagrande graphical construction on the e-log(sigma') curve to find preconsolidation pressure (with cv found separately, per increment, from the settlement-vs-log(time) curve); CRS speeds up the e-log(sigma') determination with continuous strain-controlled loading; falling-head permeameters suit the low permeability of clay, while constant-head permeameters suit more permeable sand.

lessons.label: Geophysics for Site Characterization

sections.heading: Seismic methods for depth to rock and shear-wave profiles
sections.body: Seismic refraction plants a line of geophones and records first-arrival times from a surface source, using the fact that seismic waves refract along a faster, deeper layer (typically rock) and arrive first beyond a crossover distance; inverting those travel times gives depth to rockhead and, from the rock's P-wave velocity, an estimate of rippability — whether the rock can be ripped by a dozer or requires blasting, since velocities above roughly 2,000-2,500 m/s in hard rock generally push toward blasting. For shear-wave velocity specifically, multichannel analysis of surface waves (MASW) and its close relatives spectral analysis of surface waves (SASW) and refraction microtremor (ReMi) all invert the dispersive behavior of surface (Rayleigh) waves — different wavelengths sample different depths — to build a one-dimensional Vs profile without ever drilling a hole. Crosshole and downhole seismic tests (ASTM D4428 and D7400) instead use boreholes directly, measuring travel time between known depths in one or two holes, giving layer-specific Vs values with better vertical resolution than a purely surface-based inversion.

sections.heading: Vs30 and site classification
sections.body: Vs30, the time-averaged shear-wave velocity of the top 30 m of ground, is the single parameter that drives site classification under ASCE 7 and the NEHRP provisions, because softer soil amplifies earthquake shaking relative to firm rock. Site Class D, covering stiff soil with Vs30 between about 180 and 360 m/s, is the most common classification for ordinary sedimentary sites and carries meaningfully higher design ground-motion amplification factors than the firmer Class C or the rock-like Class B above it — so a Vs30 estimate from MASW or a borehole-based downhole test can directly change a structure's seismic design forces.

sections.heading: Non-seismic methods, and the calibration principle
sections.body: Electrical resistivity tomography (ERT) injects current through ground electrodes and images subsurface resistivity contrasts, which makes it effective at locating air-filled or water-filled karst voids and old abandoned mine workings that show up as strong resistivity anomalies against surrounding rock. Microgravity surveys instead detect the subtle reduction in local gravitational pull caused by a void's missing rock mass, useful for confirming suspected cavities non-invasively. Ground-penetrating radar (GPR) images shallow stratigraphy and buried objects with fine resolution but limited depth, and its signal collapses almost entirely in electrically conductive clay, where the radar energy is absorbed rather than reflected — a well-known field failure mode, not a rare edge case. The unifying idea across all of these methods is that geophysics supplies continuous spatial coverage between the widely spaced, expensive point data of borings, but it measures a physical proxy (velocity, resistivity, gravity), not soil type directly — so every geophysical survey must be calibrated ("ground-truthed") against at least a few real borings or CPT soundings before its interpretation is trusted.

lessons.workedExample: A site suspected of overlying limestone karst is investigated with three borings spaced 100 m apart, none of which happen to hit a void, plus an ERT line run continuously between them. The ERT line reveals two localized zones of anomalously high resistivity, consistent with air-filled voids, that fall between the widely spaced borings and would otherwise have gone completely undetected. A follow-up boring placed directly over one anomaly confirms a 2 m void at 8 m depth, and that single confirming boring is what lets the engineer trust the second, unconfirmed anomaly as a likely void too — the geophysics found the anomalies, but the boring calibrated what the anomalies actually meant.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing geophysics wants to know whether a student understands that these methods measure an indirect physical proxy, not soil identity, and therefore require ground-truthing. The strongest answer volunteers that geophysics is used for continuous coverage between point borings, not as a replacement for them, and can name a specific calibration failure mode — GPR's collapse in conductive clay, or a resistivity anomaly that could be a void, a clay lens, or a change in saturation without a confirming boring. A student who presents an uncalibrated resistivity or GPR image as if it directly proves a void has skipped the step that makes the method trustworthy.

questions.prompt: Why does ground-penetrating radar (GPR) frequently fail to image anything useful in electrically conductive clay?

options.text: The radar energy is absorbed by the conductive clay rather than reflected back, collapsing the signal's effective depth and resolution
GPR physically cannot penetrate any soil type at all, including sand and gravel
Clay is too hard for the GPR antenna to be dragged across
GPR only works below the water table and clay sites are always above it

explanations.a: Correct — electrical conductivity in clay absorbs radar energy, so little signal returns to the receiver, drastically reducing GPR's effective depth and image quality in such settings.
explanations.b: GPR works well in resistive materials like dry sand or gravel; its failure mode is specific to electrically conductive material like clay, not soil in general.
explanations.c: The limitation is electrical (signal absorption), not mechanical difficulty dragging the antenna.
explanations.d: GPR's collapse in clay is about the clay's conductivity, not water table position, and clay sites are not always above the water table.

questions.prompt: Order this karst investigation workflow from first to last, based on the way geophysics and borings are typically combined.

items.text: Run a continuous ERT (or microgravity) survey across the suspected karst area
Identify localized resistivity or gravity anomalies from the survey
Drill a confirming boring directly over one anomaly
Use the confirmed boring to calibrate trust in the remaining, unconfirmed anomalies

questions.explanation: The geophysical survey is run first to get continuous coverage, anomalies are identified from that data, a boring is then used to ground-truth one anomaly, and that confirmation is what justifies extending interpretation to the remaining anomalies.

questions.prompt: Match each geophysical or in-situ seismic method to what it is primarily used to determine.

right.text: Depth to rockhead and rippability from P-wave velocity
A 1D shear-wave velocity (Vs) profile via surface-wave inversion
Layer-specific Vs with high vertical resolution using boreholes
Locating karst voids or abandoned workings via resistivity contrast

questions.explanation: Seismic refraction uses first-arrival travel times to find rockhead depth and rippability; MASW/SASW/ReMi invert surface-wave dispersion for a Vs profile; crosshole/downhole testing uses boreholes for layer-specific Vs; ERT images resistivity contrasts to find voids or old workings.

lessons.label: Instrumentation, Monitoring, and the Observational Method

sections.heading: Instruments for movement, pressure, and load
sections.body: An inclinometer lowers a probe down a grooved casing installed vertically in a slope or behind a retaining wall, measuring tilt at fixed intervals to build a profile of lateral movement with depth over repeat surveys — the standard tool for catching a developing slip surface before it becomes a visible failure. Piezometers come in two common forms with very different response times: standpipe piezometers rely on water physically flowing into an open pipe to equilibrate, which can lag badly behind real pore-pressure changes in low-permeability clay (a time lag first analyzed systematically by Hvorslev in 1951), while vibrating-wire piezometers sense pressure through a sealed diaphragm and respond essentially in real time regardless of soil permeability, at the cost of needing electronic readout equipment. Settlement plates track vertical ground movement at the surface over time, borehole extensometers measure differential settlement at multiple depths within a single hole, load cells measure force directly in a strut, anchor, or pile, and tiltmeters track rotation of a structure or wall. At a broader scale, InSAR (satellite radar interferometry) and GNSS (satellite positioning) monitor regional ground movement — subsidence, landslide creep — over kilometers, without a single instrument installed on the ground.

sections.heading: Peck's observational method
sections.body: Ralph Peck's 1969 Rankine Lecture, "Advantages and Limitations of the Observational Method in Applied Soil Mechanics," formalized an approach for designing when ground conditions are known imperfectly: rather than designing for a worst case that may never occur (and paying for it in cost) or for a best guess with no fallback (and risking failure), the engineer designs for the most probable ground condition, but works out in advance a specific range of possible deviations, a monitoring plan capable of detecting those deviations as they happen, and pre-planned contingency actions ready to deploy the moment monitoring shows the design condition is not holding. The method's power is that the contingency plan is decided calmly before construction starts, not improvised under pressure once monitoring shows a problem.

sections.heading: Trigger levels as the modern implementation
sections.body: Modern projects operationalize Peck's approach as traffic-light trigger levels tied to specific monitored values: a green level represents expected behavior with no action needed, an amber level represents a deviation requiring increased monitoring frequency and engineering review, and a red level triggers a pre-planned response such as slowing construction, adding support, or evacuating a zone. Because the response at each level was decided in advance, the observational method converts monitoring data from a passive record into an active control loop — the instrumentation is not just documentation, it is literally what tells the project which of the pre-planned actions to execute next.

lessons.workedExample: A deep excavation braced by struts is designed for the most probable soil condition, with wall deflection monitored by inclinometers behind the wall and strut loads monitored by load cells. Green level is deflection under 15 mm with normal readings continuing weekly; amber level, at 15-25 mm, triggers daily readings and a design review; red level, above 25 mm, triggers a pre-planned response of installing an additional row of struts within 48 hours. When inclinometer readings cross 16 mm in week three, the amber response executes automatically as planned — daily monitoring begins and the design team reviews the data — rather than triggering a scramble to invent a response under pressure, which is precisely the calm-before-the-fact decision-making Peck's method was built around.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask about the observational method to see whether a student understands that monitoring data is only as useful as the decision it was designed to trigger. A student who says "we put an inclinometer in to see what happens" has instrumentation without a plan; a student who can state a specific trigger level and the pre-planned action tied to it — in the spirit of Peck's 1969 Rankine Lecture — has demonstrated that monitoring was integrated into the design itself, not bolted on afterward as a safety blanket.

questions.prompt: What is the central idea of Peck's observational method, from his 1969 Rankine Lecture?

options.text: Design for the most probable ground condition, but predefine possible deviations, a monitoring plan to detect them, and contingency actions ready to deploy if they occur
Always design for the absolute worst-case ground condition regardless of cost
Skip ground investigation entirely and rely only on real-time monitoring during construction
Monitor construction only after a problem is visually observed, then decide what to do

explanations.a: Correct — Peck's method designs for the most probable condition while pre-planning both the monitoring needed to catch deviations and the contingency actions to take if they occur, avoiding both worst-case overdesign and unmonitored risk.
explanations.b: Designing purely for the worst case is the conservative alternative the observational method is specifically meant to avoid, since it can be needlessly costly.
explanations.c: The method still requires a ground investigation to establish the most probable condition; monitoring supplements, rather than replaces, that investigation.
explanations.d: The defining feature of the method is that contingency actions are planned in advance, before construction, not improvised only after a problem becomes visually apparent.

questions.prompt: Match each instrument to what it primarily measures.

right.text: Lateral movement profile with depth in a slope or wall
Pore pressure, responding essentially in real time via a sealed diaphragm
Pore pressure, but with a response lag governed by soil permeability
Regional ground movement over kilometers via satellite radar

questions.explanation: Inclinometers profile lateral movement with depth; vibrating-wire piezometers respond quickly through a sealed diaphragm; standpipe piezometers lag behind real pore-pressure changes, especially in low-permeability clay, as analyzed by Hvorslev in 1951; InSAR monitors regional-scale ground movement from satellite radar.

questions.prompt: Order these traffic-light trigger-level responses from least to most severe, as typically implemented on a monitored excavation.

items.text: Green: expected behavior, routine weekly readings continue
Amber: deviation detected, daily monitoring and engineering review begin
Red: pre-planned contingency action executed, such as adding support

questions.explanation: Trigger levels escalate from green (normal, routine monitoring), to amber (a detected deviation prompting closer monitoring and review), to red (the threshold at which the pre-planned contingency action is actually executed).

units.label: Interpreting Site Data: Bearing Capacity, Settlement, and Piles

lessons.label: Choosing Design Parameters from Scattered Data

sections.heading: A single soil, many measured values
sections.body: No soil property comes back from the lab as one number. Undrained shear strength su typically shows a coefficient of variation (COV, the standard deviation divided by the mean) of roughly 20-40% across a supposedly uniform clay layer; effective friction angle phi' is far tighter, usually 5-15% COV; hydraulic conductivity k is the outlier, routinely spanning one to three orders of magnitude within a single stratum because flow is controlled by rare high-permeability paths a bulk test can miss entirely. A designer cannot simply average every borehole result and call it the design value. Eurocode 7 formalizes the alternative: a characteristic value is a cautious estimate of the property governing the limit state, chosen with explicit regard to how much ground the failure mechanism actually mobilizes, not just the arithmetic mean of the dataset.

sections.heading: Spatial correlation length and the averaging footing
sections.body: Soil variability is not random noise at every point independently; it has structure, described by a spatial correlation length (or scale of fluctuation) over which properties tend to move together, a concept built out by Vanmarcke's random field work. A footing that is wide relative to that correlation length samples many independent patches of ground and its bearing response is governed by something close to the spatial average, so a weak pocket under one corner is compensated by stronger soil elsewhere. A narrow footing, or a pile tip bearing on a single small zone, may sit entirely within one correlation length and get whichever value that patch happens to hold, good or bad. This is why the same nominal soil profile can justify a less conservative parameter for a large raft than for a small isolated footing.

sections.heading: Turning a parameter into a safe design
sections.body: Allowable stress design (ASD) applies one lumped factor of safety, historically around 3, directly to the computed ultimate bearing capacity, folding load uncertainty, soil variability, and model error into a single number. Load and Resistance Factor Design (LRFD) separates these: load factors greater than 1 inflate the demand side, and a resistance factor less than 1 (often 0.45-0.65 for bearing capacity) discounts the nominal capacity, with both factors calibrated statistically so the design targets a reliability index beta of about 3.0-3.5 (roughly a 1-in-700 to 1-in-4,000 probability of exceeding the limit state). Eurocode 7 instead applies partial factors directly to actions, material strengths, and resistances, offered as three alternative Design Approaches (DA1, DA2, DA3) that place the margin at different points in the calculation while aiming at a comparable reliability.

lessons.workedExample: A 20 m wide raft and a 1.2 m diameter pile sit in the same clay, where su was measured at five borings ranging from 40 to 80 kPa (COV about 35%) with a spatial correlation length around 3 m. The raft mobilizes a failure zone many correlation lengths wide, so a designer can reasonably use a value close to the spatial mean, say 60 kPa. The pile's base bears on roughly one correlation length of ground, so using the mean would risk sitting the whole foundation on the single weakest patch encountered; a cautious low estimate near 45 kPa is the defensible characteristic value for that element.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'what su did you use, and why that one?' is testing whether a student understands that soil parameters are estimates from a scattered dataset, not measured facts, and that the right level of caution depends on foundation size relative to spatial correlation length. A weak answer reports a single averaged lab value with no justification; a strong answer names the scatter (a COV, a range across borings), explains why a wide footing can use a less conservative value than a narrow one, and connects the choice to whichever safety framework (ASD factor of safety, LRFD resistance factor, or Eurocode 7 partial factor) governs the design.

questions.prompt: Among su, phi', and hydraulic conductivity k, which property typically shows the widest scatter (highest coefficient of variation) within one soil layer?

options.text: phi' (effective friction angle)
su (undrained shear strength)
k (hydraulic conductivity)
All three typically show identical scatter

explanations.a: phi' is usually the tightest of the three, with a COV around 5-15%, because friction angle is controlled by fabric and mineralogy that vary less than strength or flow paths.
explanations.b: su commonly shows a COV around 20-40%, wider than phi' but far narrower than hydraulic conductivity.
explanations.c: Correct — k can span one to three orders of magnitude within a single stratum because flow is dominated by rare high-permeability pathways that bulk sampling can easily miss.
explanations.d: The three properties have distinctly different characteristic scatter; treating them as equally variable would lead to over- or under-conservative parameter choices.

questions.prompt: Why can a wide raft foundation often justify a less conservative characteristic soil value than a narrow footing or pile on the same site?

options.text: Wide foundations always settle less than narrow ones
A wide foundation's failure mechanism spans many spatial correlation lengths, so its response tracks near the spatial average rather than one local patch
Wide foundations are not subject to bearing capacity failure
Building codes simply assign lower factors of safety to wider footings

explanations.a: Settlement is a separate consideration from parameter selection and is not guaranteed to be smaller for wider foundations.
explanations.b: Correct — spatial averaging means a footing many correlation lengths wide samples both weak and strong patches, so an average value is representative, while a narrow footing may sit entirely within one weak (or strong) zone.
explanations.c: All shallow foundations are subject to bearing capacity failure; foundation width changes how variability is sampled, not whether the failure mode applies.
explanations.d: Codes do not assign safety factors by footing width directly; the averaging effect is a physical consequence of spatial correlation, which engineers account for in choosing the characteristic value itself.

questions.prompt: Order the steps in selecting a defensible design parameter for a shallow foundation.

items.text: Collect scattered property measurements across the site (borings, lab tests)
Estimate the spatial correlation length and compare it to the foundation dimension
Select a characteristic (cautious) value that reflects how much averaging the foundation actually achieves
Apply the safety framework's factor (ASD factor of safety, LRFD resistance factor, or Eurocode 7 partial factor) to reach the design value

questions.explanation: Raw data must exist before its spatial structure can be assessed; the correlation length relative to foundation size then informs how cautious the characteristic value must be; only after that value is chosen does the safety framework's factor convert it into a design value.

questions.prompt: Match each design framework to how it applies its safety margin.

right.text: A single lumped factor of safety (about 3) applied to the computed ultimate capacity
Separate load factors (>1) and a resistance factor (<1), calibrated to a target reliability index
Partial factors applied directly to actions, material strengths, and resistances, via one of several Design Approaches

questions.explanation: ASD lumps all uncertainty into one overall safety factor; LRFD splits margin between load and resistance sides and calibrates to a target reliability index (beta about 3.0-3.5); Eurocode 7 distributes partial factors across actions, materials, and resistances through its Design Approaches (DA1, DA2, DA3).

lessons.label: Bearing Capacity of Shallow Foundations

sections.heading: Terzaghi's wedge and the bearing capacity equation
sections.body: Karl Terzaghi's 1943 bearing capacity equation, qu = c*Nc + q*Nq + 0.5*gamma*B*Ngamma, sums three failure contributions for a strip footing of width B: cohesion, surcharge q beside the footing, and the self-weight of the failing soil wedge. The mechanism behind it is a rigid active wedge pushed straight down under the footing, flanked by a radial (log-spiral) shear zone, which in turn shoves a passive wedge up and outward at the ground surface — the Prandtl-Reissner mechanism, adapted from plasticity solutions Ludwig Prandtl and Hans Reissner developed for punch indentation in the 1920s. The surcharge factor has an exact closed form, Nq = e^(pi*tan(phi'))*tan^2(45+phi'/2) (Reissner, 1924), which grows steeply with friction angle: Nq is about 18 at phi'=30 degrees and about 64 at phi'=40 degrees, not passing 100 until roughly phi'=43-44 degrees.

sections.heading: The stubborn disagreement over Ngamma
sections.body: Nc and Nq both have exact plasticity solutions, but Ngamma does not — it depends on assumptions about the shape of the passive wedge and the friction mobilized along its curved boundary, so different authors get different answers from the same phi'. Meyerhof (1963), Hansen (1970), and Vesic (1973) each published Ngamma expressions that can differ by tens of percent at a given friction angle, and all three remain in active use in different codes and software, meaning the 'same' calculation can shift meaningfully depending which factor set a design follows.

sections.heading: Shape, depth, load, and drainage corrections
sections.body: Real footings are rarely infinite strips, so shape factors (sc, sq, sgamma) adjust for square, rectangular, or circular plans, and depth factors (dc, dq, dgamma) credit shear resistance above the footing base. Eccentric loads use Meyerhof's effective-width rule, replacing B with B' = B - 2e so only the portion of footing symmetric about the resultant load is treated as effective. A water table within about one footing width of the base cuts the self-weight term by substituting buoyant unit weight for total unit weight, which can roughly halve the gamma-Ngamma contribution. Terzaghi also distinguished general shear failure, a well-defined surface with peak strength mobilized in dense sand or stiff clay, from local shear, a punching-type failure in loose or soft ground where only a reduced strength (about two-thirds of c and tan phi') is mobilized before large settlements occur. The purely undrained (phi=0) special case collapses to qu = 5.14*su + q, where Nc = 2 + pi = 5.14 is the exact Prandtl (1921) plasticity value for a strip footing. Terzaghi's own 1943 general-shear tables give Nc = 5.7 for that same strip-footing geometry; the gap is a leftover of his less exact wedge-angle assumptions, not a shape correction of any kind. A genuine square or circular correction moves the number the other way — Skempton's sc = 1.2 raises 5.14 to about 6.2, close to what the Vesic shape factor used in the worked example below gives.

lessons.workedExample: A 1.5 m square footing sits at 1 m depth (q = 18 kPa, from gamma=18 kN/m3 fill) in stiff clay with su = 80 kPa, undrained loading. For a strip footing, qu = 5.14(80) + 18 = 429.2 kPa. Applying Vesic's square-footing shape factor sc = 1+(Nq/Nc) = 1+(1/5.14) = 1.195 for phi=0 gives an effective Nc*sc = 6.14 and qu = 5.14(1.195)(80)+18 = 509.4 kPa — an 18.7% increase purely from footing shape, showing why the bare strip-footing equation is only a starting point, not the final design number.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes bearing capacity because it is where students most often plug numbers into a memorized formula without knowing what the formula assumes. The revealing questions are: which factor (Nc, Nq, or Ngamma) actually has an exact solution and which is disputed, whether general or local shear governs the site's soil density, and whether a water table or eccentric load was accounted for. A student who can explain why Meyerhof, Hansen, and Vesic disagree specifically on Ngamma — not on the whole equation — has understood the mechanics behind the number rather than treated it as a lookup table.

questions.prompt: Why do Meyerhof, Hansen, and Vesic disagree on Ngamma while agreeing (essentially) on Nq?

options.text: Nq has no exact plasticity solution but Ngamma does
Ngamma depends on assumptions about the curved passive-wedge boundary with no exact closed-form solution, while Nq follows directly from Reissner's exact 1924 solution
The three authors used different definitions of friction angle
Ngamma only matters for undrained clay, where testing is less precise

explanations.a: This reverses the actual situation: Nq = e^(pi*tan phi')*tan^2(45+phi'/2) is an exact closed-form result, while Ngamma is not.
explanations.b: Correct — Nq comes from an exact plasticity solution, but Ngamma requires assumptions about the shape and friction along the passive wedge's curved boundary, so different authors' approximations diverge by tens of percent.
explanations.c: All three use the same effective friction angle definition; the disagreement is mechanical, arising from how the passive wedge geometry is idealized, not from a difference in what phi' means.
explanations.d: Ngamma appears in the drained (c, phi') equation and vanishes entirely in the undrained (phi=0) case, so it is irrelevant to undrained clay, not specific to it.

questions.prompt: A footing is placed on loose, uncompacted sand. Which failure mode and strength assumption applies?

options.text: General shear, using the full peak c and tan phi'
Local shear, using a reduced strength of roughly two-thirds of c and tan phi'
Undrained failure, using qu = 5.14*su + q
No bearing capacity check is needed on loose sand

explanations.a: General shear with full peak strength applies to dense sand or stiff clay, where a well-defined failure surface forms; loose sand instead punches.
explanations.b: Correct — Terzaghi's local (punching) shear applies to loose sand or soft clay, where large settlements occur before a full failure surface develops, so only a reduced fraction of peak strength is mobilized.
explanations.c: The undrained equation applies to saturated clay loaded quickly (phi=0 conditions), not to sand, which is generally analyzed in drained (c, phi') terms.
explanations.d: Bearing capacity must still be checked on loose sand; it simply uses the local-shear reduced-strength approach rather than the full general-shear factors.

questions.prompt: For undrained (phi=0) loading, the exact plasticity value is Nc = 2 + pi = 5.14, yet older texts quote Nc = 5.7. What is the 5.7?

options.text: The exact 5.14 after applying a square/circular footing shape correction
Terzaghi's own 1943 approximate value for the same strip-footing case, higher because his wedge-angle assumptions were less exact than the Prandtl solution
The value of Nc once a water table is present at the footing base
Nc for local (punching) shear in soft clay

explanations.a: A real square/circular shape correction applied to 5.14 gives roughly 6.1-6.2 (Skempton's sc = 1.2, or Vesic's sc = 1.195), not 5.7 — so 5.7 cannot be a shape-corrected number.
explanations.b: Correct — 5.7 is Terzaghi's strip-footing general-shear value from his 1943 formulation; it differs from the exact 5.14 only because his assumed wedge geometry was an approximation of the Prandtl-Reissner mechanism.
explanations.c: A water table changes the self-weight (gamma-Ngamma) term through buoyant unit weight; it does not change Nc, which vanishes from that term entirely in the phi=0 case.
explanations.d: Local shear reduces the mobilized strength (about two-thirds of c and tan phi'), which lowers capacity rather than raising Nc above its exact value.

questions.prompt: Order the zones of the Prandtl-Reissner bearing capacity mechanism from directly under the footing outward to the ground surface.

items.text: Active (Rankine) wedge pushed straight down under the footing
Radial (log-spiral) shear zone
Passive (Rankine) wedge heaved up at the ground surface

questions.explanation: The footing load drives a rigid active wedge downward directly beneath it; this wedge shoves outward through a radial shear zone of log-spiral shape; the radial zone in turn pushes up a passive wedge that heaves the ground surface beside the footing.

questions.prompt: Match each bearing capacity concept to its effect on the calculation.

left.text: Water table within one footing width of the base

right.text: Reduces the self-weight (gamma-Ngamma) term by substituting buoyant for total unit weight
Replaces B with an effective width B' = B - 2e
Applies shape correction factors (sc, sq, sgamma) to the strip-footing terms

questions.explanation: A shallow water table lowers effective unit weight and thus the self-weight contribution; eccentric loads are handled with Meyerhof's effective-width rule; non-strip geometries require shape factors to correct the base strip-footing bearing capacity equation.

lessons.label: Settlement Prediction and Tolerable Movement

sections.heading: Immediate settlement from CPT: Schmertmann's method
sections.body: Immediate (elastic) settlement occurs as soon as load is applied, before any pore pressure dissipates. Schmertmann's strain-influence method (1970, revised with Hartman and Brown in 1978) estimates it directly from cone penetration test (CPT) tip resistance qc without needing lab elastic moduli. It assumes the vertical strain caused by the footing follows a triangular-to-parabolic influence factor Iz with depth, peaking not at the footing base but below it — at about half the footing width B below the base for square or circular footings, or a full footing width B below the base for strip footings — because that is where the elastic solution shows the largest strain increment actually occurs; the peak value of Iz itself is typically around 0.5 to 0.6. Settlement is then the sum, layer by layer, of Iz divided by an equivalent soil modulus (correlated from qc), multiplied by the stress increase and layer thickness, with correction factors for embedment depth and load duration/creep.

sections.heading: Consolidation and secondary compression in clay
sections.body: In saturated clay, most settlement instead develops slowly as excess pore pressure dissipates. The stress increase a new load causes at depth is estimated with Boussinesq's (1885) elastic half-space solution, or its common shortcut, the 2:1 (2 vertical : 1 horizontal) approximation that spreads load through a widening prism. That stress increase, together with the compression index Cc (or recompression index Cr, for stress states below the preconsolidation pressure) measured in an oedometer test, gives primary consolidation settlement. After primary consolidation finishes, some clays continue compressing under constant effective stress — secondary compression, governed by the coefficient Calpha — which can matter over a building's decades-long service life even though it is often the smallest of the three settlement components.

sections.heading: Tolerable movement: why differential settlement governs
sections.body: Skempton and MacDonald's 1956 survey of damaged and undamaged buildings established limiting angular distortion (differential settlement divided by the span between the two points measured) rather than total settlement as the controlling design criterion: roughly 1/500 as the threshold beyond which architectural damage (cracked plaster, jammed doors) becomes likely, and roughly 1/150 as the threshold for structural damage. A building can settle uniformly by tens of millimeters with no cracking at all, because nothing bends; damage appears when one part of a structure settles more than another, straining beams, slabs, and walls. This is also why settlement, not bearing capacity failure, governs the great majority of real foundation designs: an ordinary factor of safety of about 3 on bearing capacity already keeps footings far from ultimate failure, but it does not by itself guarantee angular distortion stays under 1/500.

lessons.workedExample: A clay layer 4 m thick sits below a mat foundation, with initial effective vertical stress sigma'v0 = 80 kPa, Cc = 0.30, e0 = 0.9, and the layer normally consolidated. Boussinesq analysis gives a stress increase at mid-layer of 40 kPa. Primary consolidation settlement is Sc = [Cc*H / (1+e0)] * log10[(sigma'v0+Δsigma')/sigma'v0] = [0.30*4/1.9]*log10(120/80) = 0.632*0.176 = 0.111 m, about 111 mm. If an adjacent, stiffer column footing settles only 40 mm over a 6 m span, the angular distortion is (111-40)/6000 = 1/84 — well past Skempton and MacDonald's 1/150 structural-damage threshold, even though 111 mm of uniform settlement alone would likely cause no cracking.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about settlement because it is where 'the foundation is safe' claims usually fall apart: a design can pass bearing capacity with a comfortable factor of safety and still crack the building. The strongest answers distinguish immediate settlement (Schmertmann, from CPT) from consolidation settlement (Cc/Cr with a Boussinesq or 2:1 stress increase) and secondary compression, and then convert the numbers into angular distortion compared against Skempton and MacDonald's 1/500 and 1/150 limits — showing they understand that differential movement, not the total number, is what damages a structure.

questions.prompt: According to Skempton and MacDonald's (1956) limits, an angular distortion of about 1/150 corresponds to what?

options.text: The threshold below which no settlement analysis is required
The threshold beyond which structural damage becomes likely
The threshold beyond which only cosmetic architectural damage occurs
The maximum allowable total (not differential) settlement

explanations.a: Angular distortion limits do not exempt any design from analysis; 1/150 marks a damage threshold, not a screening cutoff.
explanations.b: Correct — Skempton and MacDonald identified roughly 1/150 as the angular distortion beyond which structural damage (not just cosmetic cracking) becomes likely.
explanations.c: Architectural (cosmetic) damage is associated with the tighter limit of about 1/500; 1/150 is the looser, structural-damage threshold.
