questions.explanation: Jet/permeation grouting suits confined sites where vibration risk rules out other methods; compaction grouting densifies loose granular soil by displacement; deep soil mixing builds stiff columns in place without spoil; lightweight fill reduces load where added weight would be a problem.

lessons.label: Building a Defensible Geotechnical Case Study

sections.heading: Pick a real hazard with a measurable local proxy
sections.body: A strong science-fair geotechnical project starts from a hazard that actually threatens infrastructure and has some property a student can measure at bench scale: karst sinkholes (dissolution of limestone or gypsum bedrock undermining foundations), expansive soils (clay that swells and shrinks with moisture, cracking slabs and roads), unstable slopes (shear strength versus driving stress on a failure surface), or land subsidence from groundwater withdrawal. Subsidence is a good anchor because it is dramatically documented: Mexico City has subsided roughly 10 meters over the past century as aquifer over-pumping let the compressible lake-bed clay beneath it consolidate, and California's San Joaquin Valley subsided up to about 8.5 meters in places by the mid-20th century from groundwater extraction for irrigation, famously documented by USGS hydrologist Joseph Poland's photographs showing a utility pole marking successive ground levels over decades. A student cannot reproduce 10 meters of subsidence, but they can measure the compressibility of a clay sample under load, which is the mechanism behind it.

sections.heading: Cheap, repeatable tests a student can actually run
sections.body: Bench-scale geotechnical testing is unusually accessible: sieve analysis and hydrometer testing classify a soil's grain-size distribution using stacked screens and a settling-column method; Atterberg limits (liquid limit via a standardized fall-cone or Casagrande cup, and plastic limit by rolling threads) quantify plasticity, the same PI values that drive liquefaction-susceptibility and expansive-soil screening; a mini-Proctor compaction test in a small mold tracks how density responds to moisture content; a small direct-shear box or a tilting slope box (raising one end of a box holding a soil sample until it slides) estimates friction angle; and a simple infiltration test (a ring pushed into the ground, timing how fast a known volume of water disappears) characterizes drainage, relevant to both slope stability and subsidence risk.

sections.heading: Sample size, controls, and surviving judge questions
sections.body: A single soil sample tested once is an anecdote, not data — geotechnical properties vary meaningfully even within one site, so a defensible project tests multiple samples (ideally from multiple depths or locations) and reports a range or standard deviation rather than one number, explicitly separating natural soil variability from measurement error. Controls matter as much as in any other experiment: if testing how moisture content changes shear strength, hold grain size and density constant across specimens; if comparing two sites, match testing method and sample preparation exactly. Judges will ask what a single data point is worth, whether the student's bench test actually measures the mechanism claimed (a tilting-box friction angle is not the same as a full triaxial test, and saying so up front beats being caught overclaiming), and how the results would change with a larger sample size — rehearsing honest answers to those questions is part of the science, not an afterthought bolted on before the presentation.

lessons.workedExample: A student investigating expansive-soil risk near a cracked driveway collects clay from three depths (0.3 m, 0.6 m, 1.0 m) at each of four locations along the crack, twelve samples total. Atterberg limits give liquid limits ranging from 48 to 61 and plasticity indices from 24 to 33 across the samples — reported as a range with a mean PI of 28 and standard deviation of 3, not a single 'PI = 28' claim. A simple free-swell test (soaking a compacted sample and measuring height increase) shows 6-9% swell depending on depth, correlating loosely with PI. The student can then honestly state that near-surface soil (0.3 m) showed the highest and most variable swell, consistent with the driveway's crack pattern concentrating near shallow soil, while flagging that free-swell testing is a simplified proxy for the standard oedometer swell-pressure test.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe methodology in a geotechnical project harder than in most fields because soil variability is large and real infrastructure failures (Mexico City's decade-scale subsidence, San Joaquin Valley's documented meters of sinking) hinge on exactly the properties a bench test only approximates. The strongest defense names the specific mechanism being proxied, reports a range across multiple samples instead of one number, states plainly what the simplified test cannot claim relative to the full standard method, and can say how many more samples or what additional control would tighten the conclusion.

questions.prompt: Why is testing only one soil sample once considered insufficient for a defensible geotechnical case study?

options.text: Because geotechnical properties vary meaningfully even within one site, so a single value cannot separate natural variability from measurement error
Because a single sample takes too long to test
Because Atterberg limit tests require at least ten samples by definition
Because soil samples cannot be tested more than once at all

explanations.a: Correct — soils are naturally heterogeneous even across a small site, so one sample's result could reflect true local variability, measurement error, or both, and a single data point cannot distinguish between them.
explanations.b: Testing time is a practical constraint but is not the reason single samples are scientifically insufficient; the issue is what one value can and cannot demonstrate.
explanations.c: There is no fixed minimum sample count built into the Atterberg limit test method itself; the need for multiple samples comes from experimental design, not the test's definition.
explanations.d: Soil samples can be retested; the concern is about representativeness across a site, not about repeatability of a single sample.

questions.prompt: Match each bench-scale test to the soil property it measures.

right.text: Grain-size distribution
Plasticity / liquid and plastic limits
Approximate friction angle
Drainage / infiltration rate

questions.explanation: Sieve/hydrometer analysis gives grain-size distribution, Atterberg limits give plasticity, a tilting slope box estimates friction angle from the slide angle, and a ring infiltration test measures drainage rate.

questions.prompt: Which documented case is an example of land subsidence driven by groundwater withdrawal?

options.text: California's San Joaquin Valley, subsiding up to roughly 8.5 meters from groundwater extraction for irrigation
The 1964 Niigata earthquake bearing-capacity failure
The Nicoll Highway excavation collapse
The 1989 Loma Prieta Marina District damage

explanations.a: Correct — the San Joaquin Valley subsided up to about 8.5 meters in places by the mid-20th century due to groundwater extraction for irrigation, documented in USGS photographs showing successive ground levels on a utility pole.
explanations.b: Niigata's Kawagishi-cho damage was an earthquake-triggered liquefaction bearing-capacity failure, not groundwater-withdrawal subsidence.
explanations.c: Nicoll Highway was a braced-excavation collapse during construction, unrelated to regional groundwater-withdrawal subsidence.
explanations.d: Loma Prieta's Marina District damage came from earthquake shaking amplification and liquefaction in hydraulic fill, not long-term groundwater-withdrawal subsidence.

questions.prompt: Order these steps in building a defensible bench-scale geotechnical case study.

items.text: Choose a real hazard with a measurable bench-scale proxy
Collect multiple samples across depths or locations with matched preparation
Run the appropriate cheap test (e.g., Atterberg limits, tilting box) on each sample
Report a range or standard deviation and state what the simplified test cannot claim

questions.explanation: A defensible case study starts by choosing a real hazard with a measurable proxy, then collects multiple controlled samples, runs the matched bench test on each, and finally reports results as a range with honest limits on what the simplified method demonstrates.
